Through the thrilling waves of international sailing competition, Italy is indeed doubling down, with Naples embodying the spirit of collaboration, embodying not just the allure of the sea, but also the promises bound within the spirit of this prestigious event. The countdown has begun, and Naples is holding its breath, on the edge of a spectacular sailing revolution that is steadily sailing towards its shores.

title: Charting New waters: UKSA's Bolstering Maritime Skills and Confidence Among the Deprived
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Charting New waters: UKSA's Bolstering Maritime Skills and Confidence Among the Deprived
summary: The UK Sailing Academy (UKSA) is steering empowering change, creating all-important ripple effects in maritime sectors.
body: A beacon of hope and opportunity, the UK Sailing Academy (UKSA), nestled on the Isle of Wight, is sowing the seeds of maritime competency among children, young adults, and adults. Directed by an ardent champion of education and youth development, the maritime training charity is anchoring their mission on empowering those with unfavorable socio-economic circumstances and arming them with skills, confidence, and qualifications for rewarding careers in sea-related occupations, particularly in the superyacht sector.

The training charity's spotlight moment? A whopping 500% surge in charitable income over the past five years. This surge has given way to more children gaining confidence on the water, more funded training placements, and a significant increase in young mariners forging a promising path from exposure to professional qualifications and employment. A staggering £1.3 million found their course to bursaries for the underprivileged, clearing their route for entry into the burgeoning superyacht industry. The resounding success is a beacon for funders and industry partners, instilling confidence in the efficacy of the initiative and fostering a long-term support network. This momentum then feeds back to the young sailors, and the cycle of success spirals upwards.

Sailing further, if the yacht industry were to embrace this philanthropic cause, the maritime world as we know it could experience jaw-dropping transformations. Simultaneously expanding access to seafaring careers, bolstering environmental initiatives, and creating enduring benefits for the communities that yachting depends on, concerted industry support could turn the tide for the better. We have but a glimpse of what's possible when dedication and shared vision converge on a cause, and the horizon looks promising indeed.

title: Experience Opulent Ocean Adventures with a Spectacular Reduction on the Archipelago, a Luxurious Moonen Motor Yacht
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Experience Opulent Ocean Adventures with a Spectacular Reduction on the Archipelago, a Luxurious Moonen Motor Yacht
summary: Fancy a tour on the high seas aboard a luxury motor yacht? There's good news. The Moonen motor yacht Archipelago is now €1M cheaper.
body: The Archipelago, a Dutch-built Moonen motor yacht, has recently undergone a significant price reduction of €1M. The responsibly for overseeing the sale belongs to Simon Goldsworthy from Edmiston. Constructed by Moonen Yachts and completed in 2005, the Archipelago represents the best of Dutch craftsmanship. Its design, helmed by Stolk Marimecs, is the epitome of contemporary elegance. The yacht's exceptional naval architecture is by Rene Van Der Velden while the stunning interior design is the creative vision of Alessandra Negrato.

The Archipelago's outdoor space is equally impressive. The main deck aft encompasses an alfresco dining area, complete with banquette and three deck chairs. Forward is an ample sunpad sheltered by an optional cover, serving as an ideal spot for sunbathing or private relaxation. Moving up to the top deck, the sundeck unveils a spacious area perfect for entertaining, complemented by a variety of seating options that facilitate flexibility. Here two large built-in sofas surrounding two tables construct a perfect dining space, covered by an optional shading for added comfort. A selection of sun beds, aft of the top deck, promise unobstructed views, and a prime sun-catching spot.

The yacht's twin Caterpillar engines boast a maximum speed of 12.7 knots and a cruising speed of 11 knots. The Archipelago's new asking price now stands at €4,900,000 including EU VAT, and is currently moored in Mandelieu-La-Napoule, France. The significant price reduction represents an amazing opportunity to delve into the exciting world of luxury yachting.

title: Dive into Adventure at the 2026 Optimum Time Phantom Inlands Sailing Regatta at Grafham Water
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Dive into Adventure at the 2026 Optimum Time Phantom Inlands Sailing Regatta at Grafham Water
summary: Experience the high-stakes contest and camaraderie that shaped the 2026 Phantom Inlands Sailing Regatta at the enchanting Grafham Water Sailing Club.
body: Ready your sails! Set yourself in the heart of the action at the iconic Grafham Water Sailing Club for the 2026 Optimum Time Phantom Inlands. This unforgettable regatta started with a rhythm of anticipation and a poignant promise of adventure. A week before the extravaganza, Richard Nurse, an East Coast legend, embarks on a mission. He accepts a request to deliver a used sail to a chap named Matt. Fast forward to Friday, Matt’s sail secure, Richard prepares for the trip to Grafham.

Arrival at Grafham signifies a happy reunion with old friends and sunny rigging delights before a briefing with PRO Peter Curtis. Knowledge is shared, plans are formulated, and a government guest even shares insights on killer shrimp. Now, it’s time for tea before a highly anticipated 12pm start out on Grafram's shimmering waters.

With the fluttering 'U' flag giving pause, the following start is a refined display of sailing decorum. Phil Worth of Delph Sailing Club takes the lead thundering around the windward mark, with Jezz Deacon of Broadwater Sailing Club nipping at his heels. But it's the second beat that proves to be the game changer.

The left side reveals its secrets, allowing Sam Coxon to rocket from high teens to the hot heels of the lead. The reigning national champion, John Rickard from Hooe Point in Plymouth, savours the rhythm of the waves, relishing the challenge right until the final hoot of the buzzer.

The Optimum Time 2026 Phantom Inlands at Grafham Water Sailing Club, a narrative steeped in strategy, camaraderie, and high-stakes navigation weaves a timeless tale of sailing adventure and resilience.

title: Day 2 of 2026 iQFOiL Open European Championships: Tense Tactics and Transforming Conditions
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Day 2 of 2026 iQFOiL Open European Championships: Tense Tactics and Transforming Conditions
summary: Day 2 of the 2026 iQFOiL Open European Championships in Portimão saw 192 athletes from 42 nations competing, with Luuc Van Opzeeland and Tamar Steinberg leading the fleets.
body: In what is proving to be an intensely-contentious championship, the 2026 iQFOiL Open European Championships in Portimão witnessed another day of high-octane competition. The second day of racing had 192 participants from 42 countries returned to the frothy waves off Praia da Rocha. The day’s racing set the stage for a fervently competitive 6-day event. Day 2 brought new hurdles to the table- with more westerly and less predictable airflows that arrived later in the day. The wind ranged between 8 and 11 knots creating a racecourse that demanded maintaining consistent speed and eagle-eyed identification of the most favourable pressure lanes. In the Bravo Race area, the men sailed in the Course Racing- an iQFOiL staple, meant to test every technical and tactical skill an athlete possesses. Athletes must strike the perfect balance between speed, positioning, and strategic decision making. Dutch Olympic bronze medallist Luuc Van Opzeeland took the overall lead, marking a consistent performance with two race wins. In the Alpha Race area, the women faced the Upwind Sprint—a brief and gunpowder-packed segment that emphasizes lightning-quick tactical execution on compact upwind courses. The format leaves absolutely no margin for error, creating intense competition and formidable spectacle. In another surprise at the 2026 iQFOiL Open European Championships, changes to the leaderboard came thick and fast, reflecting the volatile and high-stakes nature of international sailing competition.

title: How Are the EU's Newest 'No-Russia Clauses' Shaping the Circulation of Maritime Assets?
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: How Are the EU's Newest 'No-Russia Clauses' Shaping the Circulation of Maritime Assets?
summary: Following the introduction of the EU's 20th sanctions package, the maritime assets' landscape is witnessing significant shifts.
body: The 20th sanctions package introduced by the European Union (EU) propels maritime operators selling to third-country buyers into a novel operational sphere. They are now required to include contractual clauses prohibiting future resale or utilisation benefiting Russia. This bold move transcends traditional asset-freeze mechanisms and introduces parameters to control maritime assets' circulation over time, aiming primarily at the shadow tanker fleet.

The EU's evolving sanctions regime targets a broader spectrum. Apart from controlling the flow and circulation of sensitive assets, it extends to logistics chains, service providers, technical intermediaries, and jurisdictions perceived as ripe for malpractices. When sanctioned goods were systematically re-exported to Russia, the EU notably activated the anti-circumvention mechanism against Kyrgyzstan for the first time. This move signifies a drift in sanctions application, tapping into the traceability of flows, re-export chains and intermediary structures.

The implications of these clauses extend beyond Russia's shadow fleet and the energy sector. Restrictions now impact various sectors, including technical services, port infrastructure, financial operators, crypto platforms, and actors indirectly tied to Russia-related flows. This evolution is reinforced by a logic of cascading compliance, creating a ripple effect from seller to buyer, parent company to subsidiary, and supplier to reseller.

Inevitably, these changes impact the yachting market. Superyachts, which depend on a vast network of services for operational viability, face mounting sanctions risks. As a sector deeply internationalised, this signifies a distinct operational shift. The superyacht market grapples with the emergence of structured, documented liability, instead of solely prohibition. This new era of maritime operation tests companies' agility to adapt and survive, but it also promises a new dawn of transparency and traceability. Compliance may prove challenging, but those who navigate its nuances will emerge at the helm, ready to voyage into uncharted waters.

title: Gearing Up for the IRC European Championships: Insights Into Top Yacht Contenders and Their Winning Strategies
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Gearing Up for the IRC European Championships: Insights Into Top Yacht Contenders and Their Winning Strategies
summary: As anticipation mounts for the IRC European Championships, focus sharpens on contenders adopting cutting-edge technology for unrivalled performance.
body: Fierce competition waits on the horizon. The upcoming IRC European Championship sees an ocean of contenders prepping for the stellar event. Regional winners and eager debutants are sailing towards Poole Regatta for this exhilarating face-off. The championship, featuring over 50 entries, provides an arena as much for showcasing raw speed as it is for celebrating versatility. With the championship comprising an intensive series of 11 races, consistency across fluctuating conditions and varying sea states is emerging as the ultimate key to victory. Last year's winner, the dynamic Rán 7 of Niklas Zennström, is a testament to this strategy.

The seasoned sloop, Cetewayo, and the fiercely competitive Bullit from the Cape 31 class stand staunch among the contenders. Each yacht symbolises the compelling blend of classic design prowess and modern technology. While the former, originally launched in 1955, has steered through a 15-year restoration to rise back again, the latter exemplifies the razor-thin margins of high-performance tuning in contemporary racing. Both utilise smarttune on the forestay, benefiting both from enhanced performance and safeguarding their precious equipment from overload.
Regardless of the final standings, the IRC European Championship continues to be a grand showcase of the marriage between tradition and technology in the world of competitive racing.

title: The Noiseless Revolution: Sleipner's Hybrid Power Centre Takes Marine Life at Anchor to a New Level
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: The Noiseless Revolution: Sleipner's Hybrid Power Centre Takes Marine Life at Anchor to a New Level
summary: The latest innovation from Sleipner, the Hybrid Power Centre, is set to redefine the nautical etiquette at anchor with its versatility, stealth, and efficiency.
body: Sleipner, Norwegian marine technology company, just launched an off-the-shelf solution that could solve the inherent dilemma faced by large motor yacht owners. Operating big motor yachts, despite being propelled by big diesel engines, invariably requires additional generators for the ancillary systems. This means running more engines and dealing with their consequent noise and fumes. Even a tranquil bay can lose its allure amidst this incessant hubbub. Sleipner's solution, the revolutionary Hybrid Power Centre (HPC) system, promises to alleviate this issue.

The core components of the HPC system, the 48V PTO generators, are designed to work with the standard power take-offs of all significant marine diesel engines and can effortlessly generate electricity using the excess torque developed by the engines. At idle, each generator can produce up to 5kW, and at cruising speeds, they can collectively generate 50kW - enough to power a robust 100kWh lithium battery pack in just two hours.

Turkish constructor Numarine is one of the first to offer this innovation as a factory option. Marketed as the 'Mk2 Super Silent Pack', Numarine's latest 88ft explorer yacht, the 27XP can anchor for an entire night, with air-conditioners and stabilisers running, without needing to operate a generator.

Numarine, by incorporating a high capacity 92.8kWh Lithium Iron Phosphate (LiFePo4) battery bank along with Sleipner's Hybrid Power Centre, has maximised efficiency with the allowance for PTO generators to power the 48V DC bow and stern thrusters, as well as the electrically curved fin stabilisers. The introduction of the Sleipner's Hybrid Power Centre is set to tweak the nautical paradigm, offering luxurious, quiet nights at anchor.

title: Baglietto Continues Superyacht Momentum with Sale of Third T60, Eyeing a 2029 Launch
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Baglietto Continues Superyacht Momentum with Sale of Third T60, Eyeing a 2029 Launch
summary: Italian shipyard Baglietto has established itself as a key player in the yacht industry with the sale of its third T60 superyacht.
body: Baglietto, a historically prominent player in the Italian shipyard industry, has once again proven its dominance. The company has recently announced the sale of its third unit from the much-acclaimed T60 motor yacht series. The 60.6-metre superyacht is currently being constructed at Baglietto's La Spezia-based yard. Construction began under speculation in 2025 and delivery is anticipated no later than 2029. The sale was successfully secured in collaboration with James Lloyd of Edmiston, further showcasing Baglietto's adroitness in forming prosperous partnerships. Significantly, this sale secured by Baglietto follows closely on the heels of the first unit from the line, now recognised as the largest vessel built by the Italian shipyard, hitting the water. The yacht's distinctive exterior design is the innovative creation of Francesco Paszkowski Design, who also collaborated with Margherita Casprini on the interior elaborations. Naval architecture was ably taken care of by Pierluigi Ausonio, resulting in a breathtaking realization of engineering and design creativity. The third unit is being constructed in step with Baglietto's second hull, scheduled for delivery in 2027, and boasts "innovative design solutions that challenge the traditional separation of onboard spaces.", according to the shipyard. The indoor and outdoor concepts, as well as formality and informality, are deftly put together to craft a coherent, fluid on-board experience. Among the remarkable features of this model are a broad beach area flanked by a sauna, a beach lounge complete with a swimming pool, a bar, a gym, and a voluminous main saloon and dining area that seamlessly connects to the exterior through full-height glazed surfaces. Baglietto's commercial officer, Fabio Ermetto, expressed his profound satisfaction following this landmark sale, further confirming Baglietto's commitment to churning out yachts that are not only designed with modern aesthetics but also incorporate advanced technology alongside high levels of customization. Baglietto presently has approximately 18 new builds either underway or on order, including the full-custom 49.7-metre Project Farah, further broadcasting its esteemed status within the world of yacht-making. Baglietto is clearly sailing into an exciting future.

title: Venture Into the Thrill: A Look Back on the Fireball Open Meeting at Royal Torbay Yacht Club
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Venture Into the Thrill: A Look Back on the Fireball Open Meeting at Royal Torbay Yacht Club
summary: Adventurous sailors embrace challenging weather at the Fireball Open Meet, a preliminary to the Fireball World Championship, held at the distinguished Royal Torbay Yacht Club.
body: High-Risk, High-Reward is the game in the thrilling world of sailing. And it was just that at the Royal Torbay Yacht Club, where the Fireball Open Meeting ensued. Leading Fireball teams from across the UK flocked to the meeting, which served as a perfect prelude to the upcoming Fireball World Championship. The event took place over the sunny yet breezy weekend of the 16th and 17th of May.

The weekend proved challenging for both competitors and the organizing committee. The unpredictable Torbay weather threw a mix of surprises including unconventional wind directions, substantial shifts, not to mention the torrential downpour on the second day. The bright side? Crews had the chance to test new equipment and strategic ideas under conditions that they may face in the championship.

Sunday held in store a cocktail of weather - promising clear skies turned into building rain clouds, swinging 90-degree wind shifts and varying wind strength. Despite the challenges, the day succeeded in hosting three races. Great credit goes to the highly adept mark layers, managing shifts effectively amidst the rain.

Even a gear malfunction failed to stop DJ and Vyv who won the first race of the day. Pete and Richard owned the second race, followed by Georgia and Ollie winning the third. Despite the stiff competition, Tom and Shandy emerged victorious overall. It was indeed a weekend of variables, giving the sailors much to contemplate about weather and racing tactics.

In all, the Fireball Open Meeting was an exhilarating event. As teams battled the tide, they learned, strategized, and conquered. Pulling off it off, the dedicated race team and the hospitable Royal Torbay Yacht Club deserve a hearty round of applause. As the dust settles, we look ahead to the looming Fireball World Championship, enriched with insights from this eventful weekend.

title: Calling All Sea Aficionados: Award-Winning, Innovation-Driven Superyacht ODYSSEY Is Up for Grabs
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Calling All Sea Aficionados: Award-Winning, Innovation-Driven Superyacht ODYSSEY Is Up for Grabs
summary: The visionary ODYSSEY yacht, resplendent after a major 2020 refit, shatters expectations of conventional yacht design through its innovative features and luxurious accommodations.
body: Transforming the expectations associated with yacht design, the exceptional ODYSSEY welcomes a potential buyer to embark on a voyage of unparalleled luxury and comfort. The yacht, birthed from the ashes of innovation, sets a definitive standard in the arena of nautical architecture.

Delivered in 2013 with a strong emphasis on technological advances, ODYSSEY is the result of a close-knit collaboration. Her creation was jointly facilitated between CRN and the Zuccon International Project, who were accountable for both her striking external design and decadent interiors. The quality pulsates through every inch of this behemoth structure, further augmenting its appeal.

ODYSSEY bagged the coveted World Yacht Trophy in 2013 for the 'Most Innovative Yacht over 50m.' She boasts a geometric profile that nests revolutionary marine engineering solutions under its hood. Her structure, beautifully proportioned, is an exterior stylistic manifestation of her strength and stability.

Further key features of ODYSSEY include a helipad suitable for a Bell 429 or similar helicopter, an elevator, and zero-speed stabilizers. The yacht, comfortably accommodating 13 guests in six opulent staterooms, also houses 14 crew members within her spacious domain.

Dreamy sea getaways turn into reality with ODYSSEY. This extraordinary vessel, combining inspired engineering with tasteful Italian aesthetics, stands as a testament to mankind's relentless pursuit of perfection and luxury on the high seas.

title: Oyster Yachts Phases Out Southampton Facility, Prime for Evolution Learning from Rolls-Royce Heritage
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Oyster Yachts Phases Out Southampton Facility, Prime for Evolution Learning from Rolls-Royce Heritage
summary: Celebrated British sailboat constructor, Oyster Yachts, prepares not just for a production phase-out in Southampton, but for a transformative journey guided by lessons from Rolls-Royce.
body: Oyster Yachts, the esteemed builder of British sailing vessels, is charting a formidable course into the future. Not only does the brand stand on the precipice of production wind-down come end of 2026 at its leased Southampton plant, but it also plans a strategic evolution. The lead navigators in this transformative voyage are none other than Oyster's CEO Stefan Zimmermann Zschocke, and one of the pioneers of the modern automobile industry, the former CEO of Rolls-Royce Motor Cars, Torsten Müller-Ötvös. This dynamic duo is set to revitalise and modernise Oyster Yachts, widening its appeal to include a younger generation, while safeguarding its longstanding heritage. Emerging from a productive discussion between Seth Zimmermann Zschocke and Torsten Müller-Ötvös, it was clear that the key to Oyster’s future growth lies in a harmonious blend of heritage with innovation. Oyster powerfully resonates with the extraordinary loyalty exhibited by its customers who encapsulate not just ownership, but advocacy and exploration. This vital aspect is reflected in their latest 50-foot yacht, which provides more onboard space, a novel rear beach club environment, all whilst maintaining that unmistakable Oyster feel. Company growth does not just rest on innovation. It also depends on drawing parallels with the trajectory of luxury brands like Rolls-Royce. Such brands have not only stayed true to their legacy but have also opened new frontiers. As Stefan eyes the new generation of affluent buyers who may not have even heard of Oyster or know how to sail, he also realises the need for continuity with features such as sustainability, smarter energy setups, and digitalisation for existing owners and future generations. The heartening insight that the company's quality culture and craftsmanship enable the acceptance and rapid implementation of new ideas brought optimism. Feedback from owners contributes greatly to this improvement cycle. With a strategic perspective gleaned from an iconic brand like Rolls-Royce, Oyster Yachts is set to keep its ship sturdy and its sails harnessing all winds of change.

title: The Thrill of the Start: RS Tera South West Traveler Series Unfurls at Whitefriars Sailing Club
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: The Thrill of the Start: RS Tera South West Traveler Series Unfurls at Whitefriars Sailing Club
summary: The 2026 RS Tera South West Traveller Series kicked off spectacularly at the renowned Whitefriars Sailing Club, based in Cotswold Water Park.
body: Embracing its traditional role, the Whitefriars SC once again welcomed the first round of the coveted RS Tera South West Traveller Series. The event, a part of the series that explores a rich tapestry of coastal and inland clubs, began its journey in the serene and sheltered waters of Whitefriars. Here, often unpredictable, shifting winds promise an enticing challenge that lures sailors from wondrous corners of the South, South-west, and Midwest with some even traversing their way from the far-reaches of Devon. With such a diverse platter of clubs represented, it was a spectacle steeped in anticipation and camaraderie from the get-go. Race officer Chris Hargreaves charted a dynamic and engaging route for the first race, opting for a figure-of-eight course. Arabella Broughton, having switched to a Pro sail at the last minute, led and held the front position throughout. A stirring episode unfolded behind her as the rest of the pack, featuring the Sport sailors, waged their own war of prowess and resilience. Kilian Snelling, despite being a stranger to Tera fleets and the away conditions, impressed with an enviable second-place finish after Amy Heyburn, a testament to his resilient spirit. But the tournament had more excitement in store. As the day progressed, the gusts morphed, necessitating course adjustments, while the fierce competition pitting Jonas Spicer and Arabella Broughton against Amy Heyburn in the Pro fleet offered an unmissable spectacle. Heyburn ultimately reigned supreme, seizing the top honour after all races. Spicer could console himself with a top finish in the Pro category, while a spirited performance in the afternoon secured Oscar Lee the third spot. A beautiful day of sailing, competition, and forging of new friendships, undoubtedly left an indelible mark on all participants. The journey continues and the waves wait eagerly for more tales from the 2026 RS Tera South West Traveller Series.

title: Surge of Success: Australian Crews Rally at the 49er, 49erFX, and Nacra 17 Sailing Championships
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Surge of Success: Australian Crews Rally at the 49er, 49erFX, and Nacra 17 Sailing Championships
summary: Australian sailing crews have just sailed into the spotlight after a successful performance at the 49er, 49erFX & Nacra 17 World Championships.
body: The Australian crews have found their wind at the 49er, 49erFX and Nacra 17 World Championships held in Quiberon, France. The championship's diverse weather conditions provided challenging tracks, testing the mettle of the best Olympic sailors. The competitive week has presented marginal winds, shifty conditions, and brutal survival races.

Harry Price and Max Paul, the proficient pair of the Australian 49er crew, instilled excitement entering the final stages of the racing event in medal contention. Thrillingly, they held the second overall position. A nerve-wracking Finals Day saw an incredibly tight leaderboard, with almost the entire top 10 in contention for the podium. The final downwind leg of the course saw a rearrange in the standings. Despite their well-fought campaign, the pair ended at sixth overall at the conclusion of racing.

In the Nacra 17 class, Australia marked success with two Australian crews making the top-10 Final Series. Archie Gargett and Sarah Hoffman won the opening race and followed by a second-place finish, landed in fourth overall.

On the other end, the journey for fellow squad members Brin Liddell and Rhiannan Brown on the Nacra 17 has been a roller coaster ride. They had days of dominating victories followed by struggles, including in the challenging Finals, but ultimately ended tenth overall in the race.

Even in the 49erFX fleet, Australia didn’t shy away from impressing with Laura Harding and Annie Wilmot qualifying for Gold Fleet racing right at the start of the Championship successfully. This championship provided both the opportunity and the platform for the Australian crews to showcase their sailing prowess.

title: Cowes Week 2026: Two Centuries of Sail
author: Michael Hodges
imageAlt: Cowes Week 2026: Two Centuries of Sail — The World’s Longest-Running Regatta Celebrates Its 200th Anniversary in Grand Style
summary: COWES, ISLE OF WIGHT | The cannons are silent for now .. but already all eyes look to the 2026 bicentenary of the world’s oldest and most celebrated sailing regatta. Two hundred years of racing, rivalry, and revelry on the Solent — and next August, Cowes will once again take its place at the heart of global sailing culture for what promises to be a truly historic week.
body: From Seven Cutters to Seven Hundred Boats

The Cowes story began on 10 August 1826, when seven cutters gathered off Cowes Castle to compete for a gold cup worth the princely sum of £600 — a fortune at the time. There were no racing rules, no handicaps, and no race committees — just wind, tide, and nerve. At the firing of the start gun, they weighed anchor and tore off down the Solent.

The race was as chaotic as it was thrilling — including a brief grounding — but Joseph Weld’s Arrow crossed the finish line first, etching her name into maritime history. That single contest lit the fuse for a tradition that would grow into a world-class sporting institution, attracting kings, captains, Olympians, and weekend sailors alike.

Over two centuries, Cowes Week has evolved into Britain’s summer of sail, blending Corinthian spirit and professional precision in equal measure. The event has shaped modern yacht racing itself — pioneering the “rules of the road”, including the all-important port-and-starboard rule, and driving the evolution of handicapping systems that make fair racing possible across different yacht classes.

Remarkably, Cowes Week has only been cancelled three times in 200 years — during the two World Wars, and again in 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic. That resilience speaks volumes about its spirit. Even through national hardship and global upheaval, the regatta has returned stronger every time, a constant in British maritime life.
As we look toward the 200th edition, that same spirit endures — a celebration not only of competition, but of community, innovation, and adventure on the water.

The 200th Cowes Week runs from 1–8 August 2026, and early signs suggest one of the largest and liveliest fleets in recent memory. Entries for 2025 were already up 14% year-on-year, reaching 440 boats, and organisers expect between 500 and 600 entries for the bicentenary edition.
Commodore Sam Haynes of the Cruising Yacht Club of Australia summed it up best earlier this season when he called Cowes “a regatta like no other — where heritage and horsepower meet.”

In 2026, organisers are planning an event worthy of that legacy, complete with fireworks, air displays, and the return of the Red Arrows, if conditions and scheduling allow. Expect a week packed with pageantry, packed marinas, and packed pubs as sailors and spectators from across the globe descend on the Isle of Wight for this once-in-a-lifetime occasion.

The Cowes racecourse remains one of the most technically challenging and visually spectacular in the world. Tides, shifting winds, and narrow marks demand precision and patience — while the Solent’s swirling waters and crowded start lines ensure adrenaline from cannon to gun.

For 2026, organisers promise a diverse racing programme catering to everything from high-performance grand-prix machines to historic classics and Corinthian dayboats. Whether aboard a Cape 31, a Quarter Tonner, or a 6-Metre, every sailor who rounds the mark off Egypt Point will feel part of something extraordinary.
The bicentenary year will be far more than a single week — it’s set to be a summer-long festival of British yachting, with a calendar of pre-events building momentum right up to the main regatta.
Castle Trophy — classic Cowes opener.
Cape 31 Series — the Solent’s speed demons return.
Commodore’s Invitational Regatta — an elite showcase of international teams.
IRC Nationals — the backbone of UK offshore racing.
Fife & Classics Regatta — golden-age yacht design meets craftsmanship.
5.5 Metre EU Championships — elegance and precision combined.
Quarter Ton Cup — small boats, huge reputations.
Cowes Classics Week — vintage sail meets modern seamanship.
Round the Island Race — 1,500 yachts, one start line, pure chaos.
British Classic Week & 12m Regatta — nostalgia and beauty under full sail.
Cowes Week Bicentenary Regatta — the centrepiece celebration.
Round Britain & Ireland Race Start — endurance meets heritage.
Dragon Edinburgh Cup — timeless one-design class racing.
Cowes Powerboat Festival — noise, spray, and spectacle.
Global Team Racing Regatta — fast, fierce, and tactical.
RC44 World Cup — the elite grand-prix series returns to the Solent.
From varnished wood and cotton sails to foiling carbon catamarans and grand-prix racers, the 2026 season will showcase every facet of the sport — past, present, and future.

The 200th anniversary of Cowes Week is more than a date on the calendar — it’s a bridge between eras. From the gold-cup cutters of 1826 to the cutting-edge designs of today, it reflects two centuries of evolution in seamanship, design, and technology.

Yet, at its heart, it remains unchanged: a gathering of sailors drawn by wind, water, and competition. Whether you’re trimming a spinnaker, calling tactics, or cheering from the shore with a pint in hand, Cowes Week is where the sea meets the soul of sailing.

As 2026 approaches, OldSeaDogs.com will follow every development — from entry lists to race previews, classic yacht features, and behind-the-scenes stories. The countdown to the Cowes Week Bicentenary has begun, and it’s shaping up to be the sailing story of the decade.

title: Adventuring at 50 Knots: Intriguing Insights into Frauscher's 797 Spectre
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Adventuring at 50 Knots: Intriguing Insights into Frauscher's 797 Spectre
summary: Unveiling Frauscher's newest runabout, the 797 Spectre. Combining elegant design aesthetics with thrilling speed, it is sure to captivate boating enthusiasts.
body: Frauscher Boats reveals its second smallest runabout yet, the 797 Spectre, maintaining the intrinsic aesthetic that is undeniably Frauscher, while introducing a boat designed for speed. With a silhouette as smooth as silk, the 797 Spectre has scalloped hull sides, a rail-free sheerline, a seamlessly integrated swim deck, and a sunken cockpit ensconced behind a tinted windscreen. This model brims with elegance, sporting a teak-lined foredeck, and an aft sunbed that evokes a leisurely atmosphere. The 797 Spectre is powered by a standard Mercruiser 6.2L V8 350hp petrol engine, but for the speed junkies, an upgrade to a larger, more potent 8.3L MAG HO 430 engine is available. This provides the 797 Spectre with a speed range of around 50 knots. Every 797 Spectre is generously loaded with standard features. An aft platform, teak decking, a 12in MFD, the Fusion stereo, bow thruster, and fridge are included. If that's not enough to satisfy, customisation options are aplenty. From a metallic hull paint and diamond-stitched upholstery to a cockpit cover, bimini extension, and transom shower, the possibilities for personalising your 797 Spectre abound. Although the option for an electrical windlass is currently unavailable, insiders whisper about a 'Spectre Air' centre-console on the horizon, adding practicality to the list of the 797 Spectre’s attributes. Boasting breathtaking design inside and out, with exemplary power at its disposal, the 797 Spectre stakes its claim in the empire of luxury boating. It's a boat that epitomises the joy of leisurely cruising, while never compromising on the thrill of high speeds.

title: New Leadership Takes Helm: Ferretti Group Announces Stassi Anastassov as Chief Executive Officer
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: New Leadership Takes Helm: Ferretti Group Announces Stassi Anastassov as Chief Executive Officer
summary: The shipbuilding titan Ferretti Group, announces Stassi Anastassov as its new Chief Executive Officer, ushering in a new era of leadership.
body: In a decisive move that promises to chart the course for the next phase of its organizational journey, the Ferretti Group has chosen Stassi Anastassov to steer its ship as the new Chief Executive Officer. This announcement came on the coattails of the board of directors' recent Annual General Meeting and marks a clear strategic pivot for the yacht and superyacht manufacturing heavyweight.

A diverse leadership background characterizes Anastassov, who distinctly straddles both the commercial and humanitarian sectors. He holds a non-executive directorship at JS Global Lifestyle and Better Shelter and a track record of providing sound advice to global companies and investment firms on subjects including governance, operation transformation, and long-term value creation. This makes him an interesting choice to helm an organization like the Ferretti Group, which thrives on the same principles.

In accepting his new appointment as Ferretti Group's chief executive officer, Anastassov articulated his commitment towards driving growth and upholding the company's unique heritage through his leadership. Citing Italy as integral to the organization’s identity, the new CEO declared his dedication to fortifying this cultural heritage while channelling efforts towards establishing the Ferretti Group as a global standard-bearer in luxury yachting.

Anastassov plans to build on the foundation laid in recent years, acknowledging the role of humility and operational focus in achieving success. He highlighted the need for strategic consistency, ambition, and long-term vision in guiding the organization towards its lofty ambitions.

Echoing his sentiments, Tan Ning, the recently appointed chairman of the Ferretti Group, vocalized his appreciation to stakeholders for their continued support and touted their new appointment's leadership as being instrumental in boosting the company's operational excellence, global position, and future value.

The Ferretti Group, rightly recognized for its exceptional line of brands and its commitment to quality and craftsmanship, comfortably straddles a position of dominance in the yacht and superyacht industry. This leadership transition appears to be another feather in an already impressive cap, with an experienced industry player like Anastassov poised to guide them towards conquering new shores.

title: The Unveiling of the Majestic 52m Perini Navi Sailing Yacht Squall in the Luxury Yachting Market
author: Old Sea Dogs

summary: Edmiston and Y.CO have jointly announced a new central agency with the 52m Perini Navi sailing yacht Squall, a demonstration of maritime excellence and luxury.
body: The luxury yachting world has recently been adorned with the magnificence of the 52m Perini Navi sailing yacht Squall, a yacht exuding grandeur, innovation, and opulence. This nautical gem completed its most comprehensive overhaul in 2026, boasting an extensive refit and a gleaming fresh paint programme.

The renowned Perini Navi designed the Squall alongside Dubois Naval Architects, making this yacht a harmonious integration of the finest design expertise. The Squall was lauded by industry insiders as exemplifying 'the best of designer Dubois married to the best of Perini Navi'. Light polished wood and soft cream furnishing accent the chic interiors, courtesy of design mastermind Rémi Tessier, further elevating the yacht's sophisticated appeal.

Beneath deck, the master suite occupies the entire beam at the aft, accompanied by twin and double guest cabins adorning the central corridor, each equipped with en suites. Squall is suitable for ten guests across five cabins, along with nine crew members. Intricately designed walnut joiners accented with wenge intensify the elegant aesthetics aboard.

Squall is equipped with a robust Caterpillar engine, achieving a maximum speed of 14 knots. With a cruising speed of 13 knots, the yacht offers a notable range of 3,900 nautical miles. In addition, a swim platform, another spot of leisure aboard the yacht, allows easy entry into the water or a space for sunbathing.

Offering unparalleled splendor, Squall is currently listed for sale at €19,900,000; a precious maritime jewel offering an unmatched seamless voyage, merging comfort, luxury, and speed. This newly unveiled sailing yacht in the luxury market beckons all enthusiasts and connoisseurs of opulent seafaring vessels.

author: Old Sea Dogs

summary: Overcoming rough waters in the retail sector, MarineMax is making strides under the strategic stewardship of Chuck Cashman, Senior VP of Global Yacht Sales.

This audacious move is not only marking an era of change, but it is already reaping benefits and propelling MarineMax's growth even higher. title: Exquisite 30m Motor Yacht Debra One Finds New Owner in Luxurious Sale
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Exquisite 30m Motor Yacht Debra One Finds New Owner in Luxurious Sale
summary: In a recent grand deal, the magnificent 29.6-metre motor yacht, Debra One, has been successfully sold.
body: Astonishing the nautical world, the sale of Debra One, the glorious Amer Cento model motor yacht was recently finalised. This captivating vessel was commissioned in 2013 at an Italian yard; both its sturdy hull and breathtaking superstructure are crafted in GRP. With the unique distinction of never being chartered, Debra One's meticulous and devoted owner has maintained and upgraded the yacht consistently, adhering to the most stringent standards. The selling price of Debra One, with EU VAT paid, was a cool €2,200,000.

The yacht comfortably accommodates six guests across three luxurious cabins. The lower deck offers the full-beam master suite, displaying direct access to an imposing full-beam office. Each of the cabin's ensuite bathrooms is richly accentuated by large slabs of green quartz, adding an air of opulence. There is also an option to convert the lower deck office into a third VIP cabin if the need arises, thereby increasing the yacht's guest capacity to eight.

The Debra One offers ample spaces for guests to indulge in al fresco dining on the main deck aft. Simultaneously, the flybridge stands tall with a forward second helm, lounges aft, a tempting hot tub, and another dining table for added convenience. Within the bow area, sunpads and smaller tables provide great spots for cocktails and exciting games.

Powering the luxurious Debra One are twin V12 CAT engines that propel the vessel to a top-speed of 25 knots. A crown jewel in the seas, Debra One was stationed in Sanremo, Italy, when the deal was struck.

title: New York to Lorient — IMOCA Fleet Set for a Full-Noise Atlantic Crossing
author: Michael Hodges
imageAlt: The Ocean Race Atlantic 2026: Lorient Confirmed as Finish for High-Speed Transatlantic Showdown
summary: The Ocean Race Atlantic 2026 will race from New York to Lorient, bringing the world’s top IMOCA teams together for a fast, fully-crewed transatlantic showdown across the North Atlantic.
body: Some races follow history. Others start writing it. The first edition of The Ocean Race Atlantic was firmly in the second category — and with the finish now confirmed in Lorient, the shape of this new offshore test became very clear. This wasn’t just another crossing.
It was a statement.
The fleet was set to leave New York City on September 1st, pointing east across roughly 3,000 nautical miles of North Atlantic water — a route as historic as it is unforgiving. Finish line: Lorient.

Not by accident. Lorient isn’t just a port — it’s the engine room of modern offshore sailing. Known as the heart of the “Bretagne Sailing Valley,” it’s where a large part of the IMOCA fleet lives, trains and evolves. This race didn’t just end there. It belonged there. A Course Built for Speed — And Responsibility

West to east. Trades to systems. Push hard and don’t break. In reality, it was anything but. The Ocean Race organisers worked alongside 11th Hour Racing, scientists and marine advisory groups to shape a route that balanced outright performance with environmental responsibility. Avoiding high-risk zones for marine life. Reducing encounters with large mammals. Because offshore racing is changing — and this race was part of that shift.
Fully Crewed IMOCA — A Different Kind of Pressure
This wasn’t solo. This wasn’t survival sailing. This was fully-crewed IMOCA racing — fast, aggressive and relentless.
Two men Two women Plus an onboard reporter capturing every moment

That balance wasn’t just symbolic. It changed how teams functioned. Different strengths. Different decisions. Different dynamics. And when you’re crossing an ocean at full tilt, that matters. A Fleet With Serious Intent Six teams had already committed, and none were there to make up numbers:
Team Malizia 11th Hour Racing Team DMG Mori Sailing Team Oliver Heer Ocean Racing Team
Among them, sailors like Francesca Clapcich brought a personal edge to the race — crossing from the U.S., where she lives, to France, where her team is based.

That’s the thing about this race. It isn’t abstract. It’s personal. Legacy, Speed and the Next Step The boats themselves weren’t slow either. This same generation of IMOCA had already proven what they could do — including setting 24-hour distance records in previous Ocean Race campaigns.
But this time, without the stopovers.
No reset.
No second chances.
Just one long push across the Atlantic.
The arrival in Lorient wasn’t going to be quiet.
At “Lorient La Base,” the race would finish into a full public programme — Ocean Live Park, team access, fan engagement, and a proper celebration of offshore sailing culture.
Because Lorient doesn’t just host races.
It builds them.
With an ecosystem supporting hundreds of jobs and millions in economic impact, offshore sailing here isn’t a niche.
It’s industry.
The Bigger Picture — A Prologue to Something Larger
Make no mistake — this race sat in a bigger narrative.
For many teams, this wasn’t just about winning.
It was preparation.
A proving ground ahead of the next edition of The Ocean Race.
New boats. New crews. New systems.
Tested the hard way.
This one had all the right ingredients.
A proper start line. A proper finish. And an ocean in between that doesn’t care who you are.
No shortcuts. No hiding. No easy miles.
Just a straight shot across the Atlantic — and the kind of race that tells you exactly where you stand.

title: From Arctic Ice Lines to Caribbean Trades — IMOCA’s 2026 Calendar Promised a Full-Throttle Year
author: Michael Hodges
imageAlt: IMOCA 2026 Season: Five Races, Two Oceans and One Relentless Test of Offshore Sailing
summary: The IMOCA Class entered 2026 with a five-race calendar blending solo endurance and fully-crewed intensity, setting the stage for one of the most demanding and technically advanced offshore seasons yet.
body: If you want to understand where offshore sailing really lives now — you don’t look at one race.
And in 2026, the IMOCA class didn’t just put together a season — it built a proper test piece.
Five races. Different formats. Different pressures.
Same outcome: if you weren’t ready, you were going to get found out.
At the centre of it all, Class President Antoine Mermod looked ahead to his ninth season at the helm with a simple message — the numbers might ebb and flow, but the level never drops.
A Season Built on Contrast — Solo vs Crewed
What makes IMOCA different isn’t just speed.
It’s the constant shift in mindset.
One minute you’re alone, making every call, carrying every mistake.
The next, you’re in a fully-crewed machine where execution is everything and hesitation costs miles.
In 2026, that contrast was front and centre.
Solo extremes in the Vendée Arctique and Route du Rhum Fully-crewed intensity in The Ocean Race Atlantic
Two completely different disciplines.
Same boats.
Same sailors.
The season’s defining early challenge didn’t head south into sunshine.
It went north.
The Vendée Arctique left Les Sables d’Olonne and drove the fleet straight towards the Arctic Circle — into a part of the Atlantic where forecasts don’t hold and the weather writes its own rules.
This wasn’t just another qualifier.
It was a thinking sailor’s race.
Short-term forecasts. Rapid system changes. Pressure lines that shifted faster than decisions could be made.
As Mermod put it — the challenge wasn’t just distance.
It was location.
New Blood, New Boats — No Easy Entry
The 2026 fleet didn’t just carry experience — it brought fresh risk.
Six new skippers stepped into the solo IMOCA world for the first time, including:
Ambrogio Beccaria Elodie Bonafous Francesca Clapcich Violette Dorange
This isn’t a gentle learning curve.
You either adapt — or you don’t finish.
Alongside them sat proven operators like Sam Goodchild, bringing championship form into a fleet where consistency matters more than moments.
The Ocean Race Atlantic — Pressure With Nowhere to Hide
If the Arctic demanded independence, The Ocean Race Atlantic demanded control.
Starting from New York, this transatlantic crossing wasn’t just another race — it was effectively a proving ground ahead of the next edition of The Ocean Race.
Every manoeuvre is visible. Every mistake amplified.
Teams like Team Malizia, led by Boris Herrmann, lined up alongside Kojiro Shiraishi — both bringing new boats, new setups, and no shortage of ambition.
Route du Rhum — The One That Still Matters Most
For all the innovation, data, and evolution — some races still sit above the rest.
The Route du Rhum is one of them.
3,500 miles. Solo. No compromises.
From Saint-Malo to Guadeloupe, it’s a race every IMOCA skipper wants on their record.
In 2026, up to 25 boats lined up — one of the strongest entries the class has seen.
Because winning this one doesn’t just prove speed.
It proves everything.
Technology, Sustainability and the Next Battle
Behind the racing, the real arms race continued.
The IMOCA Annual General Meeting in Lorient quietly set the direction for the next phase — not just performance, but responsibility.
Increased use of RISE sails (Reduced Impact Sail Evaluation) Continued development of hydro-generators Early groundwork for the 2032 Vendée Globe rules
This is where IMOCA is ahead of the curve.
Not just faster boats.
Smarter ones.
Cleaner ones.
This wasn’t a season built for comfort.
It was built for exposure.
Different formats. Different oceans. Different pressures.
But one consistent truth:
You don’t get lucky across five races.
You either belong at this level — or the calendar proves you don’t.
And in 2026, IMOCA made sure of that.

It’s the constant shift in mindset.
One minute you’re alone, making every call, carrying every mistake.
The next, you’re in a fully-crewed machine where execution is everything and hesitation costs miles.
In 2026, that contrast was front and centre.
Solo extremes in the Vendée Arctique and Route du Rhum Fully-crewed intensity in The Ocean Race Atlantic
Two completely different disciplines.
Same boats.
Same sailors.
The season’s defining early challenge didn’t head south into sunshine.
It went north.
The Vendée Arctique left Les Sables d’Olonne and drove the fleet straight towards the Arctic Circle — into a part of the Atlantic where forecasts don’t hold and the weather writes its own rules.
This wasn’t just another qualifier.
It was a thinking sailor’s race.
Short-term forecasts. Rapid system changes. Pressure lines that shifted faster than decisions could be made.
As Mermod put it — the challenge wasn’t just distance.
It was location.
New Blood, New Boats — No Easy Entry
The 2026 fleet didn’t just carry experience — it brought fresh risk.
Six new skippers stepped into the solo IMOCA world for the first time, including:
Ambrogio Beccaria Elodie Bonafous Francesca Clapcich Violette Dorange
This isn’t a gentle learning curve.
You either adapt — or you don’t finish.
Alongside them sat proven operators like Sam Goodchild, bringing championship form into a fleet where consistency matters more than moments.
The Ocean Race Atlantic — Pressure With Nowhere to Hide
If the Arctic demanded independence, The Ocean Race Atlantic demanded control.
Starting from New York, this transatlantic crossing wasn’t just another race — it was effectively a proving ground ahead of the next edition of The Ocean Race.
Every manoeuvre is visible. Every mistake amplified.
Teams like Team Malizia, led by Boris Herrmann, lined up alongside Kojiro Shiraishi — both bringing new boats, new setups, and no shortage of ambition.
Route du Rhum — The One That Still Matters Most
For all the innovation, data, and evolution — some races still sit above the rest.
The Route du Rhum is one of them.
3,500 miles. Solo. No compromises.
From Saint-Malo to Guadeloupe, it’s a race every IMOCA skipper wants on their record.
In 2026, up to 25 boats lined up — one of the strongest entries the class has seen.
Because winning this one doesn’t just prove speed.
It proves everything.
Technology, Sustainability and the Next Battle
Behind the racing, the real arms race continued.
The IMOCA Annual General Meeting in Lorient quietly set the direction for the next phase — not just performance, but responsibility.
Increased use of RISE sails (Reduced Impact Sail Evaluation) Continued development of hydro-generators Early groundwork for the 2032 Vendée Globe rules
This is where IMOCA is ahead of the curve.
Not just faster boats.
Smarter ones.
Cleaner ones.
This wasn’t a season built for comfort.
It was built for exposure.
Different formats. Different oceans. Different pressures.
But one consistent truth:
You don’t get lucky across five races.
You either belong at this level — or the calendar proves you don’t.
And in 2026, IMOCA made sure of that.

title: Challenging Conditions Test Sailors in the Early-Season Opener of the KSSA Season at Downs Sailing Club
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Challenging Conditions Test Sailors in the Early-Season Opener of the KSSA Season at Downs Sailing Club
summary: Downs Sailing Club hosted the commendably successful opening race of the KSSA season, providing a strategic and engaging competition environment.
body: On a breezy spring day at Downs Sailing Club, located in Deal, the exciting annual opening of the Kent Schools Sailing Association (KSSA) season – known as the Opening Splash – took place. In doing so, it set the stage for an early-season test for sailors and set the tone for what to expect during the NSSA National Youth Regatta slated for later in the summer.

The event was meticulously organised with two challenging courses: the Main Fleet and the Regatta Fleet. The clever structuring served as a magnet for budding sailors while keeping the competition intense for experienced trailblazers. The turnout across the region was impressive, with Downs SC seeing a commendable representation of enthusiastic sailors.

To do well required astute tacticians who could accurately start, minimise manoeuvres, and cleverly manoeuvre pressure lines along the tidal positioning - a testament to the skills that were adjudicated across both fleets. The day also witnessed a notable wind shift that provoked a course reset, ensuring fair competition.

Front-of-fleet tensions arose throughout the day, as victories and podium places regularly exchanged hands. Sailors from Whitstable YC, Downs SC, Margate YC, and Medway YC evenly jockeyed for position across a collection of classes, including ILCA, Topper, and double-handers.

The Regatta course also offered a compelling introduction to racing, as very light winds in tandem with a pronounced tide made for tense sailing. Races were completed swiftly on a compact, inshore triangular track, allowing optimised starts and quick turnarounds. In such light airs, successful sailing was primarily dependent on cautious trim and momentum - especially for Optimist sailors, who discovered that technique and positioning were a decisive mix.

title: A Riveting Race Awaited as Seasoned Pros and Fresh Faces Gear Up for the 57th La Solitaire du Figaro Paprec
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: A Riveting Race Awaited as Seasoned Pros and Fresh Faces Gear Up for the 57th La Solitaire du Figaro Paprec
summary: Fans and competitors alike are buzzing with anticipation as the 57th edition of La Solitaire du Figaro Paprec approaches, promising an exhilarating mix of experienced pros and ambitious newcomers.
body: In a mere two days, 36 sailors, both women and men, will embark on the 57th edition of the sailing spectacle, La Solitaire du Figaro Paprec. The 2027 season opens with breathtaking scenery and an early start, as anxious participants fill the docks of Perros-Guirec, ready to set sail for Vigo, Spain. They respond enthusiastically to the call of the sea, the thrill of the race, and the lure of the legendary competition. The contest this year also invites an array of rookies who add an adventurous spirit to the competition, matched against the perseverance of the returning veterans. This delightful mix guarantees spectacular battles across all three stages, adding to the race lore. The core of this year's fleet consists of a mix of sprightly and seasoned sailors, prepped for the battle of the seas. Challenging them are four formidable frontrunners: Lois Berrehar (Banque Populaire), Adrien Hardy (Sans Nature, pas de futur!), Nicolas Lunven (PRB), and last minute entrant Martin Le Pape (Paprec), stepping in for the sidelined Yoann Richomme. The fleet boasts enriched experience with the return of these stalwarts. Collectively, they've entered the La Solitaire race 38 times. Only Lunven has tasted victory twice, in 2009 and 2017, and also won the Rookie of the Year award in his 2007 debut race. 'The timing was perfect for my return. The Figaro Bénéteau 3 is new to me. Quite different from the Figaro 2 on which I won. I still feel passionately for the class and truly relish this circuit. I return to enjoy and give it my all,' says Nicolas Lunven, brimming with anticipation for this exciting race.

These departures represent a considerable turnaround for a company that has long been at the forefront of the yachting industry. Ferrari and Domenicali's contributions to the successes of the Group over the years cannot be overstated. Their seasoned guidance, combined with their deep understanding of the sea and everything that it represents, have navigated Ferretti through both calm and stormy waters.

title: Discover the unparalleled craftsmanship and allure of the recently sold 66m Feadship superyacht, Hampshire.

summary: Highlighted by an outstanding sale, the Feadship superyacht, Hampshire, exemplifies the peak of Northern European craftsmanship, design, and long-lasting quality.
body: Craftsmanship and pedigree have been evidently intertwined in the recent sale of the 66-meter Feadship superyacht, Hampshire. This elegant motor yacht, designed by the renowned British studio Harrison Eidsgaard, was sold in a noteworthy deal involving prominent brokers Chris Cecil-Wright and Andrew Bond. Upon its listing in the market, the Hampshire was recognised for its immaculate condition, a testament to a significant engineering reset. This quality craft has successfully completed a detailed, 10-year Lloyd’s survey.

Cecil Wright, who masterfully represented the seller in this transaction, has contended that the Hampshire represents nothing short of the pinnacle of Northern European craftsmanship and design. He also emphasized the continued strong demand that exists for high-quality, pedigree yachts such as this. The sale of the Hampshire showcases the unwavering belief that potential buyers have in the reliability and lasting value of expertly-engineered yachts.

Moreover, the Hampshire provides extravagant accommodations for up to 14 guests in its generous cabins. The full beam owner’s suite is a masterpiece of luxury, complete with a private balcony and clandestine bridge access. This attention to detail extends to the crew accoommodations as well.

Entertainment and leisure get an elevated definition aboard the Hampshire. With wellness zones that encompass a beach club and an interior spa, and a sundeck adorned with a Jacuzzi and a wet bar, the Hampshire offers ample areas for relaxation and socializing. Its cruising comfort is augmented further by twin MTU engines powering the yacht to a comfortable, 13-knot speed. From its furnishings to its engineering finesse, the Hampshire is an unmatched symbol of luxury.

title: The Magnificent Mangusta 'King II' Finds New Monarch in Recent Sale
author: Old Sea Dogs

summary: The 33.5-metre Mangusta motor yacht 'King II' has found a new home following a successful sale, brokered jointly by the parties of Ocean Independence and World Yacht Group.
body: A recent transaction saw the luxe 33.5-metre Mangusta motor yacht 'King II' sailing into the arms of a new owner. The sale was facilitated by the joint efforts of Daria Tomassett of Ocean Independence and Ruben Llaudet of World Yacht Group, representing the seller and the buyer, respectively.

This magnificent vessel, whose reign commenced in 2004 when it was delivered, owes its majestic design to the creative genius of Andrea Bacigalupo. Stefano Righini took charge of crafting the yacht's naval architecture and interiors, resulting in a seamless blend of style and functionality.

Once aboard the 'King II', one encounters a saloon that exudes comfort and elegance. It houses expansive, plush settees, an entertainment centre and a bar - perfect for hosting and keeping guests engaged. The vessel also boasts a separate dining area equipped with two tables, thereby offering a grand setup to entertain numerous guests.
Space to unwind is aplenty on this yacht. The rear end of the main deck offers additional lounging opportunities with stairs descending to the swim platform, paving the way for easy sea access.
But the 'King II' is not all about comfort and luxury; it packs a punch in performance too. Capable of hitting a maximum speed of 34 knots, the yacht ensures expedient cruising at 30 knots.

This grand vessel, last priced at €1,700,000, is undoubtedly a testament to the supreme charm and timeless allure of luxury yachts. With its recent change in ownership, the 'King II' is all set to embark on a new adventure, exploring the vast oceans and indulging its inhabitants in an unrivalled sea experience.

title: The All-Conquering Cape 31 Mediterranean Fleet Set Sail for a Magnetic Med Showdown in Sardinia
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: The All-Conquering Cape 31 Mediterranean Fleet Set Sail for a Magnetic Med Showdown in Sardinia
summary: Inpatient sailing aficionados across the continents are all eyes set on Sardinia as the enthralling Cape 31 Mediterranean Circuit heads to Puntaldia for Round 2.
body: The echo of first round's concluding horn barely settled when hardy sailing enthusiasts were excitedly charting course for Round 2 of the Cape 31 Mediterranean Circuit. The crème de la crème of the sailing fraternity is making their way to the picture-perfect Sardinian coast. Puntaldia's yachting reputation precedes it, promising a weekend of high-octane races, enlivened with the stunning backdrop of Sardinia's scenic landscape, and an irresistible blend of onshore festivities and hospitality.

Following a week of gusty Mistral winds that whipped across the region, the pre-competition forecast is promising for the sailing aficionados, with the expectation of favourable racing conditions come Friday. Puntaldia's marina has been abuzz with preparations for the highly anticipated next stage of the circuit, culminating with the opening races kicking off at midday.

Undoubtedly, round 2 signals a critical acceleration for the Cape 31 Mediterranean Circuit. Teams continue to revel in both the high-performance racing and the unique concoction of sailing, high life and unique venue selections that distinguishes the circuit.

Competitive racers have descended from across the continent, including Great Britain, Germany, the Netherlands, Italy, Austria, Portugal, Turkey, Hungary, and the Isle of Man. The focal point remains the return of Round 1 champions, Alessandro Rombelli's Stig, resolved to defend their glory, while Michael Wilson's Shotgunn are ready to challenge for the top honour.
With the promising possibility of unaccustomed robust breezes on the Milesian coast, this weekend could turn tables, disrupting the leaderboard, and shaking the established pecking order.

Eye-catching at the event would be the debut of Hatari's shiny new Cape 31, shipped over from Cape Town. The fleet is on its toes to see how swiftly the new campaign finds a rhythm against their seasoned counterparts.

Pro sailing veterans including Olympic medallists, world champions, and internationally acclaimed campaigners like Luke Patience, Stu Bithell, Ian Ainslie, Sime Fantela, Sam Gilmour, and Zsombor Berecz, are set to add another layer of fierceness to the expected high-stakes competition that the three-day regatta will bring.
Come weekend, and Puntaldia port is bound to cast another indelible chapter in the illustrious and historical narrative of the Cape 31 Mediterranean Series.

title: Unveiling the 2026 Evolution of the Leopard 53PC: Enhanced Luxury, Renewed Design, and the Same Classic Spirit
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Unveiling the 2026 Evolution of the Leopard 53PC: Enhanced Luxury, Renewed Design, and the Same Classic Spirit
summary: Embodying the spirit of evolution, the award-winning Leopard 53PC is unveiled in a new avatar, blending exterior living upgrades with luxe modularity.
body: The revered flagship of the Leopard fleet, the Leopard 53PC, is bestowed with a refreshing transformation, deserving of its award-winning legacy. Following the enormous success of the previous model, which sold an impressive 142 units, it's only natural for this iconic South African brand to embrace evolutionary changes. Launched in February 2026 at the Miami International Boat Show, the primary spotlight shines on the yacht's exterior living zones. The aft cockpit now presents a choice between a set plan or an expansive deck equipped with adaptable furniture modules. New features include the option of an electric swim platform and a reimagined transom design, adding more room to the already spacious cockpit. The flybridge is enhanced with a more generous seating arrangement, modular backrests that adapt as needed, and an upgraded helm station. It also flaunts sophisticated new fabrics and a state-of-the-art wet bar, complete with an integrated sink, grill, and fridge. The interior also gets a facelift, presenting an open connection between the galley, dining, and lounge areas along with modernized lighting systems. All this while keeping the price point relatively unchanged, into a testament of the brand’s commitment towards their patrons. Retaining its appeal to both private owners and participants of the Moorings yacht charter ownership program, the Leopard 53PC offers dual layout options. Choose between a symmetrical four-cabin ensuite layout, or a three-cabin variant boasting a private owner's suite. The renowned South African shipyard, Robertson and Caine remains the constructors of its unchanged hulls and engines. Housing its major systems in a separate engine room, Leopard promises a quieter and smoother cruising experience. The Leopard 53PC marks a dynamic balance between luxury and pragmatic sophistication, proving once again that Leopard Yachts remain on the horizon of maritime evolution.

title: 60 Miles Flat Out Around the Isle of Wight as UKOPRA Returns to the Solent
author: Michael Hodges
imageAlt: Thunder Around the Isle of Wight: UKOPRA Offshore Championship Explodes Into Life for 2026
summary: Thunder Around the Isle of Wight: UKOPRA Offshore Championship Returns at Full Noise
body: There are quieter ways to spend a Saturday in the Solent. And then there’s the UKOPRA Round the Island Race.

On 16 May 2026, the south coast of England shook once again as thirty offshore powerboat teams lined up off the Isle of Wight for the opening round of the 2026 UK Offshore Powerboat Racing Association Championship.
Sixty miles. Anti-clockwise. No easing into it.
Just throttle forward and hold on.

The race started off East Lepe Buoy, opposite Gurnard, where crews gathered in the muster area beneath grey Solent skies and a growing sense of anticipation. Two rolling starts followed at midday and 12:10pm, sending the fleet charging westward around the island’s coastline. The format sounds simple. In reality, it’s brutal.
tidal shifts confused Solent chop exposed headlands changing sea states and very little margin for error at speed
Especially when the fastest UKOPRA Class 1 boats are capable of completing the full course in around 40 minutes when conditions allow. That’s not cruising. That’s sustained violence with navigation.

The fleet featured teams from across the UK and Europe competing across: Class 1 Class 1L Class 2 Class 3 And while each class carried different speeds and setups, the challenge remained exactly the same: Keep the boat alive. Keep the throttles down. And don’t lose concentration for a second. Because offshore powerboat racing isn’t circuit racing on water. It’s controlled chaos.
Part of what makes this race special is the course itself. The Isle of Wight doesn’t just sit there quietly while boats go around it. It shapes the race.

From the western approaches off The Needles to the exposed southern coastline near St Catherine's Lighthouse, crews were forced to deal with changing conditions almost corner by corner. One side of the island might offer relatively flat water. The next could feel like driving into a collapsing staircase at 100mph. That’s offshore racing. Best Seats in the House For spectators, the race once again turned the Isle of Wight into a natural amphitheatre.
Yarmouth Pier Fort Victoria Hurst Castle The Needles Ryde Pier Egypt Point

And when the boats came through at full speed, they didn’t just pass by. They arrived. The sound alone carried for miles. Shamrock Quay Became the Paddock Before the racing started, Shamrock Quay handled scrutineering and race preparations, transforming Southampton’s waterfront into a floating paddock of carbon fibre, twin engines and nervous energy.
Crews checked systems. Teams checked weather. Everyone checked everyone else.

Conditions decide everything. Safety, Respect and Clean Water UKOPRA also reminded spectator craft to remain north of the East Lepe to West Lepe line during the rolling starts. Not bureaucracy. Necessity.
At these speeds, small mistakes become very large problems very quickly. The start of an offshore race isn’t a photo opportunity. It’s one of the most dangerous moments in motorsport.

There’s something deeply British about offshore powerboat racing around the Isle of Wight. Cold spray. Big noise. Questionable life choices. And yet every year, crews come back wanting more. Because when the throttles go down and the Solent starts punching back, there’s nowhere to hide and no easy miles. Just man, machine and water.
Exactly as it should be.

title: Riding the Wave of Demand, UK's Falmouth Harbour Invests £50,000 in High-Capacity Superyacht Moorings
