So brace yourself for a nautical symphony of excitement, adventure, and camaraderie, as these sailing events promise to transform the azure expanses into a playground of victory and celebration.

title: Round the Island Race 2026 Entries Open as the Countdown to July begins
author: Michael Hodges
imageAlt: Round the Island Race 2026: The Clock Starts Now
summary: Round the Island Race 2026 — One Island, One Start Line, One Day That Matters. The countdown has officially begun for one of British sailing’s great shared experiences. The Round the Island Race is gearing up for another blockbuster edition.
body: The race itself will be sailed on Saturday 11 July, when hundreds of boats — from family cruisers and club racers to seasoned offshore campaigners — will gather off Cowes to take on the iconic 50-nautical-mile lap of the Isle of Wight.

Organised by the Island Sailing Club, the Round the Island Race remains one of the world’s largest mass-participation yacht races, and one of the few where first-timers and veterans share the same tide, the same start line, and the same long day on the water.
Momentum building ahead of launch
As preparations shift from planning to execution, Race Director Dave Atkinson says the sense of anticipation is already tangible.

“The excitement and anticipation is really building as we approach the launch of Round the Island Race 2026,” he said. “We’ve been busy behind the scenes at the Island Sailing Club getting everything ready, and now it’s time to build momentum ahead of the race in July.”
Atkinson is keen to underline what has always defined the event — its openness.
“Whether you’re a seasoned competitor or keen to take part for the first time, the race is open to all. We’d love to see you on the start line and be part of a really special occasion.”
A course etched into sailing folklore
The Round the Island Race course needs little introduction, but it never loses its impact.

The fleet will start on the famous Royal Yacht Squadron line at Cowes, before heading west down the Solent toward The Needles. From there, boats sweep south past St Catherine’s Point, continue east around the back of the Island to Bembridge Ledge Buoy, and then turn back into the Solent for the final run home to Cowes.

For some, it’s a flat-out tactical race against the clock. For others, it’s a test of seamanship, teamwork and endurance. For many, it’s simply the best possible way to spend a July Saturday under sail.
With demand traditionally high — and fleets often running into the hundreds — early entry is strongly advised.
More than a race: Cowes comes alive

The on-shore experience is a key part of the Round the Island Race weekend. A dedicated Race Village on Cowes Parade will be open throughout the event, with live music and entertainment across three days, beginning on Friday 10 July.

Whether you’re racing, supporting friends, or simply soaking up the atmosphere from the shore, the weekend delivers that rare blend of competitive sailing and summer festival energy that Cowes does better than anywhere else.
One island. One day. Every reason to be there.

For veterans, it’s a tradition that never quite repeats itself the same way twice. For newcomers, it’s a rite of passage. For everyone involved, it’s a reminder of why sailing — at its best — is about shared horizons as much as results.
Entries opened 23rd January. The race sails 11 July.
To enter or find out more, visit www.roundtheisland.org.uk .

title: SpaceCat, the Boutique Yacht Featured in 'The White Lotus', Finds a New Owner
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: SpaceCat, the Boutique Yacht Featured in 'The White Lotus', Finds a New Owner
summary: The 36m SilverYachts 'SpaceCat', whose beauty stole the show in 'The White Lotus', has been sold in a brilliant collaboration of renowned yacht brokers.
body: The 36m catamaran 'SpaceCat', crafted by Australian shipyard SilverYachts and lauded designer Espen Øeino, has found a new owner. Known for its starring role in 'The White Lotus', the sophisticated yacht was sold by sellers represented by Mark Woodmansey of Burgess and Michel Chryssicopoulos of IYC with the buyer introduced by Della Pearce of Camper & Nicholsons.

Sporting a beam of 13.3 metres, the SpaceCat distinguishes itself with its vast living spaces spread across three spacious decks. Including more than 534 square meters of lavish living space, this superyacht boasts extraordinary volume for its size.
The sale price for this superstar yacht? A cool $15M.
A saltwater pool, chic bar, and sizable aft deck make for a delightful alfresco experience while the beach club and hydraulic swim platform ensure unobstructed access to the sea.

Powered by four 920hp Volvo Penta engines, SpaceCat is capable of reaching speeds up to 23 knots and boasts an impressive range of 3,000 nautical miles at 11 knots. It is optimally designed for island hopping with its shallow 1.8-meter draught allows easy access to secluded harbours and shallow waters. Its current location is in Thailand, where it runs an established charter program and where HBO's popular social satire 'The White Lotus' was filmed.

title: Sunseeker Superhawk 34 – the Spirit of James Bond
author: Michael Hodges
imageAlt: Sunseeker Superhawk 34
summary: If ever a boat deserved to be described as iconic, the Sunseeker Superhawk 34 fits the bill. A blend of blistering performance, head-turning style, and unmistakable British engineering, this sleek open cruiser is the kind of boat that doesn’t just cut through the waves—it makes a statement.
body: If ever a boat deserved to be described as iconic, the Sunseeker Superhawk 34 fits the bill. A blend of blistering performance, head-turning style, and unmistakable British engineering, this sleek open cruiser is the kind of boat that doesn’t just cut through the waves—it makes a statement.

Made famous by its appearance in the 1999 James Bond film The World Is Not Enough, the Superhawk 34 combines Sunseeker’s high-performance DNA with refined luxury touches. Even today, more than two decades after its debut, it remains a favourite among thrill-seeking boaters and collectors alike. Whether you’re gunning it along the Côte d’Azur or pulling into a posh marina on the south coast of England, the Superhawk 34 still has the power to draw admiring glances.

At its heart, the Superhawk 34 is a driver’s boat—built for speed, responsiveness, and agility. Powered by twin petrol or diesel sterndrive engines, commonly Volvo Penta KAD44s or MerCruiser 496 MAGs, the boat boasts a combined horsepower output in the 520–700 HP range. Depending on engine spec and condition, she’ll deliver top speeds in the 40–45 knot range, with blistering acceleration and a satisfying growl from the exhaust.

The deep-V hull is designed for offshore conditions, meaning this Sunseeker isn’t just a fair-weather toy. It carves confidently through chop, holds its line in tight turns, and feels planted even at high speed. With hydraulic steering and precision throttle controls, the Superhawk 34 is as rewarding to helm as it is to ride aboard.

Mooring and low-speed handling are made manageable by her size and beam (9 ft 8 in), but this is a boat that lives to stretch its legs. She’s best suited for day runs between coastal towns, island hops, or simply high-octane fun on open water.

Above deck, the Superhawk 34 is all about socialising and open-air enjoyment. The cockpit features a triple-wide helm seat—so the skipper doesn’t have to be alone in the fun—and a spacious U-shaped aft seating area with a removable dining table. It’s an ideal layout for sipping cold drinks at anchor, hosting lunch for friends, or watching the sun dip below the horizon.

The sunpad over the engine hatch provides ample lounging space, while the integrated swim platform and ladder make it easy to dip into the sea or launch a tender. Some models feature a wet bar, and there’s good storage tucked into various lockers throughout the deck.
Optional teak decking and polished stainless-steel fittings add a touch of superyacht class, underscoring that this is no ordinary performance boat—it’s a Sunseeker, after all.

The helm is both sporty and luxurious. Well-laid-out gauges, throttles, and trim controls are all easily accessible. Visibility is excellent, thanks to the low-slung profile and the curved, wraparound windscreen. A modernised version may include upgraded chartplotters, VHF, and autopilot, but many original models still have classic analog dials and switches, which appeal to purists.
Below deck, the Superhawk 34 surprises with a well-finished and cleverly designed cabin. While this isn’t a long-range cruiser, the space is more than sufficient for weekend getaways.

The forward V-berth converts from a lounge/dinette area into a double bed, flanked by cherrywood cabinetry and padded side panels. The small galley includes a sink, stove, fridge, and basic stowage—enough to handle light meals and snacks. To starboard, the enclosed head includes a marine toilet, sink, and pull-out shower.
Headroom is modest (around 5'9"), and tall guests may need to stoop. But the fit and finish are unmistakably premium, from the upholstery to the cabinetry.
Some models of the Superhawk 34 came with options such as:
Air conditioning
Upgraded stereo systems
LCD TVs
Bow thruster
Trim tabs
Shore power and battery chargers

Because these boats are often 20+ years old, the level of modern equipment will vary significantly from vessel to vessel. Many have been tastefully updated, making them more comfortable for longer stays or more refined for entertaining.
The Superhawk 34 is now a classic, and like all older boats, condition varies widely. Key things to inspect when buying include:
Engine health: especially petrol versions, which may have high hours and thirsty fuel use
Hull integrity: gelcoat stress or repairs
Upholstery and teak deck wear
Updated electronics or rewiring
Outdrive condition: corrosion, seals, and bellows should all be carefully inspected
A professional marine survey is essential. Many owners have pampered these boats, keeping them in dry storage and under covers. Those are the gems to look for.

The Superhawk 34 is a sports cruiser, often referred to as a "gentleman's powerboat," offering impressive top-end speed, razor-sharp handling, and just enough luxury below deck to accommodate overnighting. It’s the kind of boat that turns heads at the marina and rips across coastal waters with the aggression of a race boat, but without compromising comfort or build quality.
Length Overall (LOA) 36 ft (11.30 m)
Beam 9 ft 8 in (2.95 m)
Draft 3 ft 1 in (0.94 m)
Displacement Approx. 6,500 kg (14,330 lbs)
Fuel Capacity 700 L (185 gallons)
Water Capacity 140 L (37 gallons)
Engines Twin Volvo Penta or MerCruiser (diesel or petrol)
Top Speed Up to 45 knots (varies by engine)
Cruise Speed ~30–35 knots
Accommodation Sleeps 2 + convertible dinette

Performance is where the Superhawk 34 shines. Most models were outfitted with twin petrol engines (e.g., Volvo Penta KAD44s or MerCruiser 496 MAGs), producing 520–700 horsepower combined. Some versions came with diesel engines for better fuel economy and range.

Thanks to its deep-V hull, the Superhawk 34 delivers a fast, dry, and agile ride, easily handling moderate chop at speed. Top speeds are in the 40–45 knot range, and the boat accelerates quickly, with strong midrange punch. It’s ideal for zipping between marinas, exploring coastlines, or simply enjoying fast-paced day boating.
Handling is tight and responsive, with hydraulic steering and a solid helm position offering excellent control at all speeds.

While speed is the star of the show, Sunseeker didn’t skimp on luxury. The cabin is surprisingly well-finished for a performance boat, with rich cherrywood trim, high-quality upholstery, and sleek fittings.
Forward V-berth converts to a double bed or lounging space
Dinette area with fold-out table
Compact galley includes sink, stove, and fridge
Enclosed head with marine toilet and shower
Air conditioning and TV on some models (optional upgrades)
Headroom is limited (as expected in this style of boat), but the space is comfortable enough for overnighting or escaping the sun.
Above deck, the Superhawk 34 is all about open-air thrills. The cockpit is laid out with socialising and speed in mind:
Triple-wide helm seat for pilot and companions
U-shaped rear seating area with dining table
Sunpad over engine bay
Teak decking (optional)
Integrated swim platform with ladder
Wet bar and storage lockers
It’s a boat that invites fun—sunbathing, entertaining, watersports, or simply hammering across the bay with a grin on your face.
Classic Sunseeker styling with aggressive lines and a sleek profile
Top-end speed over 40 knots
Deep-V hull delivers superb handling and offshore capability
Surprisingly refined cabin for overnight stays
Famous James Bond appearance adds to its cult status
Many boats are 20+ years old—survey and engine checks are a must
Petrol versions offer great speed but can be thirsty on fuel
Some cockpit upholstery and electronics may need updates
Cabin headroom is tight for tall passengers
The Sunseeker Superhawk 34 is not a slow cruiser—it's a driver’s boat, perfect for those who want the performance of a powerboat with the finish of a luxury yacht. It suits:
Day boaters who want style and speed
Couples or small families doing short overnight trips
James Bond fans who want to own a piece of movie history
Classic boat collectors looking for a performance icon
Ask any owner and they’ll likely rave about:
The instant power and thrilling ride
The attention the boat commands
The James Bond pedigree
The superb build quality—solid, reliable, and stylish even decades later
For those who prize speed and aesthetics, the Superhawk 34 delivers both in spades.

The Sunseeker Superhawk 34 isn’t just a boat—it’s a statement. It says you value performance, you appreciate craftsmanship, and you want your time on the water to be thrilling and memorable. For fast day boating, stylish marina-hopping, and the occasional overnight adventure, few boats in its class can match the Superhawk’s blend of heritage, handling, and high-octane fun.
If you find one in good condition, it's not just a smart buy—it's a future classic with soul.

title: Earthrace: The Iconic Trimaran That Broke Records and Stood as a Beacon for Eco-Friendly Superboats
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Earthrace: The Iconic Trimaran That Broke Records and Stood as a Beacon for Eco-Friendly Superboats
summary: Unveiling the intriguing saga of Earthrace, the silver 78ft trimaran that not only pushed design boundaries but also set new records.
body: Few boats in recent history have garnered as much attention as Earthrace - a vessel that redefined cool. The 78ft silver trimaran could have been just another eye-candy marine beauty with its sleek, metallic, and futuristic design that likened an alien spaceship. However, it chose a path of action, breaking world records and endorsing environmental conservation.

Initially conceived by New Zealander Pete Bethune, Earthrace was no less than a marvel in the field of marine engineering. Its carbon fibre and Kevlar build, together with its wave-piercing design, were all aimed at achieving speed records while emphasizing green performance. Though the original plan of electric propulsion powered by low-emission generators was later scrapped, the boat was run by marine diesels operating on pure biodiesel, a move aimed to raise awareness of alternative fuels.

A year later, Earthrace, despite all the odds, grabbed victory, marking its return to Sagunto, Spain after a record-breaking journey of just under 61 days on June 27th, 2008. The Earthrace story didn't end here though. Renamed Ady Gil, the boat joined the Sea Shepherd Conservation Society but met with an unfortunate end, sinking after a collision with a Japanese whaling vessel in 2010.

Tales about boats can often become lore whispered among fellow sailors and enthusiasts, very few captivate as Earthrace does. Aiming for speed, championing green performance, and with a strapping resilience through challenges, Earthrace carved its name forever in the annals of motor boats' history.

title: Stepping Out of Shadows: The Reveal of the 101m Masterpiece Feadship Superyacht Project 1014
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Stepping Out of Shadows: The Reveal of the 101m Masterpiece Feadship Superyacht Project 1014
summary: A bold entry to the world of yachting, the colossal 101.2-metre Feadship superyacht Project 1014 has taken its first dip.
body: Emerging from the murky mist of shrouded sheds in Makkum, the Netherlands, the grand Feadship superyacht Project 1014 has finally rippled its way into reality. Since its construction began almost three years ago in 2023, this sea beast had only been sighted a handful of times. The carefully guarded design details, once a tightly sealed secret, lay exposed for the world to admire.

An echo of the design nuances of earlier Feadship builds like Tango, Defy, Sophia, and Faith could be discerned from its uninterrupted exterior lines. However, this nautical wonder unveils some exciting new features. Project 1014 boasts of a generous glass-bottomed pool located on the main aft deck, bathing the beach club situated below in a warm aquatic glow. Dotted with multiple fold-down balconies, the beach club screams luxury. Fancy arriving in style? The prominent helipad on the foredeck has you covered. The top of this mammoth watercraft reveals a forward-facing Jacuzzi accompanying an indoor living area with additional curved windows.

Chiming in at a considerable volume of 3,840GT, the Project 1014 superyacht is accompanied by 17 other yachts currently adorning the Feadship docks. Out of these, the 72-metre Project 719 and the 82.5-metre Project 829 have also caught the eyes of yachting enthusiasts worldwide. With the Feadship superyacht Project 1014 making its inaugural sail, the yachting world awaits in anticipation for the other magnificent creations waiting in line.

title: High-Octane Drama Unfolds at ILCA UK 2026 National Open and Wessex ILCA GP Open
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: High-Octane Drama Unfolds at ILCA UK 2026 National Open and Wessex ILCA GP Open
summary: The suspenseful ILCA UK 2026 National Open and Wessex ILCA Grand Prix Open brought heart-stopping action and tactical brilliance on the waves.
body: The year 2026 debuted a double whammy of sailing action with the ILCA UK National Open co-sponsored by Ovington Boats and the Wessex ILCA Grand Prix Open, both offering a sensational showcase of tactical brilliance and resilience.

The third ILCA UK National Open unfolded on the breezy weekend of March 28-29 at the Weymouth and Portland National Sailing Academy. Seventy-one intrepid ILCA 4 sailors braved cold winds, intense gusts, and sporadic heavy showers. But despite the capricious weather, they remained undaunted to deliver an electric performance.

The first challenge was sea navigation under harsh gusts, which, to the sailors' surprise, swelled up to 40 knots. Bracing against the odds, they set out as scheduled, only to be rapidly called back by the vigilant race committee, leading to the cancellation of Saturday's events.

The inaugural race witnessed skilled manoeuvring with the leaders utilising the anticipated left shift to their advantage. Toby Turner and Thomas Knight seized the spotlight, embroiled in a neck-to-neck fight for victory, with Turner ultimately pipping Knight for the prized first place.

The adrenaline-pumping action continued at the Whitefriars Sailing Club on April 4th, marking the first qualifying event for the Wessex ILCA Grand Prix. Sailing performance reached its zenith during the second race, with the challenging wind speeds allowing sailors to flaunt their skills.
The universe of sailing indeed delivered some edge-of-the-seat racing action, blending intense rivalry with exceptional sportsmanship, offering a tantalising view into the forthcoming season.

title: Inside Look at the Sale of Ourway, the Prominent 37m Explorer Yacht by Tenix Defence
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Inside Look at the Sale of Ourway, the Prominent 37m Explorer Yacht by Tenix Defence
summary: The remarkable 37m exploration yacht, Ourway, sees ownership change in an exclusive in-house sale.
body: The 36.8-metre superyacht known as Ourway has recently made a fabulous transaction. In an in-house trade, Eugenio Cannarsa and Peter Redford of Fraser Australia represented both sides of the deal, lending their expert knowledge of luxury sea vessels. Ourway, an explorer yacht of the highest standard, was constructed by the acclaimed Australian shipyard, Tenix Defence, in 2005. Following a rigorous two-year rebuild completed in 2020, the vessel showcases brand-new systems and an interior makeover to glide into the modern era in style.

Beyond just its stunning aesthetics and amenities, Ourway houses comfortable accommodation presenting an opportunity for excitement-seekers and marine aficionados to dwell in the epitome of luxury. It accommodates 10 guests in its classy cabins, which include a full-beam master suite located on the main deck, one VIP cabin, a double suite, and two twin rooms on the lower deck. All rooms are equipped with en-suite bathrooms and comprehensive entertainment systems with flat-screen televisions. Additionally, the yacht can house up to seven crew members, ensuring top-tier service.

A comprehensive tour of the yacht reveals an array of facilities for recreation and relaxation. It is equipped with a seven-metre beach club, dedicated spaces for fishing, diving, and lounging under the stars, deck areas spread across all levels fortified with zero-speed stabilisers, a hot tub on the sundeck, and an exclusive lounging area with sun loungers. Furthermore, the bridge deck introduces another lounging space adjoining a large dining table. These shared spaces present an incredible opportunity to create unforgettable memories on the high seas.

title: Unravelling the Mystery of Alfa Nero’s Sale: A High Seas Financial Fiasco
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Unravelling the Mystery of Alfa Nero’s Sale: A High Seas Financial Fiasco
summary: The ongoing whirlwind of legal defiance surrounding the sale of the 82-metre superyacht Alfa Nero, continues to unveil new chapters in this multi-million dollar saga.
body: Unfurling like an epic adventure at sea, the ongoing legal controversy surrounding Russian billionaire Andrey Guryev’s superyacht, Alfa Nero, is chock-full of intrigue, high stakes, and international politics. The 82-metre marvel, once gracing the waters, has been caught in a complex legal wrangle that spans multiple jurisdictions and years. Yulia Guryeva-Motlokhov, Guryev's daughter, recently faced rejection from a US federal appeals court in her bid to uncover potentially impacting American banking records.

A series of dramatic events lead to Alfa Nero's predicament. Following multiple futile attempts to track its owner, the vessel was confiscated and considered abandoned by Antiguan authorities after Guryev faced sanctions from the U.S Treasury Department. This was in the aftermath of Russia's scandalous intrusion into Ukraine in 2022. The yacht was eventually auctioned off, changing hands to become the prized possession of Turkish businessman Ali Riza Yildirim.

The escalating maze of lawsuits is far from over, with legal steps being taken across multiple courts. The recent court ruling demands that any acquired documents by Guryeva-Motlokhov’s legal team be discarded, proof of compliance to be submitted. Lawyers acting for the Antiguan Prime Minister are reportedly pondering the recoupment of legal expenses accrued during the appellate process. Even the Prime Minister himself is embroiled in a defamation claim worth $10 million against certain involved entities.

As waves continue to be stirred in this tumultuous legal journey, the facts remain as mysterious and deep as the ocean itself. Irrespective of how legalese unfolds, this complex story serves as a stark reminder that the muddied waters of international politics and law can easily engulf even the most glamorous superyachts.

title: The Ultimate 45‑Foot Cruiser for Comfort & Performance
author: Michael Hodges
imageAlt: Sea Ray Sundancer 455 – The Ultimate 45‑Foot Cruiser for Comfort & Performance
summary: When you’re at sea chasing a blend of performance, luxury and weekend‑to‑extended‑cruise capability, the Sea Ray Sundancer 455 stands out. Measuring roughly 45 feet (13.7 m) in length and boasting amenity‑rich accommodation, this express cruiser ticks all the boxes for an owner‑operator or small family seeking a yacht that works equally well for coastal hops, Mediterranean jaunts or Caribbean getaways.
body: The Sea Ray Sundancer 455 features a beam of approximately 13′2″ (4.27 m) and a draft around 3′4″ (1.02 m) depending on gear selection and loading. With these dimensions, the hull delivers a well‑balanced profile: roomy enough below deck for comfortable living, yet nimble enough for tighter marina berths or quick turn‑around passages. Below deck the accommodation is generous and well thought out. Models from around 2005‑2007 specify two private cabins (a forward master with island berth and an aft guest cabin convertible lounge/berth) plus two heads and show‑casts of ample head‑room. Whether you’re hosting family or friends, the Sundancer 455 offers a genuine “home‑away‑from‑home” feel.

Up top, the cockpit is spacious with lounge seating, convertible sun‑pads, and generous walk‑around deck access. The inclusion of a hydraulic swim platform, in many examples, adds versatility for launching tenders or jet‑skis. tot-nautic.com+1 The helm station boasts good sightlines, comfortable seating and contemporary electronics (in later refits), making docking and manoeuvring a pleasure rather than a chore. Interior glazing is large, the saloon flows into a well‑specified galley outfitted with full‑size fridge/freezer, stove/microwave and abundant storage—a layout meant for more than just afternoon cruises. denisonyachtsales.com+1 On the performance front, while not an all‑out sportboat, the Sundancer 455 holds its own: twin diesel inboards (often Cummins 480‑500hp or similar) enable cruising speeds in the mid‑20s knots and top speeds in the low‑30s knots depending on load. It’s where comfort meets capability.

This yacht is engineered with cruise‑friendly systems. Generator, shore power, air‑conditioning, hydraulic platform, bow thruster and modern navigation fitments are found on many examples. On the water tank and fuel side, figures such as 378 litres fresh water and 1,268 litres fuel for late‑model units underscore its stature as a serious cruiser rather than a weekend toy. The hull construction is GRP, with a deep‑V hull and Deadrise around 18°‑19°, giving a comfortable ride while still maintaining the performance attributes expected of the class. Maintenance access is well considered, engine rooms are service‑friendly, and many broker‑ reviews highlight good build integrity, strong systems and ease of ownership compared to some European rivals. denisonyachtsales.com The result: a boat that works equally for owner operators and for professional use such as charter or corporate hospitality.

The Sundancer 455 is ideally suited for: Couples or families wanting a comfortable, well‑worked cruiser in the 45‑foot range Owners who value both style and substance: pleasing aesthetics, respectable performance, solid build Buyers seeking a good used‑boat value: many quality examples are now available, often well‑maintained Those wanting a platform for coastal cruising, weekend escapes or even low‑to‑medium range passages without sacrificing creature comforts.

Balanced size: manageable for owner‑operators but big enough for comfort Quality accommodation and systems: twin cabins, two heads, full galley Good value in the used market: established reputation Strong performance and build quality

As with any 45‑ft cruiser, maintenance costs (engines, systems, hull) should be fully factored For deeper‑drafting or heavier load configurations top speed/performance may reduce Larger yachts may offer more volume, but at higher cost and complexity Check model‑variant specifications—engine, systems and fit‑out vary significantly by year and option pack.

If you’re looking for a yacht that delivers “weekend‑on‑the‑water” ease and “extended‑cruise” capability in one package, the Sea Ray Sundancer 455 is a compelling proposition. With a quality pedigree, accumulated data on reliability and performance, and an interior layout that genuinely supports live‑aboard comfort or guest hosting, it remains a top choice for savvy yachtsmen. Whether moored in the Med, Caribbean, or cruising locally, the 455 delivers a refined, capable platform—and for many owners that’s the perfect blend.

title: Italian studio SY Design reveals innovative 45-metre yacht concept Anvil, a bold journey through contrasting design language.
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Italian studio SY Design reveals innovative 45-metre yacht concept Anvil, a bold journey through contrasting design language.
summary: SY Design, an Italian yacht design studio, introduces its striking new 45-meter explorer yacht concept, Anvil, a vessel of contrasts delivering innovation and efficiency.
body: Italian studio SY Design has completely reimagined the concept of an explorer yacht with the introduction of the 45-meter Anvil. This daring design exhibits a compact hull, a slightly inverted stern, and at a glance, reveals readable, robust volumes. This heavier design contrasts brilliantly with a distinctly lighter superstructure giving an impression of it floating, a purposeful play on the concept of contrast.

Emphasizing innovation, functionality, and a fresh interpretation of sea life, the Anvil is devised to redefine onboard living for the next generation of yacht owners. The creators prioritize guest experience in their design, as well a focus on operational efficiency by clever layout plans.

Accommodations are offered in four double guest cabins, all conceived with a focus on comfort and privacy. Similarly, the crew area holds four double cabins. Furthermore, the upper deck is dedicated exclusively to the owner, featuring 47 square meters of interior space, a private lounge area, and a generous 50-square-meter private aft deck.

Voicing their design approach, the studio quotes, "When imbalance is intentional, it becomes harmony." This fundamental belief is seen in Anvil's design, exposing a poetic balance amidst highlight contrasts.

Anvil, this extraordinarily daring venture, is not SY Design's first. The Bologna-based studio unveiled a 63-meter superyacht concept, Harmonia, last year, highlighting their dedication to evolving yacht design.

title: Wind-Whisked Weekend: Dollop Claims Victory at VX One Victorian State Titles, Brighton
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Wind-Whisked Weekend: Dollop Claims Victory at VX One Victorian State Titles, Brighton
summary: VX One Victorian State Titles at the Royal Brighton Yacht Club featured a fierce competition and some splendid sailing tactics.
body: The 2026 VX One Victorian State Titles witnessed fierce competition and remarkable sailing suspense at the Royal Brighton Yacht Club. Delivering a varied range of conditions across six races, the event saw visiting teams from interstate ruling the podium.

A robust fleet of 13 boats braced the waters of Port Phillip, with four races crowded on a Saturday that served a fresh, shifty breeze and a tumultuous sea. The following day brought more tranquil conditions, which challenged sailors with their demand for patience, as well as precision.

Among the contenders, Dollop, skippered by Rob Douglass alongside Nicole Douglass and Josh Griffith, admirably demonstrated their ability to balance speed and power, irrespective of the weather's whims. Their intelligent use of winds, superb navigating through difficult waters and consistent performance over the weekend earned them a well-deserved victory with a total score of 10 net points.

From unsettled beginnings, to managing unexpected man overboard event, the team demonstrated resilience and deftly recovered their rhythm. Their clever rig setup and focus on wave work and maintaining speed proved effective.

Rob expressed appreciation for the hospitality of the Royal Brighton Yacht Club and the fierce competition brought by visiting teams. He also recognised the Victorian VX One fleet for their warm welcome and congratulated everyone for a thrilling weekend of sailing.

The team of Dave Alexander, Mitch Young and Harry Shlager of South Australia claimed the second-place spot aboard Gidget. Their persistent performance and strategic navigation kept them in contention throughout the series. The podium was rounded-off by another South Australian team, helmed by Doug Watson aboard the Yaffayat, making for a clean sweep by interstate teams, adding an extra layer of intrigue to the event.

title: Bering Yachts Breaks Ground on Its Flagship B165 Explorer Yacht, Ushering in an Era of Luxury and Exploration
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Bering Yachts Breaks Ground on Its Flagship B165 Explorer Yacht, Ushering in an Era of Luxury and Exploration
summary: Bering Yachts is making waves with the construction of its groundbreaking 49.4-metre B165 explorer yacht, the crown jewel of the shipyard's superyacht division.
body: Renowned Turkish shipyard Bering Yachts is embarking on an exciting voyage of ingenuity as they lay the keel for the first yacht in its flagship 49.4-metre B165 explorer series. This follows the signing of the yacht contract back in January, where Aberton Yachts played a vital role in representing the owner. This monumental yacht, standing as the boldest offering from their new Superyacht division, promises to deliver an impressive 499 Gross Tonnage across its five-deck layout and is expected to exude a grandeur far beyond its actual length.

The stylistic blueprint of the yacht is the result of a noteworthy collaboration with Swiss studio Valentin Design for exterior style, Aberton Yachts for general arrangement, and Turkish studio Eureka Yachts for engineering. A pertinent part of the construction ceremony was placing a coin in the yacht's keel, a customary tradition highlighting the merging of the old with the new.

The B165's breathtaking architecture offers equally impressive highlights on board like the bridge deck. A beacon of relaxation and entertainment, it comes with an indoor-outdoor lounge, sit-up bar, open-air cinema with its own firepit, and a private crow's nest lookout presenting a captivating 360-degree panorama from the hardtop. Balancing performance with comfort, the yacht will be powered by twin 1,300 horsepower Caterpillar engines, ensuring a cruising speed of 10 knots and top speed of 15 knots alongside a range of over 5,000 nautical miles at an economical speed. The yacht will also come fitted with stabilisation systems for maximum comfort both at sea and anchor. The delivery of this engineering marvel is eagerly anticipated for 2029.

title: Gold Medallists Turn to the Cup — But the 49er Still Calls
author: Michael Hodges
imageAlt: Botín & Trittel: From Olympic Gold to America’s Cup and Back Again – The Road to LA 2028
summary: Spain’s Olympic champions Diego Botín and Florian Trittel are charting a bold course toward LA 2028, combining an America’s Cup campaign with their 49er Olympic ambitions in one of sailing’s most demanding dual programmes.
body: Some sailors win. A few dominate. Very few reset the bar — and then decide it still isn’t high enough. That’s where Diego Botín and Florian Trittel now sit.
By the end of 2025, the Spanish duo had completed what most teams spend a lifetime chasing:
Olympic Gold at Paris 2024 Olympics SailGP Season 4 Champions with the Spain SailGP Team 49er World Championship Gold in Cagliari Named World Sailors of the Year
And they didn’t just win — they did it across formats, across boats, across pressure environments. Then, instead of consolidating… they pivoted.

The 49er World Championship victory off Cagliari in October 2025 wasn’t just another line on the CV. It was the last missing piece. What made it more telling was how they did it. After stepping away for nearly a year following Olympic gold, they returned with just two months of focused 49er preparation — and still delivered.
This is not a campaign built on momentum alone. It’s built on systems, understanding and ruthless efficiency.
But rather than double down on dominance, Botín and Trittel have chosen something far harder:
In 2026, the focus shifts sharply.
The pair will join the French America’s Cup programme K-Challenge, stepping into one of the most technically demanding environments in modern sailing.
This isn’t a sideways move.
Heavier boats Foiling at extreme speeds Complex data-driven performance Team structures closer to Formula 1 than traditional sailing
It’s a different discipline entirely — one that forces even Olympic champions back into learning mode. Botín put it plainly:

“The America’s Cup represents an enormous professional challenge and a huge opportunity to grow as sailors.” They’re deliberately stepping outside their comfort zone — because that’s where the next gains are.
Balancing Three Campaigns — Not One
Most elite sailors struggle to manage one Olympic cycle.
High-performance foiling, design integration, and team-based racing.
Technical, tactical, physically demanding — and unforgiving.
Short-format, high-speed racing with the Spain SailGP Team — where decisions are made in seconds, not minutes.
Trittel confirmed the intent clearly:
“Yes, the plan is to keep doing both. Then after the Cup we’ll return fully to the 49er.”
That’s not balance. That’s controlled overload — by design.
The timeline is as aggressive as it is calculated:

2026 Full commitment to America’s Cup development Maintain 49er technical training (without full competition schedule) 2027 Return to 49er competition at the World Championships in Gdynia First Olympic qualification opportunities for LA 2028 Continue America’s Cup campaign through summer Post-Cup 2027 → 2028 Full shift back into Olympic mode Build toward defending gold at LA 2028
Too much Cup focus, and Olympic sharpness fades. Too much 49er racing, and the Cup edge is lost.
They’re walking that line deliberately.
This isn’t just about one team.
It reflects a broader shift in elite sailing:
Cross-discipline performance is becoming the norm Foiling experience is now essential Data, engineering and physical conditioning are converging
Sailors are no longer specialists.
They are becoming multi-platform performance athletes.
Botín captured the mindset:
“Combining both projects will make us better sailors.”
That’s the key point.
Amplification.
Still Hungry — And That’s the Real Story
After everything they’ve already achieved, the easy route would be obvious:
Stay in one lane. Win more. Protect the legacy.
Instead, they’ve chosen risk.
Trittel summed it up: “We’re coming off an incredible run… Now it’s time to evolve and take on new challenges.”
That’s the difference. Because at this level, talent gets you to the top. But it’s the willingness to start again from scratch that keeps you there.
By the time LA 2028 arrives, Botín and Trittel won’t just be Olympic champions returning to defend a title.
They’ll be:
America’s Cup sailors SailGP champions World champions And possibly even more complete athletes than they are today
Which is saying something.
Because right now, they’re already operating at the sharp end of the sport.

title: Wind Prediction Revolutionised: A+T Quantum 530's Innovative Quantum Technology Now Live
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Wind Prediction Revolutionised: A+T Quantum 530's Innovative Quantum Technology Now Live
summary: A+T Instruments presents a superior wind instrument, the Quantum 530, that harnesses quantum entanglement to predict wind direction and strength with startling accuracy.
body: Adventure and innovation come together in the exhilarating world of sailing with A+T Instruments' latest launch, the Quantum 530 - a wind instrument of the future. Embracing a realm of physics that evokes intrigue and mystery, the Quantum 530 exploits quantum entanglement. This phenomenon, referred to as 'spooky' by no less than Albert Einstein, describes an interconnectedness where linked particles, regardless of their distance apart, instantaneously affect each other.

In a dazzling fusion of this phenomenal physics and seafaring, the A+T team, spearheaded by Cambridge mathematician Hugh Agnew, harnessed quantum entanglement to enable sailors to foresee wind shifts with astonishing precision. With their Quantum 530, sailors can now ascertain wind force and direction up to an astounding 60 minutes into the future.

While early knowledge of wind patterns might accelerate sail calls, Agnew believes it won't necessarily ease last-minute hustle on board. After all, the thrill of sailing isn't merely in smooth navigation but also in the camaraderie and the ebullience from shared adventures and challenges.

Nick Cherry, A+T's Technical Sales and Support head, further projects how this concept can revolutionize yacht races by predicting opponents' plan even before they are made. He explains, 'With knowledge of fleet positions and wind shifts way into the future, choosing an upwind lane and planning legs pre-race becomes child's play.'
This invention, with its potential to morph strategy and dynamics of sailing, opens up a brave new world of possibilities and adventures on the high seas.

title: Cobalt Boats
author: Michael Hodges
imageAlt: Cobalt Boats
summary: In the world of luxury day boats, few names carry the prestige and trust that Cobalt Boats does. With a legacy stretching back over five decades, Cobalt has become synonymous with elegant design, high-performance hulls, and impeccable craftsmanship. These are boats built not just to perform, but to last — and to impress.
body: Whether slicing across a glassy lake, carving wakes for a surf session, or anchoring off a beach for a day in the sun, a Cobalt boat feels like a natural extension of a refined lifestyle. It’s where performance meets luxury, where practicality embraces innovation.

Founded in 1968 in Neodesha, Kansas, Cobalt Boats began as a small American builder focused on quality above all. While many competitors chased mass production, Cobalt invested in hand-laid hulls, premium materials, and a small-batch ethos that prioritised finish over volume. That philosophy continues today, and it’s the reason Cobalt owners often speak of their boats in the same breath as luxury cars.

Over the decades, Cobalt’s commitment to premium craftsmanship helped it stand apart. Every hull, stringer, and liner is bonded with precision. Stainless steel fittings are hand-polished. Upholstery is double-stitched. Electrical systems are neatly bundled, labelled, and routed with redundancy in mind. It’s not just for show — it’s for longevity, reliability, and resale value.

In 2017, Cobalt was acquired by Malibu Boats, bringing together two performance powerhouses. Yet, Cobalt retains its distinct identity and commitment to craftsmanship, operating as a semi-autonomous luxury division with its own design and production DNA.
Cobalt’s reputation isn’t built on gimmicks — it’s built on getting the fundamentals exactly right. Their boats offer:
Deep-V hulls for a smoother, drier ride
Kevlar-reinforced construction
Composite transoms (no rot, ever)
Noise-insulated engine bays
Thick gelcoat and superior finish detailing
A patented flip-down swim step, now a hallmark of the brand

The fit and finish inside a Cobalt boat rivals luxury automobiles. Expect leather-textured vinyl, stainless cupholders, hand-stitched upholstery, and responsive helm stations with digital controls and touchscreen displays.
While other builders mass-produce cookie-cutter models, Cobalt’s focus is on refined details: backlit switches, thoughtful storage, convertible seating, and polished metalwork that lasts for decades.

Cobalt builds boats ranging from 20 to 40 feet, spread across several purpose-driven lines. Whether you're looking for a ski-friendly bowrider, a luxurious surf boat, or a performance cruiser, there’s a Cobalt designed for it.
This is Cobalt’s flagship line. Think performance dayboats with open seating, luxurious appointments, and room for 10–15 passengers depending on model.
R4, R6, R8: Popular choices from 24 to 27 feet, ideal for lakes and coastal day cruising
R30, R33, R35: Larger models with twin engines, joystick control, and hardtop options
All offer massive storage, plush interiors, and head-turning lines.
Cobalt’s most luxurious range, ideal for buyers seeking high-end styling, overnighting capability, and massive cockpits.
A29: A crossover dayboat-cruiser with deep seating and a large head
A36/A36BR: Hardtop-equipped, twin-powered express boats with full galley options and joystick controls
A40 Coupe (retired): Once Cobalt’s flagship, now a collector’s gem
This series competes with brands like Formula, Sea Ray SLX, and Regal’s flagship Sport Coupe line.
Using Volvo Forward Drive or MerCruiser Bravo Four S, these boats combine the elegance of a Cobalt with a full ballast system, wake tabs, and surf-specific hull tweaks.
CS23 Surf: Entry-level surf boat with luxury fittings
R6 Surf / R8 Surf: Larger models that accommodate serious watersports without sacrificing cruising comfort
Perfect for boaters who want to surf all day and dine onboard in the evening.
More affordable without compromising quality, these are the smallest boats in the Cobalt range (CS22 and CS23), yet still feature:
Full Cobalt hull lamination
Premium seating and layout
Classic deep-V performance
Ideal for first-time buyers or lake house owners.

Cobalt boats are designed for ease of use, soft landings, and tight handling. The deep-V hull cuts cleanly through chop, while heavy construction keeps the ride stable and quiet. Joystick docking and digital throttle controls are available on most twin-engine models, as is Active Trim, GPS speed control, and surf assist tech.
These aren’t hulls designed for racing — they’re made for confident, composed cruising with plenty of power on tap.
Cobalt boats have a fiercely loyal following. Ask an owner what they love, and you’ll hear:
“It feels solid in any conditions.”
“Everything is just beautifully built.”
“I still get compliments at the dock after 10 years.”
Add to that:
Excellent resale value
Supportive dealer network
Long-lasting finishes and materials
Quiet ride thanks to hull insulation and thick laminates
Cobalts are premium boats, and their price reflects that. They typically cost more than competitors of similar size, especially new. You’re paying for:
Better materials
Superior build quality
Exclusive features
If you need cabin space or offshore range, Cobalt may not be the best fit — these boats are day-oriented luxury cruisers. But for lake and coastal performance, they’re among the best money can buy.

In a world of over-branded and under built boats, Cobalt remains a beacon of uncompromising quality. With more than 55 years of experience, this American builder continues to lead the way in crafting dayboats that not only perform beautifully, but also age with grace.
From the smallest CS to the flagship A36, every Cobalt boat is an expression of refined adventure — elegant, fast, solid underfoot, and always a joy to drive.
For those who appreciate the finer things in life — and want their time on the water to reflect that — Cobalt Boats is a brand that never disappoints.

title: Galeon 410 HTC - Review
author: Michael Hodges
imageAlt: Galeon 410 HTC - Review
summary: Galeon 410 HTC – Sleek Innovation Meets Practical Luxury In a market awash with 40-foot cruisers, few stand out quite like the Galeon 410 HTC. Built by the award-winning Polish shipyard Galeon Yachts—renowned for pushing the boundaries of design and engineering—the 410 HTC is a hardtop coupe that blends sporty styling with revolutionary features. She’s the hardtop sister to the Galeon 400 Fly, and while she trades th
body: This yacht is not just about form—it’s function, finesse, and a firm step forward in what boaters can expect from a sub-45-foot cruiser.

From the moment you lay eyes on the 410 HTC, you get a sense that this boat isn’t content to blend in. The aggressive silhouette, sweeping roofline, and gleaming hull windows all point to a yacht with performance on its mind. It’s coupe-style done with flair, and the absence of a flybridge lowers the centre of gravity and enhances the sleek, streamlined look.
At 41 feet 6 inches overall, and with a generous beam of nearly 13 feet, the 410 HTC has real presence, both in the marina and out on open water. She looks fast, even at anchor—and she is.

But one of the real party tricks of this model is Galeon’s now-iconic "Beach Mode": fold-down side balconies that transform the cockpit into a terrace-like space right over the sea. When deployed, they dramatically expand the beam and open up entirely new ways to enjoy a quiet anchorage or lively sunset gathering.

The cockpit layout is pure genius for entertaining. The aft bench seating flows into an L-shape, centred around a foldable teak table. Sliding glass doors connect the cockpit with the interior salon, creating a seamless indoor/outdoor experience. With the doors open and the hardtop sunroof retracted, the entire upper deck becomes an open-air haven.

The hydraulic swim platform (optional) makes water access effortless, and there’s space for a tender or jet ski. Wide, secure walkways lead to a spacious foredeck, complete with a sunpad and adjustable backrests—perfect for lounging underway or catching some rays dockside.

Step inside and you’re greeted by a bright, airy salon with panoramic glazing and rich woodwork that would be at home in a far larger yacht. The contemporary styling, neutral tones, and subtle LED lighting give the entire space a refined, upmarket feel. The electric sunroof in the hardtop bathes the area in natural light and lets in fresh air with the push of a button.

The aft galley, located just inside the cockpit doors, is well-positioned for serving both indoor and outdoor guests. It includes a ceramic cooktop, stainless steel sink, microwave, and fridge, with ample storage for a weekend away.

Forward in the salon is a comfortable U-shaped settee and dining area, opposite a pop-up television. Whether you’re enjoying breakfast with a view or watching a film at anchor, the layout adapts to every mood.

Below decks, the Galeon 410 HTC continues to impress. The full-beam owner’s stateroom amidships is a private retreat, with a queen-size berth, full-height wardrobe, settee, and large hull windows that flood the space with light. The en suite head features a separate walk-in shower—a luxury touch rarely seen on a boat this size.

The VIP cabin in the bow features an island double berth, hanging lockers, and direct access to the second head, which can serve as an en suite or day head. Both cabins are beautifully finished, with quality materials, excellent lighting, and whisper-quiet air conditioning (optional).

Under the surface, the 410 HTC is more than just a pretty face. Powered by twin Volvo Penta D4 or D6 engines, either sterndrives or IPS pods depending on configuration, the boat delivers responsive handling and solid fuel economy. With twin D6-440s, the 410 HTC can hit speeds around 32–35 knots, while cruising comfortably in the 22–26 knot range.
Joystick docking systems and optional bow/stern thrusters make manoeuvring in tight marinas surprisingly easy, even for less experienced skippers or short-handed crews.

Handling is confident and smooth, thanks in part to the boat’s lower profile and weight distribution. She's fun to drive—a rarity in this class where many cruisers feel more like floating condos than agile boats.
Beach Mode fold-out balconies for expanded entertaining space
Electric sunroof brings in air and light without compromising weather protection
Hydraulic swim platform for easy tender launching and sea access
Two separate heads with showers, a rare feature for a boat under 45'
Modern Euro-style interior with premium finishes
Seamless indoor-outdoor layout ideal for entertaining
Length Overall (LOA): 41'6" (12.5 m)
Fuel Capacity: 251 gallons (950 litres)
Water Capacity: 119 gallons (450 litres)
Cabins: 2
Heads: 2
Engines: Twin Volvo Penta D4 or D6 (up to 600+ HP total)
Top Speed: ~35 knots (with D6 engines)
Cruise Speed: ~22–26 knots

The Galeon 410 HTC stands out with its crisp lines, raked windshield, and low-profile hardtop. The absence of a flybridge means the centre of gravity is lower, improving handling and stability while maintaining excellent visibility from the helm.

One of the hallmark features of this model is the “Beach Mode” folding side balconies—an innovation that Galeon pioneered in this size category. With the push of a button, port and starboard sides of the cockpit fold down to dramatically expand the usable deck area, creating a terrace-on-the-sea effect that’s perfect for relaxing at anchor or entertaining guests.
Other standout exterior features include:
Wide walkaround side decks with high rails
Foredeck sunpad with reclining backrests
Hydraulic swim platform (optional)
Aft cockpit with L-shaped seating and fold-out table
Large sliding glass doors that connect the salon and cockpit

Inside, the 410 HTC boasts a bright and stylish salon with panoramic glass, natural wood finishes, and ultra-modern furnishings. The hardtop features an electric sunroof, giving you open-air cruising at the touch of a button. The salon includes:
Comfortable U-shaped settee
Fold-out dining table
Entertainment centre with TV and audio system
Galley positioned aft (starboard side), with fridge, stove, microwave, sink, and storage
Thanks to the open galley and salon configuration, guests can move freely between the cockpit and salon, making this yacht highly social and well-suited to warm-weather cruising.
Below deck, the Galeon 410 HTC features a two-cabin, two-head layout, with standout luxury for a yacht of this size:
Owner’s Stateroom (Midship): Full-beam with large hull windows, a queen-sized berth, sofa, storage, and en suite head with separate shower
VIP Cabin (Forward): Island double berth, hanging lockers, and direct access to a second head (shared or en suite depending on configuration)
Optional layouts allow for more customisation—such as adding a utility room or crew space, depending on the needs of the owner.

The Galeon 410 HTC is available with twin Volvo Penta sterndrive or IPS diesel engines (most commonly D4-300 or D6-440), offering responsive acceleration, excellent maneuverability, and joystick docking.
Top Speed: Around 32–35 knots with twin D6s
Cruise Speed: 22–26 knots
Fuel Consumption: ~30–40 GPH at cruising speed (depending on engine choice)
Optional joystick control and bow/stern thrusters make this boat easy to handle even for short-handed crews or less experienced skippers.
Beach Mode balconies extend beam for lounging or water access
Electric sunroof for convertible-style cruising
High-end interiors with contemporary Euro styling
Luxurious two-cabin layout with separate showers
Great performance with twin diesels and joystick controls
The Galeon 410 HTC is ideal for:
Couples or families looking for a sub-45-foot cruiser with yacht-like quality
Owners who prefer a coupe-style boat over a flybridge
Entertainers who love open-air social zones and innovative design
Boaters who want cutting-edge European styling, but with practical performance and reliability

The Galeon 410 HTC is a masterclass in maximising space, innovation, and luxury within a compact cruiser footprint. It offers many of the perks you’d expect on a 50-footer—folding terraces, two full heads, gourmet galley, hydraulic platform—wrapped in a sleek, manageable package that’s perfect for couples or small families. For those who don’t need a flybridge and prefer the feel of a sports coupe with serious substance, the 410 HTC is hard to beat. Whether you’re day-tripping, island-hopping, or spending long weekends onboard, this yacht invites you to enjoy every inch—and every moment.

title: Unveiling the Captivating World of Yachting: A Comprehensive Review of March 2026's Noteworthy Stories
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Unveiling the Captivating World of Yachting: A Comprehensive Review of March 2026's Noteworthy Stories
summary: Allow us to navigate you through the fascinating realm of yachting. From new launches to intriguing court cases and unexpected yacht lovers, we delve into March 2026's biggest stories.

Secondly, it seems that professional tennis players have a soft corner for the high seas. Spanish tennis ace Carlos Alcaraz, who graces the top spot in men's singles, didn't just settle for a yacht – he placed an order for a first-class 26.8-metre Sunreef Ultima 88 catamaran from the unbeatable Polish yard Sunreef Yachts. The final noteworthy bit of news came from Lürssen, the German shipyard. Sharing images of the 102.4-metre Jassj and successfully delivering the 78 metre superyacht Odisea, Lürssen further asserted its dominant presence in the yachting industry. These stories encapsulate the frantic pace at which the yachting world ebbs and flows.

title: Sunseeker Manhattan 52 - Flybridge
author: Michael Hodges
imageAlt: Sunseeker Manhattan 52 - Flybridge
summary: Sunseeker Manhattan 52 – Big-Boat Living Without the Big-Boat Hassle For years, Sunseeker has been the go-to badge for those who want more than just a motor yacht — they want a head-turning piece of floating architecture. The Manhattan 52 sits right at the sweet spot of the range, offering serious cruising comfort, flybridge living, and the unmistakable Sunseeker swagger, but without tipping into the size bracket tha
body: Launched in 2016, the Manhattan 52 replaced the outgoing Manhattan 50, and from the first show unveiling it was clear this wasn’t just an incremental update. Sunseeker’s design team went all in on open-plan living, a brighter interior, and flybridge space that would make some 60-footers blush.

From the dockside, the Manhattan 52 commands attention. The sheer line sweeps forward into a proud bow, and the profile is punctuated by elongated hull windows that flood the interior with natural light. Stainless steel detailing, sculpted hardtop supports, and Sunseeker’s signature black glazing all contribute to the upscale, almost automotive styling.

At 56 ft 6 in overall with a beam of 16 feet, she feels broad and confident in stance. The swim platform is hydraulic as standard, doubling as a launch pad for the tender or a private beach when you’re at anchor.

Climb the molded steps to the flybridge and you’ll find yourself on the yacht’s social stage. To port is an L-shaped dining area with a folding teak table, opposite a wet bar complete with sink, fridge, and optional grill. Forward are twin helm seats with full engine controls, and ahead of that, a forward sunpad big enough for a couple to stretch out without elbow wars.

The flybridge can be left open to the sun or fitted with a Bimini or even a sleek hardtop for shade. Either way, the 360-degree views make this the place to be when cruising between headlands or nosing into a new harbour.

One of the cleverest tricks in the Manhattan 52’s bag is the way Sunseeker has blurred the lines between inside and out. Sliding glass doors open from the aft cockpit straight into the galley, with a breakfast bar acting as the hand-off point between the two spaces. This means the chef — whether it’s you or a hired hand — stays in the conversation with guests in the cockpit.

The cockpit itself has aft bench seating, space for freestanding chairs, and is shaded by the flybridge overhang. Side decks are wide and well-guarded, leading to the foredeck sunpad, another lounging option when you want the breeze on your face.

Step inside and the first impression is light. Sunseeker’s designers ditched the heavy woods and darker tones of earlier models in favour of pale oak finishes, high-gloss lacquered surfaces, and soft fabrics. The saloon has a U-shaped seating area to starboard and a love seat opposite, with a folding dining table that can transform the space from cocktail lounge to dinner venue.

Forward, the lower helm has twin seats, excellent sightlines, and the kind of intuitive console layout that makes long passages less tiring. Large, one-piece windscreen glass ensures the skipper can see exactly where the bow is pointing, even in tricky crosswinds.

Below deck, the Manhattan 52 offers a full-beam master stateroom amidships, with hull-side windows that turn the waterline view into living art. There’s a vanity/desk, settee, and a generous en suite with separate shower. Forward, the VIP cabin has an island berth and private access to the day head. A twin-berth guest cabin sits to starboard, perfect for kids or occasional guests.
An optional crew cabin is tucked aft with its own head and shower — fine for short stays or for storing gear, but not intended for long-term crew living.

Power comes from twin Volvo Penta D11-725 diesel engines, giving a top speed of around 31 knots and a comfortable cruise in the 21–24 knot range. At cruising speed, the Manhattan 52 tracks straight and feels solid underfoot, a testament to Sunseeker’s deep-V hull form and resin-infused construction.

Bow and stern thrusters are standard, making close-quarters handling straightforward. For those who want fingertip control, joystick docking can be specified. The ride is quiet too, with sound insulation keeping conversation levels civilised even at higher revs.
Ask a Manhattan 52 owner what they like, and you’ll hear:
Spacious flybridge that feels like it belongs on a bigger yacht
Light-filled salon with genuine connection to the cockpit
Full-beam master cabin comfort
Manageable size for an owner-operator
Sunseeker’s brand cachet and build quality

For family cruising, the layout works beautifully. Kids can be in the guest cabin or sprawled on the flybridge, friends can take the VIP forward, and everyone has space to relax without tripping over each other.
No yacht is without compromise. On the Manhattan 52:
Galley storage is limited if you plan multi-week live-aboard trips
Crew cabin is best for occasional use
Premium pricing reflects brand and finish — you’ll pay more than some rivals of similar length
Flybridge stairs slightly pinch cockpit space
The Sunseeker Manhattan 52 is perfect for:
Couples or families moving up from a 45–50-footer, wanting more comfort without losing self-sufficiency
Entertainers who value open-plan layouts and multiple outdoor lounging zones
Style-minded buyers who want a flybridge yacht that will turn heads in any marina
Those who split time between day cruising, weekend getaways, and longer coastal runs

The Sunseeker Manhattan 52 hits a rare balance: big-boat luxury in a size you can still handle yourself. From the open-plan galley and salon to the expansive flybridge and the calm, composed ride, she feels like a yacht designed by people who actually use them.

Yes, you’ll pay for the Sunseeker name and the premium materials, but what you get is more than just a boat — it’s an experience. One that invites you to linger on the flybridge as the sun drops behind the breakwater, knowing that tomorrow’s run will be just as enjoyable as today’s.

title: Dicing with Death: A Yacht Worker's Close Call with Asphyxiation and Lessons in Maritime Safety
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Dicing with Death: A Yacht Worker's Close Call with Asphyxiation and Lessons in Maritime Safety
summary: When a casual day on a superyacht refit nearly turned deadly, it taught an invaluable lesson on maritime safety and vigilance.
body: Chronicling a day that almost ended in disaster, this is the tale of a crew member working on a superyacht refit. Responsibilities included cleaning and painting the engine room bilges, a task that brought him face to face with a potentially life-threatening situation. Deep inside the six-foot-deep main bilge sump, oblivious to the surrounding crew, he used acetone to degrease the surfaces. Unaware that acetone expands to over 300% its initial volume and is denser than air, the man unwittingly jeopardized his survival as the oxygen around him got rapidly displaced.

The incident has drawn attention to the fact that enclosed bilges present significant health and safety risks, as laid out in the CoSWP Section 15, MGN 659, and MSC A.1050(27). It's crucial for vessels to precisely identify and record all confined spaces onboard, ensuring this data reflects in the Safety Management System and risk assessments. The accident further emphasizes that VOC masks may provide a false sense of security and are not suited for certain hazards. They are protective against certain substances but can't supply oxygen or detect its depletion.

The story underscores the dangers of common solvents, which can rapidly deplete oxygen in confined or poorly ventilated spaces due to their higher vapour density. Activities like bilge cleaning may pose severe risks if performed without proper ventilation, atmospheric monitoring, and safety precautions – a lesson that the protagonist took away, and should be kept in mind by everyone in the maritime industry.

title: Jason Carroll’s Argo Resets the Antigua 360 Benchmark Ahead of the RORC Caribbean 600
author: Michael Hodges
imageAlt: Argo Unleashed: MOD70 Smashes Antigua 360 Record in 2 Hours 29 Minutes
summary: Argo Unleashed Around Antigua The lap that every Caribbean multihull crew measures themselves against just got faster. The Antigua 360 Race, organised by the Royal Ocean Racing Club in partnership with the Antigua Yacht Club, now has a new outright benchmark.
body: Jason Carroll’s MOD70 Argo stormed around the 48-nautical-mile circumnavigation in 2 hours, 29 minutes and 20 seconds, rewriting what is possible on Antigua’s classic coastal course.
The numbers tell one story. The breeze told another.

With 20 knots at the start and proper Atlantic swell wrapping the eastern flank of Antigua, the island delivered a course that was anything but flat water exhibition sailing. This was full trade-wind pressure, the kind that loads up the rig and punishes hesitation.

“It was a beautiful day for sailing and a fantastic lap around Antigua,” said owner-driver Jason Carroll. “We chose one reef at the start, which felt right. We sailed it relatively conservatively, didn’t leave much out there. One bad tack where we ended up in irons probably cost us a minute — but otherwise it was smooth all the way.”
Smooth, at 30-plus knots.
Lighting It Up at Green Island
Every MOD70 crew knows the moment the Antigua 360 truly begins. You round Green Island, bear away, and the boat transforms.
Sam Goodchild, on board for the record run and lining up again for the RORC Caribbean 600, described it plainly:

“It really comes alive once you turn at Green Island and light it up on the reach. You’re straight into proper trade-wind sailing, touching the mid-30s. That’s where preparation and precision matter.”

At those speeds, the margin for error disappears. Manoeuvres must be clean. Communication constant. Other boats close distance at alarming rates. Spray blasts through the nets and the helmsman is reading waves at motorway velocity.
Goodchild is clear about what the 360 provides:
“There are far more ways to lose a race than to win one. These days before the 600 are about detail. Getting the boat 100 percent. Getting the team dialled in.”
Zoulou Joins the Fight

MOD70 rivalry rarely lacks drama, and Final Final – Zoulou made sure of that. Skippered by Jon Desmond, Zoulou crossed the line just 18 minutes and 19 seconds after Argo — hardly distant in a race this short and this fast.
“That was unbelievable. 20 knots, big waves, proper pressure. First time lining up against Argo in a MOD70 — adrenaline was high.”
He described the defining moment familiar to all multihull sailors:
“Once you crack off and the big gennaker goes up, the boat just lights up. We saw 36 knots at times. They feel incredibly powerful, but stiff and controlled.”
That stiffness — the ability to push hard without the boat feeling loose — is what makes the MOD70 platform such a weapon in Caribbean conditions.
For Zoulou, the 360 was more than a record attempt. It was the first full test of race manoeuvres, angles and teamwork ahead of Monday’s main event.
Argo’s new elapsed time of 2:29:20 does more than sit in the record books. It resets expectations.

The Antigua 360 has long been regarded as a sharp, technical, high-speed island circuit. But this year’s conditions — mid-teens to 20 knots, Atlantic chop on the east side, flat acceleration on the leeward legs — created a course that demanded both aggression and restraint.
Carroll was candid about the balance:
“It’s great to be back with the boys pushing hard again. Now we’ve got a couple of days to cool our heels, fine-tune things and get ready.”
That readiness matters. Because the 360 is only the prelude.
Eyes on the Caribbean 600
With the course record shattered and the MOD70 rivalry fully engaged, attention turns to the 600-mile offshore test starting 23 February.

If the Antigua 360 was a dress rehearsal, the RORC Caribbean 600 will be the full production: longer legs, darker nights, routing decisions around Guadeloupe and Barbuda, and sustained trade-wind power.
Argo is quick. Zoulou is close. The trade winds are set.
And in the Caribbean, speed rarely goes unchallenged.
Salt in the air. Mid-30s on the dial.
