Low brings deep experience: an Olympic campaign at Tokyo 2020, where she and Kimberly Lim became the first Singaporean sailors to qualify for an Olympic medal race, plus an Asian Games gold medal and multiple World Cup appearances. The new partnership has been years in the making, and both sailors are already eyeing major regional targets as the long LA 2028 road begins.
Her return adds maturity and momentum to a fleet that continues to deepen in both quality and global reach.

After five intense years together, Lara Granier and Amélie Riou have formally closed their Olympic campaign. Following a narrow miss on Paris selection and a period of reflection after Cagliari, the pair chose to end a project defined by growth, resilience and shared highs on and off the water.

But endings in this fleet are rarely final. Riou is already back on the start line, forming a new partnership with Manon Peyre. With the 49erFX World Championship in Quiberon in May as their first major milestone, the focus is firmly on building foundations—fast.

Early-cycle movement continues in the multihull fleet. Sarah Newberry-Moore has announced a new Nacra 17 partnership with Hoël Menard, officially launching their LA 2028 campaign. Training is already underway, underlining just how quickly new combinations are forming across the class.
Oceanbridge Sail Auckland Regatta: early signals

The Oceanbridge Sail Auckland Regatta delivered strong international racing across the 49er fleet. Overall victory went to Seb Menzies and George Lee Rush, with Swiss Olympians and SailGP sailors Sebastian Schneiter and Arno De Planta second. Mattias Coutts and Oscar Gunn completed the podium, while Americans Nevin Snow and Ian Macdiarmid placed fourth.
All are expected back on the line for the New Zealand 49er Nationals, before heading to the Trofeo Princesa Sofia in Palma this March—one of the first true measuring sticks of the new cycle.

And finally, a name that always draws attention. Ruggero Tita has been dropping hints about a potential return to the Nacra 17. Nothing official—yet. But in a fleet where combinations shift quickly and ambition never rests, the sailing world is watching closely to see what shape that next move might take.

title: 2026 Puts Superyacht Giants on Display at the Grand Palm Beach International Boat Show
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: 2026 Puts Superyacht Giants on Display at the Grand Palm Beach International Boat Show
summary: Superyacht enthusiasts, buckle up for a thrilling showcase of opulent yachts at the 2026 Palm Beach International Boat Show.
body: The arrival of spring in March 2026 will usher in the annual Palm Beach International Boat Show (PBIBS), a nautical extravaganza, drawing yacht owners, industry cognoscenti, and aficionados towards the radiant shores of Palm Beach. Striking a chord with seasoned yachting enthusiasts, this year will see some of the most magnificent yachts offering a lavish spectacle on the azure waters. Let's dive into the splendour of the show's headliners.

The 74-metre Amels creation, Casino Royale, stands out as a crown jewel in the Amels Limited Editions Series. Its striking Tim Heywood exterior and Winch Design interior configurations present an enchanting vision. Offering luxe accommodation for 12 guests, it features a dedicated owner's deck complete with a foredeck Jacuzzi. The main deck aft transforms into a 180-square-metre party haven boasting a dance floor, bar, and a ritzy 6.5-metre infinity pool.

Finally, last year's revelation, the Amor à Vida, is set to beguile attendees yet again. This 67.6-metre work of art is the brainchild of CRN and Nuvolari Lenard. Six decks sheathed in expansive glass panels, a compact, burly profile, and sumptuous interior stylings create an airy, modern sanctuary on the sea. This catwalk of the Palm Beach International Boat Show in March 2026 promises to be a captivating spectacle, offering up a delicious blend of high-class luxury and crafted elegance.

title: Anticipation Builds as Two-Handed Powerhouses Rejoin the Fray at Pittwater to Coffs Harbour Yacht Race
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Anticipation Builds as Two-Handed Powerhouses Rejoin the Fray at Pittwater to Coffs Harbour Yacht Race
summary: The illustrious Pittwater to Coffs Harbour Yacht Race prepares to welcome back notable two-handers, assuring an exciting competition.
body: The 40th edition of the Pittwater to Coffs Harbour Yacht Race is bracing for an enthralling contest. Pre-eminent among the entrants are the celebrated two-handers, including the 2023 champion and runner-up, poised to rival again for the coveted trophy. Their ambition? Mastery of the 226 nautical mile classic.

Australia's perhaps most acclaimed two-hander, Rupert Henry, is set to resume his winning ways aboard his Lombard 34, Mistral, co-commanding with Greg O'Shea. This duo's triumph in 2023 was echoed by their commendable performance in the Rolex Sydney Hobart in the same year, placing sixth overall, succumbing only to fully-crewed yachts considerably larger than their own - a testament to their prowess and determination.

In preparation, Henry has been racing an ILCA 7 and plans to participate in the ILCA Masters Worlds in Greece come June. With his eyes set on the Route du Rhum, sailing single-handed events in Europe is on his itinerary.

Recalling their 2023 encounter, Henry shared their close victory over Disko Trooper Contender Sailcloth in largely unpredictable light conditions. Jules Hall, owner of the J/99 and co-skipper of Jan Scholten, who paralleled Mistral throughout the remarkable race and triumphed in the ORC division, seeks a rematch with Mistral this year with his new partner, Alex Knight.
As the heavyweights prepare to sail once again, anticipation builds for an enthralling face-off in the high seas.

title: Turkish Shipyard FDC Yachts Reveals Details of Their Stunning New Pocket Superyacht: Project Umai
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Turkish Shipyard FDC Yachts Reveals Details of Their Stunning New Pocket Superyacht: Project Umai
summary: FDC Yachts gives an exciting glimpse at its newest 26-metre 'pocket superyacht', the in-build Project Umai set for 2027.
body: FDC Yachts, a renowned Turkish shipyard, has recently released details of its latest customised pocket superyacht, known as ‘Project Umai.’ The 26-metre hull has already begun to take shape at the shipyard's facilities in Bodrum and is expected to be completed by May 2027. The 'Project Umai' superyacht combines steel hull and aluminium superstructure, a classic creation stemming from the effort of FDC's talented design team in tandem with FORM Yacht Design.

The new vessel reportedly embodies the essence of 'modern classic' Mediterranean design. It flawlessly marries extravagant external dimensions with contemporary onboard comfort, making it a testament to the shipbuilder's aesthetic sensibility and functional design.

One of the distinct features of this yacht is the inclusion of a silent mode option, aimed at significantly mitigating noise and vibration while at anchor, ensuring peaceful seafaring experience for the onboard guests. As for performance, 'Project Umai' is projected to reach a maximum speed of 14 knots and a cruising speed of 11 knots spanning a range of 2,500 nautical miles.

FDC Yachts asserts that Project Umai exemplifies their quality commitment, reflecting robust engineering, elegant exterior styling, and highly customisable interiors that cater to modern yachting lifestyles. This superyacht is a superb blend of long-range capability and refined Mediterranean-inspired living spaces, in a vivid demonstration of FDC Yachts' vision and expertise.

title: Kickstarting the 2026 Circuit: Trofeo Princesa Sofia Serves as Launch Pad for Olympic Sailing Season
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Kickstarting the 2026 Circuit: Trofeo Princesa Sofia Serves as Launch Pad for Olympic Sailing Season
summary: The Olympic sailing season of 2026 is set to launch with the 54th Trofeo Princesa Sofia, testing innovative changes from World Sailing.
body: The divine ballet of sails at the Trofeo Princesa Sofia is a sight to behold, the festival of yachting serving as the inaugural event for the Sailing Grand Slam of 2026. Hosted at the sublime Bay of Palma, this contest ushers in the sailing season with the sweet crescendo of competition, as the globe's finest sailors jostle for laurels. The event embarks on March 27, set to last till April 4, gathering the crème de la crème of the world's sailing elite.

Trofeo Princesa Sofia marks a significant milestone for sailing, with the debut of the mixed-crew format back in Rio 2016. From one event in Rio 2016 to a pair of mixed-crew events in Paris 2024, this pioneering shift full of promise will have its second instance in Los Angeles 2028, a testament to its success and popularity. This evolutionary shift in the composition of sailing teams brings together the finest talents of both genders on the same vessel, promising a rich blend of perspectives and skills.

Cutting a swath through the ranks of mixed-crew sailing is the Nacra 17, famously known as the 'Mixed Multihull'. Since replacing the Tornado Catamaran in Rio 2016, the Nacra 17 has encapsulated the spirit of mixed crew sailing. With its subsequent induction of foils in the Tokyo 2020 cycle, the Nacra 17 flew high into the exclusive fraternity of flying boats, propelling a revolution in sailing tournaments.

As these sailing emissaries set their sights on the azure horizon of the Trofeo Princesa Sofia, the anticipation crescendos. From John Gimson and Anna Burnet, the current world champions and defending champions to Joan Cardona and Nicole Van der Velden, new entrants with promising potential - the stage at the Trofeo Princesa Sofia 2026 is set for a thrilling show of exceptional sailing talent and high-seas drama.

title: Genova Becomes a Global Hub for Ocean Action as The Ocean Race Returns to Italy
author: Michael Hodges
imageAlt: Genova Takes Centre Stage as The Ocean Race Ignites a Week of Ocean Action
imageCredit: © © Jean-Louis Carli / The Ocean Race Europe 2025
summary: From powerful storytelling to youth-led dialogue and education, The Ocean Race will transform Genova into a focal point for ocean action during an inspiring week of events ran from 26–30 January 2026. Blending culture, science, education and advocacy, the programme brings together world-renowned voices, emerging leaders and local communities — reinforcing the Race’s belief that elite sport can be a catalyst for real-
body: At the heart of the week are three major Ocean Health initiatives, each designed to inform, inspire and mobilise the next generation. Together, they form part of Racing for the Ocean, The Ocean Race’s long-term commitment to protecting and restoring ocean health by combining competition with science, education and policy engagement.
A city awakened to the ocean challenge

Throughout the week, Genova will host a series of events that move far beyond the dockside. From the cinematic power of David Attenborough’s storytelling to direct conversations between young ocean advocates and global decision-makers, the programme reflects a growing understanding: the future of the ocean will be shaped as much in classrooms, council chambers and cultural institutions as it will on the water.
By bringing these conversations into the heart of the city, The Ocean Race is positioning Genova not just as a maritime capital, but as a place where ideas, leadership and action converge.
The Ocean Race Summit Genova: Nudging the New Ocean Society
On Wednesday 28 January, attention turned firmly toward the future with The Ocean Race Summit Genova: Nudging the New Ocean Society, hosted from 11:00–14:00 at the iconic Palazzo Ducale.

The Summit is hosted by actress and environmental advocate Bailey Bass, and brings together an intentionally diverse mix of young ocean leaders and experienced global figures — including sailors, scientists, entrepreneurs and policymakers.
This is not a traditional conference. Instead of one-way speeches, the Summit is built around participative, two-way dialogue, creating space for generations and disciplines to meet on equal terms.
Keynote speaker Mariasole Bianco, marine scientist, communicator and President of Worldrise, will open the session with a vision for a healthier, more sustainable ocean. Panel contributors include:
Francesca Santoro, Senior Programme Officer, IOC-UNESCO
Elisabetta Balzi, European Commission DG Research & Innovation
Manon Peyre, Junior World Champion and Ocean Race sailor
Adélaïde Charlier, climate activist

Through mirrored sessions, local and international youth voices will engage directly with established leaders to explore how collaboration, innovation and fresh thinking can help shape a healthier ocean and a more sustainable ocean economy. The emphasis is firmly on practical pathways — ensuring that ideas discussed translate into real-world policy influence and action.
Empowering the next generation: the first Generation Ocean Symposium
The week culminates with a landmark moment for The Ocean Race’s education programme: the first-ever Generation Ocean Symposium, hosted at Deledda International School.

Organised in collaboration with Target4Green’s Beyond COP21 Symposium series, the full-day event immerses students and educators in ocean literacy, climate action and youth leadership. Through interactive workshops, STEAM-based learning, futures thinking and hands-on activities, participants will explore how classroom knowledge connects directly to some of the planet’s most urgent environmental challenges.

True to the spirit of Racing for the Ocean, the symposium goes beyond awareness. Its purpose is to empower young people not only to understand the ocean, but to become active stewards of its future. The event also marks the launch of what The Ocean Race envisions as a growing international series of Generation Ocean initiatives.
More than a race, a movement
With Genova as its stage, The Ocean Race is underlining a simple but powerful message: protecting the ocean is not just about sailing across it — it is about racing for it.

By bringing together film, dialogue, education and youth leadership, the week’s programme ensures that the voices shaping the future of our ocean are informed, inspired and equipped to lead. For Genova, and for the wider ocean community, it is a reminder that meaningful change starts where people gather, listen — and act.

title: Codecasa Unveils the Debut of Its First 57m Superyacht, 'Legacy 4'
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Codecasa Unveils the Debut of Its First 57m Superyacht, 'Legacy 4'
summary: The lauded Italian shipyard, Codecasa, has proudly presented 'Legacy 4', a spectacular new addition to its fleet.
body: Proving once again their mastery over the seas, Italian shipyard Codecasa has made a notable splash with the unveiling of 'Legacy 4'. The first of the Codecasa 57 series, fondly referred to as hull F81 during construction, this vessel began her journey towards the horizon at a private ceremony hosted by the Codecasa Ugo Shipyards based in Viareggio.

Despite its grand stature of 56.8 meters, little was previously known about the construction of this vessel which commenced in December 2023. It was revealed that Legacy 4 would encompass a sturdy steel hull with an aluminium superstructure, meticulously crafted in line with Lloyd's Register classification standards.

Legacy 4 is endowed with an impressive accommodation repertoire, flaunting an owner's suite, five guest cabins, a dedicated captain's cabin and six twin cabins for the crew. Ensuring accessibility and a seamless connect, an in-built elevator will link all decks.

The mighty engine? Legacy 4 rumbles on twin 2,375hp Caterpillar engines. This nautical powerhouse is predicted to hit maximum speeds of 17 knots at light displacement, with a range of a whopping 5,000 nautical miles when cruising at 12 knots. While several aspects of this seaworthy marvel remain a closely guarded secret, there is no denying the promise of luxury and performance that Legacy 4 carries within its hull.

Legacy 4 is the fruit of a comprehensive team effort, with construction starting at the shipyard's facilities in Pisa before the vessel was strategically transported to Viareggio. The shipyard rightfully praised the relentless hard work, unwavering passion, dedication and professional brilliance of their entire team.

As the shipyard maps out its future with now four yachts under construction, including the seventh iteration of its Codecasa 43 yacht model due for delivery in spring 2028, the launch of Legacy 4 stands as a testament to Codecasa's commitment to delivering sheer perfection on the waves.

title: UK Match Racing Qualifier 1: London Castaways Seals Win with Late Surge
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: UK Match Racing Qualifier 1: London Castaways Seals Win with Late Surge
summary: The London Castaways dominated the UK Match Racing Qualifier 1, storming late to seize a well-earned victory in a thrilling sailing competition.
body: It was a thrilling scene as eight teams took to the water at Queen Mary SC, hosted by Royal Thames YC, to compete in the UK Match Racing Qualifier 1 on the weekend of 21/22 February. All teams aimed to secure their spot in the highly-anticipated National Match Racing Championship Grand Final in the Autumn. The race was full of adrenaline, presenting challenges not just in team boat handling but also in strategic decision making. A double round robin intensify the competition, with rapid-fire races continually unfolding. While many of the early races were tight, Hamish Taylor’s team concluded Round Robin 1 undefeated, leaving lower places passionately contested.

The semi-finals embedded more drama. Hamish Taylor upheld his dominance against Oli Hale, and Julian Fung won his first victory against Will Bradley. The final races were thrilling as victories alternated between Oli Hale and Julian Fung. However, it was the London Castaways whose skills and resilience at sea led them to take the ultimate accolade. They proved that in the sport of sailing, it’s not just about speed; it’s about strategic placement, courage, and the strength of a team working tirelessly together to claim victory.

title: Shaping the Future: Innovative Collaborative Partnership Formed between Luca Dini Design & Architecture and M3 Marine
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Shaping the Future: Innovative Collaborative Partnership Formed between Luca Dini Design & Architecture and M3 Marine
summary: Taking the world of nautical destinations by storm, Luca Dini Design & Architecture and M3 Marine join forces to redefine modern marinas and waterfronts around the globe.
body: A wave of change is set to sweep over perceived notions of marinas, waterfronts and nautical destinations. At the helm of this sea change are Luca Dini Design & Architecture and M3 Marine, the marine development consultancy firm. The two entities have recently announced a collaboration that is set to redefine the landscape of global marinas and waterfronts.

With a collective vision of shaping the next generation of world class nautical destinations, these two giants of design and marine consultancy vow to break the typical mould of present marina infrastructures. Their intent is to imbue these maritime spaces with a balance of modern design, functionality and the invaluable essence of the sea.

As we anticipate revolutionary changes in nautical destinations, this partnership further enriches the narrative of progressive design in the maritime industry. Together, Luca Dini Design & Architecture and M3 Marine not only aspire to deliver groundbreaking designs, but to also leave a lasting legacy in the world of nautical destination planning.

title: Dive Into Luxury: Explore the Best Motor Yachts Under £100,000 on the Market Today
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Dive Into Luxury: Explore the Best Motor Yachts Under £100,000 on the Market Today
summary: Luxury boating doesn't always require a fortune. Whether it's a classic cruiser or a sporty speedboat, we’ve handpicked four elegant motor yachts that cost less than £100,000.
body: The anticipation of cruising the ocean waves on a beautiful yacht is a dream many wish to make a reality, our hand-curated collection renders affordability in the lap of luxury. With a bountiful choice of secondhand boats, those prepared to roll up their sleeves will find this selection more enticing.

First, we have the British-built Sunseeker Superhawk 34, a dashing symbol of luxury boating going for £99,950. Its lineage comes from the esteemed Sunseeker, a brand long acclaimed for their sporty cruisers. The Superhawk 34 truly encapsulates this legacy with its impressive performance and sleek design, characterized by a low-profile, narrow-beam, and a race-boat aesthetic. This captivating yacht offers you the palpable glamour of the sea, without breaking the bank.

If you fancy a touch of nostalgia and grandeur, the Fairline Phantom 50 is worth considering. The flagship yacht of the Fairline range in 1989, it comes in at £99,950. It harks back to the heights of 1980s luxury, inviting you to relive a piece of maritime history.

Lastly, the Fairline Targa 39, an elegant sports cruiser, priced at £89,950. This graceful craft is astonishingly spacious, providing a home away from home. It is ideal for those seeking to embrace the limitless possibilities of the ocean. Its design is a testament to modern luxury lifestyle, balancing both comfort and style.

Our targeted choice of motor yachts are the perfect blend of luxury and affordability. Consider factors like maintenance, running costs, and functionality as you make your selection. The adventure awaits you at the helm as these vessels offer an incredibly rewarding ownership experience. Embrace the call of the sea, affordable luxury lies within your grasp.

title: First Glimpse Inside Bilgin's Majestic 80m Superyacht Al Reem of the 263 Series
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: First Glimpse Inside Bilgin's Majestic 80m Superyacht Al Reem of the 263 Series
summary: Turkish shipbuilding pioneer, Bilgin Yachts, unveils the spectacular interiors of its final Bilgin 263 series superyacht - Al Reem.
body: The legendary Turkish yard Bilgin Yachts holds a stellar reputation for magnificent sea vessels, with its 263 series causing waves the world over. The announcement of the Al Reem, the third and final unit, conjures a sense of unbridled excitement, as the project's shroud of secrecy gently lifts. Previously referred to as Project Silence, this impressive 80.1-metre motor yacht displays prowess and elegance in equal measure, carving an unforgettable silhouette against the setting sun.

These prodigious marine marvels, designed by Unique Yacht Design and London-based H2 Yacht Design, capture the essence of dynamic prowess and intricate artistry. Yet, it is Al Reem that sets a new course in bespoke craftsmanship, outperforming her sister units with an additional 100GT volume, proudly embodying her owner's 'less is more' philosophy.

A peek inside reveals a balanced palette of calm cream, white, and beige hues, creating an ambiance of serenity and spaciosity. Accentuated by organic, matte timbers, polished stainless steel, natural stones, and leather, the interiors resonate an air of luxurious tranquility.

Al Reem's design optimises every square foot, resulting in a visually unhindered main saloon. The customary bar area and entertainment systems join the band of invisible design elements, allowing unobstructed views of a custom waterfall cascading into a jacuzzi on the foredeck. In a stroke of sheer creativity, the main staircase area is now home to a bespoke art installation, turning Al Reem into a 'moving gallery'. Inhabiting every corner with mindful extravagance, Al Reem redefines oceangoing luxury and craftsmanship.

title: Dell Quay Sailing Club Sparks New Life with Celtic Longboat Winter Regatta
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Dell Quay Sailing Club Sparks New Life with Celtic Longboat Winter Regatta
summary: In an innovative move to incentivise participation, Dell Quay Sailing Club introduced rowing in its winter series, catching the attention of both current and prospective members.
body: The Dell Quay Sailing Club, nestled in the tranquil vistas of Chichester Harbour, is no stranger to sea-adventures. However, having completed a glorious century of existence, the club sought to rekindle the past glory of its members by introducing rowing as a fresh venture. Harnessing the 'have a go' spirit, they ventured into the pristine waters of the Celtic Longboat Winter Regatta, conquering both the new sport and the hearts of existing, as well as new members in one fell swoop.

The ladies rowers battled adverse conditions of strong tide and turbulent winds to clinch the fifth spot, highlighting the tenacity and energy resonating at the club. As for the men, they powered through, finishing an astounding 21 seconds ahead of every other team, leaving no question about the fierce competitive spirit pulsating throughout the Dell Quay Sailing Club.

Ultimately, the event marked a new era for the Dell Quay Sailing Club. The successful introduction of rowing in the Celtic Longboat Winter series boosted not only the spirit and competitiveness among members, but also the opportunity for higher revenues. Reinventing itself, the club has truly become a force to be reckoned with in the waters of Chichester Harbour.

title: The 2026 Wing Foiling Nationals, An Unmatched Spectacle of Speed and Balance, Readies Arrival at Worser Bay Boating Club
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: The 2026 Wing Foiling Nationals, An Unmatched Spectacle of Speed and Balance, Readies Arrival at Worser Bay Boating Club
summary: The craft of Wing Foiling is set for a thrilling national championship arrival at the Worser Bay Boating Club in 2026, promising an adrenaline-fueled event of speed and daring.
body: When the New Zealand Wing Foiling Nationals sail into the Worser Bay Boating Club in 2026, expect nothing less than a spectacular display of grit, agility, and sheer speed. Set against the stunning backdrop of a sky renowned for showcasing nature's less subtle hues, the contest promises to transform an already vibrant locale into a thrilling hub of competitive wing foiling.

Whether one is a seasoned sailor or an enthusiastic onlooker, the sight of wing foiling on Worser Bay offers an unparalleled spectacle. The sport has witnessed an astonishing evolution from being a fringe activity to a mainstream sporting event in a few seasons. Adding to the allure of the sport, a wing foil in the hand and the sight of a hydrofoil that lifts the board above the surface can captivate one and all.

The surging popularity of wing foiling across New Zealand is attributed to the exhilarating experience it offers. It blends the precision of sailing with the thrill of riding waves. The pure thrill of clean lift off from water, the humming sound of the foil cutting through the water - it’s irresistible, it’s addictive. Once sailors experience this, there's simply no returning to traditional water navigation.

While the prospect of the Wing Foiling Nationals might appear daunting, it is the spirit of healthy competition and passion for sailing that will ultimately prevail. Come March 2026, all eyes will be on Worser Bay as the New Zealand Wing Foiling Nationals takes the stage, showcasing not just the speed and balance of its competitors, but the true character and spirit inherent to the sport itself.

title: Experience a Blend of Luxury and Marine Adventure on the 40m Extra Motor Yacht L.A.U.L: Get it While it's Hot!
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Experience a Blend of Luxury and Marine Adventure on the 40m Extra Motor Yacht L.A.U.L: Get it While it's Hot!
summary: The luxurious 40m Extra motor yacht, L.A.U.L, has witnessed a €1M price reduction. Sail away in unparalleled style and comfort with this industry titan.
body: The glamourous world of yachting has been abuzz with the news of a significant €1,000,000 price reduction on the 39.6-metre Extra motor yacht, L.A.U.L. This magnificent marine model – the brainchild of the esteemed Florent Moranzoni of Denison Yachting – sets a new standard in the industry.

In recent years, the L.A.U.L has been making tremendous waves in the yachting community. The luxurious vessel made its grand first appearance at the Monaco Yacht Show in 2019. Since then, it has been the chosen private favourite of many elite yachting enthusiasts and is now available for an altered price tag of €11,950,000.

L.A.U.L stands as an epitome of harmonic colour fusion, with the dominant white and grey palette interrupted by golden orange tones. The yacht's central lounge located aft treats guests with panoramic sea views and a cosy ambience. Accompanying this lounge is a formal dining space, perfect for serving a sumptuous dinner for 12 guests.

The sleeping quarters within the L.A.U.L offer the epitome of luxury and design. The yacht features a master bedroom, complete with a dressing room, an office, and a marble en suite. Each guest cabin boasts exclusive facilities and brings a new meaning to the term 'comfort'. At every turn, this yacht has been designed to optimise space, connecting guests with the sea through its artistic aura.

The yacht’s exterior is just as impressive, with deck spaces prompting socialising and relaxation. The flybridge, in particular, stands out with a seated bar and lounge, the perfect spot to enjoy sunset cocktails while the aft lounge and al fresco dining area beckon endless chit-chat sessions.

L.A.U.L doesn't skip a beat when it comes to performance either. The twin Caterpillar engines achieve a top speed of 17 knots and a cruising speed of 15 knots. More than a yacht, L.A.U.L offers a wholesome marine adventure.

title: Brisbane Comes Alive as 56th Finn World Masters Sailing Championship Sets Sail
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Brisbane Comes Alive as 56th Finn World Masters Sailing Championship Sets Sail
summary: World-class sailors from 18 nations have flocked to Brisbane, Australia, for the opening of the 56th Finn World Masters.
body: The sailing world turned its focus to Brisbane, Australia, where the 2026 Finn World Masters was inaugurated with much aplomb. Hosted by the Royal Queensland Yacht Squadron, the event witnessed more than a hundred sailors from 18 nations, ready to compete in a series of eight races.

This competition follows closely on the heels of the Finn Gold Cup, with several sailors still nursing their wounds, from what was undoubtedly a week of high-intensity sailing. Yet, the lure of the seas is irresistible, and many familiar faces from the Gold Cup are back, complemented by fresh additions to the fleet, making the atmosphere electric.

Other names to look out for include World No 1, Laurent Hay, and Britain's Nick Craig, who despite facing equipment issues and mixed results in the previous competition, are sure to give a compelling performance.
The ceremonial opening was marked by Andy Denison, Finn Masters President, who opened the championship after receiving the Masters Gold Cup from former Finn Gold Cup winner, Thomas Schmid.

This string of Finn events in Brisbane represents the fruit of relentless efforts by the International Finn Association, Royal Queensland Yacht Squadron and numerous others who've worked tirelessly since 2016 to bring these events to life. As Brisbane basks in the glory of hosting this international sailing spectacle, the world eagerly watches on, anticipating a week of thrilling action on water.

title: Horizon II - An Adventurer's Masterpiece: Leapher Yachts' First 61m Explorer Yacht Sees Water
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Horizon II - An Adventurer's Masterpiece: Leapher Yachts' First 61m Explorer Yacht Sees Water
summary: Pioneering Dutch shipyard, Leapher Yachts, presents its debut supercraft, the 61-meter explorer yacht Horizon II, embodying luxury and exploration.
body: Horizon II, a stunning revelation in the superyacht industry, graces the waters for the first time from the docks of the finest new Dutch shipbuilder, Leapher Yachts. Once only known as Project Lazarus, the launch of Horizon II stands testament to the luxury and exploratory prowess that epitomise the brand's ethos.

Featuring a masculine grey and white profile, Horizon II is the firstborn of the shipyard's NAVIX60 model. Notably, the yacht was last spotted as a bare hull in 2024, finally emerging fully-formed after a grand showcasing ceremony in Leapher's facilities in Tolkamer, the Netherlands.

It is the large and welcoming interiors that truly amaze, affording a substantial 1,760GT of volume and allocating accommodation for 14 guests across six lavish cabins. Quintessential features for seafarers include a dedicated beach club, expansive pool, sauna, and diving room catering to diverse preference of discerning guests. Additionally, the explorer houses an avenue for water-related fun with a garage hosting an assortment of tenders and water toys.

Horizon II also has an impressive record with its performance on water. Expectations are for a top speed of 12 knots, a cruising speed of 10 knots, and an outstanding range of 9,000 nautical miles, making it truly a yacht designed for adventurous sea lovers.

Following this triumphant initiation, Horizon II now proceeds into the next stages of outfitting, commissioning, and prepping for sea trials. As Yiannis Andriotis, the visionary CEO of Leapher Yachts, declared in his conversation last year, they are not just building yachts, they're creating explorers - and Horizon II is a premium testament to that vision.

title: RORC Nelson’s Cup Series 2026 - Race Ready in Antigua
author: Michael Hodges
imageAlt: RORC Nelson’s Cup 2026: The Final Caribbean Proving Ground Before the 600
summary: From Tuesday 17 February 2026, Antigua becomes the centre of gravity for offshore racing as the RORC Nelson’s Cup Series returns to the south coast of Antigua. For many teams, this is not just another regatta — it is the final, critical proving ground before the start of the RORC Caribbean 600 on 23 February.
body: The format is deceptively simple: two days of tight coastal racing in the waters off Falmouth and English Harbour, followed by the Antigua 360 — a full circumnavigation of the island. But simplicity is not the same as ease. The Nelson’s Cup compresses decision-making, exposes weaknesses and demands precision in conditions that mirror exactly what crews will face offshore days later.
Training miles are valuable. But proper racing against serious opposition is irreplaceable.

The IRC Maxi Class this year reads like a headline act. Farr 100 Leopard 3, RP100 Galateia and Mills 100 V form a trio of 100-footers that would dominate any Mediterranean regatta. Add Wendy Schmidt’s Botin 85 Deep Blue and the Mills 72 Balthasar and the margins tighten further.

The Caribbean sea state changes everything. The waves are bigger. The loads are higher. The breeze rarely relents. Boats are driven hard — and systems are tested continuously. Ken Read, sailing master aboard the 100ft maxi V, describes the environment with characteristic clarity: owners are deeply invested, expectations are high and the boats are refined to the point where tiny mistakes carry large consequences. The Nelson’s Cup magnifies that reality because the racing is close, intense and unforgiving.

Bouwe Bekking, racing aboard Balthasar, sees Antigua as a venue that consistently delivers exactly what top teams require: wind, organisation and racecourses that reward detail. “If you want to be competitive here,” he notes, “the boat has to stay in one piece.”
That balance between pushing and preserving defines Caribbean maxi racing.

At the sharp end of IRC Zero, Niklas Zennström’s Carkeek 52 Rán returns with Steve Hayles navigating. Alongside Frederic Puzin’s Daguet 5 and James Neville’s Ino Noir, the competition becomes a study in incremental gains.

Inshore racing during the Nelson’s Cup exposes nuances that offshore legs can hide. Slight shifts in wind angle, small differences in sail crossover, a degree or two of steering — over a short course, these details become visible and measurable. Then the Antigua 360 stretches that learning into open-water decision-making.
The fleet is not solely professional programmes. One of the enduring strengths of the Nelson’s Cup is its blend of world-class maxi teams and ambitious Corinthian crews racing the same water.

Dee Caffari arrives fresh from a non-stop circumnavigation completed in under 58 days and now lines up aboard Swan 58 WaveWalker. She describes the regatta as “active recovery” — but also as a critical sharpening tool. Short races allow immediate feedback. Mistakes can be corrected the same day. Offshore, lessons often arrive too late.
That accelerated learning curve matters in a venue where heat, physical strain and Atlantic sea state combine to test even experienced crews.

Adding variety to the fleet is Mike Hennessey’s Class40 Scowling Dragon. Racing under IRC against boats optimised for the rule, Hennessey embraces the mismatch with humour but also intent. If the boat is in Antigua, he argues, it should be racing — and racing hard.

Meanwhile, the Welsh Dragon flies proudly in the Caribbean breeze. Pwllheli Sailing Club fields Mojito, Jackknife and Faenol, carrying friendly rivalries from Welsh waters into Antiguan sunshine. Jackknife, fresh from a strong RORC Transatlantic performance, relishes the opportunity to line up against larger, better-funded programmes on the same start line.
That diversity — professional precision alongside smart amateur seamanship — is not incidental. It is fundamental to the character of RORC racing.

The RORC Nelson’s Cup has evolved from a prelude into a cornerstone of the Caribbean calendar. It is where sail plans are refined, systems are stress-tested, watch routines are sharpened and decision-making is put under pressure before the Atlantic miles begin.
Two days of coastal intensity. One island circumnavigation. Then the 600-mile offshore test.
In Antigua, preparation becomes performance. By the time the fleet turns north for the start of the Caribbean 600, those who have raced hard in the Nelson’s Cup will not be guessing.

title: FPB 83 Wind Horse: A Boat Built for Unstoppable Adventure on Global Swells

Proud owners, Steve and Linda Dashew, pushed the envelope on what was possible for a cruising boat. With an admirable 37,000 nautical miles notched in the first four years of her life, Wind Horse is no ordinary 83ft aluminum yacht. This impressive vessel was meticulously designed by the Dashew couple for continuous, all-conditions cruising.

Far from their first maritime exploit, the couple's experience stems from an enchanting six-year sabbatical navigating the globe on multiple sailboats. Trading the classroom for the water, they homeschooled their children, instilling a deep-seated love for the open sea. Their wealth of experience converged in the creation of Wind Horse, their first motorboat.

A true oceanic titan, Wind Horse is more than just an industrial marvel. Its design exudes luxury, providing a comfortable lining for its multi-faceted hull with profound offshore capabilities. Following the success of Wind Horse, Dashew Marine unveiled a scaled-down 64ft version, the FPB 64, and the larger FPB 97. Unmistakably, Wind Horse remains the crowning marvel of the range, an adventure-filled testament to the power and beauty of sailing unbounded.

title: From Record-Breakers to Corinthian Triumphs, the 2026 RORC Transatlantic Race Sets a New Benchmark
author: Michael Hodges
imageAlt: 2026 RORC Transatlantic Race: Innovation, Endurance and the Ocean’s Verdict
summary: The RORC Transatlantic Race once again proved why it sits at the very top of the global offshore calendar. The 2026 edition delivered outstanding performances across a demanding and complex Atlantic course, blending cutting-edge yacht design with meticulous preparation, seamanship and resilience at the highest level of ocean racing.
body: From overall and class victories under IRC, to record-breaking multihull and monohull performances, the race showcased the depth of both professional and Corinthian talent across an international fleet. It was also a race marked by tragedy, serving as a sobering reminder of the inherent risks of offshore sailing and the importance of safety, experience and mutual support at sea. Against that backdrop, the achievements of the competitors stand as a powerful testament to endurance, teamwork and respect for the ocean.

Overall victory on IRC corrected time went to Palanad 4, the Mach 50 owned by Olivier Magre and skippered by his son Antoine Magre. Their success was not only a triumph of performance, but of belief—belief in a bold scow-bow design and in a shared campaign built on trust and preparation.

“Winning the RORC Transatlantic Race with my son is a dream come true,” said Olivier Magre. “As a father, it is the greatest result I could imagine in sailing. I am incredibly proud of Antoine. On the boat, he is the boss—he makes the decisions and the crew follows him.”

For Antoine, the result validated the concept behind the boat. “This race is a very strong first proof of concept for the Mach 50,” he said. “We believed in the potential of the scow-bow under IRC, but it had to be proven offshore. Winning overall here really sets the bar. To do it with my father on board is something I will never forget.”

At the sharp end of the fleet, the MOD70 trimarans delivered one of the most intense match races the Atlantic has seen. Argo set a new Multihull Race Record for the Lanzarote–Antigua route, stopping the clock at 4 days, 23 hours, 51 minutes and 15 seconds after a relentless duel with Zoulou, finishing just 2 hours and 32 minutes ahead.

Skipper Chad Corning described a race fought at the limit. “We knew it was going to be close, and that’s exactly how it played out. We built a small lead early, but they pushed hard the whole way. The intensity never dropped.”

“Once we hit the trades, it went to another level,” he added. “Thirty knots day after day, long dark nights—like skiing a black run blindfolded. This race was won in the preparation. Months of refit work at Marina Lanzarote paid off when it mattered most.”

The 34-metre Baltic 111 Raven, skippered by Damien Durchon, delivered one of the defining performances of the race. Raven claimed Monohull Line Honours, won the IMA Transatlantic Trophy, and set a new Monohull Race Record of 6 days, 22 hours, 27 minutes and 47 seconds—the first foil-assisted monohull of her size to complete a transatlantic race.

“Raven is incredibly stable,” said Durchon. “The better she performs, the safer she becomes. The side foils generate enormous righting moment, backed up by water ballast and hull-form stability. If a foil stalls, she simply behaves like a conventional yacht.”
“At 25 knots she already feels fast,” he added. “Above 30 knots, you’re moving quicker than the waves themselves. It’s demanding sailing—but remarkably manageable.”

Ino Noir, the Carkeek 45 owned by James Neville, finished in 9 days and 6 hours, securing second overall under IRC. The result extended a strong sequence of podium performances and underlined the value of consistency in a relentlessly tough race.

“It was windy the whole way with a brutal sea state,” Neville said. “There was no let-up. We pushed hard early, but a few days out we started breaking equipment and had to rein it in. Finishing second overall after that intensity feels very satisfying.”

Few performances captured the spirit of the race quite like Jackknife, the 30-year-old J/125 owned and skippered by Sam Hall, sailing with his father Andrew Hall. After 11 days and 13 hours at sea, Jackknife finished third overall under IRC and won IRC Two—one of the most impressive results of the entire fleet.
“Getting Jackknife across the Atlantic safely was always the first goal,” said Andrew Hall. “She’s one of the smallest and oldest boats here, but it was always Sam’s dream.”

“Winning IRC Two and finishing third overall feels incredible,” added Sam. “We hand-steered the whole way. It was about endurance, balance and looking after the crew. Racing this boat together as father and son just felt right.”

In the Double-Handed division, victory on corrected time went to Kornog 2, the Pogo 12.50 sailed by Gilles Colubi and Ivan Osselin, completing the crossing in 13 days and 1 hour. Finnish entry Stimmy, sailed by Ari Huusela and Annika Paasikivi, completed the podium after 18 days and 6 hours, embodying the adventure-driven ethos of the class.
In the Superyacht Division, the Hoek-designed Linnea Aurora emerged as the best-placed yacht under IRC, earning the Superyacht Trophy after an elapsed time of 11 days and 13 hours.

“Managing a 160-tonne yacht for 3,000 miles is a real challenge,” said Sailing Master Magnus Woxen. “But teamwork, preparation and spirit carried us through. Reaching Antigua as division winners is hugely satisfying.”
Maxitude, the Lift 45 owned and skippered by Xavier Bellouard, finished in 10 days and 12 hours, securing the Yacht Club de France Trophy for the best-placed YCF member under IRC.

“When you see the names on that trophy, they’re skippers I deeply admire,” said Bellouard. “To be associated with it is very special. This race represents one of the greatest challenges in offshore sailing.”
A race dedicated to Walross 4

The 2026 RORC Transatlantic Race is dedicated to the crew of Walross 4. Following a tragic mid-Atlantic accident resulting in the loss of a crew member, the team completed their crossing with immense courage and professionalism. The RORC, fellow competitors, Calero Marinas and the Antigua Yacht Club have all expressed their deepest condolences to the crew member’s family and to the Walross 4 team.

The 2027 edition of the race will start from Marina Lanzarote in January, continuing the partnership with the International Maxi Association and the Yacht Club de France. As part of the RORC Season’s Points Championship, the race remains a cornerstone of global offshore competition.

In 2026, the Atlantic delivered speed, innovation, heartbreak and triumph in equal measure. Above all, it reminded everyone involved that offshore racing is never just about the finish line—it is about how you cross the ocean to reach it.

title: First Look into the Luxurious Sanlorenzo SX120: The Ultimate Incontriation of Adventure and Opulence
author: Old Sea Dogs

summary: Discover the Sanlorenzo SX120, a perfect mix of luxuriant style and adventurous spirit, making its grand debut at Cannes Boat Show last year.
body: Making its grand debut at the Cannes Boat Show, the Sanlorenzo SX120 yacht certainly made a splash. With its luxurious explorative aesthetics and extravagant features such as a retractable infinity pool, it offers the perfect blend of indulgence and adventure. Extraordinary in design, this yacht unites grandeur with practicality that begins with a beach club of magnanimous proportions. Centered around an extraordinary spa pool providing breathtaking views of the sea, it doubles as a generous sea-level entertaining area and as a practical storage space for all your sea toys and tenders.

An intriguing element of its design is that the inviting sun loungers slide over the pool when it’s not in need. The yacht's chic design further incorporates multifunctional design features. Precisely, the teak benches are supported by sturdy, aesthetically pleasing stainless-steel pedestals which, in turn, act as heavy-duty winches and cleats for the stern lines.

The yacht features a main deck owner’s cabin that provides fine views through the reverse-angled front screens and has exclusive access to the foredeck lounge. Despite having a relatively smaller main saloon, with numerous alternative options available both above and below it, space is hardly an issue. A Lissoni-designed spiral staircase linking all three decks is beauty and practicality united. The bridge station claims the front end of the upper deck but the rest can be fitted as per the owner’s preference. This can range from a sky lounge to an indoor dining room. There is also an ample open deck space and a rooftop area for you to savor.

The Sanlorenzo SX120 stands out as the first leisure boat to house Volvo’s new IPS Professional platform. With a pair of robust 1,000hp engines linked to the two pod drives, it maximizes fuel efficiency at all speeds. The Sanlorenzo SX120 is an exquisite marriage of opulence and thrill, superbly showcased at the Cannes Boat Show. Its price is set at approximately €16 million ex tax.

title: Don't be Adrift: The Unexpected Legal Dilemma over Superyacht Inheritance in the European Union
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Don't be Adrift: The Unexpected Legal Dilemma over Superyacht Inheritance in the European Union
summary: Inheriting a superyacht? One may unexpectedly find themselves in legal turbulent waters due to an overlooked aspect of EU succession law.
body: To the untrained eye, European inheritance law may appear reassuringly coherent, even simplistic. But don't be fooled — the tranquillity of these waters hides some vicious undertows. The Devil, as they say, is in the detail, particularly if one has the privilege — or misfortune — of inheriting a superyacht.

The passage of EU Succession Regulation (Regulation (EU) No. 650/2012) has performed grandly in harmonising disparate laws. The principle? Simple — a person's estate is governed by the law of their habitual residence. One person, one law. The objective? Utterly laudable — clarity and coherence.

While for the most part, the objectives were delivered, an overlooked area stands out — the superyacht. Akin to a glamorous, globe-trotting persona, the luscious superyacht, is legally regarded as a 'movable asset.' But this moniker belies its unique nature – a hybrid between real estate and a regulated commercial platform.

Inheritance law dictates 'who' will inherit the yacht. Still, the national registry law holds the power to determine 'whether' this inheritance will be recognised in reality. These two legal territories, parallel yet sometimes in tension, dramatically influence the legal landscape for the inheritor of a yacht.

Adding to this is the pragmatic regulatory environment in which a yacht operates. This includes flag-state registers, ownership registers, various filings, and compliance documentation. The burden of these requirements can prove overwhelming, creating further hurdles for the unprepared inheritor.

So, dare to inherit a superyacht? Pull up the anchor of simplistic understanding; navigate carefully these legal waters. For as brilliant and luring as they are, without the necessary understanding, one might find themselves caught in a legal maelstrom.

title: Projecting a 2035 Superyacht Boom: A Deep Dive into the Future of the Mediterranean’s Prime Cruising Territory
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Projecting a 2035 Superyacht Boom: A Deep Dive into the Future of the Mediterranean’s Prime Cruising Territory
summary: The magnificent Mediterranean is a playground for superyachts, including areas from Gocek to Gibraltar, teeming with promising prospects, yet facing pressures spurred by potential growth.
body: Imagine drawing an arc from Gocek in Turkey, through Sardinia, landing in Gibraltar. This arbitrary line outlines the Mediterranean's prime cruising grounds, a sprawling expanse over 2,000 nautical miles. These waters, annually awash with thousands of superyachts, guests, and crew, form the backdrop to a lifestyle of adventure and luxury. However, with forecasts suggesting an additional 3,400 superyachts by 2035, these idyllic waters could soon face a tidal wave of infrastructure pressures and overpopulation.

Indeed, shipyard new builds and supply chains are relishing the potential advanced orders, but the infrastructure and service networks are far from celebrating. The looming influx of superyachts is set to strain the existing nautical support networks. Recognising the urgency of this issue, the Balearic Marine Cluster established the Mediterranean Superyacht Forum, a pioneering event aimed at strategic planning and readiness for the imminent challenges of the superyacht boom.

The solution lies in extensive planning and investment that strives for optimisation and readiness for the increasing existing demand and growing fleet. Regional superyacht associations across Spain, France, Monaco, Italy, Greece, Turkey, and beyond are feeling the pressure to educate stakeholders on the economic value of yachts and secure future prosperity.

This collaborative spirit displayed in the Mediterranean Superyacht Forum could potentially lead to a transformative shift in shaping the Mediterranean's future. By successfully balancing growth with preservation, the Mediterranean 'playground' of superyachts can continue to flourish as a world-class gateway to life on the seas.

title: The Moxley 12
author: Michael Hodges
imageAlt: The Moxley 12
summary: I am based on the Isle of Wight and get to see many yachts and boats of all shapes and sizes. However The Moxley 12 is a rare gem in the world of cruising catamarans—an elegant, 12-metre vessel built for those who value both performance and long-range comfort. Designed and constructed by Moxley Marine Ltd in 2015, the Moxley 12 (also known as “RA”) reflects a deep understanding of modern multihull design, bringing to
body: Measuring 11.95 metres in length with a generous beam of 6.76 metres, the Moxley 12 delivers remarkable stability at sea. This width creates a broad and comfortable platform, reducing heel and providing a smooth ride even in choppier waters—one of the key advantages of a well-designed catamaran. Its shallow draft of just 0.66 metres also means the Moxley 12 can easily access shallow harbours and anchorages that might be off-limits to deeper-keeled monohulls.

Under sail, the Moxley 12 is designed to perform. The twin-hull design offers low hydrodynamic resistance and excellent handling, while the bridge clearance of approximately 17.3 metres ensures the mainsail and rigging are well clear of deck structures, providing optimal wind performance. Whether day-sailing in local waters or heading off for a coastal passage, the Moxley 12 responds with agility and efficiency. Its sail plan is oriented toward cruising rather than racing, but the vessel’s light weight and hull shape mean it can achieve impressive speeds even in moderate wind conditions.

Below deck, the Moxley 12 offers accommodations that strike a fine balance between practicality and comfort. With sleeping quarters for up to eight people, the catamaran is well suited for extended cruising with family or guests. The twin hulls house private cabins, bathrooms, and storage, while the central saloon—bright, airy, and open—serves as a communal living and dining area. Natural light floods the interior, and the layout maximises usable space, making even longer voyages feel like home. Modern finishes and marine-grade materials complete the interior, emphasising both durability and style.

A standout feature of the Moxley 12 is its thoughtful propulsion system. It is powered by a Vetus M3.28 diesel engine producing 20 kW, paired with a custom shaft drive and Brunton H5 three-blade autoprops. This setup not only delivers reliable motoring performance when the wind dies but also contributes to fuel efficiency. The engine room is accessible and logically arranged for ease of maintenance—a detail often overlooked on smaller builds but crucial for serious cruisers. With a fuel capacity of 150 litres and freshwater tanks holding 300 litres, the Moxley 12 is built with self-sufficiency in mind. These specifications make her ideal for longer-term cruising where marina stops might be infrequent. Solar panels and other auxiliary systems are often added by owners to increase independence further, though the base configuration is already geared toward autonomy.

Currently based on the Isle of Wight, the Moxley 12 is positioned in the market as a semi-custom, performance cruising catamaran. She sits in a niche between mass-produced models and full custom builds—offering a more tailored, high-quality construction while remaining relatively accessible in pricing. The fact that she was designed and built in the UK also speaks to the craftsmanship and attention to detail embedded in her DNA.

In summary, the Moxley 12 is an exceptional example of what a well-thought-out catamaran can offer. Whether used as a liveaboard, a family cruiser, or a stylish weekender, it brings together the best of form and function. For sailors looking for something a little off the beaten path—something that combines technical finesse with a warm, livable design—the Moxley 12 might just be the perfect fit.

This two-day showcase is the perfect way for sailors, windsurfers, foilers, paddleboarders and watersports fans of all ages to kick off the 2026 season inspired, informed and ready for acti
body: Whether you’re a seasoned dinghy racer, a windsports junkie, a family looking for your next adventure or someone ready to try something new, the RYA Dinghy & Watersports Show has something for you. This isn’t just a shopping expo — it’s a celebration of maritime sport, community and water-borne discovery:

Leading coaches, elite sailors and watersports professionals will be on hand to share knowledge on race tactics, boat handling, safety, technology and training — helping visitors at every level improve their time on the water. A few highlights confirmed for the 2026 edition include well-known presenters, elite athletes and inspirational speakers who will appear across the show stages.

For many sailors and watersports enthusiasts, February can feel like the long off-season. The RYA Dinghy & Watersports Show is where that season shifts into gear. It’s where you can:

Whether you’re chasing speed on a trapeze, dreaming of your first dinghy purchase, refining your foiling technique, or simply want to get out on the water more, the RYA Dinghy & Watersports Show 2026 is the UK’s biggest, most inclusive watersports event of the year. title: Discover How Modern Technology Transforms Offshore Connectivity for Luxury Yachts
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Discover How Modern Technology Transforms Offshore Connectivity for Luxury Yachts
summary: In an interconnected world, the expectation for reliable connectivity aboard superyachts has never been more crucial. Explore the evolution of maritime communication and how it shapes the future of superyacht connectivity.
body: In a time where the earth is virtually shrunk into the palms of our hands, connectivity at sea has taken on an unprecedented importance. Superyachts crossing the high seas are no longer satisfied with the bare minimum, they now clamour for the same level of connectivity they experience onshore.

In times past, the concept would have seemed far-fetched. Maritime communication primarily rode on the back of shortwave radio frequencies ricocheting signals off the Earth's atmosphere. These were sadly limited in bandwidth and hindered by atmospheric conditions, resulting in often disrupted transmissions.

Today, the connectivity scene for superyachts has seen a revolutionary change with the advent of modern flat-panel satellite terminals. These offer reliable, stable connectivity without the baggage of legacy terminal issues.

Enhancements in technology like the flat-panel antennas have not only reduced the size, weight, and power requirements, but have also phenomenally slashed costs. These improvements have made them an attractive alternative to their predecessors.
The latter relied on weighty parabolic antennas requiring complex stabilisation systems that often grappled with lost connection due to sea conditions and manoeuvres.

Modern technology has punctuated the superyacht industry, rewriting the playbook for life at sea. It has broken barriers to global cruising, further enhancing the appeal of a life unmoored, unbound, and unlimited by geography.

title: Yamaha Transforms Boat Docking into an Exciting Video Game with its Helm Master EX
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Yamaha Transforms Boat Docking into an Exciting Video Game with its Helm Master EX
summary: Imagine piloting your boat with a portable video game-like controller. Yamaha's new Helm Master EX offers jaw-droppingly easy manoeuvres, making docking seem like child's play.
body: Yamaha has added an exciting dimension to motorboating: a wireless controller making docking as easy as gaming. With its latest innovation, Helm Master EX, Yamaha has redefined our interaction with boats, transforming the on-water experience by integrating a handheld device likened to a gaming remote control.

Graphics-interface-creating pioneer, Yamaha, has fashioned a remote controller that allows you to drive the boat from anywhere on board. It's a wireless, compact piece of technology, crafted to optimise manoeuvrability and control in the palm of your hand. Navigating, berthing, or simply holding station in the face of tide and wind has never been easier.

The remote not only allows you to move forwards, backwards or sideways, but it can also undertake intricate tasks like steering on the spot, executing gentle reactions for angling, or maintaining a precise GPS fix. It employs computer-assisted steering and throttles, making complex moves easy.

Furthermore, the handheld controller boasts a colour display showing vital information like speed, depth, and heading. Integrated with the autopilot, this allows instantaneous adjustment of the heading by five or 10 degrees, transcending the need for physically handling the helm.

Compatibility of the Helm Master EX is not an issue, as it works in harmony with the latest generation of Yamaha outboards from 150hp upwards. However, to extract its full potential, a twin rig and an integrated bow thruster from Vetus, Sleipner, or Lewmar are recommended.

In essence, Yamaha's Helm Master EX gives a video-gaming twist to boat docking, making the entire experience enjoyable and child's play. Essentially, it's boating for the digital age and might leave traditionalists astounded at how an adolescent video gamer might find controlling a Jeanneau Cap Camarat 9, with twin Yamaha F250 outboards, an effortless task.

title: Fischer and Péquin Crowned 49er Champions at Lanzarote International Regatta
author: Michael Hodges
imageAlt: Fischer & Péquin Master Lanzarote to Win 2026 International Regatta
summary: The sixth edition of the Lanzarote International Regatta concluded in emphatic fashion this week, with Erwan Fischer and Clément Péquin confirming their authority in the 49er class after four days of high-intensity Olympic racing off Marina Rubicón.
body: Across a full week of competition, the regatta delivered exactly what sailors value most at this stage of the Olympic cycle: volume, variety, and pressure. From heavy-air planing conditions and Atlantic swell to medium breezes and a tactically demanding light-wind finale, Lanzarote once again proved why it has become one of Europe’s most reliable winter proving grounds for elite sailing.

In the 49er fleet, consistency was king. Sixteen races were completed across the series — a rare achievement that underlined both the commitment of the Race Committee and the suitability of the venue. The result was a championship that rewarded adaptability, boat handling, and decision-making rather than single standout performances.

By the final day, the regatta had entered its most delicate phase. A west-southwesterly breeze of just 7–8 knots replaced the stronger conditions seen earlier in the week, compressing the fleet and placing a premium on clean starts, lane discipline, and tactical patience. It was a classic Lanzarote finish: subtle, technical, and unforgiving.

For Erwan Fischer and Clément Péquin, the lighter air changed nothing. The French pairing delivered the calm, methodical sailing that had defined their week, sealing overall victory and returning to the top step of the podium in Marina Rubicón for the second time in two years.

Their previous triumph here came in 2024 during the 49er World Championship. Winning again in 2026 only reinforced their strong connection with the venue — and their ability to perform across a full performance spectrum.
“We are very happy to be back in Lanzarote this winter,” said Péquin. “It’s a fantastic place to sail, and winning this regatta here is something very special for us.”

“We focused on being as consistent as possible all week,” he explained. “We sailed in very different conditions — strong breeze and waves, then lighter air and short chop on the final day. That’s what makes this regatta so complete and so demanding.”

Behind the winners, the margins remained narrow. Lucas Rual and Emile Amoros (FRA) claimed second place after a week-long duel at the front of the fleet, while Richard Schultheis and Fabian Rieger (GER) rounded out the podium, completing a tightly fought championship defined by depth and speed.

Across the Olympic classes — including ILCA 6 and ILCA 7 — the regatta once again fulfilled its role as a cornerstone event in the winter training calendar, blending race mileage with genuine competitive pressure.

Organised by Marina Rubicón and supported by Turismo Lanzarote, Lanzarote Sports Destination, the Cabildo of Lanzarote, and Yaiza Town Council, the regatta continues to grow in stature. Its strength lies not just in organisation, but in geography: reliable breeze, open water, and race areas that expose weaknesses quickly.
For sailors building toward major championships and future Olympic cycles, Lanzarote remains a place where results must be earned — not gifted.

As fleets now disperse to the next training blocks and early-season regattas, one thing is clear: those who perform here carry momentum forward. And for Fischer and Péquin, Marina Rubicón has once again proven fertile ground.

title: Jackknife Shines, Linnea Aurora Leads the Superyachts as the 2026 RORC Transatlantic Fleet Reaches Antigua
author: Michael Hodges
imageAlt: After Two Weeks at Sea, the 2026 RORC Transatlantic Race Comes into Focus
summary: As the RORC Transatlantic Race moves into its final hours, the shape of the IRC leaderboard is now largely set. A diverse fleet of monohulls has completed the 3,000-nautical-mile crossing from Lanzarote to Antigua, with the remainder closing fast after nearly two demanding weeks at sea.
body: What this edition has underlined—yet again—is the extraordinary breadth that defines the RORC Transatlantic Race: modern race machines and classic yachts, fully-crewed and double-handed teams, professional campaigns and deeply personal ambitions, all sharing the same ocean and the same finish line.
Jackknife delivers a defining Corinthian performance

Few results have resonated as strongly as Jackknife, the J/125 owned and skippered by Sam Hall, sailing with his father Andrew Hall. Finishing on 23 January after 11 days and 13 hours at sea, Jackknife claimed third overall under IRC and victory in IRC Two.

Raced with a Corinthian crew aboard one of the oldest boats in the fleet, the 30-year-old design delivered a masterclass in preparation, seamanship and consistency. Against newer, larger and more powerful opposition, Jackknife proved that experience and discipline still matter at the very top of offshore racing.
It is a result that will be remembered long after the spray has washed off the decks—one of the defining stories of the 2026 race.
Linnea Aurora tops the Superyacht division

In the Superyacht Class, the Hoek-designed 128-footer Linnea Aurora, skippered by Phil Martinson, has completed her crossing in an elapsed time of 11 days and 13 hours. On IRC corrected time, Linnea Aurora emerged as the leading superyacht, securing the Superyacht Trophy for the 2026 RORC Transatlantic Race.

Elegant, powerful and disciplined, Linnea Aurora combined classic long-range offshore capability with measured race management—setting a clear benchmark for how large displacement yachts can compete seriously across the Atlantic.
Maxitude completes a milestone Atlantic ambition

Maxitude, the Lift 45 owned and skippered by Xavier Bellouard, finished on 22 January after 10 days and 12 hours at sea. For Bellouard, the race represented the fulfilment of a long-held personal ambition: crossing the Atlantic in competitive mode.

The campaign was further rewarded with the Yacht Club de France Trophy, awarded to the best-placed Yacht Club de France member under IRC. For the all-French team, it capped a deeply satisfying and purposeful transatlantic passage.
MOCRA multihulls complete their race

The MOCRA multihull division is now complete. Wellness Training, sailed by offshore legend Marc Guillemot, finished on 20 January in an elapsed time of 9 days and 9 hours, securing the final podium position in class.

Calamity, the Ocean 50 sailed by Timo Tavio and Kimo Nordstrom, suffered a broken boom during the crossing. The crew are safe, and the boat is now in Jolly Harbour, Antigua, preparing for repairs ahead of the RORC Caribbean 600.
Strong depth across the IRC fleet

Further up the IRC order, Ino Noir, the Carkeek 45 owned by James Neville, finished on 20 January just after sunset, completing the race in 9 days and 6 hours. On corrected time, Ino Noir secured second overall under IRC, continuing a strong run following a podium finish in the previous edition.

NeoJivaro / Afazik Impulse, the Neo 430 sailed by Yves Grosjean, finished in 11 days and 18 hours. While just outside the podium in IRC One, the result marked a significant personal achievement after Grosjean had previously postponed his Atlantic plans due to a skiing injury.

Also completing the crossing with solid performances were the VO65 Sisi, skippered by Gerwin Janssen and Paul Lucan, finishing in 10 days and 7 hours, and the V69 Nacira, skippered by Mattia Correrini, crossing the line in 11 days and 2 hours.
Double-handed honours and the final miles
In the Two-Handed division, the 86-foot ketch Adrien, sailed by Arthur Hubert and Christoph Bachmann, was the first double-handed yacht to finish, completing the crossing in 11 days and 5 hours.
However, on corrected time, victory went to the Pogo 12.50 Kornog 2, sailed by Gilles Colubi and Ivan Osselin, who completed the race in 13 days and 1 hour, finishing at 01:31:08 UTC on 25 January.

Still racing toward Antigua are several determined crews. Rock ’n’ Roll, the Owen Clarke 40, has approximately 270 nautical miles remaining, while Solaris 55 Team 42 is closing in with around 310 miles to go. Both crews are deep into the final phase of their Atlantic crossings as the trades continue to deliver fast—but physically demanding—conditions.
Spirit of the race: Stimmy and Walross 4

The Finnish Sun Fast 3300 Stimmy, sailed double-handed by Ari Huusela and Annika Paasikivi, remains at sea around 660 nautical miles from Antigua and is expected to be the final finisher. Their race continues to embody the seamanship, patience and quiet determination that sit at the heart of the RORC Transatlantic Race.

Germany’s Walross 4 is approximately 415 nautical miles from completing her crossing, with the young crew continuing steadily west. All competitors already arrived in Antigua have expressed their deep condolences following the tragic loss of a crew member aboard Walross 4. The ASV-Berlin Yacht Club and RORC continue to provide full support and assistance as the team prepares for arrival.
A warm Caribbean welcome

The Antigua Yacht Club hosted an informal welcome gathering for arriving RORC Transatlantic Race crews, joined by local sailors following their Saturday race meeting. Complimentary food and drink were shared by more than 100 sailors, a reminder that after the miles, the fatigue and the salt, the race always ends the same way—together.
The Atlantic has spoken. The stories are written. And Antigua, once again, has welcomed them home.
