title: The Magic of Marketing Meets Seafaring Splendour: A Two-Day Convention for Superyacht Industry Leaders in Amsterdam
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: The Magic of Marketing Meets Seafaring Splendour: A Two-Day Convention for Superyacht Industry Leaders in Amsterdam
summary: This March, in Amsterdam, top-notch marketers and superyacht industry titans will converge for a two-day brainstorming marathon dubbed 'Make Your Mark ’26'.
body: In the heart of Amsterdam, on the 19th and 20th of March, an extraordinary confluence of minds will take place. Approximately 200 leaders, advisors, creators, and influencers from the superyacht marketing sphere will spend 48 riveting hours immersed in knowledge sharing, deep thinking, creative brainstorming, and inspirational presentations delivered by expert minds from the global marketing world.

'Make Your Mark ’26’ is more than a symposium. It's a highly anticipated event in the superyacht industry calendar—a beacon of knowledge and networking that's pivotal to this niche sector. Over two days, this gathering will facilitate intense debates, enlightening exchanges, and the generation of pioneering ideas that promise to reshape the superyacht communications landscape.

But the creme-de-la-creme of Make Your Mark ’26’ is beyond the hard-hitting dialogues and brainstorming. Nested in Amsterdam’s Venue Collective, right near the Olympic Stadium and Schiphol Airport, the event will offer a potent mix of inspiration and relaxation. Envision beautifully designed private spaces, meeting hubs, workshop rooms, keynote areas, and outdoor gardens—all reserved for two days of pure intellectual indulgence.

Indeed, Make Your Mark ’26’ isn't just a meeting of minds—it’s a rare business retreat that optimizes learning and networking opportunities. A place where analytical thinking is stimulated, strategic batteries recharged, and bonds forged with industry peers. In this creative and strategic hotspot, the superyacht industry will set sail towards a future steered by data, digital savvy, luxury insights, and a profound respect for sustainability. The navigation chart for the superyacht marketing journey is set—and the course promises to be an exhilarating one.

title: Discover the Exquisite Solaris Power 60 Coupé: A Masterpiece on Water
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Discover the Exquisite Solaris Power 60 Coupé: A Masterpiece on Water
summary: The latest marvel from Solaris Power, the 60 Coupé, is a true epitome of Italian boat designing excellence.
body: Known for crafting striking seafaring vessels, Solaris Power has once again charmed the yacht world with its latest masterpiece - the 60 Coupé. The boat embraces the sleek lines of a performance cruiser under the protection of a hardtop, showcasing a perfect symphony of aesthetics and functionality.

The exterior captures the essence of classic Italian design, sporting a signature vertical stem and a hull shaped with intricate yet graceful curves. Paying great attention to detail, a hydraulic tender garage conceals toys and equipment, pop-up cleats and a recessed anchor locker maintain an unbroken profile.

Despite being a 60-foot yacht, the accommodation is as impressive as a much larger vessel. An opulent full-beam owner's suite, utilising the generous width of the boat promises a luxurious experience. This is complemented by a VIP cabin and a versatile third guest cabin.

But the Solaris Power 60 Coupé doesn't just dazzle with her looks. Equipped with twin Volvo Penta IPS 1350s engines, she combines elegance with power. The yacht's low centre of gravity guarantees a smooth, dry ride even in rough waters. A fast cruise speed of 28 knots paralleled with a top speed of 36 knots redefine power in luxury yachting.

Priced at €2.1 million, the 60 Coupé is a nautical delight for those refusing to compromise between the thrill of a sporty boat and the dependability of a long-distance cruiser. Make no mistake; the 60 Coupé cements Solaris Power's reputation for creating the water's most beautiful boats.

title: Revolution Coming to Maritime Training: British Marine Unveils Plans for Digital BM Academy
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Revolution Coming to Maritime Training: British Marine Unveils Plans for Digital BM Academy
summary: British Marine is set to redefine the marine industry with the upcoming launch of its revolutionary British Marine Training Academy (BM Academy).
body: In an exciting development for the marine industry, British Marine has unveiled its plans to launch the British Marine Training Academy (BM Academy). Much more than just another learning platform, this digital academy stands to revolutionize not only training and upskilling, but also career development throughout the leisure marine sector. With this development, traditional barriers towards professional development are set to crumble, providing professionals in the United Kingdom and globally with unhindered access to various courses online, anytime they wish and at their own pace.

The BM Academy has been carefully designed to meet a broad spectrum of needs. It aims to support fresh entrants by offering introductions to the marine world. At the same time, it caters for seasoned industry professionals through its Continuing Professional Development Training. Businesses too stand to benefit, as the Academy supports them to cultivate more skilled, stronger teams.

A broad range of courses are already in development, covering technical skills, leadership, compliance, innovation, and future industry challenges. An 'Introduction to the Marine World' course is one of the first set to be rolled out, designed to support individuals new to the industry, career-switchers, and businesses training new staff. This course will act as a gateway into the industry, enabling employers to attract, engage, and retain talent while fostering growth in the leisure marine sector.

Founding partners, such as Haven Knox-Johnston Commercial, Skandinavian Agency Services S.A.C Marine Surveyors, Aqueduct Marina, and Bartons Solicitors have been instrumental in this endeavour. Their initial investment and insights have been critical in bringing the BM Academy to life, firmly aligning with the shared goal of strengthening skills, attracting newcomers and fostering a more resilient future for the marine industry.

With its imminent launch, interest is already being shown, and British Marine is encouraging HR managers, training leads, business owners, and industry professionals alike to register their interest for access details and announcements.

title: Rolex Switzerland Sail Grand Prix Returns to Geneva for 2026 SailGP Season
author: Michael Hodges
imageAlt: Rolex Switzerland Sail Grand Prix Returns to Geneva for 2026
summary: SailGP has confirmed the return of one of its most striking and successful venues, with the Rolex Switzerland Sail Grand Prix set to roar back onto Geneva’s spectacular waterfront on 19–20 September 2026. Staged once again on the deep blue theatre of Lake Geneva, the event will mark a second consecutive home race for the Switzerland SailGP Team, supported by long-standing championship and event Title Partner Rolex.
body: Following a sensational debut in September 2025, Geneva has rapidly established itself as one of SailGP’s most compelling natural stadiums. Last year’s inaugural edition drew a sold-out crowd, with more than 8,500 ticketed fans lining the lakefront to witness F50 foiling catamarans slicing across the water at astonishing speeds. The atmosphere was electric, the racing razor-close, and the setting unforgettable — even if local hopes were dashed when the Germany SailGP Team, presented by Deutsche Bank, denied Switzerland victory on home waters.

For SailGP, the return to Geneva is about far more than revisiting a successful venue. It reflects the league’s broader ambition to establish a consistent annual calendar anchored in iconic global cities.
SailGP CEO Sir Russell Coutts described the decision as a significant milestone in the championship’s growth.

“Returning to Geneva is a significant moment for SailGP and our fans, as we continue to build a consistent annual calendar in some of the world’s most iconic destinations,” said Coutts. “In 2025, the Rolex Switzerland Sail Grand Prix became one of the most attractive outdoor sporting events ever hosted in the city — and the biggest ever staged on the lake.”
He added that the 2026 event will build on that success, with an expanded fan experience ashore, enhanced viewing areas and world-class hospitality for spectators, guests and partners alike.
“Having an event in Geneva is important to SailGP’s global growth,” Coutts said. “We look forward to working closely with Rolex, the City and the Canton to host another record-setting weekend.”

For Rolex, the Geneva event carries particular resonance. The Swiss city is the spiritual home of the brand, and its continued support of SailGP reflects a partnership rooted in precision, performance and innovation.
Arnaud Boetsch, Rolex Director of Communication and Image, underlined the significance of bringing the championship back to Lake Geneva.

“We are proud to welcome the Rolex SailGP Championship back to the home of Rolex following a remarkable race weekend last September,” he said. “The event reflects the strength of our long-standing partnership and our shared commitment to shaping the future of sailing and bringing the sport to new audiences.”

Having partnered SailGP since its launch in 2019, Rolex’s involvement spans the entire championship — on and off the water — and Geneva offers a rare opportunity to showcase that relationship in a truly iconic setting.
For the Switzerland SailGP Team, the return to Geneva comes with unfinished business and renewed ambition.
Driver Sébastien Schneiter spoke openly about the motivation that comes with racing in front of a home crowd.

“We’re extremely excited to welcome SailGP back to Geneva,” he said. “A huge thank you to everyone involved in making this event possible. Racing at home gives us something extra — the energy from the crowd really does give you an edge.”

After narrowly missing out on victory in 2025, the Swiss team will arrive in 2026 determined to convert home support into home success, with Lake Geneva once again set to test the fleet’s nerve, precision and boat-handling skills.

The 2026 Rolex Switzerland Sail Grand Prix will replace Saint-Tropez’s previously scheduled September slot and will serve as the 11th stop of the 2026 SailGP Season. Crucially, it will also be the final European event before the championship heads to the Middle East for a season-defining double-header in the UAE.
That positioning only heightens the stakes. With championship points likely finely balanced, Geneva could play a decisive role in shaping the title race.

The impact of the event extends far beyond the racecourse. In 2025, the Geneva SailGP weekend delivered a significant economic and cultural boost to the city, attracting tens of thousands of spectators across the shoreline, grandstands and on-water zones, while a global television audience of 19.5 million viewers tuned in worldwide.

Fast, loud and unforgiving, SailGP’s F50s are a striking contrast to Geneva’s calm elegance — and that tension is exactly what makes the venue so compelling. When the fleet returns in September 2026, the lake will once again become a stage for elite foiling, national rivalry and stadium-style racing at its most intense.
Geneva is ready. SailGP is coming back.

title: How to Avoid Turning Wages into Anchors: An Essential Survival Guide for Yacht Owners
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: How to Avoid Turning Wages into Anchors: An Essential Survival Guide for Yacht Owners
summary: Navigating the high seas isn't just about mastering the tides. It's also about managing wage-related disputes and staying buoyant in choppy legal waters.
body: Calm seas can quickly transform into tempests in the world of sailing, and it often starts not with thunder but a whisper: a single word — arresto. Such moments fall upon one like a heavy anchor, initiated when a crewmember raises wage or leave-related issues. Particularly prevalent in European ports and notably Italy, a judicial intervention can swiftly freeze a yacht's movement exposing the need for careful navigation through legal straits.

To tackle these tumultuous seas, understanding the context is pivotal. Realize that addressing these issues with indignation or merely principles can waste precious time or money. Understanding the language that resonates with judges, lawyers, and insurers can guide the vessel back to smoother waters.
Navigating through crew claims needs a meticulous and professional approach similar to an engine overhaul, requiring forethought and preparation. Three major lessons become apparent.

First—being prepared for release requires a mindset, not just a plan. Owners must proactively set up measures to easily meet wage claims. These include having the necessary financial securities, up-to-date powers of attorney, ready-to-sign security instruments, and a list of legal counsel in frequently visited ports.

Second—employment contracts are as much about geographic specificity as they are about the fine print. Laws vary; the place where services were rendered introduces its rules and regulations. Therefore, it's vital to maintain explicit mechanisms for wage and leave records and ensure there are no loopholes for disputes to fester.

Third—maintain routine documentation like payslips, leave ledgers, confirmations of leave, etc. These 'silent witnesses' hold more weight than the loudest of verbal disagreements. Navigating these areas with forethought and meticulousness reduces the likelihood of ending up before a judge.

Sailors are often prepared for storms, but the winds of wage disputes can be just as challenging. Preparation, geographic awareness, and documentation can help keep these issues in check and your ship sailing smoothly.

title: Marvel at the Arcadia A80: A Triumph in Luxury Yachting Crafted to Thrive Amidst Mediterranean Anchoring Restrictions
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Marvel at the Arcadia A80: A Triumph in Luxury Yachting Crafted to Thrive Amidst Mediterranean Anchoring Restrictions
summary: Lo and behold, the Arcadia A80, a revolutionary luxury yacht, crafted ingeniously to pack a 90-foot volume into a sleek 24m marvel.
body: Just when we thought the realm of luxury yachting had seen every possible innovation, along comes the Arcadia A80, ready to redefine our expectations. A lesson in smart, minimalist design, this savvy vessel cleverly offers the volume of a 90-footer in a compact 24m package, born out of new anchoring restrictions in popular Mediterranean locales.

The model brings novelty to its design by expanding the yacht's extremities, which results in a vertical, towering bow that extends from the waterline all the way to the flybridge, thus elongating the decks. Including an owner’s suite on the main deck, a feature seldom found on vessels under 90ft, luxuriously endowed with large hull windows and an ensuite bathroom, the A80 deserves applause.

The entire interior is decidedly conceived around the ethos of wellness, ringed by a fleet of curved, low-set furniture cloaked in textured fabrics, pale woods, and organic shapes. From the pilothouse bridge deck, stairs lead to an open flybridge, generously shielded by a long hardtop adorned with solar panels to minimize dependence on generators.

The A80’s peaceful ambiance complements its semi-displacement hull and a Volvo IPS1200 drivetrain, engineered with a focus on noise reduction and fuel efficiency. Despite its impressive volume, the yacht can still hit 24 knots.

In the world of luxury yachting, the Arcadia A80 reigns as proof that innovation, opulence, and practical, environment-friendly design can indeed co-exist. Its unparalleled combination of compact size, vast volume, and ingenious design assuredly places it in a class of its own.

title: As the Sailing Industry Evolves So Must Its Approach to Yacht Refitting
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: As the Sailing Industry Evolves So Must Its Approach to Yacht Refitting
summary: Paint and finish demands, labour shortages, and stringent regulations are shaping the complex reality of yacht refitting in the modern era.
body: In the ever-evolving world of sailing, a focal turning point has emerged: the refitting of large, high-profile yachts. More specifically, paint jobs and finishes lie at an interesting confluence of heightened expectations, regulatory necessities, and ground-level realities. While darker hull colours and near-new-build standards are trending, balancing these aspirations with the realities of pre-existing materials, working conditions, and time constraints makes for shark-infested waters.

Adding another dimension to this complex mix are environmental regulations that have introduced a plethora of requirements, impacting how paintwork projects are planned and executed. While these regulations are generally manageable, their repercussions become painfully palpable when end-results are not up to mark, leading to extensive rework, increased timelines and inflated costs.

A closer look at the situation suggests that with more paint moving through established cycles, more labour is tied up for longer periods. Consequently, more projects are less tolerant of delay — a ripple effect that will inevitably reverberate across the market.

The takeaway here isn't that the market is doomed but rather that it must adapt, and fast. Key industry players suggest solutions ranging from the use of more sustainable, quality-maintaining coating products for durability and flexibility to forecasting higher demand by roping in advance contracts for better project planning and cost control. Some even advocate searching for alternative coating solutions that offer scope for innovation and easy repairing options.
As we sail into the future, it's clear that yacht refitting will have to navigate through an ocean of challenges and transformations to stay afloat.

title: New Nimbus 495 Coupé Ushers in an Era of Seamless Sailing Along the Great Inland Waterways
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: New Nimbus 495 Coupé Ushers in an Era of Seamless Sailing Along the Great Inland Waterways
summary: The Nimbus 495 Coupé is set to reshape liveaboard cruising with its advanced features tailored for extended stays on water.
body: Nimbus has introduced yet another masterpiece, the Nimbus 495 Coupé. Unlike its flybridge counterparts, this vessel is designed specifically for extended liveaboard cruising, offering comfort, practicality, and understated elegance. It presents as a viable solution for those planning to explore Europe and America's Great Loop inland waterways.

The Nimbus 495 Coupé is built with a larger sunroof and exterior awning system. This structure affords the luxury of shading the saloon while maintaining ventilation. Furthermore, the removal of the flybridge staircase has cleared the way for a more spacious galley, accommodating two workers and offering additional storage space. Another new addition is the aft locker where wet gear can be stored safely, keeping the interior dry and tidy.

A unique feature of the Nimbus 495 Coupé is the electrically foldable mast which reduces the air draft to less than 11ft 6in. This modification opens up the possibility of traversing the inland waterways of Europe and America's Great Loop. The vessel sports a traditional mahogany interior, offering a warm ambience favoured by long-term liveaboard cruisers.

Equipped with an easy-to-navigate helm, wide starboard side deck, intuitive driver aids, and a spacious cockpit, the 495 Coupé is a breeze to drive, even for novices. It is crafted with a robust yet lightweight vacuum-infused hull that is designed for refined cruising. The optimized design and construction ensure low sound levels while cruising at high speeds.
With its diverse range of features, the Nimbus 495 Coupé revolutionises the concept of long-term cruising, bringing a new level of ease and comfort to the boating experience.

title: Viking Marine Frostbite Series 2 Captures Spirits at Dun Laoghaire Motor Yacht Club
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Viking Marine Frostbite Series 2 Captures Spirits at Dun Laoghaire Motor Yacht Club
summary: The Viking Marine Frostbite Series 2 recently unfolded under invigorating conditions at the Dun Laoghaire Motor Yacht Club, offering participants a thrilling sailing experience.
body: The East Coast was recently left ravished by ghastly sea squalls. However, on 8th February, despite the long shadow of the storm, the sky over Dun Laoghaire Motor Yacht Club greeted the Viking Marine Frostbite Series 2 participants with optimism. Indeed, the day saw the mercury touch double digits alongside favorable sailing conditions, including a level of sunshine that belied the grey dawn. As the sailors poured in, preparations for the day's races began in earnest. The conditions were so congenial, there were speculations about conducting three races.

Launching the race fest, a three-lap Olympic course was set. However, the PY Fleet was a bit eager at the start, causing a general recall. Meanwhile, ILCA 7s and 4s made a great start while the ILCA 6s meeting the same fate as the PY fleet. The tension in the air was palpable as the race officer reset the line and initiated a U-Flag start for both fleets all in the spirit of healthy competition.

In the PY Fleet, notably, the Fireball crewed by Frank Miller and Grattan Donnelly led by a clear minute over the Aero 7 command by Thomas Chaix. Their impressive performance strengthened the spirit of the event, making it a truly memorable day at sea.

title: The Third Stage of Estonian Ice Sailing Cup Sets A New Standard with Baltic's Best
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: The Third Stage of Estonian Ice Sailing Cup Sets A New Standard with Baltic's Best
summary: Bay of Pärnu, Estonia, delivered an unforgettable third stage of the Ice Sailing Cup Series, becoming a Baltic beacon for the sport.
body: From the 7th to 8th of February 2026, the shores of Pärnu Bay in Estonia magnificently staged the third stop in the esteemed Estonian Ice Sailing Cup Series. This thrilling competition drew in the region's most formidable ice sailors, consolidating the event's stature as a premier sailing showdown within the Baltic states. The event successfully attracted robust participation, recording a total of 49 competitors. They braced the icy Baltic waters in several international ice sailing classes such as DN, Ice Optimist, Monotype XV and the DN Junior category. A particularly positive sign was the weighty youth contingent, indicative of the sport's progressive surge amongst emerging sportsmen. The scale of talent and participation from Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania underscored this regatta's informal status as the Baltic Ice Sailing Championship. Testament to Estonia’s commitment to the sport, the event was seamlessly executed with the Race Committee going above and beyond to maintain an efficient and high-quality sporting environment. The conditions were icing on the cake, with about 40 cm of solid Baltic ice punctuated with soft snowy pockets, challenging the competitors and keeping them on their toes. A consistent north-easterly wind on both days maintained the thrill and adrenaline of the competition, while the pristine Pärnu Bay offered a perfect backdrop to this icy spectacle. The DN Class, often recognized as the crème de la crème of international ice sailing, saw the 2025 European Champion, Rasmus Maalinn, holding his ground with another hard-fought victory, cementing his status as a challenging contender to beat. Runners-up included Eigo Helimets and Hardi Laurits, rounding off an impressive DN fleet of 23 sailors.

title: Cruise into the Future: Benetti Launches Two Hybrid Superyachts Blending Luxury and Sustainability
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Cruise into the Future: Benetti Launches Two Hybrid Superyachts Blending Luxury and Sustainability
summary: Italian shipyard, Benetti, unveils two superyachts packed with hybrid power, epitomising the marriage of luxury and eco-loving ingenuity.
body: The legendary Benetti shipyard has once again made headlines in the yachting world. This time, it's not just the lengths they're going to in terms of luxury, but the lengths they're going to sustainably. The Italian shipyard has proudly launched two 67-metre superyachts boasting hybrid propulsion systems from its trailblazing B.Now series.

The first of these titans, christened Symmetry, made quite a splash. Three weeks later, its dashing sibling Dagger did the same. True marvels of marine engineering, these superyachts represent not just the extra mile in luxury but, significantly, a crucial stride towards more sustainable modes of transport at sea.

The exterior design of these aluminium and steel giants was crafted by longstanding collaborator, RWD. The minds behind Reymond Langton Design and Sinot Yacht Architecture & Design worked their magic on the interiors. The result? An exquisitely designed, conscientiously powered pair of mammoth yachts that truly capture the zeitgeist.

The elemental advantage of the hybrid propulsion system lies in reducing the yacht's environmental impact, simultaneously minimising vibrations and noise, whether the vessel is sailing or anchored. This ingenious system comprises three key components - main engines, generators, and a battery pack - which synergise variably to suit different cruising profiles. It provides for a smooth sailing experience where electricity can be generated by the engines, propulsion can be supported by the generators, and loading peaks or absolute silence can be ensured by the battery pack.

Further enhancing the user experience, both Symmetry and Dagger feature the shipyard's iconic Oasis Deck - a feat of design that creates a unique, seamless indoor-outdoor living space. All in all, the new B.Now 67Ms showcase the undeniable fact that sustainability can indeed dovetail flawlessly with luxury. This is an exciting time to be alive, especially for lovers of the sea.

title: Raven Rewrites the Atlantic with Record-Breaking RORC Transatlantic Victory
author: Michael Hodges
imageAlt: Raven Unleashed — When a Monohull Redefined the Atlantic
summary: The 2026 RORC Transatlantic Race will be remembered as the moment a new benchmark was laid down in offshore monohull sailing. The 34-metre Baltic 111 Raven didn’t just win — she rewrote the record book, claiming Monohull Line Honours, securing the IMA Transatlantic Trophy, and setting a new monohull race record on the 3,000-nautical-mile passage from Lanzarote to Antigua.
body: Crossing the finish line off English Harbour at close to 30 knots of boat speed, Raven completed the Atlantic crossing in six days and 22 hours, a performance that signals a decisive shift in what modern offshore monohulls are capable of. Light for her length, foil-assisted and engineered to sustain extreme average speeds over multiple days, Raven represents not just a fast yacht — but a new design philosophy coming of age.
Skippered by Damien Durchon, Raven arrived in Antigua controlled, composed and intact — a key detail in a race where outright pace must coexist with durability.

Raven was officially welcomed into Falmouth Harbour by The Hon. Charles “Max” Fernandez, Antigua’s Minister of Tourism & Economic Development, who congratulated the crew and presented the IMA Transatlantic Trophy to the first maxi yacht to finish.

Fernandez also highlighted the significance of Antigua as the new finishing destination for the RORC Transatlantic Race — a move already proving its appeal to elite offshore programmes and international crews.

For navigator Will Oxley, the achievement carries particular weight. Oxley previously navigated Comanche to the monohull record in the 2022 edition of the race — making him uniquely placed to judge Raven’s performance in context.

“It’s fascinating to compare Raven and Comanche,” Oxley explained. “Comanche remains the global benchmark for pure VMG downwind sailing. But Raven has clear advantages at certain angles — and in this race, which is largely a classic downwind Atlantic crossing, when we’re sailing our angles, we’re faster.”
“Where Comanche still has the edge is pure VMG, and that’s something we continue to work on. But what Raven has shown here sets a very serious benchmark.”
Crucially, the record was achieved without drama — a metric the team values highly.

“Before the start, I said I’d judge this race on three things,” Oxley added. “Boat condition, crew condition, and whether the time stood up against Atlantic benchmarks. We arrived with the boat and crew in great shape — and the time speaks for itself.”
Unlike fully flying foilers, Raven generates immense righting moment through her side foils while remaining largely in the water — blending foiling performance with offshore control.
For skipper Damien Durchon, that balance is fundamental.

“This boat is incredibly stable,” he said. “The better it performs, the safer it becomes. We generate huge righting moment from the foils, supported by ten tonnes of water ballast and a strong hull form.”
“If a foil stalls, the boat simply behaves like a conventional yacht. In many respects, Raven is safer than many offshore boats.”

“At 25 knots, it already feels fast,” Durchon continued. “At 30 knots and above, you’re moving faster than the waves themselves. You’re working through the sea rather than reacting to it. It’s demanding — but the boat remains remarkably manageable.”
Sailing Master Brad Jackson was quick to emphasise that Raven’s success wasn’t about headline peak speeds, but about sustained performance.

“If you finish a race like this in under seven days, a lot has gone right,” Jackson said. “The weather was excellent, but the boat is genuinely fast through the water. This wasn’t about living on the edge — it was about letting the boat do what it’s designed to do.”
Jackson also highlighted the importance of crew cohesion on such a technically advanced platform.

“This is a complicated boat, but the crew dynamic is very strong. Everyone knows their role. We’ve spent a lot of time learning this boat together, and this was the first time we really stepped up the intensity and treated it as a full race.”

Oxley echoed the sentiment: “People want to sail this boat because of the platform — but also because of the team. There’s no friction, the humour stays, and offshore that makes an enormous difference.”
For Project Manager Claes Nyloef, Raven is not an outlier — but a signpost.

“This is a way forward,” Nyloef said. “You get foiling performance without fully flying, which is critical for ocean racing. It’s efficient, reliable, and you can sail it like a normal boat — while accessing a completely new performance level.”
“When she starts accelerating, it doesn’t stop. That sensation used to belong only to multihulls. Now you’re feeling it on a monohull of this size — and it’s extraordinary.”
Finishing at full flight
The race ended exactly as it had been sailed — with precision and confidence.
“It was a very dark night coming into Antigua,” Oxley recalled. “No moon, shifting breeze, changing pressure. We wanted to call the layline right.”
“With a bit of practice and a bit of luck, we nailed it — crossing the line doing over 30 knots. That was a pretty special way to end the race.”

“We said before the start that we’d do this in seven days,” he added. “We did it in six days and 22 hours. That tells us we understand this boat now. There’s still room to improve, but this race proved the concept.”

Raven’s performance secured Monohull Line Honours, the IMA Transatlantic Trophy, and set the benchmark IRC corrected time to beat. While challengers such as Palanad 4 remain well positioned under IRC, few boats can match Raven’s blend of speed, stability and consistency.
“This was the first transatlantic race for both the boat and the owner,” Durchon reflected. “To set a record on your first attempt is something very special.”
As Raven came to rest in Antigua, one conclusion was unavoidable. This was not just a race win.
It was a statement of intent from a new generation of offshore monohull.

title: Experiencing Luxury at Sea: Forte 47, High-End Aluminium Yacht Nears Completion
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Experiencing Luxury at Sea: Forte 47, High-End Aluminium Yacht Nears Completion
summary: Forte Yachts, Italy's latest high-end brand introduces its first offering, the Forte 47—a state-of-the-art aluminium weekender yacht with completion on the horizon.
body: Once only a concept unveiled at Cannes, the Forte 47 is now a breath away from completion. This debut model from Forte Yachts brandishes a trendy blend of luxury and performance—an elegant testimony to high-end Italian yacht craftsmanship. Fashioned entirely from aluminium, the yacht's aesthetic is characterized by a vertical bow, minimalist exterior lines, and a full-beam hardtop that encompasses more than half the vessel’s length, adding not just style but functionality.

Below deck, the yacht houses two elegantly designed cabins complemented by two proper bathrooms, ensuring a comfortable stay and privacy for guests. May it be the daring Gran Turismo model armed with triple 600hp Mercury outboards or the Lounge Deck variant equipped with full-height glazing, an enclosed saloon and twin Volvo Penta IPS 800 inboard diesel engines—pick your poison. The Forte 47 does not compromise on speed, boasting a top speed of 45 knots.

This vessel, set to redefine luxury yachting, is a testament to the innovation of Italian marine craftsmanship and the commitment of Forte Yachts to deliver unparalleled sea experience. With the Forte 47, sailing is not just an adventure—it’s an indulgence.

title: Two Visions, One Ocean: Raven and Be Cool Set to Define the 2026 RORC Transatlantic Race
author: Michael Hodges
imageAlt: 2026 RORC Transatlantic Race
summary: Two Visions, One Ocean: Raven and Be Cool Set the Tone for the 2026 RORC Transatlantic Race The RORC Transatlantic Race has always thrived on contrast. It is a race where outright pace meets endurance, where innovation rubs shoulders with tradition, and where vastly different yachts are measured by the same unforgiving yardstick: three thousand miles of Atlantic Ocean.
body: The fleet lined up off Marina Lanzarote on 11 January 2026, few pairings will capture that spirit better than Raven and Be Cool — two maxi yachts that could scarcely be more different in philosophy, yet share a single ambition: to cross the Atlantic fast, safely and competitively.

One is razor-sharp, foil-assisted and engineered for sustained high averages. The other is powerful, refined and resolutely owner-focused, blending luxury and performance in a way only a Swan can. Together, they underline exactly why this race matters — and why it remains one of offshore sailing’s most compelling proving grounds.

At 34 metres, Raven is very much a statement of intent. Built by Baltic Yachts and designed by Botin Partners, she sits firmly at the cutting edge of modern offshore design. Light for her length, foil-assisted and paired with approximately ten tonnes of water ballast, Raven has been conceived around one central idea: average speed wins ocean races.

Although Raven has already logged more than 18,000 nautical miles and crossed the Atlantic twice on delivery and passage making, the 2026 RORC Transatlantic will be her first true competitive ocean campaign. For project manager Klabbe Nylof, that distinction matters.

“This is the first time Raven is being asked real racing questions offshore,” he explains. “We’ve done long passages and pushed the boat hard, but racing for days on end is different. Consistency, resilience and system management suddenly matter as much as headline numbers.”

Those numbers, however, are impressive. Raven has already exceeded 30 knots and, more importantly, can sustain speeds in the 25–27 knot range for long periods. In the right conditions, that translates into 600-mile days — territory that until recently belonged to much larger platforms.

Crucially, Raven’s foils are designed to generate righting moment rather than pure lift. It is a subtle but important distinction, allowing the yacht to sail flatter and more efficiently without becoming dependent on foils for control.
“Redundancy offshore is everything,” says Nylof. “The boat remains strong and controllable even without foil assistance. That confidence is essential when you’re days from land.”
With Damien Duchon skippering, Will Oxley navigating and Brad Jackson managing the crew, Raven arrives in Lanzarote with an experienced offshore team — but with expectations carefully tempered.
“This race is about learning,” Nylof admits. “Proving reliability, understanding how the boat behaves when pushed continuously, and unlocking the next phase of what Raven can do.”

If Raven represents the sharp edge of innovation, Be Cool offers an equally persuasive counterpoint. At 36 metres and displacing around 136 tonnes, the Swan 128 is a performance superyacht in the truest sense — capable of crossing oceans with authority while remaining elegant, manageable and deeply comfortable.

Designed by German Frers and built by Nautor Swan, Be Cool blends proven offshore pedigree with a modern approach to owner sailing. For Boat Captain Luca Serra, the RORC Transatlantic Race is the logical next step in the yacht’s evolution.

“This will be Be Cool’s first competitive race,” Serra explains, “but the project itself is already very experienced. We’ve sailed over 5,000 miles, including from Finland to the Mediterranean. Now it’s time to test the boat properly in a serious offshore environment.”
Serra knows the Be Cool lineage well, having previously held the same role aboard the Swan 98 of the same name. But the 128 marks a significant shift in concept.

“The layout is reversed — owner forward, crew aft,” he says. “We removed the structural backstay and fitted a self-tacking jib. The goal was to make the boat safer, easier and more enjoyable to sail, including for the owner.”

Unlike Raven, Be Cool carries no water ballast. Instead, she relies on displacement, hull form and sail plan to deliver her performance. Top speeds sit around 17–18 knots, but offshore success comes from consistency rather than spikes. A steady 12-knot average and regular 350-mile days are very much her comfort zone.
Under IRC, the contrast becomes stark. Raven owes Be Cool more than 700 seconds per hour — a reminder that these yachts are playing very different games within the same race.
Crew selection reflects that philosophy. “We want to keep the spirit of a friends’ boat,” Serra says. “There will be four or five top professionals, but cohesion matters more than star power.”
Three watches of five, clear leadership and disciplined routines form the backbone of the campaign. “Good habits win ocean races,” Serra adds. “Over 3,000 miles, aggression fades. Structure endures.”

What unites Raven and Be Cool is not design, speed or rating — it is the nature of the RORC Transatlantic Race itself. This is not a straight-line drag race. It demands weather judgement, sail management, discipline and the ability to keep both boat and crew functioning under pressure, day after day.
“This race strips everything back,” says Nylof. “It shows how well you manage the boat, the systems and the people. That’s the real test.”
Serra agrees. “Crossing the Atlantic in company, in a proper race, makes sense. It’s safer, more engaging and far more meaningful than doing it alone. This is where you truly learn a boat.”

In many ways, these two yachts frame the modern offshore conversation perfectly. One pushes the frontier of sustained speed through foils and cutting-edge engineering. The other demonstrates how a refined performance superyacht can race an ocean competitively without sacrificing versatility or comfort.

The 2026 RORC Transatlantic Race, run in association with the International Maxi Association and Yacht Club de France, already boasts more than 20 confirmed entries — many of them among the most remarkable yachts afloat.
When Raven and Be Cool line up in Lanzarote this January, they will not just be racing each other. They will be showcasing two compelling answers to the same timeless offshore question:
What does fast really mean, when the ocean decides the rules?

Designed by German Frers and built by Nautor Swan, Be Cool blends proven offshore pedigree with a modern approach to owner sailing. For Boat Captain Luca Serra, the RORC Transatlantic Race is the logical next step in the yacht’s evolution.

“This will be Be Cool’s first competitive race,” Serra explains, “but the project itself is already very experienced. We’ve sailed over 5,000 miles, including from Finland to the Mediterranean. Now it’s time to test the boat properly in a serious offshore environment.”
Serra knows the Be Cool lineage well, having previously held the same role aboard the Swan 98 of the same name. But the 128 marks a significant shift in concept.

“The layout is reversed — owner forward, crew aft,” he says. “We removed the structural backstay and fitted a self-tacking jib. The goal was to make the boat safer, easier and more enjoyable to sail, including for the owner.”

Unlike Raven, Be Cool carries no water ballast. Instead, she relies on displacement, hull form and sail plan to deliver her performance. Top speeds sit around 17–18 knots, but offshore success comes from consistency rather than spikes. A steady 12-knot average and regular 350-mile days are very much her comfort zone.
Under IRC, the contrast becomes stark. Raven owes Be Cool more than 700 seconds per hour — a reminder that these yachts are playing very different games within the same race.
Crew selection reflects that philosophy. “We want to keep the spirit of a friends’ boat,” Serra says. “There will be four or five top professionals, but cohesion matters more than star power.”
Three watches of five, clear leadership and disciplined routines form the backbone of the campaign. “Good habits win ocean races,” Serra adds. “Over 3,000 miles, aggression fades. Structure endures.”

What unites Raven and Be Cool is not design, speed or rating — it is the nature of the RORC Transatlantic Race itself. This is not a straight-line drag race. It demands weather judgement, sail management, discipline and the ability to keep both boat and crew functioning under pressure, day after day.
“This race strips everything back,” says Nylof. “It shows how well you manage the boat, the systems and the people. That’s the real test.”
Serra agrees. “Crossing the Atlantic in company, in a proper race, makes sense. It’s safer, more engaging and far more meaningful than doing it alone. This is where you truly learn a boat.”

In many ways, these two yachts frame the modern offshore conversation perfectly. One pushes the frontier of sustained speed through foils and cutting-edge engineering. The other demonstrates how a refined performance superyacht can race an ocean competitively without sacrificing versatility or comfort.

The 2026 RORC Transatlantic Race, run in association with the International Maxi Association and Yacht Club de France, already boasts more than 20 confirmed entries — many of them among the most remarkable yachts afloat.
When Raven and Be Cool line up in Lanzarote this January, they will not just be racing each other. They will be showcasing two compelling answers to the same timeless offshore question:
What does fast really mean, when the ocean decides the rules?

title: Discover Klaipeda's Allure: ORC European Championship 2026 Lays out Discounted Accommodations and Traditional Gastronomy
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Discover Klaipeda's Allure: ORC European Championship 2026 Lays out Discounted Accommodations and Traditional Gastronomy
summary: The ORC European Championship 2026 gains steam as Klaipeda rolls out a comprehensive hospitality program, offering exclusive discounts and a warm Lithuanian welcome to the sailors.
body: Warm welcome signs are set up from Klaipeda, the vibrant Lithuanian city, as it gears up to host the ORC European Championship 2026. The city has rolled out an impressive hospitality program, extending discounted accommodation and dining options to the sailing teams. Even the first 20 international teams registering get an added treat — a traditional Lithuanian dinner for their entire crew. Klaipeda, a city rooted deep in its maritime traditions since 1252, is proud to host the championship. Not only does the city provide excellent offshore racing opportunities, but its location at the heart of Lithuania also makes it a prime cruising destination. Mantas Klimantavicius, the head of the event's organizing committee, shared, 'We have exclusive accommodation and dining offers specifically designed for registered participants. Teams will discover Klaipeda is a truly hospitable city, with most accommodations being central or near the yacht club.' Beyond the exclusive discount offers, the city is also preparing an exceptional shoreside program, promising a celebration of Lithuanian culture, A-level concerts featuring internationally recognized performers and a festive atmosphere throughout the week. The regatta village will double as an entertainment and education hub suitable for participating sailors and their families. Ecky von der Mosel, ORC Deputy Chairman, commented, 'I met a professional team of event organizers in Klaipeda. They are fully committed to hosting a successful event both on and off the water. I'm really looking forward to it!' The championship promises to be a memorable affair combining top-notch offshore racing with enriching cultural experiences ashore. Participants can look forward to exploring the Curonian Spit, a UNESCO World Heritage Site just across the lagoon from Klaipeda, accessible both by land and water. The event will also commemorate 100 fulfilling years of offshore sailing in Lithuania, fueled by a proud maritime heritage. So, get ready to sail into history!

title: Discover the Rising Stars: Sweden's New 49erFX Team's Meteoric Rise to Glory

Vilma, a silver medalist from the Paris Olympics, brought her experience to the table, steering their team with deftness while guiding Ebba, her less experienced yet eager-to-learn partner. Showcasing an exemplary display of focussed learning and fluid collaboration, the duo managed to claim their very first silver medal at the 2026 World Championships. This episode of their journey serves as a beacon for sailors across classes, illuminating the path to success in the highly competitive world of sailing.

title: Lürssen Superyacht Jassi Makes Its Grand Debut: Key Features and Intriguing Facts
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Lürssen Superyacht Jassi Makes Its Grand Debut: Key Features and Intriguing Facts
summary: German shipyard Lürssen's long-awaited 102.4-metre superyacht Jassi has finally been launched, showcasing a hint of luxury and nautical prowess
body: For the first time since its technical launch in December of 2023, Lürssen's superyacht Jassi has surfaced from the Rendsburg facilities in Germany. Still veiled in mystery, the full-displacement motor yacht finally makes a public appearance, punctuating the skyline with an impressive 102.4-metre silhouette stylised in steel and aluminium.

Jassi, originally dubbed 'Project Jassj', stands out with its unique exterior and interior design weaving a tale of sophistication and elegance. The artistic genius of the British design studio RWD is apparent in every feature of the yacht. This floating retreat is capable of accommodating up to 22 guests within its 11 lavish cabins. Additionally, the yacht comes fully staffed with a professional crew of 37.

This floating marvel was sold in 2021 by Moran Yacht & Ship, beginning its construction journey the following year as per details from BOATPro. As of now, all eyes are set on the much-awaited delivery, anticipated in the third quarter of 2026.

The launch of Jassi places Lürssen shipyard on the map, as the company currently has 10 more yachts measuring over 100 metres under construction. This launch punctuates a period of bustling activity for the shipyard, fresh off the news that its 110-metre new build, O3, was undergoing sea trials. All said, the Jassi marks a promising new era of maritime luxury and intrigue.

title: Somnium, the Award-Winning Feadship Motor Yacht, Finds a New Owner: A Deep Dive into its Serene Charm
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Somnium, the Award-Winning Feadship Motor Yacht, Finds a New Owner: A Deep Dive into its Serene Charm
summary: The renowned 55.2-metre Feadship motor yacht Somnium has found a new skipper, ready to embark on luxurious adventures in the high seas.
body: Signal the trumpets and hoist the sails, the exquisitely designed Feadship motor yacht, Somnium has found a new owner. Representing the seller were Feadship Resale's Folkert Schoots and senior sales broker Alex Lees-Buckley of Camper & Nicholsons. The award-winning yacht boasts a uniquely elegant look, with a sleek, all-aluminium Studio De Voogt exterior and commanding naval architecture by Feadship De Voogt.

To augment her Dutch build, Italian design studio FM - Architettura d’interni was enlisted to craft her interiors, drawing inspiration from the untamed splendour of the Galápagos Islands. Her bespoke design was recognisably superior, earning her a much-coveted Neptune at the 2022 World Superyacht Awards. And as far as price tags go, Somnium commanded an impressive €57,500,000, with VAT covered by the seller.

Among her highlights, Somnium's exterior decks are framed with a standout feature - a 9,000-litre pool offering breathtaking views of the horizon. The pool, equipped with a counter-current jet for fitness aficionados, also cleverly transforms into a lounge or entertaining area. Furthermore, she embodies the true spirit of sea adventures with a dedicated dive store and an enclosed tender garage. For privacy-seeking sun worshippers, the panoramic sundeck comes handily equipped with a Jacuzzi, sunpads and a dining table. With twin 1,224hp MTU engines, Somnium proudly manoeuvres the waves at a top speed of 15.4 knots and a cruising speed of 12 knots, whisking you and your loved ones away for adventures of a lifetime.

With the promise of such unparalleled luxury on the anvil, it is not surprising that the Bilgin 170 Superyacht has been noted for its significant charter potential.

title: Exploring the Fascinating Chronicles of the 37th America's Cup Through its Latest Arbitration Record
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Exploring the Fascinating Chronicles of the 37th America's Cup Through its Latest Arbitration Record
summary: Discover the captivating details of the 37th America's Cup as unveiled in its comprehensive arbitration book—a record of decisions, documents, and heated discussions.
body: The 37th America's Cup is known to have spun some truly enthralling controversies and debates. But nothing truly captures the entire spectacle quite as comprehensively as its sixth arbitration record. Edited by Professor Henry Peter, a distinguished panelist for multiple previous Cups and versed with the nitty-gritty details of the tournament, the document presents an indispensable look into the numerous decisions and official papers that marked the 2024 America's Cup in Barcelona. With the risk of crucial documentation being pulled off the Internet after the Cup concludes, this book stands as an unwavering beacon of reference and reliability for all Cup enthusiasts.

Every edition features a forward-looking view by the Arbitration Panel, examining the potential flow of the upcoming Cup. The sixth edition makes a step further, raising questions about the enforceability of a promise made in AC37 to continue using AC75 in AC38 during the 38th America’s Cup.

One remarkable section decodes the Deed of Gift ruling the America's Cup. It shares the ultimate classification of the Deed, complemented by pictures of the initial handwritten deed from 1857. To eliminate inaccuracies, a new transcription of the Deed was prepared with inputs from Cup historian R. Steven Tsuchiya and his colleague Dr. Hamish Ross.

A separate segment discusses the issue of a missing assignment and acceptance agreement, required by the Deed of Gift, to transition the Trophy. In this case, the agreement was not signed until 2024, despite dates indicating it should have been done in 2017. This led to a fundamental agreement that jurisdiction would remain with the New York Supreme Court, not the current defender's court system.

Among various captivating side notes, the book underlines the top speeds recorded by different teams during recent America's Cups, highlighting INEOS Britannia as the fastest team in the 2024 Louis Vuitton Cup. The volume is a treasure trove for any individual intrigued by the riveting history of the America's Cup and an essential read for commentators.

title: Supreme Turf to Lavish Turquoise: NFL Owners Rule the Seas On Off-Seasons
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Supreme Turf to Lavish Turquoise: NFL Owners Rule the Seas On Off-Seasons
summary: Off-seasons for NFL team owners invoke a different kind of competition; that of who boasts the largest and most extravagant superyacht. This piece delves into these floating marvels.
body: In the football off-season, NFL owners switch from the rough and tumble of the gridiron to the serenity and luxury of the sea. This exclusive yet growing club of NFL team owners is commissioning some of the most exquisite superyachts in existence, turning heads in harbors worldwide.

For instance, the Shahid Khan owned, 122-meter Lürssen yacht Kismet, was one of the most discussed builds of 2024. With extraordinary living spaces such as a semi-underwater indoor cinema and a Balinese spa, it's no wonder she became highly talked about. Capturing the opulence of Versailles' Hall of Mirrors in her main saloon, Kismet was crowned at the 2025 BOAT International Design and Innovation Awards. Her charter fee is testament to her grandeur, asking an eye-watering €3,000,000 per week.

The list of high-end superyacht owners does not end with Khan. Arthur Blank, the owner of the Atlanta Falcons, took delivery of two considerable superyachts over the last few years. The staggering 90-meter Oceanco DreAMBoat (now Shodan) was delivered in 2019, and swiftly followed by its 111-meter successor in 2022. These yachts further cement the status and power that these team owners have, not just on land, but also at sea.

The luxury, the extravagance, and the sheer size of these superyachts signify more than individual wealth. They are manifestations of their esteemed stand in society, their triumphs in the field, and their unending affinity towards the mystery and soothing calmness of the sea. Each NFL owner's superyacht tells a story, capturing the essence of their personality, and telegraphs their achievements in the most flamboyant of ways.

title: The Mangusta Oceano 44, Hull #8: An Unmissable Opportunity to Bypass the Waitlist
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: The Mangusta Oceano 44, Hull #8: An Unmissable Opportunity to Bypass the Waitlist
summary: Anticipation is brewing for the launch of the Mangusta Oceano 44, Hull #8, a convincing proof of Italian craftsmanship set for summer 2027 delivery.
body: The wait is almost over for the much-anticipated launch of Mangusta Oceano 44, Hull #8, promising a colossal leap in luxury sea travel. The visionary Italian shipyard is back with this unparalleled marvel, presenting a covetable opportunity to bypass the waiting list typically associated with large displacement yachts. This rare chance to takeover a well-advanced construction timeline affords potential buyers input on final details. Crafted with an extraordinary blend of steel hull and an aluminum superstructure, the Oceano 44 Hull #8 is engineered for long-range cruising. Flaunting twin MTU 12V 2000 M86 engines, with a top speed of 15 knots, she exudes an harmonious blend of comfort and performance. For those with a penchant for aesthetics, prepare to be swept away by the stunning interiors. The warm, modern material palette compels with a combination of oak and rosewood, parquet flooring, and Calacatta Gold marble detailing. An open plan main deck salon elegantly sits alongside a formal dining area, providing an ideal setting for both family use and entertaining. The vessel plays host to five en-suite staterooms for up to 12 guests. The owner's suite evokes awe with panoramic views and an en-suite bathroom. The lower deck comes equipped with two queen staterooms and two twin cabins, ensuring ample space for guests. Every corner is designed with a preference for natural light, enhancing the calming ambience onboard. From the integrated pool luxuriously nestling within the forward bow lounge to the sundeck arranged for open-air dining, every portion of the yacht promises panache and tranquillity. The aft lounge extends to the water's edge, providing a seamless waterfront platform for swimming and watersports. With a respected builder, proven platform, and well-progressed build schedule, the Oceano 44 Hull #8 stands as a mighty testament to marine expertise. The summer 2027 launch offers buyers an advanced new-build contract, allowing for last-minute refinements without the worry of construction risk or timeline uncertainty.

title: Runners & Riders Ready for the 2026 RORC Transatlantic Race from Lanzarote to Antigua
author: Michael Hodges
imageAlt: RORC Transatlantic Race 2026
summary: Runners & Riders Line Up for the 2026 RORC Transatlantic Race
body: Lanzarote to Antigua | Start Sunday 11 January 2026

The stage is set in the Canary Islands. On Sunday 11 January 2026, the RORC Transatlantic Race will once again send a diverse and compelling fleet westward from Marina Lanzarote, launching 21 teams on a 3,000-nautical-mile Atlantic crossing to Antigua.

Organised by the Royal Ocean Racing Club in association with the International Maxi Association and the Yacht Club de France, the race is both an early-season cornerstone and a statement event in the global offshore calendar. Supported by Calero Marinas and the Antigua and Barbuda Tourism Authority, the 2026 edition blends elite performance, Corinthian ambition and genuine ocean adventure.
Start day: precision before the horizon opens

The fleet will assemble off Arrecife, with monohulls starting at 12:30 UTC, followed by multihulls at 12:40. All competitors must round a turning mark off Puerto Calero before committing to the open Atlantic. From there, the fleet fans out into trade-wind tactics, routing decisions and the long, disciplined work of offshore racing.

Crews from 19 nations will line up across cutting-edge monohulls, high-performance multihulls, performance cruisers and smaller offshore racers. At the sharp end, elapsed-time contenders may finish in under a week; at the other, smaller boats will embrace the full Atlantic rhythm over two weeks or more.
The prize that matters: IRC Overall

While line honours grab headlines, the beating heart of the race is the RORC Transatlantic Race Trophy, awarded to the IRC overall winner. Since the inaugural edition in 2014, IRC has proven its levelling power — smallest to largest boats have all claimed the top step. Strategy, rating efficiency, crew work and endurance matter as much as raw speed.

Palanad 4, a new scow-bow, canting-keel 50-footer, arrives with intent. Owner Antoine Magre knows how to win, having tasted success with Palanad 3 in this race and at the Rolex Fastnet. “The goal is simple: go as fast as possible,” says Magre. “Focused crew, smart weather calls, and exploiting the boat’s strengths.”
Veteran navigator Juan Vila (aboard Ino Noir) underlines the appeal: “A January trade-wind Atlantic is very special for any navigator.” Over this distance, every system and decision is exposed.
Multihull line honours: speed at the edge

At the front of the multihull fleet, the spotlight falls on MOD70 trimarans Argo and Zoulou. For more than a decade, MOD70 duels have defined the race’s outright speed narrative — fast, physical and unforgiving.

“It’s an exhilarating experience to travel that fast for 3,000 miles,” says Jason Carroll (Argo), contesting his third edition. Ned Collier Wakefield (Zoulou) expects a tight fight: “If it turns into a downwind drag race, we’ll be glued together. Two years of refining foils, rake and balance has closed the gap.”
Monohull line honours: power with pedigree

On the monohull side, history looms large. Previous winners such as Lucky have set formidable benchmarks. This year, eyes turn to Raven, the radical Baltic 111. Though already Atlantic-tested, 2026 marks her first competitive transatlantic. Project manager Klabbe Nylof is clear-eyed: “This race is about consistency, resilience and learning how the whole system works under pressure, day after day.”

Racing under IRC and for the Superyacht Class Trophy are the fleet’s largest boats: Be Cool and Linnea Aurora. The Swan 128 Be Cool brings refined power and the ability to rack up big daily miles with civilised offshore living. Linnea Aurora, a Hoek-designed 128-footer launched in 2024, pairs classic elegance with modern performance, having already shown her pedigree with inshore success at the Superyacht Cup Palma 2025. Together, they demonstrate how the race has become a proving ground for superyachts that want to race the Atlantic, not merely cross it.
The human fleet

Beyond trophies and speed graphs lie the stories that give the race its depth. Ari Huusela and Annika Paasikivi on the Finnish Sun Fast 3300 Stimmy sail with a philosophy that transcends results: “Enjoy the sailing and finish safely.” Family legacy drives Andrew & Sam Hall (Jackknife) and Xavier & Alexandre Bellouard (Maxitude). Youthful curiosity powers teams like Walross 4, where a largely student crew embraces the Atlantic as classroom and crucible.
Antigua beckons — and records too

Finishing in Antigua opens a fresh chapter and a real chance at new elapsed-time records for both monohulls and multihulls. It also provides a natural bridge into a Caribbean campaign, with the RORC Nelson’s Cup Series and the RORC Caribbean 600 following in February. Few preparation pathways sharpen a crew like a hard Atlantic crossing straight into a 600-mile classic.
The race ahead

As the fleet prepares to depart Marina Lanzarote on 11 January 2026, anticipation is high. Whether chasing outright speed, IRC supremacy, or a deeply personal crossing, the 2026 RORC Transatlantic Race promises competition, camaraderie and the kind of miles that leave a mark long after Antigua’s palms come into view.

Prepare to set sail into oceans of knowledge and inspiration at the RYA Dinghy Show. Plot the course and see you there!

title: Meet the new Windy SR77: The largest craft in Windy's fleet that captivates with superyacht luxury and dynamic design.
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Meet the new Windy SR77: The largest craft in Windy's fleet that captivates with superyacht luxury and dynamic design.
summary: Discover Windy’s ambitious new undertaking, the SR77, a luxurious seafaring marvel poised to redefine the paradigm of superyacht design.
body: Windy, a name synonymous with luxury and innovation in watercraft construction, has embarked on its most daring venture yet. The Windy SR77, soon to be the crown jewel in the Windy fleet, promises to tantalise even the most discerning patrons with its impeccable marriage of superior performance and refined aesthetics. Crafted with precision and vision by the renowned Malcolm McKeon, the Windy SR77 directs a meaningful departure from the minimalist contours of its metallic siblings. Sweeping curves, concealed hull windows and a sleek hardtop constitute its advanced exterior, while stackable glass side doors render the enclosed helm area delightfully permeable to the gentle tryst of weather. Powering this marine titan is a pair of 1,800hp V12 MANs, mated to waterjets that effectively cut down on resistance at high speeds, bolstering its razor-sharp performance credentials. Yet, as much as it thrives on speed, the Windy SR77 is engineered with a heart for endurance. Its substantial 8,000-litre fuel reserve promises an impressive cruising range of 600nm, clocking in speeds of 30 knots or more. The vessel fashions an extensive open aft deck, wide walkaround side decks, and a sunbed-equipped bow for those sun-kissed days at sea. A Transformer stern platform permits easy dips into the sea, complete with a shower to rinse and a sunbed for tanning afterwards, crowning the Windy SR77 as an unparalleled 'fun-in-the-sun machine'. With completion slated for 2028 at Windy's Swedish yard in Vastervik, the interior of each SR77 is left to the discretion of the owner. From the choice of lounge and galley layouts to the number of ensuites and crew cabins, every Windy SR77 is a canvas awaiting personal touches. As luxury, performance, and personalisation converge in the Windy SR77, the future of superyacht design indeed appears all set for a revolutionary makeover.

title: ER Yacht Design Introduces MedEx, a Revolutionary 40m Explorer Yacht Built for Mediterranean Escapades
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: ER Yacht Design Introduces MedEx, a Revolutionary 40m Explorer Yacht Built for Mediterranean Escapades
summary: ER Yacht Design, a Vancouver-based studio, proudly unveils the MedEx, a 40-metre yacht designed with emblematic Mediterranean voyages in mind.
body: ER Yacht Design, a revered name in the world of sailing, proudly presents MedEx, a novel sailing development packed with luxury features. Designed as a maritime limousine, the 40-metre vessel sails head-high with a 9.5-metre beam and an exclusive draught of just two metres for easy access to shallow waters.

True to the concept of Mediterranean cruising, the MedEx revolutionises the boating experience with impeccably designed social spaces for enjoyable day cruising. The vessel caters to the need for luxury with its open deck areas featuring sleek removable sunshade covers, a jacuzzi, storage provisions for tenders and toys, and even an optional certified helicopter landing area.

Underlying these opulent features, the yacht intelligently capitalises on beach club configurations that extend over the water, adding to the usable deck space. Alongside supporting swim-lovers and social butterflies, these foldable side terraces accrue added advantage in hosting larger gatherings when necessary.

Aboard MedEx, living quarters are a lavish galore for 10 guests across five double cabins, four of which are located on the main deck. The owner's suite enjoys a consummate position at the aft-quarter on the bridge deck, adjacent to the optional helideck and an exclusive entrance.

Below the deck, the yacht spotlights functional spaces for 10 crew members alongside technical spaces and storage. The vessel is programmed with zero-speed stabilisers and a bow thruster, boosting comfort and manoeuvrability. Furthermore, it promises an estimated range of 5,500 nautical miles reinforcing its touring capabilities with cruise rates at 10.5 knots.

title: Navigate the High Seas with Confidence: A Comprehensive Guide to Using Buoyage
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Navigate the High Seas with Confidence: A Comprehensive Guide to Using Buoyage
summary: Avid seafarer and boating expert, Jon Mendez, unveils the secrets of navigating with buoyage, an essential skill every sailor must master.
body: As the saying goes, 'know the ropes and you'll sail a boat, know the buoys and you'll navigate the sea.' Jon Mendez, a veteran sailor and boating enthusiast, shares his insights on understanding buoyage to reassure either first-time sailers or seasoned voyagers.

Buoyage is a universal language for seafarers and knowing how to interpret and use it is crucial for safe navigation. Countries typically adopt either inland or coastal systems, with the former usually starting beyond the first sea lock. The coastal systems, however, are further divided into IALA A and B systems. The differentiation lies primarily in the color of the marks, while the shapes generally remain consistent.

System A, encompassing much of Europe, Australia and New Zealand, adopts the opposite color convention, with red pillar or can-shaped buoys on the port side and green cones on starboard, both illuminated with matching colors at night. An easy mnemonic for remembering this is that when your boat’s port and starboard navigation lights match the buoyage, you're making an inbound journey into a port.

Both systems employ safe water marks and isolated danger marks. These are crucial for avoiding hazards while at sea, indicated by their distinct colors and shapes during the day, and their unique light sequences at night. Studying these light sequences is absolutely imperative for those venturing out after dark.

Sailing is a dance between the wind and the water, but buoyage is the choreographer that makes sure no one misses a step. Confidently navigate your way to your next sailing adventure by mastering its intricacies and codes.

title: Southern Escape Complete as the 2026 RORC Transatlantic Fleet Locks into the Trade Winds
author: Michael Hodges
imageAlt: RORC Transatlantic Fleet Locks into the Trade Winds
summary: Three days into the 2026 RORC Transatlantic Race, the fleet has made its collective decision — and it’s the decision that has shaped Atlantic crossings for generations. Every boat has committed to the southern escape from the Canary Islands, pressing down the African coast before turning west for Antigua, avoiding the lighter air to the north and positioning early for the trade winds that will define the race.
body: Since departing Lanzarote on Sunday, the fleet initially compressed along the North African shoreline, bows edging steadily southwest as the wind gradient strengthened. By Day 3, that compression had eased. Courses opened, spacing increased, and the race slipped into its first true offshore phase — long miles, systems checks, watch routines and the steady accumulation of distance across open water.
This is where the RORC Transatlantic Race begins to reveal its character.
Argo and Zoulou light the blue touchpaper

At the sharp end, the MOD70 trimarans Argo and Zoulou are already deep into their element. With the breeze building, both boats have been posting eye-catching numbers, regularly pushing into the high twenties and touching over 30 knots as they run into stronger pressure.

As of 1010 UTC on Day 3, Argo held an advantage of around 40 nautical miles over Zoulou, with both multihulls entering a wind band that promises sustained, high-speed running over the next several days. The tone has been set early — wet decks, relentless pace and an Atlantic that suddenly feels very wide indeed.
“We’re still going downwind, which is good — 1700 miles to go and life on board is good,” said Sam Goodchild from Argo. “It’s a bit bumpy, which actually makes driving quite fun.”
Crewmate Charles Ogletree echoed the sentiment: “Argo is ripping along. It’s very wet in the big waves, but we’re having fun — and we’re nearly halfway to Antigua already.”
Raven commits to high-mode efficiency

Among the monohulls, Raven continues to assert herself at the head of the IRC fleet. Over the past 24 hours she logged a formidable 550-nautical-mile day, averaging 22.92 knots, while sailing a noticeably higher mode than many of her rivals.
This is Raven at her most efficient — operating at her best VMG angle and fully exploiting the benefits of her foils rather than chasing lower, faster-looking angles.

Navigator Will Oxley explained the logic: “We’re sailing a higher angle — maybe 130 degrees compared to others at 145 — so we’re definitely sailing more miles. But that’s Raven’s VMG mode. If we sail lower, we slow down, just like a multihull.”

“The sails are trimmed to apparent wind angle, and most of the time we have very little heel. Communication between the driver, trimmers and foil controller is all about staying locked into that apparent wind, with the traveller constantly adjusted to maintain the right heel angle.”
It’s disciplined, repeatable sailing — exactly what long Atlantic races reward.
Palanad 4 leads the IRC numbers

Just behind Raven, Palanad 4, skippered by Antoine Magre, is sailing a quietly impressive and measured race. At this early stage, she sits IRC overall leader on corrected time, demonstrating the consistency and positioning that so often matter more than raw pace over 3,000 miles.
“Conditions have been fantastic so far — clear nights, big stars and more breeze than we expected,” said Magre. “The boat is right on her polars and we’re very happy with how she’s performing.”

“Strong trade winds mean big speeds, but also big loads, so the focus is on sailing fast while protecting the boat. We did break a sheet yesterday, but there’s still a long way to go. We’re fully focused on our race and staying in our lane.”
It’s a classic Atlantic mindset: patience now, options later.
Jackknife settles into open-ocean rhythm

Further back in the fleet, Jackknife, co-skippered by Sam and Andrew Hall, has made a solid transition from the Canary Islands phase into true blue-water sailing. Currently leading her class and sitting fourth overall, her early progress reflects a balanced approach — pushing when it makes sense, preserving the boat when it doesn’t.

“We had a really good first 36 hours and the boat feels strong,” said Sam Hall. “The reaching conditions favour the bigger, more modern designs right now, but once we get back into VMG sailing it should get interesting.”
“There’s a long way to go and plenty of variables ahead, but we’re happy with where we are and how the boat is going.”
Superyachts: classic lines, modern miles

Among the largest yachts in the fleet, Swan 128 Be Cool, skippered by Luca Serra, has found the breeze she was built for. Reporting close to 30 knots of wind, Be Cool has remained fully under control while sustaining boat speeds over 20 knots as she stretches south and west.

She now sits almost 80 miles south of her superyacht rival Linnea Aurora, and around 50 miles ahead on the water. After IRC correction, however, Linnea Aurora currently holds a 13-hour advantage, keeping the duel finely balanced.
Despite being the largest yacht in the race, Linnea Aurora has enjoyed an excellent opening act. Navigator Tom Robinson described ideal conditions for settling into life offshore.

“So far, so good. The weather has aligned well for this race. Conditions have been gentle, which has been perfect for easing the crew into life offshore — especially as many on board are crossing an ocean for the first time.”
“It’s been sunny, with clear nights and plenty of stars, making the transition into watch systems and life at heel a positive experience.”
From a tactical perspective, Robinson notes that the race has been shaped more by big-picture positioning than direct boat-on-boat moves.

“A developing low near the Bay of Biscay compressed the Azores High over the Canaries, shortening the usual wind shadow and allowing boats to head west sooner than expected. That’s why you’re seeing such a wide north–south spread across the fleet.”
“We’re now pushing west at best speed, aiming to hook into the clockwise rotation of the Azores High and set up the final approach to Antigua.”
The Atlantic opens up

As the fleet enters its first sustained trade-wind phase, the defining traits of each campaign are beginning to show. The next few days promise stronger breeze, bigger seas and rapidly increasing daily mile counts, as crews settle fully into the long, demanding cadence of an Atlantic crossing.
The race is still young — but the direction is set, the patterns are forming, and the ocean is now very much in charge.
