summary: Dutch shipyard Feadship has released its sensational new 80-meter superyacht, Valor, capable of navigating tough Arctic conditions while maintaining a zero-emission capacity.
body: Feadship, a renowned Dutch shipyard, has introduced its exceptional new addition to the explorer yacht species - an 80-meter superyacht named Valor. With her anchorage set off the coast of Falmouth, UK, Valor is ready to make her grand entry into the esteemed Monaco Yacht Show. A repeat Feadship client commissioned this gargantuan vessel, augmenting the yard's explorer fleet which also includes prestigious names like Shinkai and Moonshadow. The steel-structured yacht is designed with a robust two-meter ice belt above and beneath the waterline, which secured her a Bureau Veritas Young Ice 2 notation, ideal for navigating the challenging Northwest Passage. But Valor isn't all about muscle. She sports an eco-friendly propulsion system that translates into zero carbon emissions for up to two days. This innovation is powered by four ultra-efficient generators paired to a water-cooled lithium-ion battery bank, offering flexible energy management. The exterior design, a unique amalgamation of a dreadnaught bow and a modern missile frigate, brings a distinctive look that the owner cited as 'recognizable from outer space'. Breaking away from the common curvy designs, this arrangement enables expansive, walk-around decks, providing a generous outdoor seating area and even a dedicated relaxation spot for the owner's three golden retrievers. Inside, Valor boasts a spacious accommodation for up to 14 guests. The main deck features six cabins, with an entire level committed to the owner's chamber offering panoramic views across the helideck and a grand dressing room. A tastefully constructed skylounge provides a formal dining space, complemented by the flexibility of sliding glass walls. The interiors of Valor have been left intriguingly undisclosed but have been hinted to exude vintage and mid-century aesthetics. These elements are further beautified by a staircase composed of 48,001 parts, including lustrous bronze and stone – a showstopper in its own right. Surrounded by high-quality furnishings from prestigious designers, Valor is a testament to Feadship's commitment to blending aesthetics, functionality, and sustainable sailing.

title: Mateusz Kusznierewicz, Bruno Prada and a Star-Filled Fleet Highlight a Day of Tactical Mastery at the 2025 Star World Championship in Croatia.
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Mateusz Kusznierewicz, Bruno Prada and a Star-Filled Fleet Highlight a Day of Tactical Mastery at the 2025 Star World Championship in Croatia.
summary: Day 2 of the 2025 Star World Championship in Split, Croatia unraveled a canvas of tactical acumen, courage, and relentless triumph on the unpredictable Adriatic waters.
body: On a day where the wind showed off its unpredictable nature, Day 2 of the 2025 Star World Championship was a true testament to sailors' tactical prowess and adaptability. Waiting ashore for 90 minutes, the 101-boat fleet took the plunge, giving spectators a breathtaking spectacle on the Adriatic. Despite an uncertain forecast, the Race Committee took a gamble and docked out at 12.30pm. Their courage paid off when, by early afternoon, a substantial 12-knot easterly graced the racecourse, accompanied by a moderate chop across the Split Channel. The race commenced at 2.30pm amid superb conditions. The Vakaros RaceSense system precisely detected all OCS boats in real time, averting a general recall and ensuring a clean getaway for the fleet. The first upwind leg quickly turned into a tactical battlefield. Amidst this intense rivalry, teams who dared to tack early toward the middle reached the top mark in front. Leading the charge were World Champions Mateusz Kusznierewicz and Bruno Prada, followed closely by Eric Doyle with Payson Infelise and the American team of Jim Buckingham and Brad Nichol. As the first downwind leg unfolded, Kusznierewicz and Prada held onto their lead. However, Buckingham/Nichol and the German duo of Hubert Merkelbach and Markus Koy didn't fall far behind, overtaking Doyle/Infelise and narrowing the gap. A tactical reshuffle in the second upwind found Merkelbach and Koy reading shifts to perfection, leading the pack at the second top mark, followed by Kusznierewicz/Prada and Italian champions, Diego Negri with Sergio Lambertenghi. Unfazed by the competition, the Italians raced a flawless final downwind leg, surfing into the lead and taking first place at the finish line, followed by Merkelbach/Koy and Kusznierewicz/Prada. Despite dramatic shifts and an absent right trend, the Italian team managed to stay on course and celebrate victory. Merkelbach was also in high spirits, commending the nice breeze of the day and the close race. With two races down, Negri and Lambertenghi lead the event's overall ranking. Eckert and Melo stand second despite finishing twelfth on the day, while Heuwinkel and Spehr, the U30 Bacardi Cup winners, sit provisionally in third. With a tumultuous forecast for Day 3, whether the conditions will play the field or lead to a pause in this sailing showdown remains an enticing question.

title: Fleet Departs Nice in Glamour Conditions as Leg 4 of The Ocean Race Europe Gets Underway
author: Michael Hodges
imageAlt: Leg 4 of The Ocean Race Europe Gets Underway
imageCredit: © Jean-Louis Carli / The Ocean Race Europe 2025
summary: The Ocean Race Europe 2025 has reached its penultimate chapter, and it opened today in pure Mediterranean style. Nice delivered a sun-splashed send-off, the Bay of Angels shimmering as seven IMOCA crews unfurled their Code Zero sails and slipped the lines for Leg 4, a 550-mile loop around Corsica before the grand finale in Genova.
body: By 1700 local time, the yachts were stacked along the Royal Yacht Squadron–style line just off the Promenade des Anglais. A light but steady eight-knot breeze carried the salt tang across the crowded shoreline as the race horns sounded. Out came the big sails, crews grinding hard to squeeze every ounce of pace as they vied for clear air on the short reach toward Monaco and the first points on offer.

It was Holcim-PRB (SUI) — this time with Nico Lunven wearing the skipper’s cap while Rosalin Kuiper takes a break — who judged it best, nailing the pin end and stretching away in clean breeze. At the other end, Paul Meilhat’s Biotherm (FRA), race leader on the overall table, punched out a strong start of their own, while Team AMAALA (SUI/KSA) rolled the dice, starting on port tack and breaking offshore in search of an early tactical edge.

From the very first tack, the stage was set: the fleet would fight tooth and nail for the Monaco scoring gate — just eight miles from the start, but carrying precious leaderboard points that could prove decisive by Genova.

The Mediterranean may look benign under blue skies, but the course the sailors face is nothing short of brutal. The fleet must skirt the entire island of Corsica, with its towering granite mountains and notorious wind shadows, before threading the needle through the Strait of Bonifacio. This eleven-kilometre stretch between Corsica and Sardinia is infamous for its funnelled gusts, eddies, and razor-sharp shoals. Crews will have to dance between strategy and survival before turning north for the final sprint to Genova, Italy’s proud maritime city and host of the 2021 inaugural Ocean Race Europe finale.

For Yoann Richomme (FRA), back at the helm of Paprec Arkéa after sitting out Leg 3, the challenge could be won or lost in the first 24 hours. “We’ve got breeze to get to Monaco, so that’s a great way to open. But tonight it’ll be light — tricky patches as we cross to Corsica. Tomorrow should bring new pressure, but around the island it’s going to be about patience and precision,” he said dockside, looking both eager and wary.

Richomme wasn’t exaggerating. Corsica rises like a fortress from the sea, mountains topping 2,700 metres that cast massive shadows over the water. Too close inshore and you risk parking up in a dead patch; too far offshore and you may miss the chance to exploit a thermal shift. “The wind shadows are huge,” Richomme warned. “We’ll have to stay sharp the whole way.”

Paprec’s campaign has been full of fight this season. Sitting tied for second overall with Holcim, the French team know they must take points here if they want a shot at the overall title. Richomme was quick to credit his crew for a solid Leg 3, led in his absence by Corentin Horeau: “They had a tough one but kept us in the game. Now, I want us back on the podium. Of course, we always want to win, but with this leg? It’ll come down to the final miles.”

For Pip Hare (GBR), racing aboard Scott Shawyer’s Canada Ocean Racing – Be Water Positive, the Mediterranean remains as unpredictable as ever. “We’re still waiting for a pattern. The models don’t agree. Under Corsica, depending on timing, you could get hammered with a gale or parked with nothing. And Genova? Thunderstorms, waterspouts, flat calms — it’s the full menu. Expect the unexpected.”
Hare has form here. She raced into Genova in the 2021 edition and knows how messy it can get: “Don’t bet the farm on anything until you see the finish line. This place rewrites its own script.”

For Ambrogio Beccaria (ITA) and Allagrande Mapei Racing, this leg carries extra fire. Genova is effectively his home waters; his Class 40 was built and launched there. After losing Leg 1 to that bruising collision in Kiel with Holcim, the Italian team are buried mid-table, but Beccaria has eyes only for redemption. “Our goal is simple — win the leg, win in Genova,” he said with trademark bluntness. “The Monaco gate? Yes, points are nice, but we’re chasing the big one.”

As the sun began to slide behind the Alpes-Maritimes, the fleet remained locked together, five boats spread within a quarter-mile. Biotherm, intent on defending their overall lead. Holcim-PRB, reborn and resurgent after early setbacks. Paprec Arkéa, looking to prove their steel. Malizia, Allagrande, Canada, AMAALA — all with scores to settle and reputations to defend.

The Mediterranean was benign at the start — eight knots, flat seas, glamour racing for the crowds onshore. But everyone knows what awaits. A long night of sail changes, hydration battles, sweat dripping below decks in the August heat. A Strait that chews boats and breaks nerves. And a final charge toward a finish that has history written all over it.

No one pretends to know how it will play out. Forecasts call for light patches, transition zones, and breeze bending around Corsica’s cliffs. The only certainty is work — relentless trimming, gybes in the dark, and no real rest until Genova’s breakwaters appear on the horizon.
As Holcim’s Franck Cammas summed it up with a wry grin: “Biotherm is ahead now, but in the Med, nothing is ever certain. There’s a long, long way to go.”

title: Adventure, Ambition, and Auction: The Grand Finale of Marine Auctions September Online Event

body: The Marine Auctions' September online showcase has been a thrilling race between bidders eager to own a slice of the maritime world. With yacht enthusiasts worldwide tuning in to place their bids, this digital exhibition of catamarans, yachts, motor boats, and sailing vessels has become a must-visit event of the season, priming excitement and anticipation.

Whether you are a seasoned collector, a seafaring enthusiast, or a novice in the marine world, these online auctions are a gateway to tossing away the mundane and embracing the adrenaline-fuelled life at sea. title: Beneteau's Swift Trawler 54 Makes a Groundbreaking UK Debut at Southampton Boat Show
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Beneteau's Swift Trawler 54 Makes a Groundbreaking UK Debut at Southampton Boat Show
summary: Gracing the Southampton Boat Show with a highly anticipated UK debut, the Beneteau Swift Trawler 54 is poising itself as the new star of long-distance cruising yachts.
body: The Southampton Boat Show has always been a stage radiating grandeur, where the finest marine innovations are unveiled. Amid this glittering display this year, the Beneteau Swift Trawler 54 made a truly memorable UK debut. With a lineage of high-volume, long-distance cruising boats, this particular trawler yacht has emerged as the crown jewel.

At first glance, the Swift Trawler 54 shares aesthetic consistencies with its smaller siblings but takes a divergence from the superyacht-inspired Grand Trawler 62. However, don't let its traditional design fool you - the ingenuity of the trawler's internal design is truly extraordinary. Each level is compartmentalised into distinct zones, leading to an enhanced sense of homeliness on board. The saloon features three areas: an upper dinette adjacent to the helm, a casual lower lounge with a coffee table, and a functional transverse galley nestled between the former two.

In addition to spacious interiors, the flybridge displays similar levels of compartmentalisation. It comprises an open aft deck for toys, central dining space and a forward companion section for lounging.

As a trawler yacht, the Beneteau Swift 54 places heavy emphasis on light, space and headroom. The innovative aft end design reveals a huge lazarette for toy storage, with the entire deck functioning as a hinge. The vessel also holds an impressive title – ‘Best Passagemaker’ at the MBY awards in January, warranting immense attention and acclaim. With an engine speed of 19 knots and a price tag from £1,125,000 ex VAT, the Beneteau Swift Trawler 54 is a game-changer and a must-see for maritime enthusiasts worldwide. Its ingenious design and extraordinary functionality make it more than just another vessel at the boat show – it is a testament to Beneteau's commitment to maritime innovation, luxury and comfort.

title: A Radical Revelation: The Innovative Princess C48, Unveiled at Cannes Yachting Festival
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: A Radical Revelation: The Innovative Princess C48, Unveiled at Cannes Yachting Festival
summary: Brace yourself for the exquisite Princess C48. This astonishing new creation is taking the yachting world by storm, turning heads at the Cannes Yachting Festival.
body: The yachting world is abuzz as the Princess C48, an all-new C-Class model from the acclaimed British yard, takes centre stage at the Cannes Yachting Festival. In a paradigm shift from its usual conservativism, the new Princess brings an exhilarating package of advancement and engineering brilliance. The C48 not only pioneers Princess's first centre console design but also its first stepped hull. Additionally, it showcases the surprising application of folding side platforms, available in two customisable iterations. From sterndrive power to outboard, the C48 isn't just an entry-level yacht - it's a class apart. With two distinct versions, the Open and the Deck Saloon, the Princess C48 caters to varied tastes. Boasting an innovative centre-console design that features deep walkaround decks, a hard-top, and a welcoming open bow, it reflects the latest yachting trends. Either you indulge in the open-air thrill with a wraparound windscreen sheltering the C48 Open's entire cockpit from the back and sides, or you enjoy an intimate enclosed saloon through glazed sides and sliding aft doors in the Deck Saloon version. Performance isn't ignored in the C48's pursuit of innovation. It holds the proud distinction of being the fastest Princess yet, potentially reaching an impressive speed of 53 knots with the option of triple 600hp Mercury V12 Verados. The expendable market versions would also feature Volvo Penta's new 480hp D6 diesel sterndrives with a top speed between 33-35 knots. Among the yacht's meticulous detailing, the folding side platforms stand out. Available in two versions - half-height hinged bulwark sections for an over-the-water seating experience or lengthy full-height platforms that create expansive terraces - it serves both aesthetic and functional purposes. Inside, the C48 consistently delivers. The cockpit sees a careful intermingling of conventional design and clever touches, including three individual helm seats behind the windshield. The seating assignments differ based on the chosen variant - the driver takes the middle seat for Open, and the starboard side for Deck Saloon. The lower deck showcases versatility with an open plan featuring a convertible Double bed dinette, a secondary galley module, and separate compartments for head and shower. A private double cabin forms a cozy retreat. In conclusion, the Princess C48 is more than a yacht - it's an emblem of the future, revolutionising the way we approach sailing journeys.

title: Rossinavi's Majestic Superyacht, the Flying Dagger III, Marks Debut on Brokerage Market with Premiere Set For Monaco Yacht Show
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Rossinavi's Majestic Superyacht, the Flying Dagger III, Marks Debut on Brokerage Market with Premiere Set For Monaco Yacht Show
summary: The 49.9-metre Rossinavi superyacht, the highlight of Italian luxury, Flying Dagger III, has finally made its way to the brokerage market.
body: Known for its intricately engineered designs and luxury statement, Rossinavi has sent one of its marvels, the 49.9-metre motor yacht 'Flying Dagger III', sailing to the brokerage market. Trusted brokerage Y.CO has acquired the yacht and plans to display it at the upcoming Monaco Yacht Show.

Boating enthusiasts will be thrilled to know that this is the first time the vessel has joined the market since its initial launch in 2018. The yacht has only been used privately, receiving well-documented and consistent upkeep. The yacht's frame, made of Aluminium, underscores a fast displacement design along with a sporty, car-like aesthetic envisioned by the innovative team at Team For Design - Enrico Gobbi. The naval architecture holds the signature touch of Arrabito Naval Architects.

The use of natural light is a prevalent design strategy within the yacht, with floor-to-ceiling windows illuminating chic, neutral-toned furnishings and furniture. The main saloon boasts of an ample lounge area and formal dining space. An upper saloon provides a relaxed ambience to unwind before dinner. Providing ample room for a crew of 10, the yacht is in the market for an asking price of €28,500,000.

title: Sanlorenzo Prospers Amid Headwinds, Reporting Steady Growth and Record Orders for First Half of 2025
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Sanlorenzo Prospers Amid Headwinds, Reporting Steady Growth and Record Orders for First Half of 2025
summary: Despite ongoing global challenges, renowned Italian brand Sanlorenzo turned heads with a resilient first half of 2025, demonstrating steady growth and signed a record number of orders.
body: Despite a global environment fraught with trade tariff uncertainties and broader economic pressures, Sanlorenzo forged ahead in the first half of 2025, recording measurable growth bolstered by sustainable revenues and healthy margins. New yacht sales contributed significantly to the resilient performance, with revenues reaching €454.1 million, an increase of 9.4% from the same period the previous year (€415.1m). Specifically, the Superyacht and Nautor Swan Divisions provided an excellent boost, even as the Yacht Division remained stout in the segment exceeding 30 metres. Notably, H1 orders saw a significant surge, growth of a staggering 29.9% YoY to €420 million. The already sold orders contributed 93% to an order backlog amounting to €1.439 million.

Sanlorenzo’s chairman and CEO, Mr Massimo Perotti, expressed confidence in the brand's performance. He attributed the impressive figures to the resilience of the company, the strength of the Sanlorenzo brand, and the timeless allure of its yachts. Especially buoyant was the demand for yachts of 30 metres and above, believed to be a testament to the vitality of the brand's made-to-measure philosophy, scarcity-driven model and successful foray into sailing with Nautor Swan. With continued wealth creation among the highest wealth cohorts, Perotti sees a promising future ahead and reaffirmed the brand’s 2025 guidance.

Besides, Sanlorenzo also performed well in diverse geographic markets. Despite facing some challenging market dynamics, particularly in the segment below 24 metres length, the Bluegame Division reported a relatively resilient performance. The Yacht Division experienced mild softness below 100 feet, but the larger models demonstrated resilience. The Superyacht Division marked a 10.2% increase compared to H1 2024, generating €137.1 million, contributing 30.2% of total revenues. The Bluegame division (13–23m) reported a small downturn of 10.9% in revenues from new yachts sales compared to H1 2024, but it still outperformed the competitive sub-24m market. The Nautor Swan recorded revenues in line with the planned business development and integration.
Evidently, Sanlorenzo’s steadfast resilience and continuous drive for innovation in its offerings, even amid global headwinds, mark it as a strong contender in the ultra-luxury yacht market.

title: Young and Talented Vaikobi 18ft Skiff Trio Leading the Charge for 2025 Australian 18 Footers League
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Young and Talented Vaikobi 18ft Skiff Trio Leading the Charge for 2025 Australian 18 Footers League
summary: The Vaikobi 18ft Skiff Team, helmed by luminary Kirk Mitchell, is gearing up to make waves in the upcoming 2025-26 Australian 18 Footers League's season.
body: The Australian 18 Footers League's 2025-26 season sees a new, spirited contender rising up in ranks - the Vaikobi 18ft Skiff Team. This vibrant team is led by the champion of the Australian Cherub class, Kirk Mitchell. Alongside him are the proficient hands of Andrew Stephenson and Daniel Barnett. Navigating their fourth season together, the team hopes for triumphant winds in their journey this time around. Having graduated from the Cherub 12ft dinghy class, the trio is seasoned in triumphing at regattas, albeit their success in the 18s is yet to match their sky-high expectations.

Mitchell and Stephenson, a formidable duo, won the Australian Cherub Championship during the 2013-14 season before sealing the runner-up spot in the next. Their seafaring legacy didn't stop there. Mitchell later teamed up with Daniel Barnett and Tim Westwood, another seasoned team, to steer Noakes Youth/Vintec in the 2017-18 season, finishing 12th in the 2018 Giltinan Championship.

Daniel Barnett carries the legacy of one of the most prominent families in the 18 footer class. His grand-father Don Barnett won the 1967 World 18 Footer Championship, and his father, Phil Barnett is a multiple World championships laureate.

The Vaikobi team, bolstered by raw talent, knows its merits exceed its current Giltinan results. Acknowledging the sting of disappointment, they are hopeful about the forthcoming season and their run at the Giltinans. The underpinnings of their optimism lie in their indisputable team ability and the steadfast support of their generous sponsor, Vaikobi.

The upcoming 2025-26 League season forecasts the Vaikobi team as one of the frontrunners. With the winds of fortune favoring them, they are all set to achieve their best result at the Giltinan Championship. The season unfurls on October 12 as the first race of the Spring Championship takes Sydney Harbour by storm.

title: Unravel the Mystique of the Bieker Moth: A Deep Dive with Sailing Champion Kyle Stoneham
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Unravel the Mystique of the Bieker Moth: A Deep Dive with Sailing Champion Kyle Stoneham
summary: Ever wondered what's beneath the polished surface of a championship racing boat? Join us as we 'unbox' the Bieker Moth with Kyle Stoneham.
body: Floating on a sea of mystique and latent beauty, the Bieker Moth has, for the longest time, fascinated seafarers and sailing enthusiasts, its alluring design adding a distinctive allure to these speedy vessels. Recently, one such avid sailor, Kyle Stoneham, took the world on a revelatory exploration of the famed vessel. The term 'unboxing' aptly characterized this endeavor as Stoneham revealed the concealed treasures of the Bieker International Moth's rigging systems. And yes, you're not drifting alone if you find unboxing videos oddly satisfying.

Ever wondered why the modern Moths insist on hiding their ropes? The journey to speed and efficiency answers that! Unearthing the carbon covers, Stoneham amuses us with the vessel's clever aerodynamic systems aimed at furnishing the boat with streamlined efficiency, making it lighter and faster. Imagine manoeuvring with clarity on a vessel that does not entangle you amongst its ropes!

Taking sailing enthusiasts on this exhilarating journey, Stoneham makes the sail into the sea of knowledge an enthralling experience. Whether you're a novice sailor or a seasoned seafarer, the covert details and sailing terminologies revealed in this expedition 'under the deck' of the Bieker Moth open up new avenues of understanding at the crossroads of science and adventure. This exploration is a tribute to those striving to push the boundaries of speed, efficiency, and elegance in the open waters. As we continue our odyssey in the world of sailing, let's keep 'unboxing' intriguing corners of knowledge and innovation, one vessel at a time.

title: Extraordinary Family Victory at Yare and Bure Open Sailing Championship on the Broad?

With the championship attracting eight boats, including sailors like Simon Daniels from Barton and Martin Thompson from Wroxham, the challenge was indeed intense. Yet, the Dugdale family sailed with exceptional skill and determination over the two days. The family's performance was extraordinary on both days, only slipping to second position in one race.

Celebrations in the form of tea and homemade cakes wrapped up the vital event. Amid all the fun and fierce competition, recognition and appreciation were also directed towards the Galley staff, cake makers, food providers, and especially Stuart Bailey and his crew.

title: Spectacular Milestone In Sea Engineering: The Largest Dutch-Built Motor Yacht By Amels, Project Tanzanite Introduces New Standard In Luxury
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Spectacular Milestone In Sea Engineering: The Largest Dutch-Built Motor Yacht By Amels, Project Tanzanite Introduces New Standard In Luxury
summary: Dutch yard, Amels, raises the bar in maritime luxury by launching the largest Dutch-built motor yacht, Project Tanzanite.
body: Famed for their maritime prowess, Dutch company Amels has yet again demonstrated expert craftsmanship with their latest venture - Project Tanzanite. This 120-metre long behemoth has grabbed the title of the largest Dutch-built motor yacht in existence, surpassing the company's previous flagship, Here Comes The Sun, by an astonishing 31 metres. With craftsmanship that's second to none, over the next year, more than 1,000 expert artisans will labor to ensure this mammoth vessel is ready to set sail by 2026.

Designed with elegance and luxury in mind, Project Tanzanite was last seen two years ago at the Damen Yachting's renowned Vlissingen facility in the Netherlands. There, it was prepped and primed for the outfitting process. Damen Yachting, responsible for the naval architecture, worked hand in hand with Deeside Maritime, representing the client throughout the construction and final stages.

This supersized beauty offers not just elegance, but also the very latest in maritime technology. Project Tanzanite boasts diesel-electric engines and Azipod electric propulsion systems to ensure a smooth and peaceful cruise, promising the lowest levels of noise and vibration ever recorded on a yacht of this size.

With its launch and continuing construction, the world awaits what could be a new era in nautical luxury. Current maritime records may see displacement as the world of yachting pushes the boundaries further. Yet, for now, Project Tanzanite stands a triumphant king of the sea, a testament to the power of innovation, design, and boundless ambition.

title: Giorgio Armani: Legendary Italian Fashion Designer and Avid Sailor Dies at 91
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Giorgio Armani: Legendary Italian Fashion Designer and Avid Sailor Dies at 91
summary: Giorgio Armani, renowned Italian fashion mogul with a fervor for yachting, has died aged 91, according to a disclosure from his company.
body: Giorgio Armani, born in the northern Italian town of Piacenza in 1934, initially aspired to become a medic. After studying medicine at the University of Milan and serving at the Military Hospital in Verona, he ventured into the world of fashion by becoming a window dresser and sales assistant at Milan's high-end department stores. This stepping stone led him to freelance for prime stylists and fashion houses, ultimately culminating in the establishment of his design office in Milan with partner Sergio Galeotti.

In 1975, Armani launched Giorgio Armani S.p.A., followed by the Giorgio Armani Corporation in 1979. Today, these companies stand amongst the global leaders in fashion, with assorted product lines including Giorgio Armani Underwear and Swimwear, Giorgio Armani Accessories, and Armani Beauty.

Armani's ardor for yachting was visible in his life and work. His company sponsored the Giorgio Armani Superyacht Regatta and he owned multiple private yachts. Included in his collection were a sub-24-metre sailing yacht and two Codecasas. The first, named Mariù, was a tribute to his mother. The successor, Main, delivered in 2008, was his crowning maritime achievement, with every detail down to the glossy dark green hull designed by Armani himself.

In recent years, Armani expanded into superyacht design. His collaboration with Admiral, a brand of The Italian Sea Group, birthed 'Project Metamorphosis', an exclusive two-yacht series expected to unveil at the upcoming Monaco Yacht Show. Characterised by unusual geometric forms and a satin gold colour scheme, the designs reflect Armani's pioneering approach to design. True to his reputation, Armani worked until his last days, nurturing the company, curating collections, and charting future projects. His legacy transcends the realms of fashion to embody a way of life, consistently ahead of times with his sharp intuition and practicality.

title: Ahead of the Cannes Yachting Festival, Maiora of NEXT Yacht Group Presents Their Impressive New 30.4-Metre Yacht, M|30
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Ahead of the Cannes Yachting Festival, Maiora of NEXT Yacht Group Presents Their Impressive New 30.4-Metre Yacht, M|30
summary: Marking another milestone, Maiora is adding to their illustrious M line with the unveiling of a new 30.4-metre yacht, the M|30.
body: Maiora, the globally recognised brand of the NEXT Yacht Group, is enriching its revered M line portfolio with a new entrant - the M|30. Spanning a grand length of 30.4 metres, the Italian shipyard will present a scintillating preview of the newest yacht at the highly anticipated 2025 Cannes Yachting Festival, with the ship slated for delivery in the summer of 2026.

Demonstrating Maiora's unyielding commitment to evolutionary design, the M|30 is a testament to integrating successful elements from its predecessors with fresh and contemporary design strategies. The resounding success of the Maiora 30 laid a robust blueprint, allowing designers to craft an updated exterior that complements the more versatile and enhanced guest spaces.

A product of Maiora’s successful ongoing collaboration with Quartostile studio and Acube Design, the M|30 is the third project from this formidable trio, who were also responsible for the M|36 and 36 Exuma's refit. Their new design straddles the line between sleek, coupé-like lines and ample volumes.

Evolving the boundaries between the interior and exterior, the visionary design includes a slim superstructure, large full-height windows and glass bulwarks. Natural materials and abundant light characterise the yacht’s interiors, reflecting Acube Design's preference for organic, soothing aesthetics. Balance and versatility form the keystone of the main deck layout, with flexible use living spaces and a master suite featuring a walk-in wardrobe, lavish en suite, and a transverse desk that doubles as a breakfast nook or home office.

For those yearning for the outdoor touch, the M|30 does not disappoint. An enlarged stern beach club reimagined as an 'al fresco veranda' connects with the main deck, promoting an organic mingling of spaces. Maiora honors its adored WalkAround concept on the upper deck, featuring step-free passages to ensure seamless movement.

A bow garage offers storage for seafaring accessories or could turn into a pool and sunbathing area, underlining the ship's emphasis on versatility. The M|30 signature is an echo of the M|36's style, a unique strip of light along the hull, further affirming Maiora's reputation for marrying practicality with aesthetic prowess.

title: The 2026 RORC Transatlantic Race
author: Michael Hodges
imageAlt: Marina Lanzarote: Atlantic Gateway for the 2026 RORC Transatlantic Race
summary: The RORC Transatlantic Race in association with the International Maxi Association and the Yacht Club de France will set sail from Marina Lanzarote on 11 January 2026.
body: Every great ocean race needs more than a start line. It needs a stage. A harbour that embodies the romance of offshore sailing, the grit of preparation, and the sense of stepping into something larger than yourself. For the RORC Transatlantic Race, that place is Marina Lanzarote – a port where volcanic ridges meet the Atlantic trades, and where decades of investment in infrastructure and community spirit converge into one perfect launchpad.

Since 2014, Marina Lanzarote has been the spiritual and logistical home of the race. What began as a one-off collaboration has matured into a decade-long partnership between the Royal Ocean Racing Club, Calero Marinas, the Government of the Canary Islands, the Government of Lanzarote, and the Real Club Náutico de Arrecife. Together, these institutions have transformed Lanzarote into a powerhouse of offshore sailing.

Calero Marinas itself is a story of vision and long-term strategy. With more than 40 years at the helm of Canarian marine development, the group has positioned its facilities not merely as mooring spaces, but as hubs of international racing excellence. Marina Lanzarote’s role in the RORC Transatlantic Race is proof of that foresight.
For competitors, Marina Lanzarote delivers the essentials of offshore readiness:
Capacity for yachts up to 60m – from sleek Class40s to towering Maxis.
A state-of-the-art boatyard with heavy-lift cranes and specialist technical services.
A full-service support network spanning rigging, sails, hydraulics, electronics, and provisioning.

This blend of infrastructure and expertise means crews arrive not just to start a race, but to fine-tune for survival. The transatlantic is 3,000 nautical miles to Antigua – and every bolt tightened in Lanzarote could prove decisive mid-Atlantic.

“Lanzarote remains the ideal starting destination for the RORC Transatlantic Race. With exceptional facilities, rich maritime heritage and year-round sailing conditions, it offers everything a race of this calibre requires.”

But world-class facilities are only half the story. What sets Lanzarote apart is the warmth and energy of its community. Each edition, the marina transforms into a race village alive with activity: skippers’ briefings, safety checks, school visits, dockside parties. Visitors from across Europe mingle with locals, and the race becomes as much a cultural festival as a sporting contest.

Edging closer to race day, the atmosphere shifts. Crews finalise provisioning, double-check safety gear, and walk the pontoons under the gaze of volcanic cliffs. Then, when the cannons fire on race morning, the fleet powers down Lanzarote’s dramatic coastline – a mix of adrenaline, pride and farewell. The island itself seems to lean out to sea, urging them forward.

The Calero Marinas group isn’t standing still. Its newest project, Marina Jandía in Fuerteventura, is under development. Designed to host 310 berths for yachts between 6 and 50 metres, it will include leisure spaces, restaurants and retail. For Fuerteventura, this represents not just a marina, but a milestone in tourism and marine infrastructure – a sign of the Canaries doubling down on their maritime identity.

The Real Club Náutico de Arrecife (RCNA), founded in 1872, underscores the cultural depth of Lanzarote’s role. From its grassroots youth programmes to its proud tradition of ocean racing, the RCNA ensures that the RORC Transatlantic Race is not just an imported spectacle, but a deeply rooted local celebration.

Lanzarote Sports Destination has also carved out a reputation as a year-round training hub, drawing Olympic teams, offshore sailors and superyacht crews. This ecosystem means that when the RORC fleet arrives, it does so into a living, breathing centre of marine excellence.

For the sailors, the start in Lanzarote is more than logistics – it is symbolism. The island is the last European foothold before the ocean swallows them whole. Each departure carries echoes of the great navigators: Columbus, Magellan, and the countless anonymous mariners who once looked west from these shores.
As one skipper remarked in 2024:
“You leave Lanzarote not just with a full fuel tank and fresh sails – you leave with the weight of history behind you.”
Why Lanzarote Matters for Offshore Racing

From a Forbes perspective, Marina Lanzarote is a case study in how strategic infrastructure, public-private partnerships, and heritage branding can create global visibility. By hosting the RORC Transatlantic Race, Lanzarote projects its name into the heart of the sailing world, attracting high-net-worth yacht owners, investment in local tourism, and international media coverage.
For Old Sea Dogs, it’s simpler: Lanzarote has the salt in its veins. It’s the perfect stage to send sailors westward into the Atlantic – a launchpad that feels both epic and intimate.

So, when the 2026 RORC Transatlantic Race fires off the line on 11 January, Marina Lanzarote will again have played its part: boats prepped, crews sharpened, families waving, and the island’s colours flying.
Because this marina is more than just a port of departure. It is the gateway to the Atlantic, the crucible of preparation, and the soul of a community that believes in the ocean.
And when the last sails disappear over the horizon, every sailor knows one thing: their race began not with the start gun, but with the warm embrace of Lanzarote.
Start: Marina Lanzarote, Canary Islands – 11 January 2026
Distance: 3,000 miles
Finish: Antigua, Caribbean
Entry: Online now at RORC.org

title: Trans-Tasman Showdown Closes Day Three at Hamilton Island Race Week
author: Michael Hodges
imageAlt: Hamilton Island Race Week
summary: Day three of Hamilton Island Race Week, powered by AMEX, was everything the Whitsundays are famous for – sunshine, steady trade winds, glamour yacht debuts and tight battles across every division – capped by a spectacular Olympic-class finale.
body: The Palm Beach Motor Yachts Trans-Tasman 49er Exhibition Series stole the show late in the day, giving crowds a taste of Brisbane 2032-level high performance. In the men’s 49er, New Zealanders Seb Menzies and George Lee Rush took top honours, while Australia’s Laura Harding and Annie Wilmot sent the home crowd into raptures with victory in the women’s 49erFX.

“Palm Beach Motor Yachts is proud to back Olympic class sailing between Australia and New Zealand. We’ll be supporting this brilliant showcase again next year,” said CEO Mark Richards, watching the spray fly off the skiffs.
Trade Winds Return, Racing Lights Up
Earlier in the day, the return of steady trades set the stage for classic island-course duels.
In Rating 1, Grant Wharington’s Wild Thing 100 stormed home first across the line in the Nautical Classic long race, but Marcus Blackmore’s TP52 Hooligan claimed the win on corrected time.
In Rating Division 2, David Hamilton’s Seeking Alpha edged victory by just seven seconds – proof of how close the racing has been this week.

The Multihull Racing division featured the debut of the 20-tonne carbon-fibre Gunboat 68 Slingshot (ex-Highland Fling 17), with skipper Dara Johnson, first-mate Maddy McLeay, and a star-studded crew including Adrienne Cahalan. They picked up handicap honours while clocking 19 knots through Whitsunday Passage – “with the coffee machine still running,” joked Johnson.

Southport duo Terry and Amy Robinson also celebrated a milestone, taking line honours aboard Miyu, their brand-new Cure 55. “It’s our first Race Week, and we love it,” Terry said dockside. “The vibe here is incredible.”

Meanwhile, Tasmania’s Ben Davidson and crew brought Sea Fever all the way from the Derwent Sailing Squadron to snatch Hamilton Island Light Blue race 3. “Good crew work made the magic,” Davidson said, even if a blown-out spinnaker kept the sail loft busy.

The Super 40s revelled in the chop of the Eastern Passage, with three sharp races in 14 knots. Sam Haynes’ Cape 31 Celestial strung together a trio of second places to climb the leaderboard, though Ray Roberts’ Team Hollywood remains the division to beat.

With the 49er showdown bringing the curtain down, Race Week pauses for its traditional lay day. Crews will patch sails, sink a few cold ones poolside, and get ready for the breeze to build again on Thursday. body: A resounding testament to human tenacity, the 14th edition of the Clipper Round the World Yacht Race recently launched in Portsmouth, UK. The fleet of ten identical 70ft racing yachts embarked on a global journey across 40,000nm. This substantial endurance trial around the world spans eleven months and is championed by twenty sailing professionals. These professionals lead their team of non-professional sailors through the trials and tribulations of the open sea.

The initial stretch of the circuit is a seemingly short 1275nm race to Puerto Sherry, Spain. However, with high winds and the dreaded Bay of Biscay's to contend with, the crews are in for a challenging start. The race director anticipates the teams will complete this first race within six to eight days, given the tough upwind conditions in the English Channel and into the Bay of Biscay.

An adrenaline-driven adventure awaits every participant, as they will endure through various harsh conditions, including hurricane force winds, infernal heat, and the seclusion of the world's oceans. With stripped back onboard facilities and close-quarter living, they'll get a taste of a sailor's life. Endurance and fortitude will indeed be the essential attributes for thriving in this exceptional expedition.

Participants from over 40 nationalities, all commoners with extraordinary determination, gear up to take on Mother Nature's whims as they circumnavigate the globe. Among them is Abigail Shanahan, a sailing writer, who harbours a dream of working as an on-board reporter for The Ocean Race. Her participation in the full circumnavigation on Team GOSH marks the beginning of her ambitious journey.

As sailing enthusiasts and viewers worldwide eagerly watch, this 14th Clipper Round the World Yacht Race is setting sail towards a journey of incredible endurance and adventure, enshrining the indomitable spirit of maritime exploration.

title: Introducing the Streaker Northern Championship 2025: A Tale of High Tides, Rigorous Challenges and Ultimate Victory
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Introducing the Streaker Northern Championship 2025: A Tale of High Tides, Rigorous Challenges and Ultimate Victory
summary: From big winds to daunting challenges; the story of Streaker Northern Championship 2025 shines a light on sailing's authentic spirit.
body: The Streaker Northern Championship 2025 at Beaver Sailing Club was not just another race. It was a spectacle of the unexpected, a showpiece of resilience and camaraderie, and a riveting portrayal of the heart-stopping action that makes the world of sailing such a fascinating place to be. On 30-31 August 2025, amidst the beckoning danger of wild winds from Scotland and the endless wide-open skies, the gallant Streaker fleet rose to the occasion for this prestigious event. Thirty-two intrepid adventurers, including eighteen local helms, daringly sailed away with the wind, gusting furiously over 30 knots. Despite the odds, the majority managed to complete all six races. Thanks to an early start before the approaching storm, they held steadfast, proving the old sailor saying, 'rough seas make better sailors.' The drama of the event was thoroughly captivating. Chief Race Officer David Nicklin devised a windward-leeward course with leeward gate, providing ample opportunities for split left or right for beats, rousing excitement and intrigue within the fleet. Moreover, Saturday's introduction of the inverted P for races three and four added two screaming reaches and a dicey gybe, pushing the boat's limits and the sailors' skill sets. Eventually, the ones who successfully executed their gybes gained a tactical upper hand, making sailing strategy as much a part of the racing process as the sail itself. The tussle for supremacy among Beaver's top three pros - Martin Penty, Giles Therkelson-Smith, and Richard Hanby - was a sight to behold. These accomplished sailors, with their unwavering focus and sea-tested expertise, made a big statement of intent by contesting the top spots in all the races, leaving the spectators in awe of their dazzling mastery. Among the other contenders, brimming with raw talent and relentless drive, James Dawes, Alan Bishop, and recent league joiner Sam Waller shone brightly for their tenacious efforts. Although James had an initial edge on Saturday, Sam's consistency paid off as he finished a commendable 4th on the more challenging Sunday morning races. In a sport where every gust can change fortunes, the Streaker Northern Championship 2025 bore testament to the mettle, grit, and relentless spirit of sailing, attending a call loud and clear to all - Dare to set sail!

title: Fresh Breeze, Fresh Battles: Fleet Accelerates Toward France After a Gruelling Night off Mallorca
author: Michael Hodges
imageAlt: The IMOCA fleet in The Ocean Race Europe have paid their dues in sweat and sleeplessness.
summary: After a long, sticky night of light airs downwind sailing close along Mallorca’s rugged northern shoreline, Paul Meilhat’s Biotherm (FRA) has emerged with an 11-nautical mile advantage over Holcim-PRB (SUI), the pair locked together for much of the night in a bruising battle of patience and precision.
body: The leg from Cartagena to Nice has already shown the full character of the Med: punishing heat, teasing calms, and now, at last, a freshening breeze carrying the seven-strong IMOCA fleet north-west toward the French coast. By midday Thursday, speeds had climbed as the leading boats found themselves in reaching mode, bows pointed toward a waypoint off the Îles d’Hyères.

If Biotherm hold the advantage now, it is only by the finest of margins after a knife-edge duel against Rosalin Kuiper’s Holcim-PRB along Mallorca’s spectacular coastline. The two crews gybed repeatedly, working every puff and shift, sometimes within sight and sound of each other as they tested inshore and offshore lanes.
“It was a proper slugfest,” admitted one Biotherm crewmember over the radio. “We were side by side, both trying to read the breeze off the cliffs. You could hear their grinders going in the night.”
By dawn, it was Meilhat’s team that had threaded the transition best, squeezing out into stronger air while Holcim found themselves momentarily parked. The difference: eleven hard-earned miles.

The move into fresher conditions has been a relief, but not a rest. Crews report a brutal workload through the long, breathless night. “I don’t know how many times we changed headsail – maybe five or six – but it was relentless,” Meilhat said this morning, clearly drained but still smiling.

Holcim’s Carolijn Brouwer painted the picture bluntly: “Hot, sticky, sweaty – but fun.” Hydration, calories, and energy management have become as critical as tactics. “You burn through so much in this heat, so we’re constantly eating, constantly drinking. And then there’s no sleep because you’re always on the sheets or changing sails.”

But even in exhaustion, there are moments to savour. Brouwer described the beauty of the night sail close under Mallorca’s cliffs: “There was enough depth to go right in, and it was spectacular. At the same time, we were locked in a duel with Biotherm. It doesn’t get more intense than that.”

Behind the leading pair, the fleet has begun to spread slightly. Allagrande Mapei (ITA), under Ambrogio Beccaria, hold third but with less than 50 miles separating them from backmarker Team Amaala (SUI), there is little breathing room.

The chasers had their own fireworks overnight. Both Team Malizia and Allagrande Mapei hit speeds above 30 knots before slamming into the same windless hole that cost Paprec Arkéa so dearly. “At one point we were touching 35 knots,” said Allagrande’s Manon Peyre. “It was a crazy ride – hanging on for dear life – and then, in minutes, it was gone. Dead calm.”
Will Harris aboard Malizia summed up the mood: “We’re happy to have someone to race against. We’re here to chase higher, not just fight for fourth or fifth. The Med keeps it all alive.”

Race Control issued a course amendment on Thursday afternoon, shifting the final turning mark away from the infamous Giraglia rock off Corsica. The decision, taken for safety reasons, will keep the fleet clear of a forecast mix of thunderstorms and gale-force squalls expected to strike the northern tip of Corsica overnight. Instead, the yachts will round a virtual waypoint 20 miles further north, sparing crews a hazardous night rounding of the rock but adding yet another tactical twist.

“It could still be messy,” warned Holcim helmsman Franck Cammas, a veteran of Med campaigns. “Biotherm have a little jump, but nothing is safe. These conditions can turn upside down in minutes. There is a long way to Nice.”

As of Thursday evening, Biotherm’s lead sat at 18 miles, with Holcim-PRB in second and Paprec Arkéa clinging to third. Less than 300 nautical miles remain, but the fleet faces one more grind: patchy breezes around the Îles d’Hyères and another collapse of wind forecast off the French Riviera.
“The finish could be anything between 6am and late afternoon Friday,” noted Race Control. “Light airs close to shore could compress the fleet again.”

For now, Biotherm have their noses in front, but after 48 hours of sweat, strain, and constant trimming, nobody is counting chickens. As Kuiper put it with a grin as she wiped salt from her eyes: “It’s full-on, and we wouldn’t have it any other way.”

title: Hamilton Island Race Week 40th: Champions, Close Calls
author: Michael Hodges
imageAlt: Hamilton Island Race Week 40th: Champions
imageCaption: Hamilton Island Orange div leaves Dent Passage on day 5 of racing
summary: As the 40th Hamilton Island Race Week, presented by AMEX, enters its final stretch, the scoreboard is beginning to reveal its champions. Some divisions are all but wrapped up, while others promise a nail-biting showdown in Saturday’s final island passage race.
body: However Race Week is about more than podiums. Success can be measured in moments as well as in points. On the Bommie Deck of the Hamilton Island Yacht Club, one sailor’s afternoon ended with an entirely different kind of victory: a marriage proposal met with a resounding yes. The bride-to-be, fresh from a day out on the water watching the fleets fly through the Whitsundays, was caught completely off guard. The crowd’s cheers proved once again that Race Week is as much about people and connections as it is about racing.

On the water, though, the serious business of winning carried on in tricky 12–14 knot south-easterlies. Marcus Blackmore’s TP52 Hooligan, skippered by Gavin Brady, put in a near-flawless display. A fourth corrected-time victory gives Blackmore the commanding position he has craved – a near-certain sixth Hamilton Island Race Week title. For Blackmore, whose history at the regatta runs deep, another win at the 40th anniversary is more than just another trophy; it’s legacy.

In Rating Division 2, Sydney’s David Hamilton has made his intentions clear. His Farr 40 Seeking Alpha has been the class act of the division, sailing with polish and precision to put the title within touching distance. With another consistent showing expected tomorrow, Seeking Alpha looks almost untouchable.

Yet amid the glamour yachts and cutting-edge carbon flyers, one of the most compelling stories belongs to the smallest, scruffiest warrior in the fleet. Graeme Etherton’s Windspeed – affectionately called The Boat – is a 36-year-old Crowther 32 catamaran that has no right to be mixing it with the multimillion-dollar giants of the Multihull Hamilton Island White division. And yet, against all odds, Etherton sits tied for first on points with the slick Gunboat 48 Mololo.

Travelling all the way from Townsville to take part, Etherton’s old-school 32-footer is proof that Race Week handicapping levels the playing field. “It’s good to race against the quality of boats here; and it’s challenging with the current and tides,” he said dockside. “Everyone’s very gentlemanly on the start line – it’s refined racing. Of course, they go past me pretty quickly!” he laughed.

On paper, Windspeed should never be able to compete with something like Terry Robinson’s Cure55 Miyu – a lightweight carbon-fibre rocket barely six months old – but that’s the magic of handicap racing: the smallest boat can still have the loudest story.

At the other end of the size spectrum sits a boat that has made Race Week its stage for decades. Ray Roberts’ Botin 40 Team Hollywood looks set to add yet another Hamilton Island triumph to its long list of victories, leading both under IRC and Super 40 handicap.

Roberts, who first raced here in 1984, admits he’s lost count of how many Race Week wins he has chalked up. What matters more is the enduring allure of the regatta and the chemistry of his team. “This boat suits the conditions here, and if you sail it well it pays you the results,” he explained. “We’ve had really good competition this week with Veloce and the Cape 31s.”

Navigator Steve Taylor, new to the Hollywood programme, has been impressed by the operation’s precision. “The culture is discipline and perfection,” he said. “When you’re the highest-rating boat in the fleet, you have to race against yourself as much as your rivals.”

Close behind is Sam Haynes’ Cape 31 Celestial, representing the Cruising Yacht Club of Australia. Haynes, twice winner of the Rolex Sydney Hobart with his other Celestial campaigns, currently sits second in the Super 40 division behind Team Hollywood and leads the Cape 31 class. “When you get the Cape tuned up, they’re very responsive,” Haynes said. “But very wet!”

Elsewhere, the Hamilton Island Pink division is set for a finale to remember. With Bobby’s Girl and Zoe tied on points, and Kerazy only a single point behind, Saturday’s passage race will be a head-to-head-to-head brawl for the title. Expect no quarter given.
