title: Baptism by Spray: Admiral’s Cup Opens With a Brutal Channel Test
author: Michael Hodges
imageAlt: Admiral’s Cup Opens With a Brutal Channel Test
summary: The Admiral’s Cup roared to life with a deceptively light start — and then reminded everyone why it’s earned its legend. The 160nm Channel Race looked tame leaving the Solent, but by sunrise the next day, the fleet limped back soaked to the skin, eyes red and salt-blasted. A confused sea, building pressure topping 25 knots, and a foaming downwind leg back from France — it was a full-pelt Atlantic slap in the face. Th
body: In AC1, Rán, Niklas Zennström’s Carkeek 52 flying KSSS colours, was first home on the water. But once the IRC numbers were crunched, it was Giovanni Lombardi Stronati’s Django — the new Wally Rocket 51 — that topped the leaderboard. Karl Kwok’s Beau Geste (TP52, RHKYC) corrected into second, just minutes ahead of Rán.

Key to Django’s win was navigator Bruno Zirilli — a name stitched into the history of Azzurra, Luna Rossa, and the TP52 circuit. “We planned hard the night before,” Zirilli said. “Worked closely with Vasco [Vascotto] to build a strategy. We knew the weather could go sideways, so we stuck to clean air and played the shifts along the north shore. When the wind flicked southeast, we were ready. That last leg — wet, fast, full canvas, and the A2 tore clean off — but we managed it. No big damage. Just good sailing.”

The win is made sweeter by Django still being new to the team. “We’re learning her, but we’ve already found her legs,” Zirilli said. “And the Admiral’s Cup? It’s special. I’ve raced everywhere — but this one? This one matters.”

Over in AC2, it was Callisto (B&C 42) that stole the show. James Murray’s Kiwi-flagged boat nailed both line honours and corrected time. With Moose Sanderson in the afterguard and Ian Moore on navigation, this is a boat with bite.

“We knew the beat out of the Solent would be brutal,” Sanderson said. “So the plan was to survive it and strike on the return. Once we hit open water, it was game on. Big breeze, tight battle with Jolt and Beau Ideal. We didn’t use a watch system — just full sprint. Everyone dug deep.”

Moore, no stranger to offshore chess, said the beat was mostly even — “tiny gains from good timing” — but the race turned on the run. “The breeze built fast — faster than I thought. We handled it well. That’s where the race was won.”

Looking ahead, Moore expects the inshore racing to be a knife fight. “The boats are all different. Some like it upwind, some down. You’ve got to strike when the conditions favour you, and hang on when they don’t. Callisto is built for versatility, but we’ll be defending hard against the likes of Jolt and Beau Ideal. Nothing is given in IRC.”
The numbers back that up. Of the 30 boats, the top six corrected-time results all came from AC2. That’s no fluke — and no comfort to the rest of the fleet.
There’s a lay day now before racing resumes on Tuesday, July 22. One thing’s for sure: the Admiral’s Cup is wide open, and no one’s holding anything back.
This isn’t just a regatta — it’s a war of attrition with wind shifts, spreadsheets, and soaked foulies.

title: Wind and Waves Shape the Dramatic Outcomes of the Snipe Women's World Championship Races in Enoshima, Japan.
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Wind and Waves Shape the Dramatic Outcomes of the Snipe Women's World Championship Races in Enoshima, Japan.
summary: The Snipe Women's World Championship 2025 Races were marked by intense competition with impressive performances under challenging sailing conditions in Enoshima, Japan.
body: The picturesque scenery of Enoshima island staged an intense opening as the Snipe Women's World Championship 2025 kicked off with high-energy races on day one. The racing commenced under a typical southwesterly Enoshima breeze and big waves, with wind speeds that escalated throughout the day.

The Japanese Team of Ai Yoshida and Honoka Miura put on an exemplary performance, leading virtually from start to finish. The Croatian team crossed the line in second place, but a U Flag unsportsmanlike penalty relegated them, clearing the path for the US Team of Sarah Alexander and Charlotte Carroll to secure second place. The second race, once again, showcased exciting nail-biting moments with the Japanese teams making a solid comeback from a trailing position.

Mimicking the weather of day two, the third day of sailing was high on action, and adrenaline with thermal gusts testing competitors' skill. The Japanese sailing pair of Ayaka Yamazaki and Aina Hokuto emerged victorious on this day, proving their upwind prowess. The race, peppered with strategic moves and counter-moves, highlights the precision and tactical acuity that is the hallmark of sailing at this level.

The Snipe Women's World Championship, with its phenomenal sailing conditions and intense competition, encapsulates the thrills and spills of the sailing world at its best, a testament to the sport's electrifying appeal.

title: Sunseeker Martinique 36 - An Owner's Review
author: Michael Hodges
imageAlt: Sunseeker Martinique 36 - A Classic Sports Cruiser
summary: The Sunseeker Martinique 36, a classic sports cruiser from the renowned British shipyard Sunseeker. I had one of these many years ago and I loved it. Nice and powerful 24 Knots on the plane, (some times a bit faster). It was my first real boat and at the time with a young family it was great. They epitomise luxury and performance for boating enthusiasts. Launched in the late 1980s and early 1990s, this model, designe
body: Typically powered by twin Volvo Penta diesel engines, such as the AQAD41 or AD41 models delivering 200hp each, the Martinique 36 combines efficiency with power. Some boats have been re-engined or upgraded, like a 1990 model reconditioned in 2003 with Volvo Penta KAD 42 engines and new DPE outdrives, enhancing reliability. The boat’s fuel capacity of around 660 litres and freshwater capacity of 204 litres make it suitable for extended coastal cruising. Accommodation is a highlight, with the Martinique 36 offering 6 berths across two cabins plus a saloon. The master cabin often features an island double berth, while a twin guest cabin provides additional sleeping space. The interior includes a well-equipped galley with a fridge, sink, and hob (sometimes induction), a spacious saloon with updated LED lighting, and a heads compartment with an electric toilet and shower. The large cockpit, often laid with synthetic teak, seats up to ten, with convertible tables for sunbathing, making it ideal for socialising.

Modern upgrades on many Martinique 36s include bow thrusters, Raymarine chartplotters, VHF radios, GPS, diesel heating, and electric windlasses, enhancing navigation and comfort. Some boats feature hydraulic gangways, air conditioning, and generators, catering to luxury cruising needs. The hull, occasionally resprayed in striking colours like pearlescent Maserati blue, adds to its timeless appeal. With a displacement of around 7,112 kg, the Martinique 36 offers stability and versatility for family outings or high-speed adventures. Its blend of classic Sunseeker styling, robust performance, and sociable layout makes it a sought-after vessel for those seeking a reliable, stylish cruiser that stands the test of time.

title: Introducing The Santasevera 52: A Taste of The Mediterranean Breeze in The Modern Cruiser Market
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Introducing The Santasevera 52: A Taste of The Mediterranean Breeze in The Modern Cruiser Market
summary: The Santasevera 52, a modern Mediterranean-sized cruiser from new Italian boat builder Santasevera, promises to bring a fresh breeze to the cruiser market.
body: The sailing world is being captivated by the newest addition to the open cruiser market, the very first offering from Italian boat builder Santasevera - the innovative Santasevera 52. Maritime architect and yacht designer Francesco Guida has tailored this striking design to encapsulate a fresh vision of modern Mediterranean cruising. Featuring a short raised foredeck complemented by a sun lounge and a walkaround deck, the Santasevera 52 optimises its space by merging the saloon, cockpit, and swim platform into a single-level, expansive socialising zone.

The boat's interior is thoughtfully designed with ample space and features three helm seats facing forward, a large starboard dinette, a port-side kitchenette, and an array of lounge furniture on the sun deck further aft. The excellent cruising capacities are further amplified by an owner’s bow cabin, which comes complete with an ensuite bathroom and a separate shower, along with a secondary guest cabin that can convert to a double. In the middle, a lounge provides extra privacy as well as a comfortable space to relax during the day.

The Santasevera 52 exhibits not just style but also performance with a set of Volvo Penta D8 600hp diesels that can be installed with IPS drives or traditional shafts, promising speeds in the mid-thirties. With a smaller 40ft model underway for 2025, it appears that the Santasevera 52 is only the beginning of Santasevera's challenging the norms of modern cruising.

title: Northwesterly to the Rock — but no headbanger, finally
author: Michael Hodges
imageAlt: Veterans of the last two Rolex Fastnet Races
imageCaption: Joost Schuijff's 100ft maxi and past line honours winner Leopard 3
summary: Its starts on Saturday 26 July 2025 Veterans of the last two Rolex Fastnet Races are checking the weather with cautious optimism. After two editions that opened with 30-knot headwinds and a battering Channel slog, the long-range forecast for this centenary running looks — dare we say it — gentle.
body: But don’t be fooled. This race is never easy. Wind or not, the tide off the south coast of England always has a say: dodging foul currents off St Alban’s Head, Start Point, the Lizard, and Land’s End is just as much part of the game as catching a shift. Then there’s the final sting in the tail: the Alderney Race, churning through the finish approach into Cherbourg.

The course remains a game of threading needles — and this year’s TSS dance is as tricky as ever. Exiting the Solent, boats must stay north of the Casquets exclusion zone, though the faster classes like Ultims and IMOCAs often head south. The Land’s End–Scilly gap is always key — shorter but tidal — while others may opt for the longer line if it pays on breeze. Past the Rock, another TSS forces a wide berth before the fleet arcs back south. Add the Scilly and Guernsey options, and there’s no shortage of tactical forks.
At present, high pressure sits out west, dominating the picture. But a low-pressure wrinkle in the Celtic Sea could throw routing into chaos — especially for the big boats.

“It’s messy,” says Leopard 3 navigator Will Best. “Yesterday’s model had us doing 2.5 days with a light windward-leeward. Today it’s shifted to a reach — much faster for a 100-footer like us. There’s a mini-system forming, and it’s changing the whole scenario daily. Normal for now, but it’ll settle closer to the start.”

Leopard 3, with her deep 5.5m keel and towering rig, can’t nip around headlands like smaller boats, but she makes tidal gates early — and if it gets light, that rig will keep her moving. They crushed the Cowes–St Malo race earlier this month in similar conditions.

RORC Rear Commodore Joe Lacey will be doublehanding Midnight Blues, a new Pogo RC 33 — one of a growing breed of lightweight offshore flyers from Nivelt and Manuard. “The high pressure’s stable,” he says. “But its exact position shifts the angles. Along the south coast, it might be a beat or a reach. Across the Irish Sea — same again. Right now, we’re looking at 12–15 knots upwind for the start, easing into a coastal reach. Ideal for us.”

The Pogo is built for reaching and downwind, not upwind slogs — and they’re up against longer boats on similar ratings. “If we’re reaching, we’re in the hunt. If it turns into too much upwind — we’ll have to hang on and fight for every second.”
The Pogo RC fleet is small but growing fast. Five are launched, with Aruba, the works boat, joining the race helmed by Achille Nebout and Tanguy Bouroullec.
In IRC Four, all eyes are on Jetpack, Mark Brown’s JPK 1010, currently leading the RORC season by over 100 points. With navigator Sam Jones onboard, they’re well-drilled and upwind quick.

“We’re probably looking at a classic northwest gradient,” says Jones. “Models are lining up — not a gale, but not dead air either. We’re a late start, so the tide gates will be tricky. Getting through St Alban’s Head could be key. Upwind into Christchurch Bay, maybe a touch of reaching by Weymouth, and then onwards.”

The Jetpack team runs six-up, unlike many doublehanded 1010s — a slight weight penalty in light stuff, but they’ll make it up with sail handling when the breeze builds. “We’re heavier than a Sun Fast 3200, but in 15 knots upwind, we’re solid — like we were beating up to Eddystone in the Myth of Malham.”
The last Fastnet ended early for them — sail damage forced a retirement. This year they’re back, leading the pack, and hungry to prove it.

The centenary race won’t be a bruiser — not yet. But between the tidal gates, tricky angles, and a forecast still shaping itself like a bar of soap, this one’s going to demand precision. The days of straight-line bashing may be behind us — but the Rolex Fastnet still takes no prisoners.

title: Black Foils Swipe Portsmouth Glory from Home Team in High-Stakes SailGP Clash
author: Michael Hodges
imageAlt: Black Foils Swipe Portsmouth Glory from Home Team in High-Stakes SailGP Clash
summary: They came, they foiled, they snatched it. Peter Burling’s Black Foils pulled off a slick, late-game heist in Portsmouth to steal a home win from Dylan Fletcher and the Emirates GBR crew — putting New Zealand on top of the 2025 SailGP leaderboard in the process.
body: Fletcher’s team, cheered on by a roaring hometown crowd, had looked sharp all weekend but fell just short in a shortened, high-drama final on the Solent. The Swiss SailGP Team, skippered by Sebastian Schneiter, grabbed third — a first-ever finals appearance for the team, and a weekend they won’t forget anytime soon.

Burling was all business on the podium. “Challenging conditions, but the team delivered,” he said. “We’re proud to be heading into the European swing as leaders. This one feels good — especially doing it in front of a British crowd.”

It wasn’t just a win — it was déjà vu. New Zealand denied Great Britain a home victory back in Plymouth during Season 3, and they did it again here, outmaneuvering both GBR and Switzerland in a tense three-boat shootout. The Kiwis now lead the series outright — and sent a clear message doing it.

For the home team, it stung. Olympic gold medallist Hannah Mills put it plainly: “Gutted. We’d bounced back from tough events, and the support here was unbelievable. Not winning hurts — but we’re proud of the team, and we’re still in the fight.”

Switzerland’s weekend was bittersweet. They were flying in the final until technical gremlins forced them to drop out near the finish. But that didn’t stop Schneiter from soaking it in. “We earned this. First final, we sailed well, we’re proud — and we’re just getting started.”

France, meanwhile, delivered the comeback story of the regatta. After a wing collapse ruled them out of Saturday’s action, the SailGP Tech Team worked overnight to get them race-ready by Sunday. Quentin Delapierre and crew came out swinging, bagging a win and a second in fleet races 6 and 7 — not bad for a team that nearly didn’t race.
“It was surreal,” Delapierre said. “Docking out at 50 knots after a night in the shed — adrenaline straight to the helm. Not our best overall result, but we're still in this.”

It wasn’t just equipment keeping the tech crews busy. Racecourse carnage, shifting breeze, and Solent chop made for tough conditions across the board. Australia missed the final for the second straight event — and Tom Slingsby didn’t hide his frustration. “Not happy,” he said. Spain finished sixth, and both now trail the Black Foils in the overall standings.
Emirates GBR remains in fourth, but with just one point separating them from the podium spots, the season is far from over.

And the fans? They turned out in force. Over 20,000 ticket-holding spectators packed the shoreline, with thousands more watching from boats and bluffs. When the final F50s crossed the line, the Southsea Race Stadium flipped straight into party mode. DJ legend Pete Tong lit up the Après Sail afterparty — a fitting finish to a weekend of high-octane sailing, heartbreak, and heroics.

title: The Exquisite Art Deco Trinity Yacht, CARPE DIEM, Makes Its Market Debut for the First Time
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: The Exquisite Art Deco Trinity Yacht, CARPE DIEM, Makes Its Market Debut for the First Time
summary: Magnificent ocean liner, CARPE DIEM, a well-maintained, one-owner Trinity boat, hits the market for the first time.
body: For lovers of the sea, the thrill of spotting a unique, well-crafted yacht isn't easily surpassed. Imagine then, the excitement mingled with the anticipation of having such admirable craftsmanship up for grabs. This is the present prospect with the CARPE DIEM, a breathtaking, one-owner Trinity yacht making its market debut.

Known as one of the most visually appealing Trinity constructions, CARPE DIEM marries functionality with an aesthetic superiority that's hard to compete with. Since delivery, she has benefited from a top-notch professional management. The yacht's continuous upgrades bear testimony to its well-maintained status, promising a smooth, rewarding boating experience for the next owner.

Constructed on Trinity's aluminium-hulled blueprint, CARPE DIEM boasts a shallow draft. Its 10-metre-wide beam does more than enhance its stability whilst cruising the high seas—it ensures an excellent internal and external volume.

CARPE DIEM was built in 2011 by Trinity Yachts. She has a semi-displacement hull and accommodates up to 12 guests. The yacht boasts top speeds of 21 knots and a cruising speed of 17 knots. With a range of 1450 nautical miles at 17 knots, extended excursions on this beauty are a delight to anticipate. She is also available for charter at a weekly rate starting from $294,000.

This unique Trinity yacht doesn't just offer a means to conquer the sea—it offers a chance to do it in grand style. So if the allure of the open ocean calls to your heart, seize the day and make the CARPE DIEM all yours.

title: Club M, Baglietto's Multi-Award-Winning Motor Yacht, Gets Sold to a New Boating Enthusiast
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Club M, Baglietto's Multi-Award-Winning Motor Yacht, Gets Sold to a New Boating Enthusiast
summary: Club M, the celebrated 39.8-metre motor yacht built by Baglietto, has attracted a new owner who appreciates its unique design and superior functionality.
body: The illustrious 39.8-metre Baglietto motor yacht, Club M, has found a new custodian. Brokers Will Christie and Felix Sowerbutts from Christie Yachts represented the seller, whereas the buyer was introduced by Jonathan Barbe of Edmiston. Crafted competently in aluminium by the renowned Italian yard and delivered in 2020, the yacht has become a symbol of superiority within the industry, winning 'Best Motor Yacht, 40-50m' at the 2021 World Superyacht Awards. It also acquired recognition for 'Best Motor Yacht, Interior Design under 499GT' at the Design & Innovation Awards.

Club M is a testament to the refined taste of an owner with three decades worth of boating experience. The owner invested three years in the design process, visiting and assessing various designers and yards across Europe. His real estate development knowledge reflected in the yacht’s well-thought-out layout and design aesthetics.

Accommodation onboard Club M is for up to 12 guests in five luxurious cabins, with the master cabin on the main deck benefiting from a vast extending balcony to starboard. This feature, as pointed out by the brokers, is typically found on a larger yacht. Additional guest cabins are conveniently located on the lower deck, with one converted into a gym but readily convertible back into a guest cabin. The yacht also houses sectors for a crew of six in three cabins.

The super yacht's fore and aft outdoor spaces are designed to encourage social interactions, meetings or leisure sunbathing, all within the confines of luxury. The Jacuzzi aft allows an uninterrupted view of the yacht's wake, a feature that adds to the naval charm one can experience on the Club M.
Baglietto's pride is powered by twin 1,600hp Caterpillar engines, which allow for a maximum speed of 17.5 knots and a cruising speed of 12 knots, promising a cruising range of 3,500 nautical miles.

Club M was built to ensure optimal operational efficiency and privacy, two essential attributes for any potential yacht owner. The guest's comfort and privacy were highly prioritised during the design and build phase, resulting in carefully concealed crew ladders and impressively low levels of sound and vibration onboard.

title: Exquisite Maiora 36 Exuma Motor Yacht Sold Ahead of Imminent 2025 Delivery
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Exquisite Maiora 36 Exuma Motor Yacht Sold Ahead of Imminent 2025 Delivery
summary: The in-the-works Maiora 36 Exuma, a 36.9-metre motor yacht, set for delivery in 2025, has been sold.
body: Riding the wave of the sea and the crest of excellence, an in-build 36.9-metre Maiora 36 Exuma motor yacht, is set for scheduled delivery next month. Still, it's already been snapped up by its new owner in an exciting sale. The transaction was managed by the yacht enthusiasts Michel Chryssicopoulos and Costas Dimopoulos from IYC.

Construction on this Italian gem began in January 2024 under speculation. Maiora, a crown jewel of the Next Yacht Group, built it out of GRP. The Italian studio Quartostile envisioned the yacht as a 'bold explorer', cementing its place as the fifth unit from the yard's prestigious Maiora 36 Exuma series. It follows in the wake of its illustrious predecessors Pesa II and Tofan.

True to their reputation, Acube Design has adorned the interiors with a contemporary style, using premium materials and a soothing palette. The creative use of curved finishes and smart storage solutions translates into a luxurious yet practical space.

The yacht's design emphasises its connection with the sea, featuring expansive windows that flood the living spaces with natural light. One can venture into the main saloon, equipped with low-profile seating and a sleek marble coffee table, to appreciate this aquatic bond. A relaxed aft deck, adorned with large sliding glass doors and floor-to-ceiling windows, further blurs the lines between indoor and outdoor living.

Among the other exciting features, a climate-controlled skylounge on the flybridge that can be transformed into an open-air space stands out. The yacht also boasts generous deck areas for lounging and dining, a jacuzzi flanked by sunpads on the foredeck, and a sunken, floating seating nestled into the bow with a sunpad spread across the sundeck.

The yacht has a beam spanning 7.9 metres. After its scheduled delivery to her owner, the new build is billed to make its grand debut at the Cannes Yachting Festival and the Monaco Yacht Show in September. The Maiora 36 Exuma is commanding an attractive tag of €20,300,000.

title: A Strong Rebound in Innovation: The New Zealand 18 Footer Skiff Community Reactivates After a Pandemic Pause
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: A Strong Rebound in Innovation: The New Zealand 18 Footer Skiff Community Reactivates After a Pandemic Pause
summary: Following a Covid-induced hiatus, New Zealand's 18 footer skiff racing community readies another action-packed season, replicating the island's long history of nautical innovation and excellence.
body: Just after the conclusion of the 2020 JJ Giltinan World Championship on Sydney Harbour, where David McDiarmid's Honda Marine 18 footer team scored a memorable three-in-a-row win, the sailing world came to a standstill due to the Covid pandemic. With enthusiasm and dedication worthy of a sailor, New Zealand's 18ft skiff racing community, led by Graham Catley, Suellen Hurling and seasoned campaigner Alex Vallings, has managed to navigate through this tempest and is on its way to another top-class campaign by 2026.

The Australian crew, led by skipper Bert Swinbourne in Taree, came out on top but controversy entangled the title when a following regatta in Auckland saw Swinbourne disqualified and the title awarded to New Zealand's Gordon Chamberlin and Manu. This dispute, finally settled in 1946, notwithstanding, a victorious tradition, and an innovative spirit were born within the New Zealand 18ft Skiff Racing community.

In 1950, Jack Logan made another notable mark in this ongoing legacy. Faced with a perceived disadvantage against Australian counterparts, he decided to innovate rather than retreat. Rummaging through his late father's designs, Logan found an old skiff design that he modified, cut, and reshaped into a revolutionary vessel, calling it 'Komutu' or 'surprise' in Maori. Logan's 'surprise' out-sailed and shocked the Australian teams at the Auckland championship with its blistering pace, defeating them by considerable margins. This win further affirmed Kiwi's innovative spirit while instigating a tradition of on-water creativity that persists to this day.

Undeterred by interruptions to their sailing calendar, New Zealand's 18 footer skiff community draws from a deep wellspring of determination, ingenuity and a celebration of tradition and community. As they gear up for the forthcoming 2026 campaign, there is little doubt that the world will be thrilled once again by the Kiwi spirit of innovative competition with relentless pursuit of victory.

title: Unveiling the Thrill of the 2025 Admiral's Cup Inshore Races: A Visual Tour
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Unveiling the Thrill of the 2025 Admiral's Cup Inshore Races: A Visual Tour
summary: 2025 brought impressive inshore races to the Admiral's Cup competition. Tag along through iconic visuals capturing the exhilarating maritime contest.
body: Ahoy, there! If you've ever dreamed of feeling the thrill of a sailing race without setting foot on a deck, you're in luck. Recently, the Admiral's Cup 2025 competition took sail enthusiasts on a thrilling journey during a series of inshore races. These electrifying races, held in the traditional Solent conditions, were masterfully captured on film by two renowned photographers, David Maynard and Paul Wyeth.

The first of these races showcased sailboats navigating the robust South Westerly winds of 15 to 20 knots. Both a short and a long inshore race added to the excitement, with channel markers marking the turning points. David Maynard, an acclaimed maritime photographer, was on the spot, lens at the ready. His series of photographs vividly illustrate the dramatic tension and high-stakes competition inherent in these races.

By contrast, Paul Wyeth's photographs snapped later that Wednesday revealed slightly milder, overcast conditions. However, the heart-pounding action and strategic tussles of these races were unabated. Wyeth beautifully captured the unfolding drama, encapsulating the intensity of the sailors' experiences.

Through the lenses of Maynard and Wyeth, the true adrenaline, strategy, and camaraderie of 2025's Admiral's Cup inshore races were brought to vivid life, filling viewers with a sense of awe and respect for the raw power and thrill of the oceanic sporting event. For anyone keen on experiencing the joys and trials of sailing, these images are a feast for the eyes, providing a sense of being right in the thick of the action without so much as a drop of sea-spray on one's face. To put it briefly, these photographs are nothing less than the essence of sailing distilled!

title: Revitalized IGY Ibiza Marina Opens, Superyachts Welcome: A Significant €5M Investment Fully Redeveloped
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Revitalized IGY Ibiza Marina Opens, Superyachts Welcome: A Significant €5M Investment Fully Redeveloped
summary: IGY Ibiza Marina, now fully redeveloped under a €5M investment, invites larger vessels, including superyachts. The fresh layout can accommodate crafts from 20 to 150 meters.
body: There's an exhilarating energy surrounding the newly redeveloped IGY Ibiza Marina. A notable project backed by a €5M investment, it ushers in a new era for the yachting industry. Spearheaded by Ocean Capital Partners (OCP), Grupo Empresas Matutes, and Island Global Yachting (IGY), this transformational move is set to propel Ibiza into the limelight for seafarers in search of top-tier facilities for their behemoth masterpieces of the sea. The marina, now entirely reconfigured and refitted, can communicate a warm 'ahoy!' to vessels extending up to 150 meters. Superyachts, once merely admired from afar, have indeed received a grand welcome on the scenic Spanish coast. This significant development, while retaining the charm and essence of Ibiza, ensures that the marina is now prepared to accommodate a diverse range of vessels, elevating its stature in the global marine landscape. Now, whether you own a compact sailing boat or a lavishly decked out superyacht, the IGY Ibiza Marina is unequivocally ready for you. This marina, displaying its sparkling new features, symbolises a growing trend towards infrastructural inclusivity within the yachting community. By adapting to accommodate larger vessels, it encourages a spirit of unity among sea-going enthusiasts across the spectrum. In the world of yachting, one element rings true: progress is relentless. Destinations like the IGY Ibiza Marina, enriched by substantial investments and strategic enhancements, are blossoming into hotspots for yachting connoisseurs. Without a doubt, the winds of change are set to steer more superyachts towards this captivating Spanish marina.

title: Unleashing Power: Williams Introduces the Evene Superyacht Tenders, Promising More Capacity and Enhanced Design Features
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Unleashing Power: Williams Introduces the Evene Superyacht Tenders, Promising More Capacity and Enhanced Design Features
summary: Williams, a renowned UK jet-tender specialist, introduces a brand new range of superyacht tenders, Evene, boasting higher passenger capacity and innovative design.
body: In the thrilling world of luxury sea vessels, Williams, a renowned jet-tender specialist based in the UK, has launched an enticing new range of superyacht tenders, the Evene Series. The new line, named Evene, showcases two initial models - the 5.7m Origin 57 and the 7.1m Origin 71. With their distinctive designs, it's expected that this launch will soon be followed by larger versions.

Despite the different ship lengths (LOAs), both models share a similar design foundation with a 2.25m beam dimension. Unlike the rest of Williams' Jet Tender range, the Evene vessels do not sport inflatable RIB tubes. They instead boast a solid GRP hull coupled with an innovative Petestep underwater design.

The Evene vessels pack a serious punch when it comes to power. Each is powered by a single Yanmar 4LV diesel engine, complemented by one of Williams’ own waterjet designs. The Origin 57 engine is rated at 195hp while the 71's is 250hp, and both vessels can achieve an estimated top speed of 36 knots. The fuel capacity also sees an improvement, with the 71 model boasting an expanded capacity from 100 litres to 140 litres compared to the 57 model.

Despite the absence of extra buoyancy from the inflatable tubes, the seating arrangement in these vessels is impressive. The smaller model, intended for yachts over 30m, comfortably seats up to nine people, whereas the larger version can accommodate up to 13, catering to yachts over 40m.

In line with Williams' commitment to sustainability, the engines have been designed to run on HVO100 (hydrotreated vegetable oil) alongside regular diesel. The fitout also incorporates decks made from plantation-grown cork and upholstery stitched from recycled PET bottles.

Lastly, the Evene line is fully customizable according to the owner's preferences, right from seating layouts to array of optional equipment, and even the name and colorways tailored to match the mother vessel. With prices yet to be announced, the Evene vessels will make their public debut at Cannes Yachting Festival in September, promising a taste of a refined onsea adventure in a sleek, powerful, and sustainable boating masterpiece.

title: Stepping in 'Go's Footprints, Tankoa Celebrates the Launch of Its Second T450 Yacht – Singolare
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Stepping in 'Go's Footprints, Tankoa Celebrates the Launch of Its Second T450 Yacht – Singolare
summary: Welcoming the successor to 'Go', Tankoa Yachts exhibits Singolare, the latest entry in its T450 series focused on versatility and customization.
body: Italian shipyard Tankoa Yachts is making waves with the launch of its second yacht in the impressive T450 series – 'Singolare'. Following in the wake of the series’ first unit, 'Go', Singolare is the latest model to hit the waters, making its grand debut at the yard's base in Genoa, Italy.

Singolare sets a new bar for versatility and personalization. Crafted with meticulous attention to detail by the renowned Italian designer Giorgio M. Cassetta, this luxury vessel is tailored to reflect the lifestyle of its South American owner. Exceptional features such as the innovative interiors reimagined by the acclaimed Brazilian architect Debora Aguiar, to a hardtop with a fully-enclosed veranda which converts into a climate-controlled saloon, ensures Singolare stands out from the crowd.

The upper deck, committed to relaxation and entertainment, boasts a gym, sauna, and private cinema with a forward-facing view. Thanks, in part, to a smooth and clear foredeck, a well-integrated, watertight tender garage is successfully concealed onboard.

The new vice president of Tankoa Yachts, Guido Orsi, stated that the launch of Singolare represents a significant stepping stone for the company in strengthening their standing in the international luxury yacht markets, with a particular focus on the South American stage.

Delivery of Singolare is set for this summer. Its maiden voyage will traverse the crystal-clear waters of the Mediterranean, with a winter season in the Caribbean to follow. This superyacht's debut journey is sure to set the tone for many marvelous voyages to come.

title: Jongert Sailing Yacht Scarena Witnessing a Stunning 20% Price Drop: Now Yours for an Astounding €610k Less
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Jongert Sailing Yacht Scarena Witnessing a Stunning 20% Price Drop: Now Yours for an Astounding €610k Less
summary: There's an exciting new opportunity on the horizon for sailing enthusiasts with a lavish taste, as the Jongert sailing yacht Scarena sees a substantial €610,000 reduction in price.
body: If you find the elegance of Dutch craftsmanship irresistible, then you surely can't overlook the Jongert yacht Scarena. Built in 1995 in steel and aluminium, this 30-metre sailing yacht has proven her worth over time. Designed by the ingenious Ron Holland, and with naval architecture by Doug Peterson, Scarena truly is a jewel of the Jongert 2900M model series. Not to mention her interior, beautifully adorned with pear wood and teak, is the work of esteemed designer Peter Sijm.

True to her pedigree, Scarena has been continuously improved and updated. Significant refits made in 2007 and 2017 further increased her value and appeal. With the additional, most recent improvements carried out in 2024.

Scarena's above deck calling is her generous offering of twin cockpits and sunbathing area. Add a semi-enclosed deck saloon with a push-button sliding hard top for a weather-friendly gourmet rendezvous, and we have indulgence redefined! The yacht also comes with a hydraulically-operated garage featuring a bathing platform to further the enjoyment of life aboard. Plus, it’s a great host for a selection of water toys, such as paddleboards, kayaks, diving gear, fishing equipment and inflatables.

The Scarena, under power, roars with a 345hp MTU diesel engine, propelling the 109GT yacht to a top speed of 12 knots and a cruising speed of 8.5 knots, rounding off with a respectable range of 1,550 nm. Suited for charter or private use, she comes with a Greek charter license valid until 2027 and a Malta commercial licence valid until 2029.

Enrico Solinaos, of Ocean Independence, has listed Scarena at an asking price of €1,990,000. This is following her significant value deduction of €610,000. A price drop to such an extent is, surely a fine occasion for sailing aficionados of refined tastes to take note.

title: Experience the Thrill of the 2025 Admiral's Cup’s Inshore Races, Captured by Top Photographer David Maynard
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Experience the Thrill of the 2025 Admiral's Cup’s Inshore Races, Captured by Top Photographer David Maynard

The challenging and thrilling event raised the spectre of maritime racing to new heights. Two races were held that day, a short and a long inshore race, expertly navigating round channel markers.

Navigating the windswept chaos and capturing the thrill of the moment was top photographer David Maynard. Armed with his camera, he set off on the water, catching scene after breathtaking scene of the thrilling races. The result was a collection of superb photos that brilliantly preserve the exhilarating tension, the electrifying excitement, and the unspoken camaraderie that characterized the race.

The raw energy, the grace of the boats cutting through the water, and the palpable excitement of the competitors brought a unique vibrancy to the event that Maynard managed to encapsulate in his spectacular photo gallery. These photos do more than merely record the event; they transport viewers in the heart of the thrilling races of the 2025 Admiral's Cup, offering a tantalizing taste of the serene chaos that is inshore racing.

title: Transpac 2025 - Full Moon and Full Throttle
author: Michael Hodges
imageAlt: Transpac 2025: Halfway to Hawaii, Full Moon and Full Throttle
imageCaption: Transpac 2025 - The Crew of the Westerly
summary: With just under a week left to run, the 2025 Transpac fleet is officially past halfway, surfing westward across the Pacific towards Honolulu’s Diamond Head. After setting off in staggered starts on July 1, 3, and 5, 53 yachts of every style and strategy—ranging from 35 to 88 feet—have now picked up the trades, leaving behind fickle calms and early retirements (four boats have dropped out). The leaderboard is starting
body: At the head of the fleet is Bryon Ehrhart’s 88-foot Lucky (formerly Rambler 88), chewing through the final 350 miles in big breezes, clocking over 400 miles in a day. Despite starting nearly four days after the first batch, Lucky’s aiming squarely at the Barn Door Trophy for fastest elapsed time. Navigator Stan Honey predicts landfall in the early hours of Friday, July 11. The prestigious King Kalakaua Trophy, awarded for best corrected time, remains undecided until the last boat finishes.

The Pacific, though vast, hasn’t played fair. Roy P. Disney, aboard Pyewacket, described their passage as being rerouted around what he calls the “Pacific Pothole”—a weather hole of stubborn light air. “The seas haven’t really organized,” said Disney. “We’re doing 12 knots in 15 knots of wind. It’s been like this for days.”

This Transpac, Disney’s 26th, also marks the first-ever offshore race for 19-year-old Oscar Perry, sailing aboard the Cal Maritime entry Oaxaca. “My longest race before this was maybe 20 miles,” said Perry. “Now I’m getting hit by flying squid at night and watching dolphins in bioluminescence. It’s surreal.”

Back aboard the Santa Cruz 52 Heroic Heart, the Firestone brothers—Dan and Steve—along with old mate Mike Wolfe, are reliving their teenage circumnavigation roots. Though seasoned sailors, this is their first proper ocean race. “I asked for a refund after 24 hours in the lull,” joked Wolfe. But once the kite went up, spirits rose. “Getting shaken awake and gybing the kite in the dark? That’s what we came for,” said Dan. The crew’s already compiling a “next time” list. Top item? “Don’t bring the J3.”

Meanwhile, Tom Holthus and son Kelly are on their ninth and fifth Transpacs, respectively, aboard BadPak. Kelly, now 20, is no longer the wide-eyed 12-year-old he was on his first crossing—he’s now on the bow, surrounded by three college mates and their fathers. “Put a tiller in their hands and they sail the boat like a dinghy,” said Holthus.

Weather-wise, Tom Furlong’s Reichel/Pugh 52 Vitesse has found the race unusually gentle. “No big squalls. Some rain, some breeze. But it’s not the punchy stuff we’re used to,” he said. “Still, we’re into that sweet spot now—planing breeze, just under 20 knots, and flat seas.”

Over on Zero Gravity 51, things are calmer still—unless you count the snack economy. “We joke that the snacks are free, but you pay for whatever’s still in your snack bag at the end,” said skipper Ivan Batanov. "Snack trading starts soon—it's a whole secondary market."

Despite a sail break, spirits remain high thanks to hot meals and crew dinners under the stars. “Last night, we had steak, asparagus, and potatoes. We’re now thinking about installing a gimballed wine rack,” Batanov quipped.
And tonight? It’s a full moon. Roy Disney put it best: “When you’re surfing downwind into the moon path—that’s when it becomes magic. Every night gets better.”

For the 49 boats still chasing Honolulu, this race is about more than speed—it’s about shared watches, salt in your beard, late-night helm chats, and seeing land for the first time after 2,225 miles. For veterans and rookies alike, Transpac 2025 is delivering all the right conditions for lifelong memories.

title: Dutch Dark Horse Sails to a Nail-biting Win at the Celebrated Picasso Cup
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Dutch Dark Horse Sails to a Nail-biting Win at the Celebrated Picasso Cup
summary: After a season's absence, Team Leeloo racks up a stunning last-minute surge to clinch the Picasso Cup held in stunning Kristinehamn.
body: The highly anticipated M32 sailing series witnessed a spectacular comeback thriller as Team Leeloo seized a nail-biting victory at the fabled Picasso Cup in the tranquil setting of Kristinehamn. The Dutch crew, with their experienced skipper Harold Vermeulen at the helm, proved that they have lost none of their mettle. Despite their hiatus, they triumphed in a breathtaking final showdown, sending ripples of excitement throughout the sailing community.

Typifying the true spirit of M32 racing, the competition was fierce right up to the final moments. The scoreboard teetered on the brink of predictability as Team Leeloo sparred with top-flight adversaries, including Team Liros, skippered by Youth America's Cup savvy Oscar Engström, and the previous Picasso Cup champions, The Vikings, captained by M32 veteran Håkan Svensson.

An added pull to the circuit is the individuality of the Picasso Cup. This event provides fully rigged boats, allowing international teams to sidestep the cumbersome process of shipping their gear. Entrants simply turn up, step onto their assigned vessels, and compete. As if plucked from a storybook, this happened amidst the picture-perfect archipelago of Kristinehamn during the celebrated Archipelago Festival, an event that brings together sport, food, and music. For a week, summer and sailing synergized in a celebration of cultural and maritime tradition.

title: Its that a car or a boat - Jet Car / Boat ?
author: Michael Hodges
imageAlt: Jet Car Boats: The Thrill of a Sports Car, the Freedom of a Speedboat !
summary: Here's a bit of fun....!! In recent years, a striking new trend has emerged on lakes, marinas, and coastal waters: the jet car boat. At first glance, they resemble sleek sports cars—low-slung, aerodynamic bodies, aggressive grilles, and detailed paintwork—but don’t be fooled. These are not amphibious vehicles or floating gimmicks. Jet car boats are high-performance personal watercraft (PWCs) built for speed, style, a
body: A jet car boat is a water-only vehicle designed to look like a road-going supercar. Built on a fiberglass or composite hull and powered by high-output jet propulsion systems—often sourced from Yamaha or Sea-Doo engines—these machines blend the visceral aesthetics of a Lamborghini or McLaren with the hydroplaning agility of a jet ski. Unlike amphibious vehicles (which drive on land and float or cruise on water), jet car boats do not function on land. Instead, they are launched via trailer and driven exclusively on water, combining the familiarity of a car-style cockpit with the adrenaline of a jet-powered ride.
The first thing anyone notices about a jet car boat is the look. Most feature:

From a few feet away, especially in a marina setting, they can easily be mistaken for a luxury sports car that’s somehow floating. It's this visual deception—this magic trick of industrial design—that gives jet car boats their unique appeal.
Most jet car boats, like the Model L from Water sports Car (watersportscar.com), use high-displacement jet-ski engines. A typical setup includes:
The interior of a jet car boat continues the illusion. Many models feature:
It feels like sitting inside a two-seater convertible—but instead of a road ahead, there’s open water in every direction.

They are also gaining traction at boat shows and waterfront events, where they routinely steal the spotlight from traditional yachts and PWCs.

They’re loud, bold, and built for thrill-seekers who want to turn heads and have fun doing it. While not practical for everyone, they are redefining the personal watercraft market with style, speed, and imagination. In a sea of sameness, they stand out. Literally.

title: UKOPRA Offshore Powerboat Championships
author: Michael Hodges
imageAlt: Round Three of the UKOPRA Offshore Powerboat Championships
imageCaption: Good Boy Vodka (1-25) clinching first place in the "Solent 80
summary: Under blazing skies and with the Solent simmering in summer heat, the UKOPRA Offshore Powerboat Championships roared back into action on Saturday with the third round of the series: the legendary “Solent 80.” Eighteen boats took on the demanding clockwise circuit around the Isle of Wight, delivering drama, mechanical heartbreak, and spectacular performances—classic offshore racing in all its noisy, unpredictable glor
body: Headlining the day was the emphatic return of Good Boy Vodka (1-25), driven by Rob Lockyer and American offshore ace Tim Linden. After a patchy start to the season, the Anglo-American pairing made their mark in style—blasting to victory with an average speed of 95.11 mph, leaving the Class 1 field trailing in their rooster tails.

It wasn’t plain sailing for early favourites and current championship leaders Double Trouble, the Falmouth-based team. After a strong opening burst, they were forced to shut down for a frustrating eight-minute pause due to an electrical gremlin. That moment opened the door for Lockyer and Linden, who grabbed the lead and never looked back.

Behind them, Silverline struggled with power loss on one engine, while the Swedish entry Sture Gold suffered a race-ending gearbox failure—proving again that in offshore racing, it’s not just speed but survival that counts.

Meanwhile, in Class 1L, local interest was reignited by a name from the past. Peter Hall, Isle of Wight publican and offshore enthusiast, pulled off a near-impossible feat. Having only acquired the 1973 classic Cigarette “Dry Martini” days before the race, Hall and his all-Islander crew—Tristan Ormiston and Richard Jackson—took to the water with just four hours of practice. The result? Fourth overall and a Class 1L win in their debut outing. A fine return to form for both the team and the boat.

In the highly competitive Class 3E, it was once again the silver catamaran Oblivion (E-2), driven by Marcus Dodd and Sean Girdler, that dominated proceedings. They kept things smooth and fast, outpacing their closest rivals, the Cougar monohull Renegade 2 (E-280), piloted by Andy Foster and Simon Matthews. Third place went to another well-loved hull: “Blast from the Past” (E-17), a Souter-built classic manned by Steven Tenant and Leslie Horner—proof that vintage powerboats still have what it takes to mix it with the modern machines.

There was less luck for Team NEAFS (E-24), a new outfit running a V24 hull. Despite retiring early due to technical issues, the team remains upbeat, vowing to come back stronger—and with their eyes firmly on a podium finish next time out.

With round three now complete, attention turns to the next showdown at Southampton’s Shamrock Quay on Saturday, August 9th, where rivalries will be renewed, engines will roar once more, and the championship battle will move up another gear. Expect more thrills, spills, and the kind of racing that has made offshore powerboating one of the most exhilarating motorsports on water.

title: Discover the awe-inspiring adventure of a sailor who journeyed from simplistic canoeing to owning a cutting-edge Dale Classic 37 yacht
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Discover the awe-inspiring adventure of a sailor who journeyed from simplistic canoeing to owning a cutting-edge Dale Classic 37 yacht
summary: Recall your sheer childhood joy of water adventures, as this tale uniquely captures the romantic transition from canoe paddling to sailing an elegant yacht.
body: Who doesn't enjoy the euphoria of life's simplest pleasures? For our protagonist, this euphoria was birthed on the local rivers and canals of his hometown, aboard a Canadian canoe built by his father. These were the days of delightful exploration, paddling down the River Wye to the tune of the dawn chorus, or gallantly navigating a kayak alone across the harbour during a family camping trip.

As years soared by, life found Tim Steel and his lovely wife Annette celebrating more of their days on the South Devon coast. By 2017, Tim's exploration cravings had outgrown a paddle's purpose, drawing him into the captivating world of modern maritime vessels. Here, he found comfort and excitement in the XO 270, a cool, fast, and seaworthy charmer that transported them across the majestical coastlines of South Devon and Cornwall. However, frequent day trips were the limit of this platform.

The quest for the ideal 'bigger boat,' capable of hosting grander adventures, began. Their wishlist included desiring a vessel capable of comfortably cruising the Channel Islands, France, Scillies, Wales, and Ireland for weeks on end. The boat needed to be spacious, consisting of two well-equipped cabins, a workable galley, and a comfortable heads with a good shower. Size was also a factor, decking a boat that is not greater than 40ft for easy harbour manoeuvering and reducing docking costs. Finally, it had to be smooth riding, stylish, and durable enough to persevere the test of time.

The journey explored various brands, planing and semi-displacement boats. However, the journey concluded on deck of a Dale Classic 37, a vessel that harmonized every note in their wishlist. This exquisite boat is an impressive display of excellent craftsmanship, superior seamanship, and striking heritage - a dream come true for Tim and his family

title: Spectacular Scenes as Yachting World Dayboat Open Captivates Poole
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Spectacular Scenes as Yachting World Dayboat Open Captivates Poole
summary: The exciting Yachting World Dayboat Open unfolded at Poole Yacht club generating high octane action over two days.
body: The revered Poole Yacht Club was abuzz with excitement as it played host to the Yachting World Dayboat Open. Despite the imminent Dayboat championships in Falmouth and the forecast of stormy weather, the event saw 12 boats vying for victory, attesting to the steely resilience of the participants. Balancing meticulous strategy and skilful sailing, the open unfolded over two captivating days, putting the participants and their yachts to the ultimate test.

Day one saw two action-packed long-distance races around the picturesque harbour islands. Only six boats braved the erratic conditions during the morning session. A race littered with giant shifts and areas devoid of breeze transformed the route to Green Island into a high-stakes gamble. However, Sue and Howard Clayton emerged victorious, overcoming challenges, keeping to the marked channels and capitalising on the rising tide at the harbour entrance.

The final day of the tournament brought fierce winds, shrinking the turnout to six steadfast boats. As the yachts cleaved through break-neck winds of up to 28 knots, a thrilling spectacle unfolded on triangle/sausage courses. Despite an unfortunate rudder breakage, the sailors exhibited nothing less than masterful prowess as they tamed the tempestuous weather.

The Yachting World Dayboat Open serves to highlight the enduring strength and tenacity of these talented sailors. Weathering storms both literal and metaphorical, they continue to inspire, delivering a spectacle that draws the attention of the world.

title: Could two shiny new JPK 1050s cause trouble in IRC Two?
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: JPK 1050: Fast, French and Ready to Shake Up IRC Two
summary: Wouldn’t be the first time a Jean-Pierre Kelbert design came in sideways and stole the silverware. His initials are stamped on the transom — literally — and his boats have a reputation for upsetting the pecking order in offshore racing. The 34-foot JPK 1050 might just be the sharpest new weapon in a fleet of 73, and it’s already shown a flash of brilliance.
body: Case in point: Léon, the works boat, borrowed by Hervé Chataigner and offshore legend Gildas Morvan for June’s Transmanche dash across the Channel. Not content with simply showing up, they smashed the course record. And this was before Chataigner had even taken delivery of his own 1050, Pilou. One gets the feeling they’ve barely begun to scratch the surface of what the boat can do.

Chataigner’s secret weapon is Morvan — a sailor with serious credentials: America’s Cup in ‘95, Olympics in ‘96, two decades on the Figaro circuit, multiple transatlantic races in IMOCA 60s, and a resume built on grit and podiums. Together, they’re aiming Pilou squarely at Léon — which will be helmed by Jean-Pierre Kelbert himself, alongside none other than Alexis Loison. That name should ring bells. Loison and his father Pascal won the 2013 Fastnet overall — still the only doublehanded crew to ever claim the big trophy.

Loison is back on board Léon, a boat from the same design family as Lann Ael 3. “Fast reaching and downwind,” he says. “She’s lighter than the last one.” That might be understatement. Ludovic Gérard thinks so too — he’s bringing his new JPK 1050 Solenn for Pure Ocean to the line, teamed up with Eliott Coville. After eight seasons with the JPK 1080 version of Solenn, Gérard’s expecting speed and smiles from the new ride.

Meanwhile, the latest Lann Ael has already proven her point. Didier Gaudoux’s semi-scow Manuard-Nivelt NM 35 tore it up in last year’s blustery Loro Piana Giraglia, slicing through the 241-mile course in under 25 hours with co-skipper Erwan Tabarly. She’s built for this kind of thing. Light, fast, and designed to surf, Lann Ael 3 also won the first IRC Two-Handed European Championship and comes with the weighty honour of Gaudoux’s 2017 Fastnet win on Lann Ael 2.
Bottom line? When the breeze is hot and on the quarter, these easily-driven, twin-rudder rocket ships are going to be hard to touch. But IRC Two isn’t just a scow-sailed playground.

At the top of the leaderboard in the RORC Season's Points is Scarlet Oyster, a boat with more bluewater miles than most of the fleet combined. Ross Applebey’s Lightwave 48 has crossed the Atlantic 13 times and logged more than 150,000 miles. She’s a family heirloom, racing since 1999, and aside from one Fastnet missed in 2009 for charity work, she’s been a podium regular: five seconds and two firsts.

Then there’s the rise of the Pogos. Midnight Blues, a 34ft Pogo RC with a hungry crew, is turning heads. Owned by RORC committee man Jean-Eudes Renier and co-skippered by Rear Commodore Joe Lacey, it’s a boat with French offshore pedigree and a helm with serious RORC roots.

Not to be overlooked is Codiam, a well-bedded-in Grand Soleil 43 campaigned by IRC veterans Nicolas Loday and Jean-Claude Nicoleau. Loday, now 74, has sailed the Fastnet more times than most have had hot dinners. A 505 World Champion in 1972, he later coached France to Olympic bronze in ‘84 and even did a leg of the Whitbread. This guy teaches history and geography — and has made both on the water.

Another Grand Soleil 43 to watch: Ikigaï, making her Fastnet debut with a Belgian university crew representing KYCN. Skipper Benoît Stevens wants stories, memories, and a touch of Tabarly-esque adventure. “It’s about seamanship, friendship and unpredictability,” he says — which might as well be the mission statement of this whole race.

Further north, the student crew on Löwe von Bremen, a Sun Fast 3600 skippered by Frederick Nabor, are flying the flag for Germany’s Segelkameradschaft “Das Wappen von Bremen.” From medicine to politics, their academic mix rivals their sail trim.

From New Caledonia comes Alofi, a Figaro 3 fresh from Solitaire campaigns. Skipper Thierry Levayer and offshore thoroughbred Philippe Delamare (fresh off winning the Global Solo Challenge) are here for training — but with over 100,000 miles in the logbook, they’ll be competitive too.

Prime Suspect, a Mills 36 Custom out of Rosslare Harbour, knows Irish waters well and wears RNLI ties on her sleeve. Owned by Keith Miller, Tom O’Connor, and Donal McLoughlin, she’s got Round Ireland and D2D experience and a lifeboatman at the helm.

From across the pond, Avanti, a Hanse 430 out of the USA, brings firepower in the form of Jeremi Jablonski and Marek Mirota — fresh off the Transatlantic Race, no less, and past IRC Two-Handed winners in the RORC Transatlantic.

And flying the flag for Fastnet’s golden age: Crusade, a 1969 Gurney 64 once owned by Sir Max Aitken. Line honours in the Sydney-Hobart, Admiral’s Cup veteran — and yet she’s still racing at the front. A third-place finish in the recent Myth of Malham proves she’s more than just a piece of yachting history.

Just behind her in that same race? Rogan Josh, Richard Powell’s First 40 and the new 2025 IRC Two National Champion. Royal Thames crew, fully amateur, but proving that teamwork and consistency still count for something.

The J/Boat fleet is deep and dangerous in IRC Two. Corazon, Lawrence Herbert’s J/133, took second in the Myth of Malham and boasts a crew of under-30s with three solid RORC seasons under their belt. Vice Commodore Derek Shakespeare’s Bulldog, a J/122, won the De Guingand Bowl last year and remains a threat whenever the breeze picks up.

With conditions looking likely to favour the light, planing hulls, the JPK 1050s and Lann Ael 3 could well rocket ahead. But this division’s deeper than the Mariana Trench — full of history, heavyweights, and hungry newcomers.
You wouldn’t bet the rum on any one winner just yet.

title: Massive €1.5M Price Drop for Mangusta's Newest 50-meter Superyacht Big On Luxurious Perks
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Massive €1.5M Price Drop for Mangusta's Newest 50-meter Superyacht Big On Luxurious Perks
summary: A notable €1.5 million price cut for Felicità, Mangusta's latest 50-meter superyacht, has recently been announced, sparking a buzz among luxury yacht enthusiasts.
body: Get ready for a wave of enthusiasm in the luxury yacht market as the Felicità, a brand-new, 50-meter superyacht by Mangusta, has recently undergone a hefty price reduction of €1.5 million. Currently in the final stages of construction, Felicità is a proud addition to the Mangusta Oceano 50 series — a celebrated line of yachts known for their shimmering allure and top-notch performance.

Designed by the famed Alberto Mancini and Mangusta Yachts' in-house team, this superyacht is a remarkable vessel constructed with a durable steel hull and an aluminium superstructure. The interior dons a contemporary design by Overmarine's in-house team, in collaboration with Pierluigi Ausonio PLANA.

Apart from the aesthetically pleasing living spaces, she also showcases an 'expansive' beach club aft, an open cine theatre on the upper deck, an oversized gymnasium, and a stunning blue marble and mosaic-tiled Hammam. Felicità also offers ample enjoyments for the water sports enthusiasts.
Guests can enjoy the Jacuzzi pool on the sundeck or unwind in the freestanding lounge seating on the vast foredeck above the garage where tenders and toys are stowed.

Powering Felicità are twin 1,700hp MTU engines. These engines equip her with a max speed of 16 knots and a cruising speed of 12 knots. Her range takes you 4,500 nautical miles at an economical 11 knots. All of this luxury and power are now available for €36,000,000, from the previous price of €37,500,000. The Felicità superyacht is scheduled for delivery by Summer 2025.

title: Breaking Boundaries: The Most Exciting Superyachts to Attend the Monaco Yacht Show 2025
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Breaking Boundaries: The Most Exciting Superyachts to Attend the Monaco Yacht Show 2025
summary: The Monaco Yacht Show 2025, a pinnacle event in the superyacht calendar, is set to showcase some of the world's most remarkable megayachts.
body: An event that turns heads and stirs excitement in the boating world, the Monaco Yacht Show never fails to astonish spectators with a collection of the world's most prestigious yachts. The anticipation for the 2025 show is no exception, as it is set to host over 30 entries in the 50-metre-plus range at Port Hercule from 24 to 27 September. The yachts to be displayed exemplify seamless fusion of indulgence, cutting-edge technology, and extravagant design.

Adding to the stellar line-up is 'Gigia', an 85-meter vessel by Lürssen, designed with paramount focus on privacy. It offers accommodation for 20 guests across 10 lavish cabins, alongside features like a sprawling dining table, an extensive wine presentation area, and a private owner's deck.

'Bilgin Yachts' introduces yet another masterpiece, 'Al Reem', an 80-meter yacht boasting more volume than its predecessors and a fresh new layout for heightened privacy. Feadship's 'Valor' and 'Amels' Energy' have also made it to the list of this year's elite display of superyachts, promising an experience that will redefine luxury and innovation in yachting. With each promising unmatched opulence, advanced naval architecture, and ground-breaking design, the Monaco Yacht Show 2025 is set to be an event of unrivalled maritime luxury and engineering brilliance.

title: High-Tension Drama as Tornado Open, Mixed and Youth World Championships Kick Off
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: High-Tension Drama as Tornado Open, Mixed and Youth World Championships Kick Off
summary: The opener for the 2025 Tornado Open, Mixed and Youth World Championships marked a spectacular start brimming with high-seas drama.
body: The 2025 Tornado Open, Mixed and Youth World Championships got off to a cracking start with an exhilarating first day of racing. Competitors were met with light winds and challenging conditions, all amid the vibrant atmosphere of what promises to be a thrilling showcase of talent.

As the second race unfurled, the breeze freshened to 7-9 knots and rivalry was rife. Michaela & Marek and Mavros & Parianos found themselves in a bow-to-bow battle throughout the contest, each vying for the lead as they skillfully adapted to the shifting winds. Finally, it was Michaela & Marek who swept ahead, securing their first 'bullet' win of the championship, with Mavros & Parianos trailing close in second place.

After the enthralling first day, Michaela Pavlisova & Marek Pavlis emerged as frontrunners in the Open Mixed and Youth categories; however, Nikolaos Mavros & Polykarpos Parianos are hot on their heels, with matching points on the score-board. The Tornado Class recognises 'youth teams' as those where both sailors are under 26 years old, offering a thrilling competition landscape for talent born in 2000 or later.

Once ashore, the racers were treated to a Traditional Pita Party—a fitting finish to an action-packed opening day. Expectations are now set sky-high for the rest of the championship as the world's top sailors prepare to take on their next challenge.

title: Numarine's Latest Marvel: Miouch, the 40MXP Model Raising the Bar in Luxury Yachting
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Numarine's Latest Marvel: Miouch, the 40MXP Model Raising the Bar in Luxury Yachting
summary: The Turkish shipyard, Numarine, launches its new flagship explorer yacht, the 40MXP model, Miouch, catwalk ready and making waves in the industry.
body: The Turkish marine titan, Numarine, has unveiled a spectacle from its Gebze dockyard. This time it radiates not just with another seafaring beauty, but its flagship explorer yacht, the 40MXP model, christened Miouch. It is this innovative shipyard's latest gem, an evolution of the highly popular 37XP model, now packaged with a bigger and grander appeal. As described by Numarine's chairman, Ömer Malaz, Miouch carries forward the yard's ethos of designing high-volume, low-maintenance yachts with significant long-range capabilities.

What sets Miouch, the flagship build, apart are her extended aft decks. The upper deck, ordained with a glass-fronted dip pool, adds an exclusive touch. The shipyard's general manager, Murat Şen, marveled at the overwhelming response from the market, with three 40MXP hulls sold already before the first launch. Undoubtedly, a notable success in the industry.

Miouch boasts two extra meters than her antecedent, with a significant portion of additional space dedicated to the aft deck. This layout entails a sizable alfresco dining space, an inviting bar, a comfortable lounge, and an aft pool with a glass transom, all contributing to an elevated experience of opulence. According to Malaz, the new aft layout enhances an owner's indulgence in everything the yacht has on offer, making it a fitting place to unwind with family and friends by the water.

Miouch is also a storage marvel. It can accommodate a nine-meter tender and house three Jet Skis, still leaving room for additional water sports equipment. With 11 yachts currently in build or on order, Numarine continues to shape the luxury yachting industry with its magnificent creations.

title: Revolutionising Yacht Management: The Voly Group Software Suite's Bold Vision for the Future
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Revolutionising Yacht Management: The Voly Group Software Suite's Bold Vision for the Future
summary: Pioneering innovation in the yachting industry, the Voly Group Software Suite aims to revolutionise yacht management with comprehensive digital solutions.
body: Sailing steadily into the harbours of the future, the Voly Group Software Suite navigates the management of superyachts with an unprecedented digital elegance. Tailored for the yachting industry, this suite unifies real-time reporting, global transactions, interactive project management tools and efficient crew payroll systems - all in one seamless platform. The intent behind this technological leap? To enhance the day-to-day ease of yacht operations.

Having successfully attracted an array of brands under its banner, the Voly Group aims to streamline the yacht management companies' operations, placing it at the forefront of modern yacht management technology. Not looking to replace yacht management companies, but rather to support them by providing a robust toolkit

Experts predict that, by 2026, the Voly Group Software Suite will catapult yacht management to the next level, offering a unified dashboard to keep track of every yacht detail. Whether one is a captain, crew member, yacht manager or family office member – everyone can benefit from this streamlined system. Yacht managers can now effortlessly manage payroll, review refit items, load pre-paid cards, and handle more tasks without juggling with spreadsheets or chasing updates.

Voly Group also offers some remarkable flagship products like Voly Financial Management, a financial management tool tailored specifically for yachts, and Voly APA Charter Management that profoundly alters the way Advance Provisioning Allowance (APA) is managed. With these and many more sophisticated tools under its belt, Voly Group Software Suite sails confidently towards a future where managing yachts is a breeze, irrespective of one's location in the world.

title: Admiral Launches Spectacular 78m Superyacht with Revolutionary Propulsion System
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Admiral Launches Spectacular 78m Superyacht with Revolutionary Propulsion System
summary: Admiral, part of The Italian Sea Group, has unveiled their latest innovation, a custom-built 78 metre superyacht, complete with a pioneering hybrid propulsion system.
body: The Italian Sea Group (TISG) recently unleashed its newest marvel on the water. Admiral, a division of TISG, delivered a beautifully bespoke 78-meter superyacht. She stands neck and neck with the yard-standing colossus Platinum. Revealed to the public for the first time in January, the mega-vessel cuts a striking figure with her distinctive aqua-blue hull.

This superyacht's exterior design symbolises elegance and finesse. Combining a polished aesthetic with high-end finishings, the architectural design is the fruit of hard-driven creativity and craftmanship of Sinot Yacht Architecture and Design, who also curated the interiors. The yacht’s naval engineering was executed in-house at TISG.

The comfort and luxury on this artistic composition do not stop at the water's edge. The breakthrough superyacht offers accommodation for 12 guests and high-class lifestyle features including a six-meter swimming pool, spa, dive area, gym and a dedicated helipad for efficient arrivals and departures from the shore.

In a statement that mirrors their visionary approach to yacht construction, TISG founder and CEO Giovanni Costantino commented, 'The Admiral 78M goes beyond being a mega yacht, she promises treasured experiences at sea, seamlessly blending innovation, elegance and a profound respect for the environment.'

These are busy times for TISG. While the commanding delivery of this opulent superyacht has raised the bar, the company currently has a further 16 Admiral projects in pipeline. This includes the notable 100-metre hybrid superyacht, recently reaching a significant stage in its construction. If the company's recent feats and current ventures are any indication, then maritime enthusiasts can expect innovative brilliance ahead of its anticipated 2026 completion.

title: Riva Debuts Sports-Luxury Redesign with Launch of First 112 Dolcevita Super Model
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Riva Debuts Sports-Luxury Redesign with Launch of First 112 Dolcevita Super Model
summary: Celebrated Italian yacht brand Riva introduces a game-changing restyling with the grand debut of its first 112 Dolcevita Super model.
body: La Spezia, Italy, is abuzz with the launch of the first 112 Dolcevita Super model yacht, courtesy of Italian yard Riva. The much-awaited event signals the brand's radical restyling of its classic models, and it was all achieved by the impeccable craftsmanship of the award-winning Officina Italiana Design studio.

The new model, part of the illustrious Ferretti Group, stands out in her 34.4-metre length, proudly displaying the sporty, assertive profile that is the hallmark of all Riva flybridge yachts. However, the boat's outstanding feature lies in its truly unique outdoor space. The beach club, with its ultra-low 35-square-metre platform, offers incomparable access to the open sea. This haven houses an extra-large, sun-drenched sofa lounge – made even more useful with a ventilated storage space for safekeeping of the two SeaBobs. Under the sunpad, one finds a large garage, spacious enough to house a tender and a Jet Ski.

The yacht's interior also raises the bar, with the main saloon offered in two distinctive configurations – dining area aft and the lounge midships, or the more traditional lounge area by the entry and the dining area centrally placed - both reflecting the superb design elements seen on her smaller sibling, the Riva 102 Corsaro Super. The extensive use of high-gloss rosewood and decorative black leather adds a lavish touch to the yacht's interior, emphasising guest comfort. Additions like a reinforced lower deck bulkhead and redesigned flooring enhance the overall acoustic experience, providing a tranquil environment unmatched by others.

As a testament to Riva's commitment to innovation, the flybridge furnishings have been entirely revamped on the 112 Dolcevita Super. It flaunts a new welcoming and versatile style, with a cocktail bar featuring stools and a television facing a large sofa lounge. The model effortlessly embodies sport-luxury at its finest, promising an exceptional experience on the high seas.

With a range of projects in the pipeline, including a 70-metre hybrid superyacht commissioned by a loyal Riva customer, the future is looking bright and promising for this trusted brand. It seems that Riva, with its radical restyling and unwavering commitment to luxury, will continue to keep us intrigued and spellbound.

title: Intense Competition, High Spirits Mark Long Beach 2025 Olympic Classes Regatta
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Intense Competition, High Spirits Mark Long Beach 2025 Olympic Classes Regatta
summary: The 2025 Long Beach Olympic Classes Regatta witnessed top-drawer competition defining a week of sailing supremacy.
body: The Long Beach Olympic Classes Regatta made waves in Southern California as the competing sailors navigated through wind gusts and waves under sun-soaked skies. The regatta was a sight for champions with competitors delivering high-octane races that had spectators riveted to the edge of their seats.

In the 49er FX class division, the Swedish team of Vilma Bobeck, an established world-class helm and 2024 Olympic silver medalist, and Ebba Berntsson, an emerging FX sailor, led the fleet. The competitive pair delivered a show-stopping performance, with Bobeck's finesse at steering and Berntsson's increasing skill from participating in top-tier regattas.

Meanwhile, USA's Paris Henken and Helena Scutt, who created history by being the first USA duo to compete in the 49erFX at Olympic level at Rio in 2016, returned for another showdown. The duo displayed their continued aptitude for sailing on a high level, sparking formidable competition.

Results declared saw regatta podiums filled with top competitors from different divisions like the FX, 49er, Nacra 17, Women's iQFOil and Men's iQFOil. The regatta set an effective precedence for sailing's rising stars offering them a pivotal experience and an opportunity to showcase their sailing prowess into the upcoming LA28 Olympic Games.

title: Cruise further, cruise safer: tackling the beautiful coastline from Poole to Penzance
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Cruise further, cruise safer: tackling the beautiful coastline from Poole to Penzance
summary: Join adventure-seeker Simon Ellis on his thrilling three-month sabbatical travelling from Poole to Penzance, stopping at every bay, harbour, and marina along the way.
body: Imagine the thrill of a coastal cruise, every day a new chapter in the diary of a lifelong love for the sea. This was just the case for Simon Ellis, who used his sabbatical to traverse the picturesque sea route between Poole and Penzance. Each day brought fresh sea breezes, lungfuls of salty air and breathtaking coastal landscapes. Join Simon as he tours every bay, marina, and harbour on his way to the majestic Scilly Isles.

On their 16th day, Babbacombe Bay welcomed them with sun-soaked serenity, prompting the decision to spend the day and night at anchor. The joy on deck was infectious, with laughter and banter permeating the sea air, while sipping on sundown drinks at the Cary Arms. However, the chilliness of the water kept their swimming ambitions at bay.

The following day, the crew made its way back to Torquay, following a breakfast fit for kings. As they strolled through Paignton, they admired the unrivalled views from the terrace of the Redcliff Hotel. Back at the marina, they witnessed the nurturing instincts of swans tending to their clutch of eggs, adding to the beauty of their surroundings.

Day 18 brought more sunshine and an easterly swell, leading them to explore Brixham, adding another gem to their coastal treasure trove. The sea, however, remained unfit for a dip. On the cards for the day were activities that ranged from stand-up paddleboarding to onboard Thai culinary sessions, rounding off yet another day of their life-affirming journey.

title: Shaping the Future of the Superyacht Industry: An Urgent Call for Resolute Measures to Improve Safety Features in Vessel Design
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Shaping the Future of the Superyacht Industry: An Urgent Call for Resolute Measures to Improve Safety Features in Vessel Design
summary: Embracing the journey of enhancing superyacht safety, this piece highlights essential design concerns in the maritime industry, underscoring the dire need for design improvements.
body: An insightful analysis from CHIRP Maritime's Superyacht Feedback addresses the rising safety concerns in the superyacht industry. Through the detailed narrative of a reporter who recently joined a vessel under construction, this initiative highlights theSuperyacht Maritime Advisory Board's commitment to improving maritime safety through anonymous reporting and sharing critical insights.

The reporter underlined the requirement for 'pad eyes'- robust points enabling safe work practice at heights. While more pad eyes were deemed necessary, the request for additional ones was rebuffed by the shipyard. They claimed the design, already sanctioned by the owner, architects, and classification society, negated the need for modifications.

This matter underlines the much-needed emphasis on soliciting and assimilating the experiences of operators during the design stage. It's absolutely integral to prioritize safety implications for crew and passengers right from the design phase. A rigid feedback process is propitious, enabling the integration of experiential learning into future builds.

Active participation from owners, classification societies, and Flag states is essential during the design phase. Equally, crews should provide feedback regarding design flaws to Flag states. It's imperative to instill a proactive safety culture instead of a merely calculative one, where essential compliance is the bare minimum.

The salient points derived from this report entail promoting a proactive safety culture, emphasizing on additional safety features, and encouraging robust communication around safety designs. CHIRP's commendable initiatives serve to encourage active participation in the pursuit of enhanced operational safety for crews working on superyachts. With this, it's full steam ahead for the safety revolution in the superyacht industry.

title: A Riveting Weekend of Sailing as SailGP Makes Waves in Portsmouth
