body: Tucked along the rugged northeastern coast of Sardinia, Italy, Porto Cervo is a name that resonates across the world’s yachting elite. A purpose-built haven for sailors, jet-setters, and sun-seekers alike, it stands as the undisputed capital of the Costa Smeralda – the Emerald Coast – famous for its turquoise waters, unspoiled beaches, and luxurious Mediterranean lifestyle. But at the heart of Porto Cervo’s appeal lies its deep and enduring connection to the sea.

Porto Cervo was conceived in the early 1960s by Prince Karim Aga Khan IV, who fell in love with Sardinia’s wild beauty. Alongside a group of international investors and renowned architects, he envisioned a coastal village that would preserve the island’s character while offering discreet luxury to Europe’s elite. What emerged is one of the most exclusive and tastefully designed resorts in the Mediterranean.

The town itself is compact, with winding alleys, pastel buildings, and manicured piazzas. There’s no high-rise glamour here – instead, Porto Cervo offers understated elegance that blends harmoniously into the surrounding landscape. Yet make no mistake: this is a destination where superyachts replace taxis, and designer boutiques outnumber beach bars.

At the centre of Porto Cervo’s maritime life is the Yacht Club Costa Smeralda (YCCS), founded in 1967 by the Aga Khan. It has since become one of the world’s most prestigious sailing institutions, on par with the Royal Yacht Squadron or the New York Yacht Club. The YCCS is a magnet for both traditional yacht owners and cutting-edge racers, thanks to its impeccable facilities and a racing calendar that reads like a who’s who of international regattas.

Annual events include the Rolex Swan Cup, the Loro Piana Superyacht Regatta, the Maxi Yacht Rolex Cup, and various 12 Metre and J-Class events. These attract sailing legends, Olympic champions, and billionaire boat owners to compete in one of the most visually stunning backdrops on the planet.

Yachting and the Yacht Club Costa Smeralda (YCCS) The heart of the yachting scene is the Yacht Club Costa Smeralda (YCCS), founded in 1967. It's one of the world’s top yacht clubs, renowned for hosting premier international regattas including:
Rolex Swan Cup
Maxi Yacht Rolex Cup
Loro Piana Superyacht Regatta
12 Metre Championships
Perini Navi Cup
Yacht Club Costa Smeralda features a state-of-the-art marina and clubhouse with bars, terraces, lounges, and a restaurant offering panoramic views of the marina and Tyrrhenian Sea.

Berths: ~700 (including for megayachts up to 120m) Services: 24/7 security, fuel dock, power & water hookups, waste disposal, Wi-Fi, repairs, provisioning, concierge Facilities: Shipyard services, technical assistance, private tender dock, helipad access nearby

The clubhouse itself is elegant but relaxed – with panoramic terraces, a fine dining restaurant, a members’ bar, and open-air lounges that overlook the harbour. For visiting sailors, the YCCS also offers top-tier berthing and concierge services.

The Marina di Porto Cervo, adjacent to the yacht club, is divided into the Old Port (Porto Vecchio) and the New Marina. Together, they offer over 700 berths, including spaces for megayachts up to 120 metres. Facilities are world-class, with everything from 24/7 security, electricity and water supply, high-speed Wi-Fi, fuel dock, and black water disposal, to full shipyard services, chandlery, provisioning, and even helicopter access nearby.
It’s no exaggeration to say the marina is one of the most advanced and best-maintained in the world, designed to meet the demands of royalty, celebrities, and serious offshore competitors alike.

Once ashore, Porto Cervo offers a lifestyle that is effortlessly luxurious. From Michelin-starred dining at places like Cervo Restaurant or La Pergola, to late nights at Billionaire Club or Ritual, there is no shortage of high-end experiences. For shoppers, the waterfront is lined with flagship stores from Gucci, Versace, Dolce & Gabbana, and more.

Yet, the true charm of Porto Cervo is the ease with which you can escape it all. A short sail or drive reveals hidden coves, unspoilt beaches, and local trattorias far from the spotlight. Many visiting yachts stay longer than planned – and few leave unimpressed.

title: Puerto del Rey Marina
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Puerto del Rey Marina
summary: Situated on the northeastern tip of Puerto Rico, Puerto del Rey Marina (now part of the Safe Harbor network) is widely regarded as one of the largest and most capable marinas in the Caribbean. It combines scale, service, and strategic location to serve as both a comfortable home base and an efficient stepping stone to the Virgin Islands and beyond.
body: Situated on the northeastern tip of Puerto Rico, Puerto del Rey Marina (now part of the Safe Harbor network) is widely regarded as one of the largest and most capable marinas in the Caribbean. It combines scale, service, and strategic location to serve as both a comfortable home base and an efficient stepping stone to the Virgin Islands and beyond.
The marina's address is 4900 State Rd. 3, Km 51.4, Fajardo, PR 00738
It sits inside a naturally protected bay, with a significant breakwater to shelter from storms and ocean surge.

Originally completed around 1988 and later refurbished (notably in 2014) Puerto del Rey now operates near full capacity. The marina is laid out on concrete fixed docks, floating piers, and a dry-stack storage yard, covering roughly 60 acres of waterfront property.
Puerto del Rey is notable for its sheer numbers:
Over 1,000 wet slips for yachts up to 180 feet LOA.
Drafts up to 15 feet (~4.6 m) are supported in many slips.
Dry stack storage for smaller vessels, with space to stack boats three high and spacing of fairways and docks are generous, which reduces the stress of maneuvering in a crowded facility.
Given its dimensions and the number of slips, Puerto del Rey is often dubbed the largest marina in the Caribbean.
Puerto del Rey doesn’t just rest on scale—it supports a broad suite of services for cruiser and yacht needs:
Utilities: Shore power (various amperages), metered water, Wi-Fi, and pump-out services are available throughout the marina.
Fuel Dock: Diesel and gasoline delivery to slips is offered.
Shuttle & Mobility: Because the docks are far-flung, the marina operates golf cart shuttle service to ferry crew and provisioning items.
Haul-out & Repairs: A 165‑ton travel lift, dry storage, and space for repair contractors are available on-site.
Security & Access: The marina offers 24/7 security, gated access, and monitored perimeter systems.
Customs & Immigration: As Puerto del Rey is designated as a sea port of entry, on-site immigration, customs, coast guard, and regulatory offices simplify arrivals.
Lodging & Amenities: Beyond marine services, the marina offers rooms, dining, game rooms, gym, a convenience store, and the ability to arrange excursions.

One reviewer guest described the marina as “massive but still manages to offer excellent customer service. The slips and fairways are generously sized, and the golf cart shuttle service makes navigating such a large facility manageable.”
Operational Strengths & Weaknesses
Strategic staging point: Its location is ideal for transitions between Puerto Rico and the Virgin Islands, or for long passages toward the west or south. Discover Puerto Rico
Resilience: The marina’s structure is known to have endured storms (e.g. Hurricane Maria) with its concrete docks proving reliable.
Comprehensive services: The marina's broad scope—from utilities to repairs to guest amenities—makes it a self-contained base.
Scale with navigation ease: Despite its size, features like shuttle service, wide fairways, and clear signage help reduce the logistical burden of moving among hundreds of slips.
Distance & walking: Slips can be a long walk from the marina office or parking; relying on shuttle service is common. Sailing Satori
Provisioning scale: On-site marine stores and convenience items are good, but for full provisioning crews often have to drive into Fajardo or San Juan for larger supermarkets.
Booking in peak season: Given its reputation and size, transient slips may fill up, so early reservations are advisable.
Connectivity hiccups: Some users report occasional Wi-Fi or electrical metering glitches, though these are not deal-breakers for most.

From a visitor’s perspective, Puerto del Rey is both welcoming and impressive. Many cruisers report that the staff are responsive, the marina layout is logical, and the amenities make longer stays comfortable. Some recount special generosity, with complimentary stay offers in exchange for visibility.

Crew and captains enjoy the ability to handle multiple tasks ashore—immigration, provisioning, technical maintenance, and leisure—without constant repositioning. The marina essentially functions as a one-stop hub on the east coast of Puerto Rico.
For boats gearing to cross to the Virgin Islands, Puerto del Rey is a logical staging ground. It also offers comfort and service for those staying longer, given its location, security, and scale.

Puerto del Rey Marina is a rare blend—massive in scale, strong in infrastructure, and rooted in cruising practicality. While not perfect, its strengths far outweigh its limitations for most bluewater voyagers and seasonal basers alike. For those seeking a central, well-equipped launchpad into the Caribbean or a long-term base with robust facilities, Puerto del Rey delivers. It is not just a marina — it is a maritime community built for serious travellers.

title: Puerto Portals - Mallorca
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Puerto Portals - Mallorca
summary: Located just a short drive from the historic city of Palma, Puerto Portals is one of the most prestigious and glamorous marinas in the Mediterranean. Nestled along the southwest coast of Mallorca, this exclusive port has become a magnet for superyacht owners, celebrities, and those seeking the perfect balance of luxury, lifestyle, and nautical adventure. Offering first-class facilities, chic surroundings, and a vibra
body: Located just a short drive from the historic city of Palma, Puerto Portals is one of the most prestigious and glamorous marinas in the Mediterranean. Nestled along the southwest coast of Mallorca, this exclusive port has become a magnet for superyacht owners, celebrities, and those seeking the perfect balance of luxury, lifestyle, and nautical adventure. Offering first-class facilities, chic surroundings, and a vibrant social scene, Puerto Portals is much more than a marina—it's a destination in itself.

The marina boasts over 600 berths, accommodating vessels from 8 to 60 meters in length, with limited space for even larger superyachts. Its deep-water access and sheltered position in Bay of Palma make it a safe and reliable harbour throughout the year. Due to its popularity, especially in summer, advance reservations are essential for those looking to secure a berth during peak months. Each berth is serviced with electricity (up to 125 amps), fresh water, Wi-Fi, and grey/black water disposal. The marina also offers 24/7 security, dockside assistance, and customs and immigration services. A dedicated fuel dock, chandlery, and marine services area provide essential support for maintenance, repairs, and provisioning. Whether you're stopping in for a few days or planning a longer stay, the marina’s professional staff ensure that every detail is taken care of.

What truly sets Puerto Portals apart is its sophisticated atmosphere and stylish infrastructure. The waterfront promenade is lined with high-end boutiques, designer stores, and fine dining restaurants, many with terraces overlooking the yachts. Well-known brands like Louis Vuitton, Hermes, and Rolex sit comfortably beside independent fashion outlets and luxury lifestyle stores, making it a shopping haven for discerning visitors. Dining in Puerto Portals is a social experience. The marina is home to some of the island’s most celebrated restaurants and lounges, including Baiben, led by Michelin-starred chef Fernando P. Arellano, and the ever-popular Ritzi, a hotspot for fine Italian cuisine and evening cocktails. Trendy bars such as Social Club and Wellies offer the perfect setting for people-watching and sipping champagne while the sun sets behind the masts. Puerto Portals is also famous for its calendar of glamorous events, including international sailing regattas, fashion shows, and classic car exhibitions. These occasions draw an international crowd and add to the marina's electric atmosphere, particularly in the summer months.

The location is ideal for exploring the Balearics. From Puerto Portals, it’s an easy cruise to Cabrera National Park, the coves of Andratx, or the crystalline waters of Es Trenc. It also serves as a convenient jumping-off point for longer voyages to Ibiza or Menorca.

Weather-wise, Mallorca offers a Mediterranean climate with over 300 days of sunshine a year. Summers (June to September) are warm and dry, with average temperatures between 27–33°C (81–91°F), and light sea breezes that make for pleasant sailing conditions. Spring and autumn are also fantastic times to visit, with fewer crowds and equally gorgeous weather.

In summary, Puerto Portals is where nautical excellence meets island glamour. With its flawless service, chic atmosphere, and access to some of the most beautiful cruising grounds in the Med, it remains one of the most desirable marinas in Europe for those who love both sailing and style. Known as the St. Tropez of Spain. Superyacht playground meets upscale shopping.

author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Safe Harbor Newport Shipyard
summary: Nestled in the heart of historic Newport, Rhode Island—long hailed as the yachting capital of the U.S.—Safe Harbor Newport Shipyard is one of the premier marina destinations in North America. Famed for its capacity to handle everything from modest cruisers to world-class super yachts, this facility blends maritime tradition with state-of-the-art services. Whether you're a visiting sailor, professional crew, or yacht
body: Nestled in the heart of historic Newport, Rhode Island—long hailed as the yachting capital of the U.S.—Safe Harbor Newport Shipyard is one of the premier marina destinations in North America. Famed for its capacity to handle everything from modest cruisers to world-class super yachts, this facility blends maritime tradition with state-of-the-art services. Whether you're a visiting sailor, professional crew, or yacht owner, Newport Shipyard offers unmatched access to the vibrant marine culture of Narragansett Bay.

The marina provides 154 berths, including slips for super yachts up to 350 feet (107 meters) in length, with deepwater access and robust dockage infrastructure. It is the preferred base for many of the globe’s largest sailing and motor yachts—frequently hosting regattas, racing teams, and events such as the Newport Bermuda Race and the Ocean Race stopovers.
Facilities and Services Safe Harbor Newport Shipyard is exceptionally well-equipped, providing a full spectrum of modern amenities:
Fuel Dock: The marina offers high-speed, in-slip fueling with both diesel and gasoline available. Fuel bunkering for large vessels is also supported.
Wi-Fi: Complimentary high-speed Wi-Fi is available throughout the marina for visiting vessels.
Waste Disposal: Pump-out services and environmentally friendly waste disposal options are available at every slip.
Food and Drink: The onsite Belle’s Café is a local favorite—offering breakfast, lunch, and dockside dining with views of the harbor. Catering is available for yachts.
Fresh Water: Potable fresh water is available dockside at all slips.

Maintenance & Shipyard Services: The facility features a 500-ton Travelift (the largest in New England), as well as on-site mechanical, electrical, painting, rigging, and carpentry services. Ideal for both emergency repairs and full refits.
Showers & Laundry: Clean and secure restroom, shower, and laundry facilities are provided for visiting crews.
Security & Parking: The Shipyard is gated with 24/7 surveillance. Reserved parking is available for guests and crew.
Visitors will also find on-site marine vendors, crew services, provisioning, and event planning support—making it not just a marina but a thriving maritime village.

Whether you're pulling in for a short stay or planning a full seasonal layover, Safe Harbor Newport Shipyard combines a deep respect for seafaring history with some of the finest marina services on the East Coast. Its close proximity to downtown Newport also means easy access to boutique shopping, historic mansions, and the vibrant waterfront dining scene. For yachtsmen seeking excellence in both service and setting, it remains a top-tier destination year after year.

title: Santa Pola
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Santa Pola
summary: Situated along the sun-drenched coastline of Spain’s Costa Blanca, Club Náutico Santa Pola is a well-regarded marina that blends nautical tradition with top-class modern amenities. Located in the vibrant town of Santa Pola, this yacht club and marina serves as a gateway to the Mediterranean for both local boaters and international cruising sailors. With its ideal location, excellent services, and welcoming atmosphere
body: Situated along the sun-drenched coastline of Spain’s Costa Blanca, Club Náutico Santa Pola is a well-regarded marina that blends nautical tradition with top-class modern amenities. Located in the vibrant town of Santa Pola, this yacht club and marina serves as a gateway to the Mediterranean for both local boaters and international cruising sailors. With its ideal location, excellent services, and welcoming atmosphere, Club Náutico Santa Pola has become a favourite among yachtsmen navigating the waters between Alicante and Cartagena.

Club Náutico Santa Pola boasts more than 490 berths, accommodating boats from 6 to 20 metres in length. The marina is sheltered from prevailing winds by a robust breakwater and offers easy access to the open sea, making arrivals and departures smooth and safe. The marina caters to both permanent berth holders and visiting yachts, with a generous allocation of transient berths available year-round.

Each berth is equipped with electricity (220V), fresh water supply, and free Wi-Fi, ensuring visiting sailors enjoy a hassle-free and comfortable stay. The marina can support monohulls and catamarans and offers ample manoeuvring space, even for less experienced helmsmen.
Whether you’re stopping overnight or planning an extended stay, Club Náutico Santa Pola provides a full suite of services to meet the needs of every sailor. Key facilities include:
24-hour security and CCTV surveillance for peace of mind
Fuel dock with diesel and petrol
Toilets and hot showers, kept immaculately clean
Laundry services and vending machines
Boat repair and maintenance services, including crane and dry dock
Weather forecast updates and navigation support from marina staff
Ample parking for berth holders and guests
A friendly reception and marina office is open daily, offering assistance in Spanish and English, and can help with berth reservations, tourist information, and onward travel arrangements.

The Club is also home to a seafront restaurant and café, where guests can enjoy Spanish tapas, seafood paella, and a glass of local wine with a view of the harbour. Several nautical shops and provisioning stores are within walking distance, along with supermarkets, pharmacies, and a lively town centre full of charm.

For those looking to explore, Santa Pola offers a beautiful promenade, pristine beaches, and nearby attractions such as the Salt Museum, Santa Pola Fortress, and the ferry to Tabarca Island, Spain’s only inhabited island in the Mediterranean.

Club Náutico Santa Pola hosts regattas and social sailing events throughout the year, making it a lively and engaging place to meet other sailors. The club has a strong local membership and a reputation for hospitality, regularly welcoming cruisers from across Europe.

body: Tucked away just off the coast of Tortola in the British Virgin Islands, Scrub Island Marina offers an exclusive and luxurious haven for yachts and their owners. As part of the private Scrub Island Resort, Spa & Marina, this boutique marina combines high-end amenities, first-class service, and breathtaking Caribbean scenery. Accessible only by boat, this destination is a favourite for those looking to escape the crowds while still enjoying world-class yachting and island living.

The marina is situated in Cam Bay, a well-protected harbour with calm waters and easy access to the Sir Francis Drake Channel. It features 55 deep-water slips, including 10 specifically designed for mega yachts up to 160 feet. The marina’s location and layout provide natural protection from swells and weather, making it ideal for both overnight stays and longer-term mooring. With draft depths of up to 15 feet, even larger vessels can be accommodated comfortably. Each slip is fully equipped with water, 30/50/100 amp electricity, complimentary Wi-Fi, waste pump-out, and 24-hour security. The marina also offers customs and immigration clearance, a major convenience for those arriving from international waters. Fuel services are available at the adjacent fuel dock, and marina staff assist with docking, provisioning, and logistics, offering a seamless experience from arrival to departure. But Scrub Island Marina is much more than a place to park your yacht—it’s a gateway to luxury island living. Guests at the marina have full access to the Scrub Island Resort, a 5-star Autograph Collection resort that includes elegant villas, beachfront suites, a full-service spa, fine dining, and two infinity pools overlooking the marina and Caribbean Sea. The resort’s Ixora Spa is perched on a hilltop, offering panoramic views and a menu of treatments inspired by the natural surroundings.

Dining options range from fresh-caught seafood at Cardamom & Co. to casual poolside fare at One Shoe Beach Bar & Grill. There are also gourmet provisioning services available for yacht guests who prefer dining aboard.

The lifestyle at Scrub Island is private, polished, and indulgent. The island’s exclusivity creates a serene atmosphere, while its proximity to Tortola (just 10 minutes by ferry or tender) ensures easy access to urban amenities, charter bases, and international connections. Many yacht owners use Scrub Island as a launch point to explore the rest of the British Virgin Islands, including Norman Island, Jost Van Dyke, and Virgin Gorda—all within easy cruising range. The weather in the BVI is near-perfect year-round, with average temperatures ranging from 26–31°C (79–88°F). The region enjoys consistent trade winds, especially from November through May, making it one of the most reliable sailing destinations in the world. Rain is generally brief and refreshing, and hurricanes are rare outside of the June–November season.

In essence, Scrub Island Marina offers the perfect blend of practicality and paradise. With its five-star service, stunning natural surroundings, and luxury resort amenities, it provides an unforgettable experience for yacht owners, charter guests, and adventurers seeking a refined Caribbean escape.

body: Located in one of the most charming coastal towns of southwestern Turkey, Setur Marina Kaş offers a tranquil yet fully equipped haven for yachters exploring the Turkish Riviera. Set in the picturesque town of Kaş, on the edge of the Lycian Coast, this marina combines modern facilities with unspoiled natural beauty, ancient history, and a relaxed Mediterranean lifestyle. It’s the perfect base for those seeking both adventure and serenity in equal measure. Setur Marina Kaş is part of the Setur Marinas Group, one of Turkey’s leading marina operators, known for its quality infrastructure and exceptional service. The marina features 472 berths, including space for 80 vessels on land and the capacity to accommodate yachts up to 50 meters (164 feet) in length. The marina’s depth ranges from 4 to 12 meters, allowing deep-draft vessels to berth comfortably. It is well sheltered from winds, making it a safe and secure harbour throughout the year.

Each berth is fully serviced with electricity (up to 125A), fresh water, black and grey water discharge systems, high-speed Wi-Fi, and satellite TV. The marina also provides 24-hour security, video surveillance, and professional mooring assistance, ensuring a hassle-free stay. On-site customs and immigration services make international arrivals and departures smooth and convenient. A fuel dock with diesel and gasoline is available, and the boatyard is equipped with a 100-ton travel lift, hardstanding areas, and technical services for maintenance and repairs.

The marina’s amenities extend beyond the practical. Within the complex, you’ll find a chandlery, mini market, restaurants, a yacht club, and a fitness centre. Additional services include laundry, showers, car rentals, and shuttle services into Kaş town centre, which is only a few minutes away. The marina is eco-conscious and certified with the Blue Flag, reflecting its commitment to sustainability and environmental care.

What makes Setur Marina Kaş especially appealing is its location. The town of Kaş is a delightful blend of Turkish authenticity and understated sophistication. Strolling through its narrow streets, you’ll find boutique hotels, local artisans, wine bars, open-air cafés, and restaurants offering both traditional Turkish cuisine and international fare. The atmosphere is friendly, relaxed, and less commercialized than other tourist-heavy spots along the coast.

While not as glitzy as Bodrum or Göcek, Kaş has its own brand of glamour—quiet luxury, intimate venues, and a strong connection to nature and history. Yachters often use Setur Marina Kaş as a base for exploring Kekova Island and its sunken city, Patara Beach, or the ancient ruins of Antiphellos, all accessible via day trips. The waters around Kaş are renowned for diving, snorkeling, paddleboarding, and kayaking, with crystal-clear visibility and abundant marine life. The climate in Kaş is typically Mediterranean, with hot, dry summers and mild, wet winters. From May through October, expect clear skies, temperatures between 28–34°C (82–93°F), and gentle sea breezes. The sailing conditions are excellent, especially in late spring and early autumn when the sea is warm and the winds are favourable.

In summary, Setur Marina Kaş offers a perfect mix of modern yachting facilities and relaxed, coastal living. It’s ideal for cruisers seeking natural beauty, cultural richness, and quiet sophistication—all in one of Turkey’s most enchanting maritime settings.

body: Situated on the shimmering Broadwater of Queensland’s stunning Gold Coast, the Southport Yacht Club Marina (SYC) is one of Australia’s most prestigious and well-equipped marina destinations. It’s the flagship marina of Southport Yacht Club—established in 1946—and is revered for both its top-tier service and vibrant social atmosphere. A gateway to the Coral Sea, the Great Barrier Reef, and the Pacific, this marina caters to everyone from bluewater cruisers to luxury motor yacht owners.

The SYC Marina features over 300 berths, including dedicated superyacht moorings that can accommodate vessels up to 75 metres (246 feet). The marina is a certified Clean Marina and a Gold Anchor-accredited facility, offering modern infrastructure and a wide array of services that make it a highly sought-after stop for both local and international vessels.
Facilities for Visiting Sailors Fuel: Onsite 24-hour high-flow fuel dock supplying both diesel and unleaded petrol. Diesel bunkering is available for large vessels.
Wi-Fi: Complimentary high-speed Wi-Fi access is available throughout the marina precinct.
Electricity: 15, 32, 63, and 100 amp single and three-phase shore power is available, suitable for a range of vessel sizes.
Fresh Water: Potable water available at all berths.
Waste Disposal: Includes general waste, recycling, oil disposal, and black water pump-out facilities.
Food & Drink: The SYC Waterfront Restaurant and Bar offers fine dining with marina views. There are also casual dining options, a members’ lounge, and regular social events.

Maintenance & Marine Services: Onsite chandlery and access to nearby shipwrights, mechanics, electricians, riggers, and boat cleaners. The club maintains strong relationships with many nearby haul-out and repair facilities.
Crew & Guest Amenities: Secure gated entry, clean shower and restroom blocks, laundry facilities, car parking, concierge services, and customs/immigration assistance for international arrivals.
Recreational Facilities: Access to sailing and powerboat events, youth sailing programs, and reciprocal privileges with other major yacht clubs globally.

Perfectly positioned near Surfers Paradise, with quick access to both offshore and inland waterways, the Southport Yacht Club Marina offers a luxurious and practical base for sailors exploring Australia’s east coast. Whether you're cruising north to the Whitsundays or south toward Sydney, SYC is a premium marina that blends classic yachting hospitality with modern marine excellence.

title: V&A Waterfront Marina
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: V&A Waterfront Marina
summary: V&A Waterfront Marina – Cape Town, South Africa “Where Table Mountain towers above the mastheads”
body: V&A Waterfront Marina – Cape Town, South Africa “Where Table Mountain towers above the mastheads”

There are few places in the world where you can moor your yacht in the heart of a bustling city, step off the gangway, and walk into a cultural, culinary, and retail playground — all while having a world-famous mountain standing guard over your shoulder. But that’s exactly what you get at the V&A Waterfront Marina in Cape Town, South Africa.
For the salty old dogs, globe-trotting cruisers, and luxury-loving adventurers alike, this is where the lines between marina and metropolis blur in the best possible way.

Tucked within the historic Victoria & Alfred Waterfront — a working harbour turned world-class leisure destination — the marina sits like a polished jewel in Table Bay. Cape Town’s iconic Table Mountain looms behind, and the open waters of the South Atlantic Ocean shimmer out front. The dockside hums with the activity of tourists, artisans, fishermen, and superyacht crew.

Originally built in the 1800s to shelter merchant ships from winter storms, the V&A has evolved into a mixed-use wonderland: 450+ shops, 80+ restaurants and bars, museums, galleries, craft breweries, a world-famous aquarium, and even a Ferris wheel. It’s Disneyland for grown-ups with an ocean addiction.

The V&A Waterfront Marina isn’t the largest in Africa, nor is it the most technically advanced, but what it offers is unique: safe, secure mooring in the beating heart of one of the world’s most iconic cities.

The marina itself offers limited berths — especially for larger vessels — so booking ahead is essential. Superyachts can be accommodated with advance notice, though space is tight, and berthing is coordinated via strict port control protocols.
While it lacks the private-club feel of Mediterranean megamarinas, it delivers seamless access to services through a well-run Yacht Office and friendly dock team.
Access isn’t as simple as pulling up to a lazy Caribbean mooring buoy. All vessels must:
Hail Cape Town Port Control on VHF Channel 14
Contact “Swing Bridge” on VHF Channel 71 to request entry through the basin gate
Follow timed bridge openings into the secure inner marina
These layers of control help manage the mix of working freight, tour boats, ferries, and visiting yachts. It’s a civilised dance — like threading a needle between a container ship and a seal.
This is where V&A Marina earns its crown.
Once you're tied up and lines are snug, the gangplank becomes your front door to one of the most vibrant waterfronts in the world.
Cafés, bars, and fine dining line the harbour edge — from sushi to steak, tapas to African fusion.
The Watershed market is a treasure trove of African crafts, local textiles, and handmade gifts.
Zeitz MOCAA, the Museum of Contemporary Art Africa, sits in a converted grain silo and hosts some of the continent’s boldest modern exhibitions.
Two Oceans Aquarium is steps away and showcases the rich marine life of the Atlantic and Indian Oceans.
Live music, pop-up art shows, and bustling markets keep the quay alive long into the night.

There’s also every convenience for the long-range cruiser — supermarkets, pharmacies, barbers, and chandlers are within walking distance. And if you’re heading to or from the airport, you’re just 25 minutes from Cape Town International.

This marina isn’t a sleepy sailor’s hideaway. It’s plugged into city life. Expect joggers on the quay, tour groups snapping selfies at every turn, and local boatbuilders chatting with visiting captains at the dock gate. It’s international and distinctly African — polished but real.

Don’t be surprised to find a mega-cat moored next to a local day-sailer, or a solo circumnavigator swapping stories with a charter crew on shore leave. This is a maritime melting pot, and it’s part of what makes the V&A so special.

V&A Waterfront Marina isn’t just a stopover — it’s a front-row berth to everything Cape Town has to offer. The infrastructure is solid, the location unbeatable, and the lifestyle is second to none. Whether you’re provisioning for a South Atlantic crossing, wintering in the Southern Hemisphere, or just treating guests to a few nights under Table Mountain, this marina delivers.

Whether you’re a global circumnaviga
body: Tucked into the heart of Auckland’s bustling waterfront, Viaduct Harbour is more than just a marina—it’s New Zealand’s most prestigious yachting destination. A vibrant hub for superyachts, cruisers, and high-performance racing boats, the harbour offers top-tier facilities, world-class service, and direct access to one of the Southern Hemisphere’s most dynamic waterfront districts. Whether you’re a global circumnavigator, a racer fresh off a regatta, or a leisure cruiser chasing the Pacific sun, Viaduct Harbour delivers a seamless mix of maritime excellence and metropolitan energy.

Originally developed for the 2000 America’s Cup, Viaduct Harbour has since grown into a refined, full-service marina catering to vessels of all sizes—from 10-metre keelboats to 60-metre superyachts. It boasts around 150 berths, including stern-to and alongside options, and offers 5+ metres of depth at low tide, ensuring safe, accessible mooring even for the largest yachts.

The marina is designed with the international sailor in mind. Power (single and three-phase) and fresh water are available at every berth, along with high-speed fibre-optic internet, black and grey water pump-out, and 24/7 security with gated access and CCTV coverage. Berths can be booked for short stays, seasonal layovers, or long-term mooring, and there’s always a helpful marina team on hand to assist with docking and logistics.

Viaduct Harbour is surrounded by a dense network of marine professionals and services. Within walking distance, you’ll find everything from marine engineering firms and sailmakers to electronics specialists, chandleries, and full-service refit yards. Auckland’s marine industry is renowned globally, and many of the region’s marine trades supported previous America’s Cup challengers and round-the-world race teams.
The marina also provides concierge-style support, including:
Customs and biosecurity clearance on arrival
Bunkering and fuel delivery
Provisioning and catering
Crew accommodation and visa assistance
Travel and transport arrangements
This is especially valuable for international arrivals looking for a stress-free port of entry into New Zealand.

What makes Viaduct Harbour so unique is its unbeatable lifestyle offering. Step off your boat and you’re in the heart of Auckland’s dining and entertainment district. Fine restaurants like Soul Bar & Bistro, Baduzzi, and Hello Beasty line the waterfront, offering everything from freshly caught seafood to pan-Asian street food. Cafés, craft beer bars, art galleries, and luxury shops are all within minutes of the docks.

The marina is also a short walk from Auckland’s central business district, Sky Tower, and the Auckland Maritime Museum, offering a perfect blend of maritime history and modern city living. With views across the Waitematā Harbour and the iconic Auckland skyline behind you, it’s easy to see why Viaduct is the preferred berth for many global yacht owners.

Viaduct Harbour is more than a destination—it’s also a strategic launchpad. From here, cruisers can head north to the stunning Bay of Islands, south to the Coromandel Peninsula, or out to Great Barrier Island. For long-haul sailors, New Zealand’s position makes it a vital Pacific waypoint between Australia, Tahiti, and Southeast Asia.

The sailing season typically runs from November to April, with warm, dry weather and consistent breezes. Average summer temperatures hover around 22–26°C (72–78°F), creating ideal conditions for coastal cruising and regatta participation.

title: Exploring the Upcoming Innovations: The Most Anticipated Yachting Startups for 2025
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Exploring the Upcoming Innovations: The Most Anticipated Yachting Startups for 2025
summary: Uncovering the potential of yachting start-ups on the horizon, as championed by industry mavens Yachting Ventures.
body: Since its inception in 2020, Yachting Ventures has been an avid supporter of burgeoning businesses within the yachting industry. Led by Gabbi Richardson and Lucy Wright, the initiative has collaborated with over 300 enterprises across 25 countries, facilitating approximately £500 million in total funding. Besides financial assistance, Yachting Ventures has provided these fledgling firms with a significant platform, boasting over 20,000 followers, to ensure visibility and connectivity with crucial industry stakeholders.

Almost half a decade on, the expertise accrued by Richardson and Wright has afforded them a unique perspective on the industry's evolving landscape. They've witnessed the emergence of novel market segments, changing customer demands, and greater operational efficiency in the sector. As we steer our attention to the horizon of 2025, we delve into the promising start-ups that are set to define the future of yachting.

A prime trend is the ascent of AI-powered solutions across the industry. Start-ups are beginning to harness AI's capabilities in various manifestations such as predictive maintenance, route optimisation, customer service automation, and personalised experiences. Richardson elaborates that this shift is catching the eye of other start-ups, investors, and considerable industry players who acknowledge the added benefit it could bring to their operations.

Alongside the global acceptance of AI, the Middle East is creating a significant ripple in the industry. Richardson observes increasing interest from startups in exploring the region’s opportunities, given its growing inclination toward advanced technologies and sustainable marine solutions. Rising events like the Abu Dhabi International Boat Show and the GCC Smart Yachting Days encapsulate the region's expanding influence and are becoming key platforms for young companies.

title: The Yacht Environmental Transparency Index (YETI): A Catalyst for Greening the High Seas
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: The Yacht Environmental Transparency Index (YETI): A Catalyst for Greening the High Seas
summary: The Yacht Environmental Transparency Index (YETI) heralds a new era in sustainable yachting, assessing and improving ecological impacts in an unprecedented way.
body: The Yacht Environmental Transparency Index (YETI) represents the vanguard in yachting's sustainability evolution. Born from discussions regarding 'green' yachting and its quantification, YETI presents a reliable, systematic approach to assess a yacht's environmental footprint and identify ways to enhance it. Consequently, guiding refitting projects in an eco-friendly direction is now more feasible than it ever was.

Launched in 2019, YETI has been on a roll, with every iteration contributing meaningfully to its growth. Its latest offering – a dedicated website with bespoke software for the revamped YETI Lite and the familiar YETI Pro – is a testament to such progress.

Spearheaded by Bram Jongepier, senior specialist at Studio De Voogt, YETI was initiated as an antidote to rampant greenwashing in the yachting industry. When weighing alternatives for energy carriers, a collaboration between De Voogt and Delft University gave birth to a tool that allowed quantification of sustainability impact.

YETI's intention transcends merely examining the impact of yacht operations on global warming. Instead, recognizing and rewarding improvements made on the vessels that lead to positive environmental outcomes is a crucial aspect of its design. As such, YETI introduced Ecopoints, which reflect the total environmental load of a product throughout its lifecycle. Such a tool encompasses a broad spectrum of impact factors across three categories: human health, ecosystem quality, and resources. With the Ecopoint system and the capability to calculate CO2 equivalent impacts, YETI provides yacht owners with an accessible platform to promote and pursue sustainability, making it an increasingly integral part of the yachting landscape.

The dialogues reflected the collective aspiration of the leaders for a more organised, efficient, and well-detailed future for the superyacht refit industry, whilst acknowledging the challenges that lie ahead. title: Talent Shortages in Boating: A Case for Rethinking Hiring Strategies and Exploring Untapped Young Potential

body: The boating industry is steering into choppy waters. Faced with a dwindling talent pool and unsteady retention rates, the industry urgently needs to reimagine its hiring practices. The recruitment problem is dire, calling for a paradigm shift away from the insular networks and familiar faces that have traditionally dominated the sector.

By remaining locked in these circles of familiarity, the industry is sailing past an ocean number of young individuals bursting with enthusiasm and potential, often from backgrounds less traditionally associated with sea life. As the needs for skilled crew and artisanal craftsmen grows, the industry needs to cast its recruitment net wider. The bustling cityscape, brimming with fresh talents, provides a refreshing alternative to the usual networks of coastal towns.

The common view of the younger generation as soft or spoilt, harboring an aversion to manual labor, is misguided and potentially detrimental to the industry's rejuvenation. In truth, the education systems, particularly in countries like the UK, often fail to provide exposure or encouragement to industries such as sailing. Instead, the focus on university-based education forges a potent reinforcement of office-based positions rather than maritime-based skilled trades.

By tapping into this youthful reservoir and diverging from the education culture overly centered on university degrees, the boating industry can introduce a new wave of engineers, welders, and carpenters onto the scene, thereby injecting fresh life into the industry and steering it forward into calmer waters.

However, for those preferring less demanding ventures, post-war projects, especially from the 1960s through to the 1980s, furnish a good variety of options. Bryan notes that these modern classics, when restored to their original radiance with a bit of future-proofing, uplift the cachet of any marina they are birthed in, drawing attention amidst a sea of predictable and indistinct yachts.

title: Attitude Versus Training in Yachting: The Indomitable Spirit of Sailors Unearthed
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Attitude Versus Training in Yachting: The Indomitable Spirit of Sailors Unearthed
summary: In the unrelenting world of sailing, attitude often rules over training, redefining the survivalist spirit of seafarers amidst the unforgiving ocean tides.
body: A sailing ship is charted as much by the course it treads as by the people that steer it. In the nuanced world of yachting, crew management isn't merely firsthand training and skill but a question of attitude and resilience. Take the evocative tale of M/Y Santa Cruz Tres and its relentless crew, who were put to the test with their tireless washing duties, primed with two 6kg Miele washing machines and sleep-deprived overnight shifts. The demands, though harsh, set a zealous standard in an era bereft of modern conveniences and ease of communication to rally on. The onus then lay on the captains, who faced the brunt of quaint shipyard rules and direct owner-liaisons, long before the advent of advanced boat handling techniques, mobile phones, and internet. Despite all this, the heart of yachting remained unchanged: the loyal symbiosis between the captain, crew, and owners or guests. Today, however, a concern arises when this admirable commitment and grit are overlooked. Discussions veer towards logistical concerns, such as the number of uniform changes, which deviate from the primal yachting spirit. Crew selection agencies and training companies are championing the need for crews to 'feel valued, skilled and motivated', with an overemphasis on mental health. However, consider the crews of 1986, of yachts like the 48-metre Azteca and Paraiso, who course-corrected at head-spinning 22 knots at night with no navigation aids but their instinct. Would their survival rely on mental health workshops, or would it hinge on an unfaltering attitude, a survival instinct, and an unyielding spirit? Through such trials and tribulations was the seafarer's code of honour born - the code of resilience. The sea is a fickle friend; its vast, everlasting draught warrants a kind of hardiness and mettle that usurps formal training. And so it is, that the true spirit of a sailor is measured not by his crew's seamanship, but by their shared resolve to stay afloat amidst the oceans' relentless churn.

title: Revealing the Momentous Tale of a Near Fatal Superyacht Event: Criticality of Watertight Security
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Revealing the Momentous Tale of a Near Fatal Superyacht Event: Criticality of Watertight Security
summary: Delving into a compelling case study that brings to light dangers seafarers face due to unsecured hull openings onboard superyachts.
body: Embarking on a fascinating narrative, we plunge into a case study following a 50-meter-plus sailing superyacht's ordeal. The vessel had just set sail when an unusual amount of spray was spotted on one of its decks. The root cause – a rogue shell door, a boarding platform with a cavity for guest amenities, left wide open. Despite not providing direct ingress to the yacht's interiors, the open door could have caused considerable harm, even potentially rupturing hydraulic hoses had it not been identified in time.

Pre-departure checks (PDCs) underscored the significance of securing all hull openings. However, the yacht's design, coupled with the door and hull's shape, meant that identifying this vulnerability required an overboard glance. Complicating matters further, the shell door's associated sensor was known to be problematic, often giving false readings thereby compromising the monitoring system and sounding false alarms.

The report highlights several elements that jeopardized safety. A lurking design flaw made it challenging to detect if the shell door was indeed secure. Aggravating the situation further, the faulty sensor, known for its unreliability, was left unattended, further undermining safety alarms.

Drawing vital lessons from this alarming incident, it's crucial to recognize that a prompt pre-departure check can avoid a panoply of potential dangers, fortifying the watertight integrity of the ship and guaranteeing smooth sailing for all aboard.

title: The Superyacht Industry Blueprint: Navigating the Voyage to Net Zero by 2050
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: The Superyacht Industry Blueprint: Navigating the Voyage to Net Zero by 2050
summary: Key industry stakeholders chart an ambitious course for the superyacht industry to achieve net-zero emissions by mid-century.
body: The luminaries of the superyacht world are charting a bold and sustainability-focused course to a future of net zero emissions by the year 2050. Leaders and stakeholders across the diverse stages of a superyacht's lifecycle came together to shed light on the mechanisms and actions required to hit this lofty target. The game plan was introduced by Vienna Eleuteri, the visionary behind Water Revolution Foundation, who championed the '3R' model for sustainability.

'Reduce, Remove, Restore' - the 3R model sets clear goals. The 'reduce' element aims at minimizing the negative impacts across all stages of a yacht's life, such as improving on-board system efficiencies and utilizing low-emission power methods. 'Remove' involves embracing bio-based build materials and biofuels. 'Restore' calls for active investments in ecosystem restoration to achieve net-zero outcomes, an imperative upshot of which is blue carbon development throughout marine environments.

Eleuteri cited the Red Sea as an encouraging example. Its rich biodiversity and stunning marine ecosystems are being safeguarded by an 'environmental protection mechanism' ingrained in their marine-based tourism industry. This sustainability-centric approach is indeed a ray of hope. However, she stresses, the voyage toward net zero will require the participation and commitment of every stakeholder involved in the lifecycle of a superyacht - from design, to build, to refit, to operation. Each stage has unique powers and potentials, and it's only by harnessing them all that the industry can steer itself toward a future of net zero emissions.

title: Nobiskrug and Flensburger Schiffbau-Gesellschaft File for Insolvency, Signaling Deep Crisis in Tennor Group
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Nobiskrug and Flensburger Schiffbau-Gesellschaft File for Insolvency, Signaling Deep Crisis in Tennor Group
summary: High profile shipbuilders, Nobiskrug and Flensburger Schiffbau-Gesellschaft (FSG), under the Tennor Group, have filed for insolvency, causing ripples in the maritime industry.
body: In a game-changing twist for the boating industry, prominent shipbuilders Flensburger Schiffbau-Gesellschaft (FSG) and superyacht shipyard Nobiskrug officially declared bankruptcy. The move signals a deepening crisis for their parent entity, Tennor Group, and its beleaguered owner, Lars Windhorst. District courts in Flensburg and Neumünster named lawyers Christoph Morgen and Hendrik Gittermann as the provisional insolvency administrators. It's a sobering finale to a harrowing saga of reported mismanagement and financial turmoil. The severity of the predicament came to light when the SH public utility company threatened to halt the power supply at the Rendsburg facility over long-overdue payments. The only thing that saved the facilities from a blackout was the presence of a federal police ship requiring repairs.

The takeover of FSG by Lars Windhorst's Tennor Group in 2019 has ultimately led to the current situation. Despite promises of a rebirth as 'FSG 2.0' and future projects galore, they only saw unmet deadlines and unfulfilled promises. The result? A once-thriving shipyard left vulnerable.

title: Land and Sea Unite: Shedding Light on the Crucial Stability of Yachts and How to Perfect the Balance
author: Old Sea Dogs
imageAlt: Land and Sea Unite: Shedding Light on the Crucial Stability of Yachts and How to Perfect the Balance
summary: Understanding the delicate dance of stability in yachting promises an unparalleled grasp on maritime safety while unlocking incredible adventures.
body: Yachting, a world often associated with blissful seascapes and luxurious experiences, presents multifaceted technical and operational challenges that often go unseen by the seafaring amateur. The stability of a yacht is one such enigmatic concept that demands a keen understanding and careful monitoring. Failing to pay heed may tip the balance from a leisurely soiree on the water to a potential calamity. As such, the clandestine workings of a yacht's stability are indispensable for those cruising in the yacht life. At its core, yacht stability is simply a measure of how effortlessly a yacht can regain its upright position after a disturbance, like a gust of wind or a wave. This balance is influenced by a myriad of complex parameters, such as the yacht's weight, loaded weight and vertical centre of gravity, to name a few. Such values, although abstract and non-measurable by a standard ruler, are incredibly susceptible to change. For a yacht to confidently navigate the ocean waves, it must maintain an equanimity between these factors. Notably, the stability parameters are detailed in a yacht's Stability Information Booklet, an essential manual for understanding and mitigating stability challenges. Standing quayside at a placid harbour on a windless day still can reveal the nuances of yacht stability. Witnessing yachts of comparable size and form exhibit diverse reactions to gentle waves provides a practical glimpse into the concept. Without adequate stability, even a robust, undamaged yacht could succumb to a temperamental ocean, as tragically illustrated by the sinking of Bayesian. Therefore, achieving and maintaining stability, irrespective of the yacht's size, form or condition is paramount for sailing enthusiasts. As the industry continues to focus on fire safety, a renewed awareness is required for yacht stability. Remember, when setting sail, whether it's crossing the Atlantic or just mooring with a clear view of the horizon, stability is the golden key that keeps the yacht afloat and your adventures boundless.
